It must also be noted that, according to the number of the days of the left side, three hundred and ninety loaves baked under the ashes are ordered to be made and eaten one each day, while about loaves for the forty days of the right side there is complete silence, so that Holy Scripture may signify in a hidden way that the punishment is not the same for a sinning people, provided it still has the knowledge of God, and for one that has wholly departed from the religion of the true God. We can also say this, according to the spiritual understanding: that the Jewish people, since its offense against God, eats to this day loaves baked under the ashes, mixed of wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet and oats, of which the one is the food of men, the other of beasts of burden: for in that they seem to believe in one God, they have something of wheat too; but in that they deny the Son, they feed on the barley of beasts of burden and on beans, by which the belly of those who eat them is puffed up and the mind is said to be weighed down, so much so that it is a food abhorred even by the Pythagoreans. For lentils Esau lost his birthright; millet is the food of rustics and countrymen and of fattened fowl; on oats, or vetch and olyra, brute animals are fed.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The scantiness of the food is increased by the scantiness of the water: for he is commanded to drink each day the sixth part of the Hebrew measure called 'hin' — now a 'hin' makes two Attic 'chois' [choes, an Attic liquid measure], which we can call two Italian 'sextarii', so that the 'hin' is the measure of the Jewish sextarius and of our military one, whose sixth part makes a third of an Italian sextarius —; and this food and drink, in the words of the renowned orator, gives no strength, but keeps off death. As for his saying: From time to time you shall eat (or drink) it, it means from evening to evening, although some wrongly think it is to be understood from year to year.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the loaves themselves are made like a barley loaf baked under the ashes; and he is told to cover them with human dung, not with those who are to eat them unaware — for in such a situation ignorance usually tempers miseries — but with them seeing, and before their eyes, so that one may endure the horror of the sight before the nausea of the taste.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And that it is written, according to the Seventy, that Elijah, fleeing Jezebel, found a ὀλυρίτην [made of olyra] loaf, 'baked under the ashes', is a sign of persecution and want; hence he is also fed by ravens, and, because he had found no food in Israel, he was fed with the nourishment of the nations, which were unclean. The Law itself too, which they read and do not understand, is a loaf baked under the ashes, and it is covered with human dung; for which reason Paul the Apostle too says that he counted the gains of the Law and the observance of the former ceremonies as dung, that he might gain Christ.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the Lord said: Thus shall the sons of Israel eat their bread polluted among the nations to which I will cast them out. And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, my soul is not polluted, and what died of itself and what was torn by beasts I have not eaten from my infancy until now, and no unclean flesh has entered my mouth. And he said to me: Behold, I have given you the dung of oxen instead of human excrement, and you shall make your bread in it. That the prophets, according to Zechariah, are men of portent, who portend things to come by their deeds, and of whom God says: In the hands of the prophets I have been likened, we read very often in many places. Just as, therefore, Ezekiel eats bread in dung, so the sons of Israel too, or the whole people of the Jews, or, as others think, the ten tribes, will eat polluted bread among the nations; although the threat is not addressed to those who have already been cast out, but to those who were still to be cast out of the land of promise.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 5

I have recalled that the prophet Ezekiel too says something similar, when the Lord had commanded him to cook loaves for himself "in human dung". For he answered the Lord and said: "O Lord, never has my soul been defiled, and carrion or anything unclean has not entered into my mouth. But neither has yesterday's flesh entered into my mouth". Concerning which I often used to inquire within myself, what this exultation of the prophet might be, by which he brought forth before God as something great and said: "I have never eaten yesterday's flesh". But, as I see, taught from this and imbued with these mysteries, the prophet spoke thus to the Lord: I am not so cast down and degenerate a priest as to "feed on yesterday's", that is, on old "flesh". Hear these things, all you priests of the Lord, and understand more attentively what is said. The flesh which from the sacrifices is assigned to the priests is "the word of God" which they teach in the Church. For this, then, they are admonished by mystical figures, that when they begin to bring forth discourse to the people, they should not bring forth "yesterday's", should not speak forth old things which are according to the letter, but through the grace of God should always bring forth new things and always find spiritual things.
Commentary on Ezekiel

When the prophet had learned this, according to Aquila he expressed his abhorrence three times: 'Ah, ah, ah', but according to Symmachus and the Seventy he answered: Μηδαμῶς, which in Latin is said 'By no means', for which Theodotion translated: 'O Lord God'; lest we should think that he is contradicting the Lord's command, rather than giving reasons, or rather pleading, why he cannot do this; and in the end he obtains what he asked, and the severity of the sentence was tempered by a milder command. It is asked why Ezekiel refused easier things, while Hosea was at once joined to a harlot and did not object, or rather reply, that he had a chaste body and ought not to be stained by union with a prostitute, as the Apostle says: He who cleaves to a prostitute becomes one body with her; from this it is shown that it was a figure of the Synagogue or of the Church, not truly carried out according to the letter, as we discussed more fully when expounding that prophet himself. 'What died of itself' is the name for that which loses its life without the shedding of blood, and in which the soul dies; 'torn by beasts', for what in Greek is called θηριάλωτον.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And that the dung of oxen is granted in place of human dung signifies lighter evils, since he is indeed commanded to eat bread baked in ox dung, but to be far from the uncleanness of human dung; and to this day this sentence is kept among the people of the Jews: they do not eat their bread in human dung — for they neither serve idols nor worship the various monstrous forms of demons — but in ox dung, since they do everything for the sake of the flesh and the belly and the good things of this earth, according to what is said: He who does them shall live in them. But we who despise earthly things not only trample on the foods of human dung and count earthly delights as nothing, but eat the bread which came down from heaven and enjoy that food of which the psalmist sings: Man ate the bread of angels, living not at all on Egyptian meats but on the fineness of manna.
Commentary on Ezekiel

What he had shown by deed was to come, he also declares by word; and the whole sleeping on the left and the right side, and the bread baked under the ashes and mixed from a variety of six kinds, signifying the evils of the world, tends to this: to proclaim the want of food in Jerusalem and an incredible scarcity of water, so that each one collapses upon his brother, hoping from another for the help that he does not see to be in himself — for it is the nature of men that, when evils press and the weight of distress, they put their confidence in their neighbor rather than in themselves —, and they waste away in their iniquities, while they suffer all things for their iniquities. And I fear that this breaking of bread may be found in our Jerusalem too, in which the vision of peace is discerned: bread which the Lord breaks when he is angry and judges us unworthy of his bread; and would that we might at least deserve to receive it by weight and in anxiety, and that the tip of Lazarus's finger might moisten our tongue, parched with excessive dryness. But when the bread and water of the Church fail, a man will collapse against his brother, and everywhere there is discord, as we tear the tunic of Christ which not even the soldiers dared to tear at the passion of the Savior, and waste away in our iniquities, while we do not have the righteousness of God.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he said to me: Son of man, behold, I will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem, and they shall eat bread by weight and in anxiety, and they shall drink water by measure and in distress, so that, bread and water failing, each one may collapse upon his brother, and they may waste away in their iniquities. The Hebrew word 'mate' the first edition of Aquila translated 'staff', while the second, and Symmachus and Theodotion, translated στήριγμα, that is, 'support'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

It is written in Jeremiah that the little ones, that is, the common people of the Church, asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them; but Paul, who was a man and knew that Christ had broken the loaves of the Law and given them to the disciples to be distributed, speaks confidently. And those who need the milk of infancy and are not able to take solid food cannot eat the staff or strength of bread; and nothing so strengthens the mind of the one who eats as the bread of life, of which it is written: And bread strengthens the heart of man.

n: That. Hebrew, "the scissors of clippers." The same term is used for clipping sheep as for cutting hair. Shaving was not probably then in use. --- Beard, as in mourning or for ignominy, 2 Kings x. 4., and Jeremias xlvii. 5. --- Balance, to shew that God does nothing unjustly. (Calmet) --- The hair. Literally, "them." (Haydock) --- This was to be done before he lay down. Hew was to burn, cut, and divide the hair as the siege represented on the tile advanced, to denote that some should perish in the city by famine, others by the sword, while a few should be scattered among the nations: yet of these a small number should be gathered round Godolias, and perish with him, or in Egypt, &c., and the rest be thence led captive to Babylon.

Third. Septuagint and Theodotion read "a fourth," as also [in] ver. 12., (Calmet) thus assigning half to be burnt by death (pestilence) and famine. The other half of the people falls a prey to the sword and to captivity. The pestilence, famine, and the sword, were the three usual scourges left to David's choice, (2 Kings xxiv.) which here destroy each a fourth part, while the rest become captives. Yet even of this third or fourth part, many engage in civil broils, and perish. St. Jerome hints that the Septuagint is interpolated from Theodotion, ver. 12, and that their version only comprised the pentateuch. But the other books went at least under the same title; and there must be some mistake in the words asterisked, since they occur in the Hebrew, Vulgate, &c., third being only substituted for fourth: "And a fourth part of thee shall fall by the sword." The Hebrew is rather less degrading to the Jews, as there would be thus at most one-third preserved, instead of a part only of one-fourth. See Deuteronomy xxvii. 4., and Jeremias lii. 28. --- Take. Septuagint add here, "a fourth part; and shalt burn it in the midst of it; and a fourth thou shalt cut," &c. (Haydock) --- He was thus to deal with a part of the hair during 390 days, (Menochius) or at the end of them. (R. Salom.) --- Round, in the cities near Jerusalem, (Worthington) or round the picture of it, chap. iv. 1.
Out of it. Some rose up against Godolias, Jeremias xl., &c. (Calmet) --- The divisions of the Jews brought on the persecution of Epiphanes, (Sanctius) and introduced Pompey. (St. Jerome) (Haydock)
Midst, distinguished above the rest. Many have supposed that the city was in the exact middle of Palestine, or of the world, Psalm lxxiii. 12. (Calmet)

Surpassed in numbers, (Symmachus) or rather in wickedness. (Chaldean) (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "because you have been incited by the," &c. (Haydock) --- Judgments. You have been less attached to my service than the Gentiles have been to their idols. Some think that not is here superfluous, as it is omitted [in] chap. xi. 12. But it is wrong to imitate the Gentiles, and worse to surpass them in crimes.
Like. The ruin of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans was terrible, (Calmet) but that by the Romans was more so. (St. Jerome) --- The reasons were different.

Fathers. This is not specified in history. Famine prevailed, 4 Kings xxv. 3.; and we find something similar, Lamentations iv. 10., (Calmet) and Baruch ii. (Worthington) --- It is probable, therefore, that these threats were realized. (Theodoret) (Deuteronomy xxviii. 53.) --- Scatter. Literally, "winnow." (Haydock) --- The Jewish nation was never again all together in the promised land.
Pestilence. Septuagint, "death;" so they usually denote pestilence. They add, "and a fourth part of thee shall be," &c., ver. 2. (Haydock)
Comforted, or revenged, chap. xxiv. 14., and Isaias i. 24.
And a. Septuagint, "and thy daughters (dependances. Calmet) round," &c. (Haydock)
Scoff. Literally, "blasphemy;" which is here used improperly, to denote derision. (Worthington)
Arrows; inclemency of the seasons, &c., which bring on famine. (Menochius)
Beasts. They usually take possession of abandoned countries. (St. Jerome) --- The Chaldeans may also be meant, chap. xvii. 3.

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

Moreover, just as in the hair of the head and the beard there is a token of beauty and manhood, and if they are shaved off a shameful nakedness appears, and the outermost and, so to speak, dead part of the whole body is in the hair of the head and the hairs of the beard, so Jerusalem and its people, dead and separated from the living body of God, is handed over to famine and pestilence, to slaughter and the sword, to captivity and dispersion. From this dispersion, under the figure of the hairs, some part is bound in the height of the cloak, so that a small amount is again handed over to burning, from which an infinite flame and the whole devastation of punishment goes forth into all the house of Israel.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword like a barbers' razor (or shaving the hairs), and draw it across your head and your beard, and you shall take for yourself a balance of weight and divide them. A third part you shall burn with fire in the midst of the city, according to the completion of the days of the enclosure; and a third part you shall cut down with the sword round about it; but the other third you shall scatter into the wind, and I will bare the sword after them. And you shall take from there a small number, and you shall bind them in the top of the cloak; and from them again you shall take, and cast them into the midst of the fire, and burn them; from it a fire shall go forth into all the house of Israel. Instead of the 'three' parts of the hair of the head and of the beard, of which one is burned in the midst of the city, another is cut down with the sword round about it, and the third is scattered, to be snatched hither and thither by the wind, from which a little is taken and bound in the edge of the cloak, and again some small amount of the third part is cast into the fire, from which a flame goes forth into all the house of Israel, the Seventy translated 'four' parts; and when they had said: A fourth part you shall burn with fire in the midst of the city, and a fourth you shall slay with the sword round about it, and a fourth you shall scatter into the wind, because another fourth part remained to them, they added of their own: And a fourth part you shall take and burn it in the midst of the city, as if it were not the same as the first, and he had said one thing in the first and another in this one which has been added. Finally, in what follows too, the Lord himself explains through the prophet the αἴνιγμα [riddle] of the hairs divided into three parts, saying: A third part of you shall die by pestilence and be consumed by famine in the midst of you, signifying that famine and pestilence are the fire; and a third part of you shall fall by the sword round about you, describing the slaughters and wars outside; but the third part of you, he says, I will scatter into every wind, showing that these are the ones who are to be led into captivity. After these he says that he bares or pours out his sword, so that not even captivity should be the last of evils, and that he takes from those very ones who were scattered and made captive, and binds at the top of his cloak those who are to return from captivity to Jerusalem, and from them too takes some part and consumes it with fire and flame, signifying the Macedonians, under whom the inhabitants of Judea, and especially of Jerusalem, suffered harsh things.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But as to his saying: From it (that is, from the people of the Jews, or according to the Seventy: From her, so that the city of Jerusalem is understood) a fire shall go forth into all the house of Israel, the history of the Maccabees relates it: that a certain part of the Jews gave themselves over to Antiochus Epiphanes and stirred him up to the persecution of the people, and many other things which are written in the same history and in the volumes of Josephus, and especially the dissension of Hyrcanus and Alexander, through the occasion of which Gnaeus Pompey took Jerusalem and subjected it to Roman dominion; and afterwards, under Titus and Vespasian, the city was taken and the temple overthrown, and, after fifty years, under Aelius Hadrian the city was burned down to the ground and destroyed, so that it lost even its former name.
Commentary on Ezekiel

She was set, therefore, in the midst of the nations so that, since God was known in Judea, and in Israel his name was great, all the nations round about might follow her examples; but she, following the impiety of the nations placed around her, surpassed even them in her wickedness. Symmachus translated this beautifully: This Jerusalem, which I set in the midst of the nations, and the regions around her, has exchanged my judgments for impieties which she learned from the nations, and my justifications from the regions which are round about her, because they have rejected my ordinances, and in my judgments they have not walked. But that what the Seventy said: My justifications unjustly from the nations, and my ordinances from the regions which are round about her, has no coherence is clear even if I keep silent.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God: This is Jerusalem; in the midst of the nations I have set her, and round about her lands; and she despised my judgments, so as to be more impious than the nations, and my precepts more than the lands which are round about her: for they have cast away my judgments, and in my precepts they have not walked. That Jerusalem is situated in the middle of the world this same prophet testifies, showing that she is the navel of the earth; and the psalmist, expressing the nativity of the Lord: Truth, he says, has sprung from the earth; and then, the passion: He has wrought, he says, salvation in the midst of the earth. For on the side of the east she is girded by the region which is called Asia; on the side of the west, by that which is called Europe; on the south and the south wind, by Libya and Africa; on the north, by the Scythians, Armenia and Persia and all the nations of Pontus.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'Why,' he says, 'should I complain that you have not walked in my precepts and have not done my judgments, when you have even surpassed all the nations round about in your wickedness, and have not done what they often did by the natural law written in their hearts? Therefore not through angels nor through any ministers, but I myself will execute judgments in you, with all looking on, such as I have not done in you before and will not do again'. And by saying 'judgments' he shows the truth of the sentence, lest his wrath should seem to exceed the measure of the punishments.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have surpassed the nations that are round about you, you have not walked in my precepts, and have not done my judgments, and have not acted according to the judgments of the nations that are round about you, therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I myself will execute judgments in the midst of you in the eyes of the nations. And I will do in you what I have not done, and the like of which I will not do again, because of all your abominations. (In place of what we translated: Because you have surpassed the nations that are round about you, Symmachus translated: Because your multitude was from the nations that are round about you. Aquila's second edition: Because you have been numbered among the nations that are round about you; and further, LXX: "Because your occasion is from the nations that are round about you".) And the sense is: either that Jerusalem by her crimes surpassed all the nations round about, or that her multitude is to be called not the people of Israel but a crowd of the other nations, or certainly that they were turned into the number of the other nations which are round about, or that they took every occasion from the nations whom they ought rather to have taught toward the good.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Nor did he do in any nation such things as he did in Jerusalem; and the mighty shall suffer torments mightily; and: The like, he says, I will not do again. He said well: I will not do the like, for after the killing of Christ he was going to do much harsher things: for it is one thing to have worshiped idols at times, for which they had been punished before, and another to have slaughtered the Son of God.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore fathers shall eat sons in the midst of you, and sons shall eat their fathers, and I will execute judgments in you, and I will winnow all your remnants into every wind. To what he had said above: Because you have surpassed the nations that are round about you (or Because your occasion is from the nations that are round about you), you have not walked in my precepts, and have not done my judgments, he has referred 'therefore' three times. First thus: Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I myself will execute judgments in the midst of you; secondly: Therefore fathers shall eat sons in the midst of you; thirdly: Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, unless because you have violated my holy place with all your offenses, and the rest. Yet it must be noted that where things are seemly and honorable, and in accordance with the merit of those who undergo them, God professes that he does them himself; but where they are sad and not worthy of God, he says indeed that they happen, but not by him, as in the present passage: Therefore fathers shall eat sons in the midst of you, and sons shall eat their fathers; for he did not say: 'I will make fathers eat their sons in the midst of you, and sons eat their fathers'; but what was seemly and did not seem unworthy of the majesty of God, he says he does himself, for there follows: And I will execute judgments in you, and I will winnow all your remnants into every wind. Something of the sort we shall be able to find also in the curses of Deuteronomy, and especially in that passage: Those who glorify me I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be brought to nothing; for those who glorify him he himself glorifies, but those who despise him will not be despised or brought to nothing by the Lord — for this is what would have followed for him to say —, but they will be brought to nothing absolutely, not by God but for their own deserts and sins. We read in the volume of Kings that, under the compulsion of famine, a son was devoured by his mother; Josephus too records many things of this kind done in the siege of Jerusalem; but when fathers ate their sons or sons their fathers, no history relates, unless perhaps it is to be believed that in many evil necessities these things too were done. This very thing can also be referred to our Jerusalem, when masters against disciples, that is, fathers against sons, and disciples against masters, that is, sons against fathers, are stirred up in mutual strife, and that is fulfilled which is said through the Apostle: But if you bite and accuse one another, see that you are not consumed by one another. Hence the prophet too sang in mystical speech: When those who afflict me drew near against me to eat my flesh, and Job says something similar: If indeed my maidservants have said: Who will give us of his flesh, that we may eat?, and concerning masters who pursue gain from their disciples and have no care for their salvation it is said: Who devour my people like a meal of bread, of whom the Apostle too says: And they eat, he says, the houses of widows. We can understand the fathers who ate sons and the sons who ate fathers not only in the Babylonian but also in the Roman siege; what is said: And I will winnow all your remnants into every wind, pertains rather to the Roman captivity, when they were scattered throughout the whole world, and this is the dispersion of the hair of head and beard into every wind.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God, unless because you have violated my holy place with all your offenses and with all your abominations, I too will break (or according to the Seventy I will cast you off), and my eye shall not spare, and I will not have pity. This is said properly to Jerusalem: 'Because you have violated my holy things by deserting me, and have worshiped idols in my temple, I too will break all your idols and crush and cut them down, or I will cast you off because you first cast me off, and my eye will not spare when I see you submitting your neck to famine, the sword and slavery, nor will I have pity, because you do not deserve mercy', for it is written: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. This same thing must be understood in the Church too, that God could daily say to masters and priests who have acted negligently: 'Because you have violated my holy things with all your offenses and with all your abominations which you have committed, I too will crush and break you, and I will repay through myself what you perpetrated against my people. Concerning this the same prophet speaks more fully against the shepherds: that they clothe themselves with the wool of the sheep and feed on the milk and the cheese, and do not seek out the broken and sick flock.
Commentary on Ezekiel

A third part of you shall die by pestilence and be consumed by famine in the midst of you, and a third part of you shall fall by the sword round about you, but the third part of you I will scatter into every wind, and I will unsheathe the sword after them. And I will fulfill my fury and make my indignation rest upon them, and I will be consoled; and they shall know that I the Lord have spoken in my zeal, when I have fulfilled my indignation upon them. (The Seventy, because above they had set down four parts, whereas the prophetic word proved that there are only three, in the ravaging by burning and by sword and by dispersion, so that superfluously the one part of burning was divided into two parts, in this place too divided that same first part into two, so as to say: A fourth part of you shall be worn away by death, and a fourth part of you shall be consumed by famine in the midst of you, and a fourth part of you shall fall round about you, and a fourth part of you I will scatter into every wind; although what we have set down: And a fourth part of you shall fall by the sword has been added from the edition of Theodotion under asterisks.) But it is clear, as the Hebrew truth contains, that there are three parts, of the first of which it is said: And a third part of you shall die by pestilence and be consumed by famine in the midst of you. And it would have been much better to translate what is written than to seek a defense for a thing badly translated; nor do we say that this was done by those to whom antiquity has given authority, but that it was corrupted over many centuries by the fault of copyists and readers, although both Aristeas and Josephus and the whole school of the Jews assert that only the five books of Moses were translated by the Seventy; and since we have spoken of this point above, it seems that it should now be passed over.
Commentary on Ezekiel

This only I will add, which is necessary, regarding what he says: And I will fulfill my fury and make my indignation rest upon them, and I will be consoled; and they shall know that I the Lord have spoken in my zeal, when I have fulfilled my indignation upon them: how the fury and indignation and zeal of God are to be understood, we have often explained, namely that God speaks with human affections, not that he himself is angry, but that we, through punishments and torments, may feel God to be angry. Zeal, moreover, is to be taken under the μετάφορᾳ [metaphor] of a husband and wife: a husband, as long as he loves his wife, is jealous; if he has neglected her, he says what we shall say in what follows: My zeal shall depart from you; and I will no longer be angry with you. And as to what is joined: And they shall know that I the Lord have spoken in my zeal: not those who have been consumed by famine and pestilence, nor those who have fallen by the sword round about the city, but those who will be scattered into every wind will, by the deaths of others and by their own miseries, feel God angry, whom they were unwilling to feel merciful.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will give you into a desert, (and what follows:) and into a reproach to the nations which are round about you (is not found in the Seventy, in place of which they added of their own: and your daughters round about you; and again according to both editions:) in the sight of everyone passing by. Now it profits Jerusalem that all the vices in her should be made desolate and reduced to a desert, and that she should recognize her own sins, so that she who ought to have been an example of virtues to the other nations may be an example of miseries. Her daughters, moreover, we can understand as cities or villages, or as the churches scattered throughout the whole world, so that whoever is a pilgrim of this age, and says with the psalmist: I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, as all my fathers, and of whom it is said: Those who passed by did not say: The blessing of the Lord be upon you, may see her reproach and grieve.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you shall be a reproach and a blasphemy, an example and an astonishment among the nations which are round about you (in place of which in the Seventy is read: And she shall be στενακτὴ — that is, 'worthy of groaning'; and from Theodotion there has been added: — καὶ δηλαϊστὴ, a word of which we have no knowledge; in place of which the three other translators rendered 'blasphemy', which in the Hebrew is called 'geddupha'. And there follows:), when I have executed judgments in you in fury and indignation and in rebukes of wrath, which I the Lord have spoken. That Jerusalem is worthy of groaning when she has offended God, and he has executed judgments in her in fury and indignation, Paul too testifies, who says: We were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest, and again: We who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened; and we speak with Jerusalem: I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him. Δηλαϊστὴν or δηλαίαν some wish to be understood as 'unhappy' and 'wretched', others as 'conspicuous' and 'exposed to miseries'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

When I send the most evil arrows of famine, which will be deadly, and which I will send to destroy you, and I will gather famine upon you, and I will crush the support (or staff) of bread. That famine and pestilence and most evil beasts and whatever other evils we endure in this world come because of our sins is manifest. Hence also that famine which is recorded to have happened in Ruth, and in the volume of Kings under Elijah, when the heaven was shut for three years and six months, and under Elisha, whose incredible want a sudden abundance made good, was sent by the judgment of God. And this was not only done then in Jerusalem, but is done also in our Jerusalem, in which, because of the greatness of our sins, first a famine of hearing the word of God is sent; then death follows the famine, so that we who did not hear: Taste and see that the Lord is sweet, may afterwards experience: The death of sinners is most evil. Of the support and staff of bread we have spoken above.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will send upon you famine and most evil beasts, even to utter destruction, and pestilence and blood shall pass through you, and I will bring the sword upon you; I the Lord have spoken. That most evil beasts are brought upon a land of desolation which has been laid waste by famine, sword and pestilence, the present times also show, when dogs, domestic animals, are roused to madness against the flesh of their masters, and the land is filled with bears and wolves and all other kinds of beasts; and by pestilence and blood passing through it he signifies disease and the sword. But into our Jerusalem too most evil beasts are sent, when we are given over to passions of ignominy and to a reprobate mind and to the consciousness of sins, which torment and tear apart our soul. Dissensions, heresies, schisms, rivalries, envies, sorrows, detractions, many desires, avarice — which is the root of all evils —, these are most evil beasts; and when they are in us, we deserve to hear: 'Your transgression shall chastise you', and we pray and say: Do not deliver to the beasts a soul that confesses to you.

n: Mountains, where idols were chiefly adored. Here their votaries find death. (Worthington) --- Israel, including all God's people, as the sacred writers make no distinction (Calmet) after the destruction of Samaria.
Idols. Protestant marginal note, "sun-images," as [in] ver. 6. The sun was much worshipped, chap. viii. 16. (Haydock)
Bones. The Chaldeans violated the tombs, Baruch ii. 24., and Jeremias viii. 1. (Calmet)
Some. Providence still preserves some faithful or penitent souls. (Worthington)
Broken. Adversity has made them repent.
Foot, through indignation or pity. (Calmet)
From, or, "more than," (Haydock) as Hebrew may signify. Deblatha was in the land of Moab, Numbers xxxiii. 46. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel, and you shall prophesy to them, and you shall say: Mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord God. Thus says the Lord God to the mountains and the hills, to the crags and the valleys. Since 'Adonai' the Lord is often said in this prophet, it seems that it should be briefly explained for the sake of the Greeks and Latins who have no knowledge of the Hebrew language: 'Adonai' is one name among the ten names of God, and it means 'lord', which we often use of men as well — indeed Sarah too, calling Abraham her 'lord', called him by this name; and where it is said: My lord king, 'Adonai' is written — ; when therefore two names, 'lord' and 'Lord', are joined, the first name is common, the second is properly God's, the one which is called ἄρρητον, that is, 'ineffable', and which was written on the golden plate that was on the forehead of the high priest. Now the mountains of Israel, which had been occupied by the images of demons, hear and understand their Creator not with ears but by the command and power of their Maker — just as the sea saw and fled, the Jordan was turned back, surely not with eyes of flesh, which it lacked; and to the sea it is said: Be still, be silent, and the blasts of the winds are commanded, and the worm that struck Jonah's shelter is given its order; and of this same earth it is written: Who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble — ; to them the prophet speaks, indicating that the idols are to be destroyed, and that the altars and all the ceremonies with which they had previously served the idols are to be crushed. We can take the mountains of Israel as both the princes and those who excelled in power and wisdom and knowledge and riches. And this must be noted: that the face is indeed set firm and placed against the mountains, but he speaks by no means to the mountains alone, but also to the hills and to the crags and to the valleys, in which a lower rank and degree of prudence and knowledge is recognized. Tropologically, it seems to me, the mountains are those who have arrived at perfect knowledge; the hills, those who are a little lower; the crags, those who, having no knowledge and trusting only in their manner of life, presume something for themselves concerning the interpretation of the Scriptures, having, according to the Apostle, a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; and that those are called valleys who are the last in the Church, who, though lower both in life and in knowledge, nevertheless do not withdraw from the gathering of the Lord's household; all of whom are commanded to hear the word of God, so that each one may understand, according to his own small measure and sense, what the Lord commands.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places; and I will demolish your altars, and your images shall be broken, and I will cast down your slain before your idols. And I will lay the corpses of the sons of Israel before the face of your images, and I will scatter your bones around your altars, in all your dwellings. It is said to the mountains of Israel that God will destroy their high places, on which men worshiped fashioned gods, and will break the altars and images, and will cause their worshipers to be slain in the sight of the shrines, so that the corpses of the dead may lie where the victims formerly lay, and the bones may be scattered — not of the mountains, but of those who lay on the mountains — round about the altars and in all the cities and villages of Israel. This according to the letter.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But otherwise, upon those also who are lifted up into pride, and of whom the Apostle speaks: Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up, a sword is brought, so that all their images, which they have fashioned from their own mind, may be crushed, and they may lie slain and perceive that they are dead, seeing that their images and fictions profit them nothing.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And as for his saying that he scatters the bones of the mountains around the altars, he indicates that all the strongest of them are to be separated from one another — for it profits perverse knowledge that the wicked be divided from the wicked — ; and as those who, with a most wicked consensus, were building a tower were, for their own benefit, scattered and their tongues divided, lest the most wicked consensus make them worse, so the bones of the mountains are scattered, that they may understand their vain endeavors. (This which we have put: And I will lay the corpses of the sons of Israel before the face of your images, is not found in the Seventy.)
Commentary on Ezekiel

Through these words an occasion is given us rather to follow the spiritual understanding, so that the cities of the heretics, which are interpreted as churches, and the high places of their pride and the altars of their perverse doctrines may be broken, and the idols may perish which they had feigned for themselves out of their own heart, and the shrines may be crushed — for these are the temples which had risen up against the temple of the Lord, and which in the Greek tongue are called τεμένη, that is, 'fanes' and 'shrines' — , and all the works of the mountains may be crushed which are not works of God but of the masters of false knowledge.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The cities shall be deserted, and the high places shall be demolished, and your altars shall be scattered and shall perish, and your idols shall be broken and shall cease, and your shrines shall be crushed, and your works shall be blotted out; and the slain shall fall in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord. The reason is plain why the cities of the mountains are to be deserted: namely, that the high places and altars may be demolished, and the idols destroyed, and the shrines perish, and all worship of images cease; that the slain may fall in the midst of the mountains, and they may know that he himself is the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when the slain have fallen in the midst of the mountains — either those whom the mountains themselves had slain, or the men of the Church who had slain them, living wickedly as they were, unto their salvation — then there will be an end of the proud mountains, so that they may know that he himself is the Lord. It may also happen that, out of the one people of the mountains of Israel, when some have been slain, the others come to know: for when the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will be wiser.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will leave among you those who escape the sword among the nations, when I have scattered you into the lands; and your freed ones shall remember me among the nations to which they have been led captive. That which the Lord says to Elijah: I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal, and which the apostle Paul writes: And now in this time a remnant according to the election of grace has been saved, can fit this passage. For the apostles too, who were of the seed of Israel and had escaped the sword, were preserved for this reason: that they might be scattered among the nations, and preach the Gospel in the lands, and remember God among the nations in which they were dwelling in the time of captivity. This can also be said: that some from the Jewish captivity were preserved for this reason, that among the nations they might remember his name and proclaim his power. Of the peoples of the heretics also, those who have been able to escape the sword of their perdition and the most wicked faction which had been stirred up against God, scattered hither and thither, will remember the name of God, doing penance, and will exult that they have been taken captive by men of the Church.
Commentary on Ezekiel

It profits the heretics too that their heart be crushed, that most evil treasury of perverse doctrines, because it has departed from the Lord, and their eyes, fornicating after their own inventions; and they, when they have remembered the Lord, will be displeased with themselves in all their abominations, and, understanding the truth of the true faith, will know that he himself is the Lord. And for this reason he often brings on tribulation, which seems ruinous and most grievous to those who suffer it: that they may be turned to penance.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Because I have crushed their heart, fornicating and departing from me, and their eyes fornicating after their idols; and they shall be displeased with themselves over the evils which they had done in all their abominations, and they shall know that I the Lord have not spoken in vain, that I would do this evil to them. (Much of this passage has been passed over by the Seventy, and this has been changed: I swore to their fornicating heart, in place of which we have put: I have crushed their heart, fornicating.) Now he swore and decreed that he would do what he showed in deed; or else, he crushed the heart fornicating and departing from God — the heart of those to whom he speaks through Hosea: They have been led astray by a spirit of fornication — , and the eyes fornicating after idols — through whose windows death is said to have entered: for which reason in Daniel too the two elders ordered Susanna to be unveiled, that they might enjoy the beauty of her bared body — .
Commentary on Ezekiel

Nor has the Lord spoken in vain, that he would do evil or evils, when at his threat those who lay under the sentence do penance; but if the heart is hard and untamable, not perceiving, even through punishments, the benefits of the one who corrects, it is said to them: In vain have I struck your sons; you have not received discipline.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God: Strike with your hand and stamp your foot, and say: Alas, for all the abominations of the evils of the house of Israel. The prophet is commanded to show the magnitude of the sins with hands and feet and speech, so that, by the gesture of his body and the lowering of his voice, he may display the bearing of one stunned and amazed and weeping. For just as, whenever we behold something new and astonishing, we shudder in body as much as in mind, so that we clap our hands and strike our feet on the ground and lower our voice to weeping, so now the prophet, discerning with the eyes of the mind the punishments to come, speaks concerning all the abominations of the evils of the house of Israel which follow. Spiritually, we strike with the hand when we separate ourselves from evil works; we stamp the foot when we do not walk in the way of sinners; we lament and weep when the things that are done displease us, which is shown by the word 'alas' — for which Aquila translated ἀᾶ [ah!], Symmachus σχετλίασον, which means 'lament' or 'mourn', the Seventy or Theodotion εὖγε [well done!], which belongs rather to one who mocks than to one who mourns — .
Commentary on Ezekiel

Who are to fall by sword, famine, pestilence. This is the cause of mourning: that the inhabitants of the mountains and the worshipers of the altars of the idols are to fall by sword, famine, pestilence. Those who are led about by various errors and change their faith daily and are carried about by every wind of doctrine, these are cut down by the sword and divided into parts, abandoning the unity of the Church's faith. But he who does not have spiritual food dies of famine, not knowing him who said: I am the life. Further, he who, given over either to single vices or to several, cannot be separated from them, falls by pestilence, as if by a kind of lethargy.
Commentary on Ezekiel

He who is far off shall die by pestilence, but he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who is left and besieged shall die by famine, and I will fulfill my indignation upon them. He who escapes the siege of the city and moves away to the deserts will die by pestilence; he who is near will fall by the sword of the enemy; but he whom the hostile army surrounds will perish by famine and want; and in all these the indignation of God will be fulfilled, so that those who remain may know that he himself is the Lord. Whoever also withdraws from the Church will at once die by pestilence; he who seems to himself a man of some learning and diligent will, unless he takes care, be struck by the sword of the enemy; he who is content with simple faith — like the brute animals he does indeed spend his time in the Church, yet he brings nothing to completion in any good work, nor is he an imitator of the ant, which in harvest prepares food for itself and carries it in — , he will die of famine; and in all these the wrath of the Lord will be fulfilled.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you shall know that I am the Lord, when your slain are in the midst of your idols, round about your altars, on every lofty hill and on all the summits of the mountains, and under every shady tree, and under every leafy oak, the place where they burned sweet-smelling incense to all their idols. It is plain according to the letter and needs no interpretation, that on the mountains of Israel and on the lofty hills, among the very altars of the idols and the groves, which are called shady trees, the army of Israel was cut down, so that where they had sinned, there they would be punished. According to ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense] let us follow the order set forth. When the masters of the heretics have been crushed and overcome by men of the Church who are instructed in the knowledge of the Scriptures, we see the slain of the perverse doctrines lying among the images which they had fashioned, and those who lifted themselves up against the knowledge of God laid low on the mountains and hills under every shady tree: they had pompous words and the shade of leaves, and did not have the fruits of good works; they were under every leafy oak, which bears fruit not for men but for swine, where they burned sweet-smelling incense, not to God but to their idols; nor could they say what is written of Noah: The Lord smelled the odor of good fragrance, and that which Paul says: We are the good odor of Christ to God in every place — but just as the saint delights God with his odor, so the sinner, in whose person that psalm is sung: My scars have rotted and become corrupt before the face of my folly, burns stinking incense to his idols — . (That which we have translated: On all the summits of the mountains, and a little after: And under every leafy oak, the Seventy left out.)
Commentary on Ezekiel

I will stretch out my hand over them, and I will make the land desolate and forsaken from the desert of Deblatha in all their dwellings; and they shall know that I am the Lord. O mountains of Israel, when your slain have fallen in the midst of the altars of your idols, on every lofty hill, on all the summits of the mountains, and I have filled with the corpses of the dead your groves, in which they once burned sweet-smelling incense to their idols, then I will stretch out my hand for vengeance, which until now had been held back, and I will reduce the whole land of Israel to a wilderness, from the desert of Deblatha — which is in the land of Hamath, which today is called Ἐπιφάνεια [Epiphania] of Syria — in all their dwellings, so that it may be plain to all that there is nothing between the wilderness and the Great Sea which the enemy's blade has not consumed — many think that it is the same place of which it is written in Jeremiah: And they seized Zedekiah in the desert which is near Jericho, and all his retinue fled from him. And when they had taken the king, they brought him to the king of Babylon at Reblatha, which is in the land of Hamath, and that, on account of the nearness, or rather the likeness, of the Hebrew letters 'daleth' and 'res', which are distinguished by a small stroke, it is called either Deblatha or Reblatha — . But according to the mystical senses, the Lord stretches out his hand over all who had been deceived by heretical error, to make their land, which is interpreted as the Church, desolate from the desert of Deblatha — which in our language means παλάθη, that is, 'a mass of figs' 'and of dried figs pressed together' — , so that, after they have found bitterness in a feigned sweetness, which belonged not to cultivated land but to the wilderness, they may then know that he himself is the Lord: For honey drips from the lips of a harlot woman, which for a time fattens the throats of those who eat, and afterward is found more bitter than gall. This is also signified by the two baskets of figs which were set in Jeremiah before the face of the temple, one of very good figs and one of very bad, of which the one refers to the Church of Christ, the other to the congregation of the wicked.

n: Israel, or Judea, in all its parts. (Worthington) --- In five or six years' time all shall be destroyed.
Set, as accusers, to increase thy confusion.
One. A second shall not be necessary, Nahum i. 9. (Calmet)
Awaked. Justice seems to have slept. (Haydock) See ver. 10., and Jeremias i. 12.

Destruction, (contritio.) St. Jerome reads "contraction," as also [in] ver. 10. Protestants, "the morning." (Haydock) --- Chaldean, "the reign." (Calmet) --- Hebrew tsephira, is variously rendered. (Haydock) --- Joy. Hebrew, "echo or cry" of people in the vintage.

Budded; figurative expressions, denoting a speedy vengeance. (Calmet) --- Chaldean, "the reign is open, the ruler has flourished, the wicked hath appeared." In this reign of Nabuchodonosor ye shall be chastised. (Haydock) --- Septuagint or rather Theodotion, from whom many things have bee supplied according to St. Jerome, (Calmet) have, "The deceit (or thick foliage; ploke) has gone forth, the rod," &c. (Haydock)
Iniquity. What other fruit could be expected from wickedness? It draws on chastisement. --- Noise, or grandees. None will repent, and therefore none shall escape, from the highest to the lowest.

Sold, as in the year of jubilee, Leviticus xxv. 25. (Calmet) --- Now there shall be no recovery. (Worthington) --- They shall be driven from the land. --- Although. By supplying the former negation, (Calmet) we may render "Nor," &c., (Haydock) which seems better. (Calmet) --- It may also mean, "those who are now alive" shall witness these things. (Haydock) Back. It is not a mere threat.
Ready. He describes the vain attempts of the Jews to make resistance.
Doves, not daring to vent their complaints. (Calmet)
Water; urine, (St. Jerome) sweat, &c., the usual effects of fear.
Heads. They cut their hair in times of penance and of mourning.
Iniquity. Riches have fostered their passions: they will not now procure food or liberty, Sophonias i. 18. (Calmet) --- The riches of the idols invited the enemy to plunder. (Worthington)

And. Protestants, "As for the beauty of his ornament, he set it in majesty: but they made the," &c. The sacred ornaments of the temple, appointed by God, (Haydock) have been converted into idols, and shall be carried to Babylon, ver. 21. (Calmet)
Secret: the inward sanctuary, the holy of holies. (Challoner) --- God would guard it no longer. (Calmet)
Shutting up. Hebrew, "chain," for imprisonment and captivity. (Challoner) --- Pronounce sentence upon all.
Sanctuary; the temple of God, or of idols, chap. vi. 3.
Distress. When the enemy is before the city, they will see their error; but it will be too late. They shall not obtain peace, Jeremias xxxviii. 1.

Ancients. Priests shall afford no consolation, nor counsellors any advice. They shall be all confounded. (Calmet) --- During the captivity a few only were found to give instruction, Malachias ii. (Worthington)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, thus says the Lord God to the land of Israel: The end has come, the end upon the four 'wings of the earth'. These we have translated 'regions of the world': namely the east and the west, the south and the north; of which wings Isaiah also speaks: Lord, from the wings (or ends) of the earth we have heard wonders, which were being wrought throughout the whole world by the apostles; and of the saints it is written: If you sleep in the midst of the lots, wings of a dove silvered over, and its hinder parts in the greenness of gold; whence the Lord too, when he had drawn near and seen Jerusalem, wept and said: How often I would have gathered your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not?; he it is who, in the song of Deuteronomy, spread out his wings, took them up and bore them on his shoulders. A certain writer sets down as the spiritual wings of the earth, by which we fly up to heavenly things, four kinds of believers: the house of Aaron and the house of Levi and the house of Israel and those who fear the Lord — of whom the psalmist sings: House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord —, understanding by Aaron the priesthood, by Levi the temple-keepers and ministers, by Israel the whole people, by those who fear the proselytes. We, however, think it should be explained simply: that after the threat against the mountains of Israel the prophetic word is directed to the whole land of Israel, whether of the ten or of the twelve tribes, and that the prophet by no means announces a captivity to come but sees one already bearing down. For in the fifth year of Zedekiah Ezekiel began to prophesy to the captives in Babylon, and in the ninth year Nebuchadnezzar came and besieged Jerusalem, and he took it in the eleventh year of Zedekiah. From this it is clear that the end had come and drawn near, not upon mountains and hills and crags and valleys, but upon the four regions of the land on every side of Israel; not of the whole earth — for had he said that, it could have been believed to concern the whole world —, but simply of the land, which signifies Israel; for thus he had begun: Thus says the Lord God to the land of Israel: The end has come, the end upon the four regions of the land.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now the end is upon you, and I will send my fury against you, and I will judge you according to your ways, and I will set against you all your abominations. And my eye will not spare you, and I will not have mercy, but I will set your ways upon you, and your abominations will be in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord. (In this chapter, in the Seventy translators, the order has been changed and confused, so that the first things are last and the last either first or in the middle, and the middle things themselves are moved now to the end, now to the beginning; wherefore we, following both the Hebrew itself and the other translators, have set down the order of the truth.) To the land of Israel, then, the word is directed: that the end and consummation has come upon it, and that the Lord sends forth his fury against it, a fury not unjust nor coming merely from indignation, but full of equity and reason, so that he may judge it according to its ways and show it all its abominations, that it may remember its works and understand what wrong it has done.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And as for his saying: My eye will not spare you, and I will not have mercy, like a most merciful physician who wishes to cut away rotten flesh and to burn out decayed wounds with the cautery, he does not spare so that he may spare, he does not have mercy so that he may have mercy the more, lest anything rotten remain in the body that would corrupt the living flesh by its nearness. But the Lord strikes the one whom he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives; to this understanding belongs that saying: I will strike and I will heal, for every medicine has bitterness for a time, but afterwards the fruit of the pain is shown in health; something of this kind God speaks through Amos: Since I have known you out of all the tribes of the earth, therefore I will avenge upon you all your sins; for the Lord knows those who are his. 'And her ways', he says, 'and the course of her whole life, and her abominations and stains I will set in her midst', so that the former sins may be set before the eyes of the sinful woman, who is punished for her healing; and when the Lord has done this, those who have been tormented will know that he himself is the Lord. That testimony too sounds this very thing: I will avenge Jacob according to his ways, and according to his devices I will repay him.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God: One affliction, an affliction, behold, comes. The end comes, the end comes; it has awakened against you, behold, it comes. Crushing comes upon you who dwell in the land. (These words are not found in the Seventy, but in their edition they were added under asterisks from the translation of Theodotion; let us, however, follow the Hebrew.) In place of 'affliction', which we have put for the sake of clarity following Symmachus, who translated κάκωσιν [ill-treatment], both in the Hebrew and in the Greek κακία or πονηρία is written, that is, 'malice'. And it is said that the time of the final sin of the land of Israel has arrived, so that it no longer escapes the sentence of God which it had long been deserving. And because it had not yet filled up its sins, the punishment was for that reason being deferred, according to that which is written: For the sins of the Amorites are not yet complete; whence the Lord too says to the Jews: You also, he says, fill up the measure of your fathers. Misery, then, has come upon you, affliction has come, and captivity has come. And lest you think that I am again threatening things to come, I point with my finger and show it: Behold, it comes, the end comes, the end comes; he who until now seemed to you to be dozing and at rest has suddenly awakened against you and risen up.
Commentary on Ezekiel

We can also interpret this place spiritually against the people of the Jews, upon whom came the end and consummation from the blood of Abel the righteous to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom they slew between the temple and the altar. For as long as they did not lay hands on the Son of God, the Lord's sentence dozed for them and was put off; but when they killed the heir so that the inheritance might perish, then it awoke against them, and the whole order and tangle of miseries rose up, because they did not seek heavenly things but desired to cling to the earth.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'Crushing' has come — which in the Hebrew is called 'sephphira', and which Aquila translated προσκόπησιν, that is, 'contemplation' and 'looking forward' — which you, ever fearful, dreaded would come upon you — and which Theodotion translated πλοκὴν, that is, the 'order and connected web' of all evils —. Further, what is said: Upon you who dwell in the land, we ought to take according to that saying of the Ἀποκαλύψεως [Revelation] of John: Woe upon all who dwell on the earth — for the saint is not a dweller on the earth but a stranger and sojourner, and he says: I am a stranger and a sojourner, as all my fathers were. For this reason Abraham too is called 'a Hebrew', that is, περάτης, and 'sojourner' and 'passer-through' and 'wayfarer', hastening to pass from the present age to the things to come —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The time has come, the day of slaughter is near, and not of the glory of the mountains. The Hebrew word 'adarim', which we, dividing it into two words, the first 'ad', the second 'arim', have translated following Theodotion as 'glory of the mountains', Symmachus turned into 'postponement' and said: And the time is near, a day of haste and not of postponement. (But the Seventy translated thus: The time has come, the day has drawn near, not with disturbance nor with pains.) Theodotion: The time has come, the day of famine is near, and not of the glory of the mountains. And the time of slaughter and of famine is proven even now in the Jewish people, which has neither prophets nor the word of God by which the soul of believers is fed. By the mountains understand the teachers and those who have knowledge of the Scriptures, of whom it is said in another place too: You give light wonderfully from the everlasting mountains. But the Seventy, who said: Not with disturbance and not with pains, signify this: that they have such ignorance of God and blindness of soul that they are neither disturbed in their crimes nor tormented by the pain of repentance.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now from near at hand I will pour out my wrath upon you, and I will unfold my fury upon you, and I will judge you according to your ways, and I will lay (or give) upon you all your abominations. If we wish to reckon from the fifth year of the exile of King Jeconiah to the ninth year of the reign of Zedekiah, when Nebuchadnezzar came and besieged Jerusalem, there will be three years in between. Hence it is rightly said: 'Now from near at hand I will pour out my wrath upon you; I will by no means foretell things to come to you nor threaten things that will happen long afterwards; now I will fulfil my fury upon you: and this fury and wrath is not without judgment, but is so that it may repay your ways upon your head and make you feel all your abominations'. We can also speak of the final captivity: that after the killing of Christ, when the end came upon them and sin awoke against them, there was fulfilled that which the apostle Paul writes: Now the wrath of God has come upon them to the end; when Jerusalem was encircled by Titus and Vespasian and its desolation came and there was fulfilled: Behold, your house will be left to you deserted, then they were judged according to their ways and the blasphemies by which they denied the Lord, and they felt the fury of God, and all his indignation was poured out upon them and they received back their crimes, so that the destruction of the temple remains until the consummation.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And my eye will not spare, nor will I have mercy, but your ways I will lay (or give) upon you, and your abominations will be in your midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord who strikes. The causes of the severity and harshness, or, as the heretics think, of the cruelty of God, in that 'my eye will not spare, nor have mercy', he adds, saying: 'I will give you your ways, and your abominations will be in your midst, so that you may feel what you have done and, seeing your abominations set either before your eyes or in the midst of all, may correct your error by repentance, and, withdrawing from your former works, when you hate what you have done, then you will know that he himself is the Lord who strikes for this reason: to correct, and: He chastises every son whom he receives'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But the Seventy, according to that sense in which it is written: For you do not know what the coming day may bring forth, said: 'Behold, the day gives birth to what it had conceived long before, and the end comes, and the encompassing has gone forth, which is to encompass and hold all your evils (or, as Symmachus translated, inspection, so that the Lord may see all that you have done and consider your works and render to each what he deserves)'. And on what they likewise translated: The rod has blossomed, we can use that testimony: Do not take the rod away from your son, and that of the apostle: What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?; and God too resounds through the mouth of the psalmist: I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; but my mercy I will not take away from them.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Behold the day, behold, it comes, contraction has gone forth; the rod has blossomed, pride has budded; iniquity has risen up in the rod of impiety: not from them, and not from the people, nor from their noise; and there will be no rest for them. (LXX: "Behold, the day gives birth, behold, the end comes, the encompassing has gone forth, and the rod has blossomed, pride has budded, injury has been roused, and it will crush the strength of the wicked, and not with disturbance nor with haste, and they are not of them, nor is there beauty in them.") 'The day', he says, 'has been contracted and shortened, and the captivity presses close at hand; the rod which for a long time threatened you has blossomed, and from the blossom it is bringing forth the fruit of blows; your pride has budded what you deserved, so that over the rod of your impiety, with which you impiously beat those subject to you, there rises up iniquity which is not from the wretched people, nor from those who are led like brute animals by their teachers, nor from their clamor and noise with which they shout in vain, led astray by the priests and Pharisees, so that they cried out with one voice and said: Crucify, crucify such a one; hence there will be no rest for them, but everlasting captivity'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For this reason, then, the Lord visits and strikes: that all the pride which long lay hidden, shut in, may spring up and lie open, and injury may be roused against the pride that has sprung up and is budding, and the strength of the wicked may be crushed, not with disturbance nor with haste; for the end of the blossoming rod is health and correction, which comes not by the merit of those who are corrected, nor by a beauty which they do not have in themselves, but by the mercy of the Lord. A difficult place, and one in which the Hebrew and the Seventy differ greatly; many things have been added to the Seventy from the edition of Theodotion, so that they might seem to have some coherence.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The time has come, the day has drawn near. It is not only to Jerusalem that it is said that the time of its captivity has come and the day has drawn near on which it is to be walled in by the Babylonian army; but to him too who exulted over his barns built and enlarged, the Lord speaks: Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?; whence the apostle too: The time, he says, has been shortened; and in another place: For the figure of this world is passing away; and it must be noted that he did not defer it to the future but spoke of the present, 'is passing away', and that daily 'the figure of the world' slips by: for it never remains in the same state, but the figure of things growing and diminishing ever flies past and is changed; whence the Lord too: Heaven, he says, and earth will pass away. But if these things, by which all that is in the world is contained, pass away and go by, what in human affairs can be everlasting?
Commentary on Ezekiel

Let him who buys not rejoice, and let him who sells not mourn. It is natural to rejoice in the purchase of possessions and to mourn in their sale. But when slavery and captivity are pressing, both joy and sorrow are vain in either case. Hence the apostle too: The time has been shortened; for the rest, let those who have wives be as though they had none, and those who weep as though they did not weep, and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, and those who buy as though they did not possess, and those who use this world as though they did not make full use of it; for the flood too overwhelmed those buying and selling, as the Lord says in the Gospel.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For wrath is upon all its people. (This is not found in the Seventy.) For 'people' one may also take 'multitude' and 'crowd' according to the Hebrew: for this is what 'amona' signifies. And the reason is clear why he who buys ought not to rejoice and he who sells should cease to weep: because the wrath of God is shortly to come upon the whole multitude of the land of Judea, or of Jerusalem; for this is understood from the preceding words, in which it is written: Thus says the Lord God to the land of Israel, and the rest.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For he who sells will not return to what he has sold. He speaks according to the Hebrew custom: for every purchase used to return to the seller in the fiftieth year, the year of release, which among them was called the jubilee; before the year of release comes, then, when possessions return to their former owners, captivity will burst in, which will take away the whole accustomed life of the city. But what the Seventy translated: For he who buys will not return to the seller, though according to the history it does not hang together at all, according to anagogy can have this sense, so that we may say that he who had been deceived by heretical error, when he has understood the fraudulence of his teacher, by no means returns to the seller, that is, to the teacher, but despises and scorns him.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And still their life is among the living: for the vision to all its multitude will not go back. Just as the possession will not return to its former owner, since the overthrow of the city is impending, so the vision and prophetic threat, which is directed to the whole multitude of the city, will by no means go back and become void, but will be fulfilled in fact, while those to whom the prophetic word is directed are still living. And he says this to show the captivity is imminent, lest according to their custom they should say: 'This vision is for many days hence and will be fulfilled after long times'. We can also say this: that after the prophetic vision withdrew from the Jews — The law, indeed, and the prophets until John the Baptist —, after the killing of the Savior it by no means goes back to them, nor do they any longer deserve to have prophets. And significantly: 'To all', he says, 'the multitude the vision will not go back'; therefore it will go back to those of the Jews who believed in the Lord, namely the apostles, and the remnant of the Jewish people which has been saved out of Israel. (But neither are these two verses found in the edition of the Seventy.)
Commentary on Ezekiel

And a man in the iniquity of his life will not be strengthened. (LXX: "And a man in the eyes of his life will not obtain.") And the sense according to the Hebrew is: his iniquity will not profit a man, nor will it furnish him any strength; according to the Seventy: even the man who desired what he thought precious in the world will not obtain it, but, as liberty perishes, all that is beautiful will be lost. Now the ambiguity of the Hebrew letters 'iod' and 'uau', which are distinguished only by size, caused some to translate 'iniquity' and others 'eyes'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Sound the trumpet, let all be made ready. (LXX: "Blow the trumpet and judge all things.") Of the blast and sound of trumpets we read in many places, as there: Lift up your voice like a trumpet, and elsewhere: Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of our solemnity, and in the apostle: For the Lord himself, at the command and at the voice of the archangel and at the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven, and in the Gospel: Do not blow a trumpet before you; and the history of Numbers tells of beaten and silver trumpets, which are compared to the prophetic word and to the apostolic teaching. And now it is commanded that all be made ready for wars at the signal of the blast of the horn. But as for what the Seventy said: And judge all things, no one doubts that it befits the power of the apostles, who, after the trumpet of the angels has sounded, are to judge the twelve tribes of Israel on twelve thrones; one of whom, Paul, said: We shall judge angels, and elsewhere: In you the world will be judged. But according to the present sense, those who are bound to this office are bidden, by irony, to blow the trumpet, so that all may be made ready against the Babylonian army.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And there is no one who goes to battle; for my wrath is upon all its multitude. (These words too are not found in the Seventy.) God had commanded that they sound the trumpet to make ready an army which could resist the strength of the Babylonians, but it did no good to have commanded it, since there is no one among the people who dares to go forth to wars. And the people has been unnerved and lacks the strength to fight for this reason: because the whole wrath of God is upon all its multitude, that is, understood, of the city of Jerusalem or of the land of Judea; but also of the Jerusalem of our land: when either public persecution or the incitements of various vices strive to overcome us, in vain do the teachers sound the trumpet and hasten to make us ready for wars, since there is no strength in the people, which has been withdrawn for this reason, that present sins have deserved the wrath of the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The sword without, pestilence and famine within; he who is in the field will die by the sword, and those who are in the city will be devoured by pestilence and famine. And those of them who flee will be saved, and they will be on the mountains like doves of the valleys, all trembling, each in his iniquity. (The Seventy were entirely silent about 'doves of the valleys', or, as Theodotion translated, 'meditating'.) And what we have translated: All trembling, each in his iniquity, Theodotion translated thus: All murmuring, each one in her iniquity, so that under the metaphor of meditating doves he signifies that each one of the people weeps for his own sin and understands and perceives why he suffers these things. Now the three parts — of some who are to die in the city by pestilence and famine, and of others whom the sword will kill outside, and of those who have escaped captivity by flight — we read of above; of these, he who is saved will pass over to the mountains and, like murmuring doves, will trembling bewail his sins. Tropologically, however, it is to be understood thus: that he who is in the field and the plain, outside the bounds of the Lord's city, which means the Church, is struck by the adversary's blade; but he who in the city has acted negligently and has not prepared for himself the foods of which it is written in Proverbs: He who works his land will be filled with bread, he will die by famine and pestilence; while the few who have escaped either the sword of the heretics or the famine and death of their own sloth will not be saved except on the mountains, and if they have taken the wings of a dove and flown away and found rest — doves which, as long as they are in the valleys, tremble and dread every single thing, whose innocence we are commanded to imitate, and of which it is written in the psalm: If you sleep in the midst of the lots, wings of a dove silvered over, and its hinder parts in the paleness of gold, in whose form the Holy Spirit descended and remained upon the Lord Savior; and beautifully, following Theodotion, we shall call a meditating dove him who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, and of whom it is written: The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom.
Commentary on Ezekiel

All hands will be weakened and all knees will flow with waters. And they will gird themselves with sackcloth, and dread will cover them. (For 'knees flowing with waters' the Seventy translated: Thighs will be defiled with moisture.) When all have trembled and fled to the mountains, the hands of all will be weakened, and no one will be able to resist the enemy, and through the greatness of their fear urine will defile their knees, nor will the bladder be able to hold back the waters flowing forth; they will gird themselves with sackcloth, and trembling will possess all things; granted that this was done in that people not only under the Babylonians but also under the Romans, when the wrath of God came upon them to the end. But also in our Judea, in which is the confession of the Lord, when iniquities have multiplied and the love of many has grown cold, all hands of good works will be weakened, and all knees, or thighs, will flow with waters, those of the men who seek unlawful couplings and whom Scripture in the law calls γονορρυεῖς, that is, 'suffering a flow of seed' and 'unclean'; hence those who are such ought to gird themselves with the sackcloth of repentance and to dread the judgment to come, and he who does this will deserve to hear Isaiah saying: Be strengthened, weakened hands and feeble knees, be made strong.
Commentary on Ezekiel

On every face shame, and on all heads baldness. The blush of the face is a sign of shame, and the consciousness of sins shines out in the face, and there is hope of salvation when shamefacedness follows wrongdoing; hence to her who with hard heart gloried in her sins it was said: The face of a harlot has become yours, you do not know how to blush.
