Baldness of the head too signifies mourning, when the hair loses its comeliness and we lose the beauty of our locks; accordingly it is said to Jerusalem: For the ornament of your head you have baldness, because of your works, and another prophet: All heads, he says, in every place will be shorn, and every beard will be shaved; Micah also to the same Jerusalem: Make yourself bald, he says, and be shorn for the children of your delights; enlarge your baldness like the eagle; and over the dead baldness is commanded to be made, but only the holy, that is, the Nazirites, and those who have been found worthy to attain the high priesthood of the Lord, do not shave their heads, for they neither have works of death nor are unclean, because they are Nazirites, that is, holy ones of the Lord; and if anyone dies beside them, all the former days of their sanctification will not be reckoned; Samuel was a holy one of God, and therefore possessed everlasting ornaments of the head, and he heard that saying from the Song of Songs: Your locks are black as a raven; but Samson, because he lost his hair, lost his strength, and as his hair gradually grew back his former strength returned, so that in dying he killed many more than while alive; Elisha, though he had baldness of body, nevertheless, because he was a Nazirite of the Lord, enjoyed the locks of the head; hence the little boys, because they were little and had not yet reached a man's age, mocking his baldness and saying: Go up, baldhead, go up, baldhead, were torn by the bites of wild beasts, whose dwelling is the glades and forests.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Their silver will be cast outside, and their gold will be in the dunghill. (LXX: "Their silver will be cast into the streets, and their gold will be for contempt.") As flight and captivity compel them, they will cast their riches, the weights of gold and silver, into the streets, desiring only to save their lives, so that what were formerly their luxuries may not be a burden. Otherwise, according to anagogy, all the silver of the captives and of those fleeing from Jerusalem will be cast into the streets, onto the broad and spacious way that leads to death, because they have abandoned the narrow path of salvation; but all the gold will be for contempt and will be reckoned as a dunghill and uncleanness: for what is outside the Church of the Lord cannot have cleanness.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Their silver and their gold will not be able to deliver them on the day of the fury of the Lord. (And this is not found in the Seventy.) No one doubts that in the time of siege and famine gold and silver do not deliver the hungry, and that teeth dashed against the most precious metal are blunted as on the hardest stone. Accordingly there follows:
Commentary on Ezekiel

They will not satisfy their soul, and their bellies will not be filled. By present evils we have learned that many rich men, amid silk, gems and weights of gold and silver, worn out by want, have had the end of beggars. But that the silver and gold of those who are outside the Church do not deliver the souls of their possessors on the day of the fury of the Lord, but that they have everlasting hunger and are tormented with an empty belly, is shown by that testimony in which it is said: The ransom of a man's soul is his own riches. His own riches are those which the truth of Christ has taught us, who commanded us to make for ourselves friends of the mammon of iniquity, who may receive us into the eternal tabernacles.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For it has become the stumbling block of their iniquity. 'Therefore', he says, 'neither will the soul of those who possess gold and silver be satisfied nor their belly be filled: because this very gold and silver has become the stumbling block of their crimes'. And he signifies the idols which, fashioned of gold and silver, condemn their own makers. (But the Seventy translated: For torment was their iniquity, so that the wicked may be tormented in their own error and understand that they have wickedly turned the gifts of God into blasphemy).
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the ornament of their necklaces they set for pride, and they made of it the images of their abominations and idols. (LXX: "The choice things of the world they set for pride, and the images of their abominations and their stumbling blocks they made of them.") 'What I', he says, 'had given as an ornament and as riches to those who possessed them, they turned to pride, so that from the very things by which they could have freed their soul through almsgiving and good works they took material for arrogance; then from the gold and silver they made idols and turned my gifts into images of demons'. But as for what the Seventy said: The choice things of the world they set for pride, it is to be referred to gold and silver, than which nothing in the world is thought more precious; and as for what follows: Their stumbling blocks, let us know that it was added from the edition of Theodotion. And the tropology is easy: that the gold and silver, the senses and words of the Scriptures, which are the choice things of the world and have been given to us for an ornament, the heretics have set as tinder and material of pride, and have made of them images of their various doctrines and of their abominations and stumbling blocks, so that through the very things by which they could have worshiped and adored God, by these they offended God.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For this reason I have given it to them for uncleanness. And I will give it into the hands of strangers to be plundered, and to the impious of the earth for a prey, and they will defile it. (LXX: "For this reason I have given them to them for uncleanness. And I will hand them over into the hands of strangers that they may plunder them; and to the pestilent of the earth for a prey, and they will pollute them.") 'Because from the gold and silver, that is, from the ornaments of the necklaces which I had given them, they made for themselves images of their abominations and idols, for this reason I have given those things to them for uncleanness and for dung', for which Symmachus translated nausea, wishing to express the filth of idols. 'And I will hand them over', he says, 'into the hands of enemies that they may plunder everything, and so that I may not so much defile them as show to have been defiled the things which earlier seemed most holy'. We too are handed over into the hands of enemies and of those estranged from God, when we make our ornaments into images of demons, and all our glory is possessed by the impious or the pestilent of the earth, so that they may subject us to their power.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will turn away my face from them, and they will violate my secret place; and there will enter into it emissaries (or, as the Seventy translated, rashly, or, as Symmachus and Theodotion, 'those bursting in' and 'the pestilent') and they will defile it. 'When', he says, 'for the causes given above, the abominations of the people, I turn my face away from them and by no means judge them worthy of my eyes, then they will violate my secret place (which signifies 'the Holy of Holies', for which the Seventy translated vision, to show that the presence of God had been in the holy places), and the impious and pestilent of the earth will burst into those places which, apart from the priests and the high priest alone, no one else dared to enter'. This we know was done both by the Babylonians, and by King Antiochus and Gnaeus Pompey, and, finally, under Vespasian and Titus, when the temple was taken and overthrown, and all things were perpetrated which the prophet's following discourse embraces. At our evil works too God turns away his face, and because his face is turned away, therefore the secret place of God is violated, so that in place of the priests and saints of God the pestilent enter and defile all things, so that what ought to have been a place of holiness becomes a place of uncleanness, according to that Gospel saying: My Father's house will be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Make a conclusion, for the land is full of the judgment of bloods, and the city is full of iniquity. (LXX: "And I will bring disturbance, for the land full of the judgment of bloods, and the city full of iniquities.") The Hebrew word 'arethic' Aquila translated 'conclusion', Symmachus and Theodotion καθήλωσιν, that is, 'nailing fast', for which the Seventy put φυρμόν, which we have rendered as 'disturbance'. 'Therefore, O prophet, conclude my wrath upon the land of Judea and upon the city of Jerusalem in a brief word: so that, as the land is full of the judgment of bloods — for all are judged in blood, shedding innocent blood, as Scripture records the Jews also did in the person of Naboth —, so their own gore too may be shed and the city shown to be full of iniquity — for under Manasseh too the city of Jerusalem was filled from gate to gate with the blood of the prophets —. And conclusion and disturbance and nailing fast will come upon them, so that no one can escape the impending miseries'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will bring the worst of the nations, and they will possess their houses. (And this is not found in the Seventy.) 'In place of priests and prophets I will bring the Babylonians, the worst of all the nations, that they may possess your houses and subject you to slavery'. But our houses too, that is, our souls — for we are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in us —, the worst demons will possess, if our land is full of bloods and our dwelling full of iniquity.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will make the pride of the mighty cease, and they will possess their sanctuaries. (LXX: "And I will turn away the roaring of their strength, and their holy things will be polluted.") All pride offends God. Therefore the worst of the nations will possess the houses of the mighty and the proud and will take hold of their sanctuaries, because the unclean man enters the place of holiness and defiles it with his uncleanness. And significantly, because the holy things of God had been polluted and the secret place violated, he did not say: 'They will possess my sanctuaries', but: 'their' sanctuaries, which after their defilement ceased to be 'mine'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Anguish is at hand. (LXX: "Propitiation will come.") — According to the preceding order Aquila and Theodotion rightly translated that 'anguish' is at hand, and Symmachus 'grief'; but the Seventy, in the midst of all the sorrowful things, put a word of gladness, so that the mind of the mourner may be sustained and may hope for better things amid adversities, and for the Lord propitious, of whom it is written: The Lord raises up those who are dashed down. — We, however, following Symmachus, have joined the former sentence to the latter, so as to say: As anguish comes upon them, they will seek peace and there will be none, which according to the Seventy cannot stand at all: for if 'propitiation will come', how 'will they seek peace and not find it'? And he will seek peace and not find it who heard from the apostles: Peace to this house, and did not keep it nor make it rest in his mind; but, put to flight by evil works, it cannot be found. And it is that peace which surpasses all understanding, which the Savior, ascending victorious to the Father, left to the apostles.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Trouble upon trouble will come, and report upon report. (LXX: "Woe upon woe will be, and messenger upon messenger.") Just as it is said to the saints: Rejoice, again I say: rejoice, and of them it is written: They will go from strength to strength, so that they may heap future goods upon present goods, so also to these, upon whom anguish has come and who have sought peace and not found it, there will come trouble upon trouble, or woe upon woe — according to what is written in Revelation too: One woe has passed, and another woe will come —, and report will come upon report, and messenger upon messenger — according to that saying of blessed Job: While one was still speaking, another messenger came, adding evils to evils, and describing the roaring and the throng of the approaching Babylonian —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And they will seek a vision from the prophet, and the law will perish from the priest, and counsel from the elders. Properly, each thing is sought from each: the prophecy of things to come is sought from the prophet; the interpretation of the law is the priest's office; prudent counsel is what mature age searches out, according to that which is written: In the counsel of the saints and in the congregation, great are the works of the Lord. And these things were sought from the prophets and elders and priests not only at that time, when the Babylonian army was coming against Jerusalem, but they are required daily in the churches, which, if they have lost vision, law and counsel, boast in vain that they have prophets and priests and elders.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The king will mourn and the prince will be clothed with grief (or, according to the Seventy, with destruction; who, intending I know not what, were entirely silent about what we have expressed from the Hebrew speech: The king will mourn.) That Zedekiah mourned, and that all the princes of the people of the Jews were covered with grief, Holy Scripture records. But we can — although at first sight this may seem blasphemous — say that the king who mourns our vices and sins is Christ, who speaks in the Psalms: What profit is there in my blood, while I go down into corruption? and who, drawing near to Jerusalem, wept over it and said: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I would have gathered your children as a hen gathers her chicks under wings, and you would not? The princes too will be either, in a good sense, the apostles who mourn sinners, or, in the contrary sense, those to whom it is said: Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom. And he will be clothed, according to the Seventy, with destruction, who does not have the armor of God, nor has put on Christ: For as many as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the hands of the people of the land will be troubled. (Or, according to the Seventy, will be weakened.) When there is no vision in the prophet and no knowledge of the law in the priest and no counsel in the elders, and the king has mourned and the prince is in grief or in destruction, consequently the hands of the people too will be troubled, losing their order, or will be weakened, no longer having their ancient strength. And beautifully the people whose hands will be troubled, and whose citizenship is not in heaven, is called not the people of God but the people of the land, of whom it is written: Let those who depart be written upon the earth.
Commentary on Ezekiel

According to their way I will do to them, and according to their judgments I will judge them. (Or, as the Seventy translated, I will avenge myself on them.) To sinners God renders according to their ways, so as to keep the truth of judgment; but toward the saints he exceeds the measure of mercy: The sufferings of this time, indeed, are not worthy of the future glory which will be revealed in us. For the wages of sin is death, which the sinner receives according to his ways and his works; but the virtue of the righteous enjoys the Lord's bounty, of which Paul speaks: The gift of God is eternal life. And what he added: And according to their judgments I will judge them, sounds that Gospel saying: With what judgment you judge, it will be judged of you, and that apostolic one: In that in which you judge another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And they shall know that I am the Lord. This little verse is often set down in this prophet, because the knowledge of God follows punishments and torments, so that him whom they do not understand through benefits they may come to know through torments.

n: Sixth of the prophet's captivity, (Calmet) in August, the year of the world 3411. (Usher) --- He had rested on his left or right side, whenever he slept during 430 days, and on the following had this vision. (Worthington) --- He was stationed in spirit at the northern gate leading to the court of the priests, and beheld the glory of God and the idol of jealousy. He saw the people, men and women, adoring idols, and priests worshipping the sun, chap. ix. God rests on the gate of the temple, and orders a man to sign those who were to live, and six others to destroy the rest. The prophet prays, chap. x. God orders the man clothed in linen to take coals from the cherubim, and sprinkle them through the city. The throne goes to receive the Lord, chap. xi. Ezechiel prophesies against many, at the eastern gate; and God informs him that the former captives shall return, but that the wicked at Jerusalem shall perish. His chariot then rests on the mountain to the east of the city. Thus his reasons for punishing the people become evident.
Likeness. Septuagint add, "of a man," as it had appeared [in] chap. i. 27.

Lock, like Habacuc; (Daniel xiv. 35.) or by a bandage, on which parts of the law were written. (Hebrew) (Calmet) --- Of jealousy; Baal, (St. Jerome) or any other idol, (Haydock) particularly Adonis, ver. 14. He fell a victim to the jealousy of Mars.

About. This was the council chamber, Jeremias xxvi. 10. They durst not publicly adore the Egyptian, &c., idols. (Calmet) --- They denied Providence, ver. 12. (Haydock) --- The wicked do not regard it, and hence fall into idolatry. (Worthington)
Jezonias. He probably was over the temple, as his father had been, 4 Kings xxii. 3. (Calmet)

Adonis, the favourite of Venus, slain by a wild boar, as feigned by the heathen poets, and which being here represented by an idol, is lamented by the female worshippers of that goddess. In Hebrew the name is Tammuz, (Challoner) which means "concealed," as Adonis signifies "my lord." This idol, which the Egyptians called Osiris, was placed in a coffin, and bewailed till it was pretended he was come to life, when rejoicings took place. Obscene pictures were carried about; and the more honest pagans were ashamed of these practices, which began in Egypt, and became almost general. Moses alludes to them, Leviticus xix. 27., and Deuteronomy xiv. 1. (Calmet) --- David and Solomon say that the image was made of brass, with eyes of lead, which seemed to weep, melting when it was hot. (Worthington) --- But this is destitute of proof.

Men. Twelve priests and as many Levites officiated daily. The high priest made the twenty-fifth, 1 Paralipomenon xxiv. --- Sun. They prayed to God, turning their faces to the west: but here they despised him, and adored the sun, Job xxxi. 26. (Calmet) --- This posture was common. Illi ad surgentem conversi lumina solum. (Virgil, Æneid xii.) (Serv.) --- Christians did the like, though the reason is not ascertained. (Calmet) --- It might be because Christ is the orient, and not to resemble the Jews. There was no danger of their being taken for idolaters. (Haydock)

Nose, to hide their faces respectfully, (Calmet) when they look at the sun rising. (Haydock) --- A thyrsus was used in honour of Bacchus, who is often confounded with the sun. Various improbable versions of this text are given. It may signify Hebrew, "they threw their instruments down before their faces," like the twenty-four elders, Apocalypse v. 8. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth of the month: I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting before me. We read that the preceding vision came to the prophet in the fifth year of the exile of Jeconiah, in the fourth month, on the fifth of the month. But this one, which we now wish to expound, is recorded to have taken place in the sixth year of the same king, in the sixth month, on the fifth of the month. From this it is clear that these things which are written took place a year and two months later, and that either the prophecy was interrupted for a year and two months, or the things which the preceding discourse wove together were carried out over the whole fourteen months. Now, that the prophecy was made in the sixth year and the sixth month and on the fifth day of the month (numbers which refer to the making of the world and to the fleshly senses, which look upon earthly things and do not yet contemplate heavenly ones) will not surprise anyone who has understood that the discourse is directed to the presbyters of Judah, and to those among whom seventy were holding censers and twenty-five were worshiping the sun in the temple. And the prophet was sitting in his house, fleeing the throng of the multitude, and the elders of Judah were sitting before him, either eager to hear the prophet's words or lying in wait for his sayings. And it is significant that they are called the elders of Judah, so that we may understand that nothing is said to Israel, that is, to the ten tribes which had been taken captive earlier, but to those of the tribe of Judah who had been led into captivity with Jeconiah.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the hand of the Lord God fell upon me there, and I saw: and behold, a likeness as the appearance of fire; from the appearance of his loins and downward, fire, and from his loins and upward as the appearance of brightness, as the vision of electrum. (LXX: "And the hand of Adonai the Lord came upon me there, and I saw, and behold, a likeness as the form of a man; from his loins and downward, fire; from his loins and upward ※ as the vision of a breeze: as the vision of electrum.") The Hebrew text does not contain 'man'; and the 'vision' 'of a breeze', which is not found in the Seventy, we have added from Theodotion; and where we said: The hand of the Lord fell upon me, Symmachus translated: The hand of the Lord befell me, which in the Hebrew is said 'thephphol' [it fell]; and the hand signifies ἐνέργειαν, that is, 'working', so that he might be able to know the mysteries of the vision.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And this must be considered: that he does not see the truth itself but the likeness of fire, since from the loins downward fire appeared, and from the loins upward as the appearance of brightness, as the vision of electrum. For 'brightness', which in the Hebrew is called 'zor', Theodotion translated 'breeze', so as to show the refreshments of God in the upper parts. Indeed, in the volume of Kings too, blessed Elijah beholds the coming of the Lord not in the storm and the whirlwind, not in the blazing of fire, but in the appearance of a breeze, thin and most gentle, so as to prove the mildness of almighty God. Now the works of intercourse, which are signified by the loins, downward, are purged by fire, and the works of the virtues, which rise from the loins to the higher parts, have brightness and splendor; and yet neither is the fire said to reach to the feet, nor the brightness of electrum to the head, but only 'downward' and 'upward', so that, in sinners as well as in saints, according to the diversity of merits, one may reach as far as this or that member, another as far as these or those. And just as those who hold the perfection of holiness reach all the way to the crown of the head, so those who are in the depth of sins must be believed to hold the soles of the fiery feet.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the likeness of a hand, sent forth, took hold of me by a lock of my head (LXX: "And he stretched out the likeness of a hand and took me up by the fringe of my crown.") Here too it is the likeness of a hand, not the hand itself, that is stretched out: for there is nothing bodily in God; and a hand is seen, as a member of the human body, so that by its familiarity it may in no way terrify him who is taken up and seized: for if it had touched the prophet in the likeness of a snake or of any other of the beasts, the very unlikeness of the members would have terrified the one taken up. And a part of the hair is seized, because human nature cannot bear the grasping of the whole head. For 'lock' the Seventy translated κράσπεδον, that is, 'fringe', of which the one is usually taken of hair, the other of garments.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven. First he is seized by the likeness of a hand; afterwards he is lifted up by the spirit, and the spirit does not raise him at once to heaven, but between earth and heaven, so that, leaving earthly things behind for the time being, he may hasten toward heaven. We can also say this: that the prophet was seized by the likeness of God's hand on account of good works, and is lifted up by the spirit on account of the knowledge of spiritual things.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he brought me to Jerusalem, in the vision of God, near the inner door that looked toward the north, where the idol of jealousy had been set up to provoke rivalry. And behold, there was the glory of the God of Israel, according to the vision that I had seen in the plain. (LXX: "And he brought me into Jerusalem, in the vision of God, to the vestibule of the gate that looks toward the north, where was the statue of the possessor." But this, which is found in certain codices, ※ And in the statue the image of jealousy: has been added from Theodotion. The rest likewise.) When he says: He brought me to Jerusalem in the vision of God, he shows that he was carried over not in the body, but in the spirit. According to this kind of vision we too can behold both the heavens and the depths of the sea and the lower regions, while we embrace in thought the principles of each. First, however, he comes to the vestibule that looks toward the north, so as to see there the statue of the idol of jealousy, to provoke rivalry, so that from that place he may penetrate to the inner parts and discern the rest, which are described afterward; and history relates that a statue of the idol Baal was placed in the temple of God; and it is aptly called 'the idol of jealousy', because it provokes the Lord to rivalry and jealousy, according to what is said in Deuteronomy: They provoked me to jealousy with that which was not God; and I will provoke them to jealousy with a nation which is not; further, because 'jealousy' and 'possession' are called by the same name, which in Hebrew is said 'cena', for 'the statue of jealousy' the Seventy translated 'the statue of the possessor'; indeed, when Cain was born, his parent said: I have possessed, a man through God, alluding by the possession of a man to the name Cain.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the glory of the God of Israel was there, not because it took delight in such a neighbor, but so that by its presence it might destroy the idol of jealousy and the temple; hence the overthrow of the city and of the temple also follows after a short time; and it is written in Isaiah that a narrow bed can by no means hold two, and a short cloak cannot cover both, Scripture signifying that saying of the Apostle: What agreement has Christ with Belial? The temple of God with an idol?
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he said to me: Son of man, lift up your eyes toward the way of the north. And I lifted up my eyes toward the way of the north, and behold, to the north of the gate of the altar, the idol of jealousy in the very entrance. (Where we have put: To the north of the gate of the altar, the idol of jealousy in the very entrance, the Seventy translated: From the north toward the eastern gate, which is not found in the Hebrew, leaving out the other things which are written there.) 'He said to me,' he says, '(either the glory of God which I had seen in the plain, or the spirit which lifted me up between heaven and earth), and he spoke to me after he had carried me over into Jerusalem and made me see either the city or the temple, and he commanded me to lift up my eyes toward the way of the north; for there the statue of Baal had been set, which he calls the idol of jealousy, in the very entrance of the gate'. But those who refer the idol of jealousy, or of the possessor, to the glory of God or to the spirit act impiously, interchanging the person of the idol with the majesty of God.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he said to me: Son of man, do you think you see what these are doing, the great abominations which the house of Israel is doing here, so that I should withdraw far from my sanctuary? And turning again you will see greater abominations. 'Lest you think,' he says, 'that I abandon the temple unjustly and leave the city to be overthrown, look at what they do in the temple; and when you have beheld those things, do not think that this is the end of their crimes: you will behold still greater things'. This can indeed also be understood of our Jerusalem and our temple, when, after the example of Hophni and Phinehas, we work the crimes of idols in the tabernacle of God, and commit fornication with those women who have vowed themselves to the warfare and ministry of God, and pluck off the first portions of his sacrifices, giving them for the use of clients and servants, and do everything for the sake of gain. But if these things which we see are so great, how much greater must those be reckoned which escape human awareness?
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he brought me in to the door of the court, and I saw, and behold, one hole in the wall; and he said to me: Son of man, dig through the wall; and when I had dug through the wall, one door appeared. And he said to me: Go in, and see the most wicked abominations which these are doing here. (This which I translated: And I saw, and behold, one hole in the wall, is not found in the Seventy.) And because everything is shown as if in an image and a painting, he says that he saw one hole in the wall, and that he was ordered to dig it through and make it larger, so that, the hole having been opened, he might enter more widely and see what he could not see while placed outside. By this it is shown that, in the churches as well as in each of us individually, greater vices are revealed through small ones, and that through certain holes, as it were, one arrives at the greatest abominations: for by the fruits the tree is known, and out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. Words that burst out are a sign of the inner man, just as a foul word sometimes exposes the lustful man who cunningly hides his vices, and desire for a trifling thing betrays the avarice lurking within: for greater things are revealed by lesser ones, and the conscience cannot be disguised by face and eyes, since a wanton and lascivious mind shines out in the face, and the secrets of the heart are disclosed by the movement of the body and by gestures.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I went in and saw, and behold, every likeness of creeping things and of animals, an abomination, and all the idols of the house of Israel were painted on the wall round about, throughout. Not only did the idol of jealousy stand at the entrance of the north gate, but all the walls of the temple too were painted with various images of idols, so that there was no beast which the painting on the wall did not show. This we see to this day in the shrines of idols and the temples of the Gentiles: that a foolish religion worships every kind of beast; whence Vergil too: And of every sort, he says, of gods the monsters and barking Anubis — as if those which he praises were not monsters too —, against Neptune and Venus and against Minerva. We too can point out idols painted on the walls of our temple, when we are subject to all vices and paint in our heart the consciousness of sins and various images, of which it is said in the psalm too: O Lord, in your city you will scatter their image, and in another place: Yet man walks about in an image. That is, there is no one among men who does not have some image, whether of holiness or of sin; for which reason it is said of the furious and the wrathful: Their fury is after the likeness of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voices of the charmers; and of wicked men: Generation of vipers, who showed you to flee from the wrath to come?; and of the shifty and deceitful: Go, tell this fox; and of lovers of women: They have become to me horses mad for females; each one neighed after his neighbor's wife; and also of the brutish and senseless: Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding; and again: With bit and bridle bind fast their jaws, who do not draw near to you; and many things of this kind. (But this which we have put: Behold, every likeness of creeping things and of animals, is not found in the Seventy.)
Commentary on Ezekiel

And seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, and Jaazaniah son of Shaphan was standing in the midst of them, who were standing before the paintings, and each one had a censer in his hand, and a vapor of cloud was rising up from the incense. When he says that there were seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel who held censers in their hands, he shows that there were many other presbyters too who were not doing this, but were perhaps held fast by other sins, and that one, Jaazaniah son of Shaphan by name, stood in their midst, as the prince of the crime and sacrilege of those who, having abandoned the worship of God, were worshiping idols, and in the temple were adoring not God, whose temple it was, but the paintings on the walls. And it is aptly said: Jaazaniah son of Shaphan was standing, that is, of his own 'judgment' and 'condemnation', in the midst of the standing presbyters, because both the prince and those whose prince he was stood with a firm step in their crimes, and did not waver in evil, but persisted most stoutly; and the vapor of cloud, of confusion and of whirlwind, which rose from the incense, displayed the sacrileges of those who offered it. Let this have happened at that time according to the letter. But we too must pray that the elders of the house of Israel, multiplying the number seven, which is holy, into seven decades, may not stand in their errors and adore the paintings of idols, and that the vapor of sacrilege may not ascend, or rise up, resisting God. When we see a most wicked people gathered together, of which it is written: I have hated the church of evildoers, and overseers worse than the people, and a still more wicked prince, who has been set over the people and the presbyters, let us say that Jaazaniah is standing before the paintings, and that each one has a censer in his hands, adoring not the majesty of God but their own opinions, and that it is by no means an odor of good fragrance that reaches God, but a stench that reaches the idols.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he said to me: Surely you see, son of man, what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the darkness, each one in the secret of his bedchamber; for they say: The Lord does not see us, the Lord has forsaken the earth. 'From what they do in the temple when gathered together,' he says, 'it is shown what each one does in his own chamber'. But according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense] it can better be understood that some princes of the churches do in darkness things which are shameful even to speak of. This is the hidden man of the heart, of whom it is said: Enter into your chamber, and again: He who sees in secret will repay you. Let each one call his conscience to mind and recall the works of darkness in darkness, and let him know that it is written: Everyone who does evil hates the light, lest he be reproved by the light, and he will understand that this has been fulfilled in himself: He who is drunken is drunken by night, which cannot stand according to the letter: for how many are drunken at luncheons and banquets by day?; but because the drunkenness of the heart, which offends God, belongs to darkness and not to light, therefore: Whoever is drunken is drunken in the night. And when the elders of the house of Israel have done evil in darkness and in the secret of their chambers, and have thought that they could hide from God, then they will consequently say: The Lord does not see us, the Lord has forsaken the earth. And many are sinners, walking according to their own thoughts, who do not reckon that God cares for mortal things, or that our vices concern him. Certainly, when we sin, if we thought that God sees and is present, we would never do what displeases him. Further, what follows, The Lord has forsaken the earth, is also the opinion of certain philosophers, who, from the course and substance of the stars, suppose that there is providence in heavenly things, but that it despises earthly things, since nothing right or according to order is done on earth.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he said to me: Turning again you will see greater abominations which these are doing. And he brought me in through the door of the gate of the house of the Lord which looked toward the north, and behold, women were sitting lamenting Adonis. What we have translated 'Adonis', both the Hebrew and the Syriac language call 'thamuz'; hence, because according to the pagan fable the lover of Venus, a most beautiful youth, is said to have been slain in the month of July and afterwards to have come back to life, they call that same month of July by the same name and celebrate an annual festival for him, in which he is lamented by women as though dead, and afterwards, coming back to life, he is sung of and praised. And consistently, after it has been shown what the princes and elders of the house of Israel did in the temple and in darkness and in their chambers, the vices of the women too are described, who lament when deprived of the company of their lovers, and exult if they have been able to obtain them. And since that same paganism interprets subtly fables of the poets of this kind, which contain shamefulness, accompanying the slaying and the resurrection of Adonis with lamentation and with joy (of which it thinks the one is shown in the seeds that die in the earth, the other in the crops in which the dead seeds are born again), let us too call women those who are either saddened or exultant at the evils and goods of the world, being of a soft and effeminate mind, and let us say that they lament 'thamuz', that is to say, those things which are reckoned most beautiful in the affairs of the world.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And since we read above, after the idol of jealousy which appeared at the north gate: Turning again you will see greater abominations, and, after the paintings of all the beasts had been shown along the wall, which the seventy presbyters and Jaazaniah son of Shaphan were adoring, holding censers in their hands, it is said a second time: Turning again you will see greater abominations which these are doing, because women were sitting lamenting Adonis, so after the third sin too it is said: Turning again you will see abominations greater than these. But what abomination is greater than the three preceding crimes? Clearly the fourth, which follows: And behold, at the door of the temple of the Lord, between the vestibule and the altar, about twenty-five men with their backs toward the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the east, and they were worshiping the rising of the sun, because, despising the Lord, that is, the Creator, they were adoring the sun, that is, the Lord's creature, although the Lord himself had commanded through Moses that they should by no means adore God facing the east after the custom of the Gentiles, but, in whatever part of the world they might be, whether to the east, or to the west, or to the south, or to the north, they should adore facing the temple, where the Lord was believed to inhabit the Holy of Holies; which indeed we know Daniel too did in Babylon, who, with the windows of his upper room open, adored the Lord facing the temple which stands in Jerusalem. No one doubts that this, according to the letter, was a matter of sacrilege. According to the ἀναγωγὴν, that all heretics are worse than the earlier things, that is, than the idol of jealousy and the figures of living creatures painted on the wall and the lamentation for Adonis, through which idolatry and pleasure are shown, he will be able to know who has understood the prophet saying: But you have hated discipline, and have cast my words behind you, and in another place: They turned their shoulders against me, departing; or are we ignorant that Marcion and the other heretics who tear the Old Testament to pieces, despising the Creator, that is, the righteous God, worship and adore some other, good God whom they have fashioned out of their own heart, and that all the heretics of our time, who preach the Son of God as a creature and yet adore him, having left the temple of the divinity and holding it behind their back, say by their own confession that they adore a creature? But we so adore the sun of righteousness that we adore God in the temple of the Old Testament, where the Law and the prophets are, where the cherubim and the mercy seat are. Where we translated 'twenty-five' men, the Seventy put 'twenty', and in certain copies the 'five' have been added from Theodotion.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he said to me: Surely you have seen, son of man; turning again you will see abominations greater than these. And he brought me into the inner court of the house of the Lord, and behold, at the door of the temple of the Lord, between the vestibule and the altar, about twenty-five men with their backs toward the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the east, and they were worshiping toward the rising of the sun. What we have translated 'vestibule' following Symmachus, who put πρόπυλον [gateway], where the Seventy and Theodotion translated the Hebrew word itself, 'aelam', Aquila's first edition translated προστάδα [porch] and the second the 'aelam' of the temple; this we can express as the 'portico' of the temple, or the unroofed 'court' which was between the temple and the altar.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he said to me: Surely you have seen, son of man; is it a light thing to the house of Judah that they should do these abominations which they have done here, because, filling the earth with iniquity, they have turned to provoke me? And behold, they put the branch to their nostrils. (Where we said: And behold, they put the branch to their nostrils, the Seventy translated: And behold, they themselves like men sneering, to which there was added from Theodotion: They stretch out the branch, so that the whole together reads: And behold, they themselves stretch out the branch as if sneering, for which Symmachus translated: As if sending out a sound in the likeness of a song through his nostrils.) It signifies that the twenty-five men, who are set firm in a square in a solid station and, from the five senses, by five times five form the figure of a square, not only have the temple behind their back in figure, but, after the manner of idols, put the branch to their nostrils — no doubt a branch of the palms which in the Greek language they call βαΐα —, so that by this it may signify that they adore idols. Indeed Job too says that among his other virtues he had this as well: that never, looking upon the sky and the sun and the moon and the shining stars, had he kissed his hand, that is, adored creatures. But Symmachus' translation signifies a foul and hoarse sound proceeding from the nostrils in contempt of God. And all heretics, who have filled the earth with iniquity and have turned to the knowledge falsely so called, so as to provoke the Lord to anger, must be reckoned, when they have wished to praise God, rather to blaspheme with a foul sound, or to hold the God of the Old Testament in low esteem, to deride, to despise.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore I too will act in fury: my eye will not spare, nor will I have mercy, (and what follows:) and when they cry to my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them (is not found in the Seventy). 'For all these things,' he says, 'which they have done, I too will act in fury and my eye will not spare, nor will I have mercy'. Hearing this, the heretics of old slander the Creator as cruel and bloodthirsty, and do not consider that the apostle Paul, who is surely the apostle of the good God — as they themselves would have it —, writes to the Corinthians: If I come again I will not spare, so as to chastise offenders with the rod and draw back the erring to salvation; for those who do not understand what is profitable for them, and often pray for contrary things, it is expedient that they not be heard by the Lord. Hence in the prayer too we say: Your will be done; not our will, which is accustomed to err, but your will, which knows the things to come; and it is sometimes a great happiness not to merit mercy for the present. These, therefore, who are of the house of Judah and have withdrawn from the confession of the Church, the Lord will not spare; and when they cry out with a loud voice, of which the Lord said: Their cry has come to me, the Lord will nevertheless not hear them, so that, compelled by evils, they may understand what they have done.

n: Upper, leading to the court of the priests. These were six angels, representing the army coming from Babylon. The seventh was an angel of peace. (Calmet) --- God never abandons his whole Church. (Worthington)
House; to the holy place, shewing that he abondoned those in the temple. (Calmet)

Mark Thau. Thau, or Tau, is the last letter in the Hebrew alphabet, and signifies a sign or a mark: which is the reason why some translators render this place set a mark, or mark a mark, without specifying what this mark was. But St. Jerome, and other interpreters, conclude it was the form of the letter thau, which, in the ancient Hebrew character, was the form of a cross. (Challoner) --- Of this many inscriptions still extant bear witness. (Montfaucon.) --- Some Rabbins allow that the last letter was used but in honour of "the law," Thorah. The cross is supposed to be the hieroglyphic of a future life, (Hist. Rufini. ii. 29.) and found frequently in the pictures or (Haydock) in the tables of Isis. But it rather represents a key. Soldiers who were acquitted received the letter T, and those who were sentenced to die had Th, (Calmet) alluding to Thanatos, "death." (Haydock) --- We may, however, suppose that if God designated any letter, it would be some letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and accordingly the last had formerly the figure of †. x. though this text may signify "a sign" in general. The virtuous would be discriminated from the guilty, as if they were marked. (Calmet) --- The door-posts of the Hebrews were stained with blood, in Egypt, to shew that all should be redeemed by that of Christ; and here those who shall be saved, received the mark of his cross. This sign has always been held in veneration among Christians, (Worthington) and used in conferring baptism, consecrating the blessed Eucharist, &c. (St. Chrysostom, hom. lv. in Matthew, and lxxxiv. in John) (St. Augustine, tr. cxviii. in John, and ser. ci. de temp., &c.) --- It appeared to Constantine with this inscription, "In this conquer;" (Eusebius, vit. i. 22.) and again over Jerusalem; (St. Cyril, ep. ad Constantium.) and will be borne before Christ, at his last coming, (Matthew xxiv.) to the joy of those who have performed their baptismal promises, and to the confusion (Worthington) of the enemies of the cross of Christ. (Haydock)

Sanctuary. Aquila, "temple," or people (Calmet) consecrated to my service, (Septuagint; Tirinus) particularly (Calmet) the twenty-five idolaters, the ancients and women, (Calmet) chap. viii. 16. --- Judgment beginneth at the house of God, (1 Peter iv. 17.) and those (Haydock) who abuse holy things are justly cut off. (Worthington)
Defile. Septuagint, "you have defiled." I regard the place no longer. (Calmet)
Perverseness, in "wresting of judgment." (Protestant marginal note) What else can be expected, when the judges deny Providence? (Haydock)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying: The visitations of the city have drawn near. For 'visitations' the Seventy translated 'vengeance': for Mine indeed is vengeance, and I will repay, says the Lord, and every vengeance is a visitation, as of one who is sick, as of one who has wounds, as of one who awaits the hands of physicians, according to what is written elsewhere: I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with scourges; but my mercy I will not take away from them. And rightly, as we said above, visitation or vengeance is said to draw near, with the captivity close at hand.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And each one has a vessel of slaughter in his hand. He did not say 'had', as the Seventy translated, for he is not narrating things past, but shows things present and future. Whoever, therefore, strikes the wicked in that they are wicked, and has vessels of slaughter to kill the worst, is a minister of the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And behold, six men were coming from the way of the upper gate which looks toward the north, and each one a vessel of destruction in his hand; and one man in their midst clothed in linen, and a writer's inkhorn at his reins; and they went in and stood beside the bronze altar. And the glory of the Lord of Israel was taken up from the Cherub over whom it was, to the threshold of the house; and he called the man who was clothed in linen and had a writer's inkhorn at his loins. For 'linen', which we translated following Symmachus, the Seventy translated ποδήρη [a robe reaching to the feet], Theodotion the Hebrew word itself, 'baddim', Aquila 'choice things'; again, where we said: And a writer's inkhorn at his reins, the Seventy put: And a sapphire girdle upon his reins, Theodotion: Κάστυ [inkhorn] of the scribe in his hand, Aquila: Μελανοδοχεῖον (that is, Inkhorn) of the scribe at his loins, Symmachus: He had a writer's tablets at his reins; and where we translated 'threshold of the house', the Seventy and Theodotion put τὸ αἴθριον, that is, a 'vestibule' under the open sky; for 'vessel' also, which each of the men had in his hands, the Seventy alone translated 'axe'. To blot out, therefore, the sins of men, who were made on the sixth day of the fashioning of the world, six men come and descend from the upper gate (or, as the Seventy translated, 'the high one') toward the north; and each one had an axe in his hands, of which John speaks: For already the axe has been laid to the roots of the trees; every tree that does not bear fruit will be cut down and sent into the fire. And in the midst of the six men was one, that is, a seventh, in the attire of a high priest, clothed in linen garments, and he had a writer's inkhorn at his reins, with which to write down the sins of all and to separate the number of the saints from the sinners; or a sapphire girdle, of the color of the sapphire stone which is among the ornaments of the chief of the priests. And the six men went out and stood beside the bronze altar — for there were two altars: one of incense, of gold, within, and the other before the temple, the bronze altar of holocausts. They are said to stand beside the altar ready for the command of the one giving orders, so that whoever they saw had not had his sins forgiven there, they might know him to be subject to the sentence of the Lord and to slaughter —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Some interpret the six men as six angels who obey the will of God, and understand that one, who had the high priest's garments, as the Savior, according to the fact that the angel of great counsel is a priest, and to what is said: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Now ποδήρη, which the Seventy translated, is one of the eight garments of the high priest, which in Latin is called 'talaris' [ankle-length]; and from the fact that it comes down to the feet, it was allotted this name — I know that many years ago I published a book on the vesture of the high priest, to whose explanation I send the reader, for I cannot say everything in every place —. And as to what Aquila's first edition and Theodotion called κάστυ, for which in the Hebrew one reads 'cesath': when I asked a Hebrew what it meant, he answered me 'that in the Greek tongue it is called καλαμάριον [pen-case], from the fact that pens are stored in it'; we say 'atramentarium' [inkhorn], from the fact that it holds atramentum [ink]; many, more expressively, call them 'thecae' [cases], from the fact that they are cases for writers' pens. Of the four Cherubim, one Cherub is sent from the glory of the Lord's majesty, to speak to him who was clothed in the vestments of the high priest — and although most think that τά χερουβεὶμ [the cherubim] is said in the neuter gender and the plural number, we ought to know that 'Cherub' is in the singular number, of the masculine gender, and in the plural, of the same gender, 'Cherubim'; not that there is sex among the ministers of God, but that each thing is called by different genders according to the property of its own language: angels are called in the plural number 'Malachim', and 'Cherubim' and 'Seraphim', of the same gender and number; whereas 'sabaoth', which means 'of warfares' or 'of hosts' and 'of powers', are said in the feminine gender and the plural number, and end in the final syllable 'oth'. — Those, however, who wish the Savior to be understood under the figure of the high priest use an example from the Revelation of John, in which it is written: And I turned and saw the voice that was speaking with me; and having turned I beheld seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The glory of the Lord of Israel also went up, or was taken up, from the one Cherub, and went to the threshold, or to the open-air part of the court of the house and of the vestibule, which is in no way pressed down by a roof but enjoys the freedom of the air. This very glory of the Lord called the man who was in the attire of a high priest and had the inkhorn at his loins, and said what Scripture attests.
Treatise V. An Address to Demetrianus 22

God says that only those can escape who have been reborn and signed with the sign of Christ; when sending his angels to lay waste the world and to destroy the human race he threatens more seriously than the last time.… This sign pertains to the passion and blood of Christ and that he is kept safe and unharmed whoever is found in this sign.
LETTER TO THE BISHOPS OF EGYPT 1:2

Thus he suffers and is dishonoured; and although he still ventures with shameless confidence to disguise himself, yet now, wretched spirit, he is detected the rather by them that bear the Sign on their foreheads; yea, more, he is rejected of them, and is humbled, and put to shame. For even if, now that he is a creeping serpent, he shall transform himself into an angel of light, yet his deception will not profit him; for we have been taught that `though an angel from heaven preach unto us any other gospel than that we have received, he is anathema.'
Concerning the Statues, Homily 18

And I have heard many, after such experience, blame themselves, and say, What advantage is it that I have grieved? I have not recovered my money, and I have injured myself. But if thou hast grieved on account of sin, thou hast blotted it out, and hast reaped the greatest pleasure. If thou hast grieved for thy brethren who have fallen, thou hast both encouraged and comforted thyself, and hast also restored them; and even if thou wert not to profit them, thou hast an abundant recompense. And that thou mayest learn that this grieving for those who have fallen, though we should not at all benefit them, still brings us a large reward, hear what Ezekiel says; or rather, what God Himself speaks through him. For when He had sent certain messengers to overturn the city, and to consume all the dwellings with sword and fire, along with their inhabitants, He thus charges one of them: "Set a mark upon the forehead of the men that groan, and are in anguish." And after charging the others, and saying, "Begin ye from mine holy ones," He goes on to add, "But upon whomsoever the sign is, touch them not." For what reason, tell me? Because although they avail nothing, they nevertheless lament the things which are done, and deplore them.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the Lord said to him: Pass through the midst of the city, in the midst of Jerusalem, and mark a tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are done in its midst. And to those he said, in my hearing: Pass through the city following him, strike; let your eye not spare, nor have pity: old man, youth and virgin, little child and women, kill to utter destruction; anyone upon whom you see the tau, do not kill, and begin from my sanctuary. He who was clothed in an ankle-length garment, or a linen one, and displayed priestly attire, is commanded to put a sign upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are done in the midst of Jerusalem. For 'sign', which the Seventy, Aquila and Symmachus translated, Theodotion put the Hebrew itself, 'tau', which among the Hebrews is the last of the twenty-two letters, so as to show perfect knowledge in the men who groan and grieve; or, as the Hebrews assert, because 'law' is called 'thora' among them, which is written with this letter at the beginning of its name, those received this seal who had fulfilled the precepts of the law. And to come to our own: in the ancient letters of the Hebrews, which the Samaritans use to this day, the last letter, 'tau', has the likeness of a cross, which is painted on the foreheads of Christians and is signed by the frequent tracing of the hand; there are those who think that, from the fact that this is the last letter according to the Hebrew alphabet, it is shown that in the multitude of sinners a remnant of the saints survives. Those who groan and grieve, therefore, are saved, who not only did not consent to evil works but also lamented the sins of others, as Samuel too lamented over Saul, and the apostle Paul over those who after sinning did not do penance; whence he himself also said: We who are in the tabernacle groan, and elsewhere: I have great sorrow, and unceasing pain of my heart.
SERMON 107:7

But maybe that person wasn't yet a Christian. We at least, brothers and sisters, should listen; we to whom as believers the gospel is chanted, we by whom the one who said all this is worshiped, whose sign is worn by us on our foreheads and held in our hearts. It makes a great deal of difference, you see, where a person keeps the sign of Christ, whether on the forehead or both on the forehead and in the heart. You heard, when the holy prophet Ezekiel was speaking, how before God sent an exterminator of a wicked people, he first sent a marker and said to him, "Go and mark with a sign the foreheads of those who groan and grieve over the sins of my people, which are committed among them." Yet for all that they groan and grieve; and this is why they have been marked with a sign on the forehead—the forehead of the inner self, not the outer one. There is a forehead of the face, you see, and a forehead of the conscience. In fact, sometimes the inner forehead gets a knock, and the outer one blushes; it either blushes for shame or turns pale with fright.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the six men are commanded, apart from those who can say: The light of your countenance has been signed upon us, O Lord, to kill all: to spare not the old man, not the young man, not the virgin, not the little child, not the woman — according to the mystical senses, the old men are those in the Church of whom it is said: A man's gray hairs are his prudence; the young men, those who are most ready for the battles of faith; the virgins, those who keep chastity with their whole mind; the little children, those who are given the milk of infancy to drink and do not yet take solid food; the women, those who attest the frailty of their sex by the weakness of their soul — ; none of whom is spared if they believe themselves to be anything apart from the seal of Christ.
Commentary on Ezekiel

They began, therefore, with the elder men who were before the face of the house. And he said to them: Defile the house and fill the courts with the slain. For 'courts', which in Hebrew are called 'aseroth', the Seventy put 'ways'. Now the elder men are slain, of whom we read above that they had censers and burned incense to idols. Nor is there any sanctity of the temple left, because, the God of religion having been offended, all things have been defiled, so that whence came the sin, thence may come the judgment. And the courts in the temple are filled with corpses, and not the ways, which surely were outside, unless perhaps we can understand the ways as the streets of the city. Nor could the angels have dared to defile with the blood of the dead the temple in which the glory of God had formerly dwelt, had not the Lord of the departing glory commanded this. Everyone who is dead through sin defiles the courts of the temple and the ways of the city of the Lord in which he lives; he who rises with Christ ceases to be dead.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And what follows: And begin from my sanctuary (or, as the Seventy translated: And begin from my holy ones) signifies either the priests who busied themselves in the temple and worshiped idols, or those who, by the merit of their priesthood, were called holy among the people and who had been the cause of sin among the peoples, and these were the first to deserve punishment: for it is time for judgment to begin from the house of God.
SERMON 107:7

So there is a forehead of the inner self. That is where those people were marked, to save them from being wiped out. Because even if they did not put right the sins that were committed among them, at least they were pained by them, and by their very pain they set themselves apart; while set apart for God, they were mixed together in the eyes of people. They are marked with a sign in secret; they escape harm in public. The destroyer is sent next and is told, "Go, destroy, do not spare young, old, male, female; but do not go near those who have the sign on their foreheads." What a sure guarantee has been given you, my brothers and sisters, you among this people who are groaning and grieving over the wicked deeds committed in your midst and are not committing them!
Commentary on Ezekiel
And they went out, and struck those who were in the city. (Or, as others translated: They struck the city, naming the city itself in place of those who were in the city.)
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when the slaughter was complete, I remained, and I fell upon my face and, crying out, I say: Alas, Lord God; will you then destroy all the remnant of Israel, pouring out your fury upon Jerusalem? When all who did not have the seal had been laid low in the slaughter, the prophet fell on his face, thinking, because of the multitude of the slain, that no one but himself had remained. Because this seemed to be contrary to the sentence by which the Lord had ordered that the men with signed foreheads were not to be slain, it was for that reason removed in the common edition; but we, following the Hebrew truth, have put: I remained; and it must be noted that he had not said 'alone', for had he said that, it would have seemed contrary, but: I remained, so that 'with the others' who had sealed foreheads may be understood — and that we may know that this was said pointedly: I remained: in the volume of Kings, when Elijah speaks to God: They have torn down your altars, and I have been left alone, and they seek to take away my life, he put 'alone' because he did not know that others had remained —. Some think that this can also be understood from the person of the Lord, in whose type Ezekiel went before, concerning the people of the Jews: When all turned aside, together they became useless; and the prophet testifies: Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed; for the Lord was found 'alone' who did no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth. And as to what he added: Pouring out your fury upon Jerusalem, the word of pouring out shows the greatness of the punishments, as we read elsewhere: Contempt has been poured out upon princes, and again: My steps had almost been poured out, and in a good sense: The love of God has been poured out in our hearts, and: Grace has been poured out on your lips, and in the contrary sense: Pour out your fury upon the nations that have not understood you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name, and: Pour out the spear and close in from the opposite side against those who persecute me.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he said to me: The iniquity of the house of Israel and of Judah is great, exceedingly, very much; and the land is filled with bloods, and the city is filled with turning away. For they said: The Lord has forsaken the land, and: The Lord does not see; therefore my eye too will not spare, nor will I have pity: I will repay their ways upon their head. The Lord, seeing his prophet weep for the people and marvel at the greatness of the indignation, gives the reasons, not, as he thought, of a punishment unjust or exceeding measure, but of a deserved and just sentence: 'The iniquity,' he says, 'of the ten tribes of Israel and of the two tribes of Judah is great, and not only great but exceedingly great'; nor was it enough to have said this, but he added 'very much', so that the greatness of the punishment might match the greatness of the iniquity. From this we learn that sins are not equal, as many think and especially the Stoics, but either great or small, and that according to the quality and measure of those who sin there is diversity in the punishing judgment. The land, he says, is filled with bloods (or, as the Seventy translated, with peoples), and the city is filled with turning away (or, as the common edition has, with iniquity and uncleanness); no moderate amount of blood was shed, but from gate to gate, and the whole city turned aside from the worship of God, and in its place it is full of uncleanness, namely the filth of idolatry. The cause of such great crimes is this: that they thought there was no providence over the earth, and that God did not care for mortal things, according to what we read elsewhere: Of course this is a labor for those above, this is a care that troubles them in their quiet! ...
Commentary on Ezekiel

Since, therefore, they thought either that there was no providence, or that the providence which had formerly been among the peoples had at this time abandoned its own people, for that reason God's eye too will not spare, nor will he have pity: so that, raging against vices, he may be placable to virtues, and may repay their ways and sins upon their heads, either upon the ruling part of the heart or upon the princes of the people, according to the book of Numbers, in which the heads of the peoples are said to be princes.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And behold, the man who was clothed in linen, who had the inkhorn at his loins, answered, saying: I have done as you commanded me. (LXX: "And behold, the man who was clothed in a podere — that is, an ankle-length garment —, and girded as to his loins with a girdle, and he answered a word, saying: I have done as you charged me.") He is the man who was ordered to pass through the midst of Jerusalem and to put a sign on the foreheads of the men groaning and grieving over all their iniquities. He says, therefore, that he has fulfilled the Lord's commands and has armed the foreheads of those who mourn with the seal of the letter 'tau'. But the six men, whom the Lord had commanded, saying: Pass through the midst of the city following him, and strike; and have pity on no one, to utter destruction, report nothing of the kind; for to carry out a sentence that is proved not by word but by deed is a matter not of gladness but of grief. And in this place, for 'podere', that is, 'ankle-length garment', which the Seventy translated, Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, 'baddim', Symmachus 'linen', Aquila 'choice' or 'robe'; for 'girdle' also Symmachus put 'tablets', Aquila 'inkhorn', Theodotion κάστυ.

n: Throne. It was a sky blue crystal or sapphire colour, (chap. i. 22, 26.) and was now empty, chap. i. The Lord spoke from the temple door, ver. 4. (Haydock)
Out, to purify (St. Jerome) or punish the city, (Theodoret) which would shortly be reduced to ashes. (Vatable) (Menochius)
Right, south of the priests' court.
Lifted up, before chap. ix. 3. (Calmet) --- A man seemed to be on the throne, (Worthington) or rather over the door of the holy place.
Court of the people. --- Speaking in thunder.
Wings. They would seem to be distinct, or (Calmet) fingers appeared at the end of the wings. (Grotius)
Stone. Hebrew Tharsis. Symmachus, "Hyacinth." (Chap. i. 16.) (Calmet)
By four ways. That is, by any of the four ways, forward, backward, to the right, or to the left. (Challoner) (Worthington)
Wheels. These, as well as (Haydock) the cherubim, (Theodoret) were full of eyes. (Calmet)

Voluble. That is, rolling wheels: galgal, (Challoner) which means "rolling:" (Haydock) or "he said to the wheels, Turn around about." (Theodoret) --- This is the real import of Hebrew. (Calmet) --- Protestants have, "O wheel." (Haydock)

Cherub, or "ox." All four seem to have had the resemblance of a man, but one more than the rest, which had respectively the appearance rather of an ox, a lion, or an eagle: (Worthington) or the ox was predominant in all, as both the head and feet were of it; (Calmet) which, however, does not constitute the greatest part, chap. i. 5. (Haydock)

Creature. What I saw, was properly called cherubim. Charab, in Syriac means "to labour;" (Spencer) or cherubim may imply any composed and unusual figure, or "mixture," Exodus xxv. 18. (Calmet) --- Ezechiel being a priest, saw that the creatures resembled the cherubim of the temple. (Tirinus)
Life. They were not mere machines; (Haydock) or they were pushed forward by an impetuous wind.
East gate, leading from the city to the court of the people. (Calmet) -- How unwilling is this good father to leave his house! (Tirinus)
Creature. The cherubim and all the throne seemed alive. (Haydock)
Forward, thus shewing God's decree to abandon the synagogue. (Tirinus)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And I looked, and behold, in the firmament that was above the head of the Cherubim, as it were a sapphire stone, as it were the appearance of the likeness of a throne appeared above it. And he spoke to the man who was clothed in linen, and said: Go in into the midst of the wheels that are beneath the Cherub, and fill your hands with coals of fire that are between the Cherubim, and pour them out upon the city. Concerning the firmament that was above the Cherub, and the sapphire stone that had the likeness of a throne, and the wheels that followed the living creatures, let it suffice to have spoken above, and let the reader be content with the explanation of those things.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But now, as for the command given to the man who was clothed in linen — for which the Seventy in this place translated 'robe' — that he should take coals of fire from the midst of the Cherubim and pour them out, or scatter them, upon the city, it seems to me to show this: that after the slaying and slaughter of many, and the corpses of the dead in the streets, coals of fire are taken up to purge, or cleanse, Jerusalem, according to what is written in Isaiah: He will sanctify him in burning fire, and will devour the material like hay. These are the coals which, as a remedy for the tongue and for lying, laying waste vices and sins, the prophet, when questioned, longs for: What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you against a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals; and we shall be able to find many things of this kind in the holy Scriptures, of which we have often spoken. This only is to be noted: that in Isaiah, who had sinned only in speech and had said that he had unclean lips, a single coal is taken up with tongs to purge him; here, however, since the city was full of iniquity and, after the punishments, of the corpses of the dead, many coals of fire are taken up, and not with one hand but with both, so that all Jerusalem may be purged — although this too may be understood: that the coals of fire are to be taken up not for purging but for punishments and torments, to be poured out upon Jerusalem —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he went in in my sight. Now the Cherubim were standing on the right side of the house when the man went in, and a cloud filled the inner court. And the glory of the Lord was lifted up from above the Cherub to the threshold of the house, and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the Lord. And the sound of the wings of the Cherubim was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God almighty speaking. And when he had commanded the man who was clothed in linen, saying: Take fire from the midst of the wheels that are between the Cherubim, he went in and stood beside the wheel; and a Cherub stretched out his hand from the midst of the Cherubim to the fire that was between the Cherubim, and took it, and gave it into the hand of him who was clothed in linen; who, receiving it, went out. And there appeared in the Cherubim the likeness of a man's hand beneath their wings. While the prophet looks on, the man goes in who was clothed in a garment reaching to the feet, or in linen — and, as the Seventy now change their rendering, in a 'holy robe', although among the Hebrews there is one and the same word, 'baddim' [linen garments], and the other translators persist in the rendering they began with —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now as the man who was clothed in linen garments went in, the Cherubim were standing on the right side of the house, so that the holy powers on high might be seen to hold the right-hand part of the house of God, and those that are sent for punishments — of whom it is written: A sending through most evil angels — may be believed to occupy the left-hand parts. And when the glory of the Lord had been lifted up from the Cherub who was about to hand the coals of fire to the man, and had passed over to the threshold of the house, at once the inner court is filled with cloud, darkness and gloom; for punishments are not carried out while the majesty of the Lord is present, and the glory of the Lord is seen in the court, of which it is written: The sound of the wings of the Cherubim was heard as far as the outer court. For 'sound' the Hebrew has 'voice', and this voice had the likeness of the voice of God almighty speaking — for which the Seventy translated 'like the voice of God saddai', which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion translated as ἱκανόν, which signifies 'strong and mighty' —.
On the Tabernacle 1:5.25:18-21

The prophet Ezekiel clearly declares that "cherubim" is the name of the angelic powers that he describes as having appeared to him with wings, according to the pattern in which they are ordered to be deployed here.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he goes in, as is said a second time, into the midst of the wheels that are beneath the Cherubim, to fill his hands with coals of fire. When he had gone in, he only stood beside the wheel and, stunned either by sorrow for Jerusalem that was to be punished or by the greatness of the glory, did not himself put his hand to the fire; but one of the Cherubim, that is, a Cherub, put out his hand and took the fire that was in the midst of the Cherubim and gave it into the hand of him who was clothed in linen garments; who, receiving it, went out; and yet Scripture does not say what he did when he had gone out, so as to leave the narration of a sad event to our understanding rather than set it before our eyes.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Note, reader, in what points the former vision and this one agree or disagree, so that from the comparison of the two, without any prompting from us, you may understand the divine mysteries; note also what I pointed out before: how in the firmament, and in the throne, and in the hand of a man, not the reality but the likeness is spoken of; for we do not contemplate the glory of the Lord face to face with unveiled countenance, but we see all things in likeness and image, as long as we are encompassed by a frail and corruptible body.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I looked, and behold, four wheels beside the Cherubim; one wheel beside one Cherub, and another wheel beside one Cherub, and the appearance of the wheels was like the sight of a chrysolite stone, and their aspect was one likeness for the four, as if a wheel were in the midst of a wheel. And when they went in four directions, they went and did not turn back as they went, but to the place to which the first one turned to go, the others also followed and did not turn about. And their whole body and necks and hands and wings and rims were full of eyes round about the four wheels; and these wheels he called whirling, in my hearing. Now one had four faces: the one face the face of a Cherub, and the second face the face of a man, and in the third the face of a lion, and in the fourth the face of an eagle. And the Cherubim were lifted up. Observe that earlier, according to the Seventy, the appearance of the wheels was Like the sight of 'tharsis', but now, according to the same: Like the sight of 'carbuncle', so that by the fire that is handed over by the Cherub a likeness of the punishments may be shown — although in the Hebrew, both above and here, 'tharsis' is written, which Aquila translated 'chrysolite' and Symmachus 'hyacinth' —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And again, where we rendered: And their whole 'body', with 'of the wheels' understood, in the Hebrew it is written: And all their 'fleshes', and necks and hands and wings and rims; note that flesh is spoken of in the heavenly powers, so that, when we read: Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God, nor corruption incorruption, we may know that not the substance of the flesh but its works are condemned: for 'basar', which is written in this place, signifies not 'body' but 'flesh'. Now by the rims of the wheels he meant the iron tires by which the roundness of the wood is bound and held tight. These wheels, moreover, have not only fleshes, or a body, or members, but also necks, hands and wings, so that in each of these we may perceive the workings of things, not images of members.
Pastoral Rule, Part 3, Chapter 4

Wherefore those who are over others are to be admonished, that through earnestness of circumspection they have eyes watchful within and round about, and strive to become living creatures of heaven. For the living creatures of heaven are described as full of eyes round about and within. And so it is meet that those who are over others should have eyes within and round about, so as both in themselves to study to please the inward judge, and also, affording outwardly examples of life, to detect the things that should be corrected in others.

Subjects are to be admonished that they judge not rashly the lives of their superiors, if perchance they see them act blamably in anything, lest whence they rightly find fault with evil they thence be sunk by the impulse of elation to lower depths.
