They are to be admonished that, when they consider the faults of their superiors, they grow not too bold against them, but, if any of their deeds are exceedingly bad, so judge of them within themselves that, constrained by the fear of God, they still refuse not to bear the yoke of reverence under them.
Commentary on Ezekiel
Further, what follows: In my hearing, up to the place where it is written: The Cherubim were lifted up, is not found in the Seventy but has been added from the Hebrew.
Commentary on Ezekiel
The 'wheels' themselves, too, are called in the Hebrew tongue 'gelgel', which Symmachus translated 'whirling' and Aquila 'wheel'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

In this it must be observed that it is by no means as is said above: The face of a man, and the face of a lion four, and the face of a calf on the left four, and the face of an eagle four on the right, so that, of course, some might be believed to be on the left and others on the right; rather, an equal order of them all is described, as Scripture says: Now one had four faces: the one face the face of a Cherub, and the second face the face of a man, and in the third the face of a lion, and in the fourth the face of an eagle, so that the first and second and third and fourth face is described not by a difference of place, right and left, but in a single order, by degrees. Now the one face, that is, the first, he called Cherub, where above he had said the face of a calf; from which it is understood that the face of a Cherub is the face of a calf. The sense of all these things is contained in the explanation of the former vision.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But as for what is said: This is the living creature that I had seen beside the river Chebar, Scripture shows that in the exposition of the living creature we ought to understand the same things that we understood above.
Commentary on Ezekiel

This is the living creature that I had seen beside the river Chebar. And when the Cherubim went, the wheels also went alongside them; and when the Cherubim lifted their wings to be raised up from the earth, the wheels did not hold back, but they too were beside them. When those stood, these stood, and when those were lifted up, these were lifted up, for the spirit of life was in them. All things live to God and perceive their own Creator: He is not, you see, the God of the dead, but of the living. Hence also all the bodies of the wheels are full of eyes. And in the psalm it is said: The heavens tell the works of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands. Day to day pours forth a word, and night to night shows knowledge; the sun too and the moon, the sea and the rivers, the mountains and the hills praise God, and the elements revolve in their own circuit year by year, and we discern on earth the order of the heavens, so that, keeping the order of the ancient law, they revolve and run, and we see nothing new upon the earth.
LETTER 108.12

I linger long in the land of the midday sun, for it was there and then that the spouse found her bridegroom at rest and Joseph drank wine with his brothers once more. I will return to Jerusalem and, passing through Tekoa the home of Amos, I will look on the glistening cross of Mount Olive from which the Savior made his ascension to the Father. Here year by year a red heifer was burned as an offering to the Lord, and its ashes were used to purify the children of Israel. Here also according to Ezekiel the cherubim after leaving the temple founded the church of the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the glory of the Lord went out from the threshold of the temple, and stood above the Cherubim; and the Cherubim, lifting their wings, were raised up from the earth before me, and as they went out the wheels also followed; and it stood at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, and the glory of the God of Israel was above them. This is the living creature that I saw beneath the God of Israel beside the river Chebar, and I understood that they were Cherubim. Four by four faces to one, and four wings to one, and the likeness of a man's hand under their wings; and the likeness of their faces, the very faces that I had seen beside the river Chebar, and their gaze, and the onrush of each to go forward before its face. The glory of the Lord, or the majesty that had stood at the threshold of the temple, stood above the Cherubim, which, lifting their wings, were raised up while the prophet watched, the wheels following alike, and it stood at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, and little by little the protection of God left Israel. First it was in the temple; then it stood in the court of the temple, or at the threshold, and as it withdrew from the temple, cloud and gloom filled the inner recesses of the temple; and again the glory itself sat upon the Cherubim and, as they at once flew off and went away to the outer parts, the wheels followed; and the glory stood at the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, not at the door of the temple, but beyond the court and the threshold, at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

When the prophet had seen this: This is, he says, the living creature that I saw beneath the God of Israel beside the river Chebar, and I understood that they were Cherubim. For what new thing did he see, that he should understand that they were Cherubim, which he had not understood before? 'Cherubim' in our language is 'multitude of knowledge', the knowledge of the mysteries of God, and his throne and resting place; hence also in the psalm it is said: You who sit upon the Cherubim, be made manifest; for the glory of the Lord always sits in the multitude of knowledge, and it is made manifest then: when all things are shown to be ruled by providence, and nothing to happen by chance, and no one to say: The Lord has forsaken the earth, and the Lord does not see; hence also the gaze of the Cherubim and their desire is to forget the things that are past and to stretch themselves forward to the things to come.

n: Me. The prophet in Chaldea, saw in spirit what was doing at Jerusalem. (Worthington) --- Men. Magistrates. (Prado.) (Tirinus) (Menochius) --- Jezonias, perhaps mentioned [in] chap. viii. 11. (Calmet)

Built, &c. These men despised the predictions and threats of the prophets; who declared to them from God, that the city should be destroyed and the inhabitants carried into captivity: and they made use of this kind of argument against the prophets, that the city so far from being like to be destroyed, had lately been augmented by the building of new houses; from whence they further inferred, by way of a proverb, using the similitude of a cauldron, out of which the flesh is not taken till it is thoroughly boiled and fit to be eaten, that they should not be carried away out of their city, but there end their days in peace. (Challoner) --- They thought themselves secure, (Worthington) and laughed at the menaces of Jeremias, i. 15. (Calmet) --- Hebrew, "The destruction is not soon coming. Let us build;" (Pagnin; Menochius) or, "It is not time to build." (Calmet)
Slain, under Manasses, &c. (Tirinus)

Cauldron. I will explain the prediction, which you turn to ridicule. Those whom you have slain, are like the flesh (Calmet) boiled. (Haydock) --- But you shall be treated still worse, being led captives and slain. (Calmet) --- They feared wars, but had no dread of captivity. (Worthington)

Israel. They pretended that they should die in peace in Jerusalem: God tells them it should not be so, but that they should be judged and condemned, and fall by the sword in the borders of Israel; viz., in Reblatha, in the land of Emath, where all their chief men were put to death by order of Nabuchodonosor, 4 Kings xxv., and Jeremias lii. 10, 27. (Challoner)
But you. Some copies of Septuagint have, "neither have you done," chap. v. 7.

Pheltias, the prince, (ver. 1.; Haydock) or false prophet, whose death Ezechiel does not bewail, but fears the great destruction of the people; (Worthington; Menochius) though, if Pheltias died impenitent, his death might justly call for tears. (Haydock) --- This happened in a vision. Yet (Calmet) he probably died suddenly about his time. (Lyranus)

Thy brethren, &c. He speaks of them that had been carried away captives before, who were despised by them that remained in Jerusalem; but, as the prophet here declares to them from God, should be in a more happy condition than they, and after some time return from their captivity. (Challoner) --- David had been insulted in like manner, 1 Kings xxvi. 19. (Calmet)

A little. Hebrew, "for a short time, a sanctuary," or temple. They shall find all things in me. The Christian Church was never more pure than during the first persecutions, when her children could not assemble freely, or build temples. (Calmet) --- God will never totally abandon her, Jeremias iv. 27., &c. (Worthington)
Scandals: idols. They relapsed no more into idolatry, (Calmet) as a nation, though some fell in the persecution of Epiphanes. (Haydock)
One. Septuagint, "another." They have read (Calmet) acher for echad, "one." (Haydock)
Head. I will punish them as their crimes deserve. (Calmet)

Mount Olivet, whence he might behold the conflagration of the city, before his ascent into heaven. (Menochius) --- He leaves his habitation by degrees, to shew how Jerusalem would be treated, and the Jews suffer after the ascension of our Saviour. Theodoret well observes, that the person on the throne represented Him, the upper part of the body being different from the lower, (chap. i. 26.) to denote the two natures. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the spirit lifted me up, and brought me in to the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, which looks toward the rising of the sun. Since the glory of the Lord had gone forth from the threshold of the temple and stood above the Cherubim, and afterward, as the Cherubim flew away, the glory itself stood at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, the prophet too — he could not go to it by himself — was lifted up by the spirit and led to the same eastern gate of the house of the Lord, which looks toward the sun of righteousness, of whom it is written: Behold a man, the Orient is his name, so that he should by no means remain in the temple, which was confounded by the cloud of ignorance, but, standing in the gate of the house of the Lord on the east, might come to know the mysteries that follow.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And behold, at the entrance of the gate twenty-five men, and I saw in their midst Jaazaniah the son of Azur and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people. And he said to me: Son of man, these are the men who devise iniquity, and handle a most wicked counsel in this city, saying: Were not the houses built long ago? This is the cauldron, and we are the flesh. Therefore prophesy concerning them; prophesy, son of man. And the spirit of the Lord rushed upon me and said to me: Speak. Thus says the Lord: So have you spoken, house of Israel, and the thoughts of your heart I know. You have killed very many in this city, and you have filled its streets with the slain. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Your slain, whom you have laid in its midst, they are the flesh, and this is the cauldron; and I will bring you out of its midst. You have feared the sword, and the sword I will bring upon you, says the Lord God. And I will cast you out of its midst, and I will give you into the hand of enemies, and I will execute judgments upon you. By the sword you shall fall; in the borders of Israel I will judge you, and you shall know that I am the Lord. This shall not be to you for a cauldron, and you shall not be in its midst for flesh: in the borders of Israel I will judge you; and you shall know that I am the Lord. (What follows is not found in the Seventy but has been added from the Hebrew:) Because you have not walked in my precepts, and you have not done my judgments, but you have acted according to the judgments of the nations which are round about you. The prophet is taken up, according to what is written: The Lord taking up the meek, or he is lifted up from the earth and brought in to the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, so that he may come to know the mysteries of the twenty-five men who were at the entrance of the gate, and of Jaazaniah the son of Azur and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And since what is said is plain according to the letter, setting aside for a little while the names of Jaazaniah and Azur, Pelatiah and Benaiah, which we reserve for another time, this must be said: that to this day in the Church, which is the house of God, both before the eastern gate and at the entrance, or in the way, of the gate, which signifies the Savior, through whom we enter to the Father, there are twenty-five men, referring all things to the senses — and, so far as it does not escape my memory, I have never been able to find this number in a good sense, although in Leviticus men are chosen for the priestly ministry from twenty-five years of age; for in the Hebrew it does not have this number which is given in the Seventy, but the number thirty, which is contained in the opening of this prophet and in the age of the Lord when he came to the streams of the Jordan and was baptized by John; but if in the Gospel five wise virgins and five foolish are found, let us know that this number is placed in the middle and, according to the quality of those who use it, can be applied either to the good or to the bad side —. These men, then, who refer all things to the senses, and have two princes, of whom we spoke above, are contained in the dual number, which splits unity and, in the number of the second day, is not seen by the Lord, according to the Hebrew truth — whence also into the ark of Noah the unclean are brought in two and two; but the Lord, drawing the division together into one, made both one and loosed the middle wall, condemning the enmities in his flesh; whence also he says something more august and more sublime: I and the Father are one, so that he may call us back from the Jewish duality into the union of the Christian faith; finally, when the high priesthood of the Jews had been lost, the Lord suffers by no means under one prince, but under two, Annas and Caiaphas, so that he might show the divided error of their religion —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

There are many at the entrance of this gate, before the eastern house of the Lord, who by their vices are compared to the nations, and from the consciousness of their sins despair of salvation, and say: 'The city in which we dwell is a cauldron, and we are all flesh, and we shall be consumed by the Babylonian burning, whose darts are fiery', unwilling to do penance and despairing of salvation; therefore they hear that they themselves are not the flesh of the past and lost city, but those whom they have scandalized, whom they have killed; and for that reason the sword is brought upon them: so that, after they have been judged in the borders of Israel, by no means among the nations but among Christians, then they may know that he himself is the Lord, according to what is read in the Psalms: When he slew them, they sought him, so that him whom they had not perceived through benefits, they may come to know through torments.
Commentary on Ezekiel

These, then, who were at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, despairing of salvation and, from the consciousness of their crimes, ready for destruction, and unwilling to correct their sins through repentance, say: 'Although the houses which had earlier collapsed have lately, after the first captivity, been built, yet we know that this city is like a cauldron and we are for flesh, so that in it we may be consumed and burned up together, according to what is written in Isaiah: The tempest, if it passes through, will not take us'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

As they say these things, the spirit of the Lord rushed upon the prophet, and commanded him a second time to prophesy and to say: 'Since you have said these things, and the secrets of your hearts do not escape me, I will interpret to you how the city is to be reckoned a cauldron and you flesh, not according to the sense in which you spoke, but according to another which you do not fear: the city is indeed in the likeness of a cauldron, but it will not be filled with your flesh, but with that of those whom you have killed; you, however, who think that you will die in this city, I will bring out of the midst of the city and hand over into the hands of enemies, and I will execute judgments upon you, so that, when you have fallen by the sword, by no means in the city nor outside the bounds of Israel but in the borders of your own province, then too you may know that I am the Lord'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And a second time it is said: 'In the borders of Israel I will judge you, and you shall know that I am the Lord; and all these things you will suffer, because you have not walked in my precepts and have not done my judgments, but have wrought the crimes of the other nations round about'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And it came to pass, while I was prophesying, Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died; and I fell on my face, crying out with a loud voice, and I said: Alas, alas, alas, Lord God, you are making a consummation of the remnant of Israel. As the prophet prophesies, one of the two princes, Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, dies, whose name means 'a fall turning aside', and he is the son of a 'builder' or 'mason' — for οἰκοδόμος cannot be rendered into our language otherwise —; the other of the princes, Jaazaniah, is kept safe — Jaazaniah signifies 'his ear', by which 'of the soul' is understood; Azur, however, 'support' or 'help' —. He, then, who by falling had turned aside from the Lord and was of a most wicked building, rightly falls while he whom God strengthened is prophesying; but he who obeyed the precepts of God and was sustained and supported by his help rightly remains in command of the people — we read in Exodus that, when Pharaoh king of Egypt had died, the sons of Israel groaned from the works of clay, of straw and of brick, and cried out to the Lord, upon whom, while he lived, they could not call; Isaiah also, when Uzziah the leprous king had died, saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and the Seraphim standing around him, and, understanding that he had unclean lips and dwelt among a people having unclean lips, he merits that a coal be sent from the altar and purge his unclean lips; here, however, as the strength of God prophesies, the prince who had turned aside from the service of the Lord falls, so that he may be raised up by Christ: for if the Lord is the resurrection, the devil is the fall; in which it is asked how it is said of the Savior: Behold, this one is set for the fall and the resurrection of many in Israel: for the fall of those who stood most wickedly, and the resurrection of such as had fallen —. When the prophet had seen this, he fell on his face, not by the desert of one who sins but with the feeling of one who mourns, and with a loud voice, which came from the great ardor of faith, he cried out three times and said: Alas, alas, alas, Lord God, you are making a consummation of the remnant of Israel; and the sense is: 'Even the very remnant which seemed to be among the people is being destroyed in your indignation'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The word of the Lord, therefore, came to Ezekiel, who had said: Alas, alas, alas, Lord God, you are making a consummation of the remnant of Israel, namely in the death of Pelatiah and of those who were killed with him: that by no means were those the remnant which the prophet supposed in Jerusalem, but those who were seen to be captives in Babylon; and the sense is: 'O son of man, your brothers, begotten of the same stock with you, your brothers, I say, to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: You have gone away from the Lord, because you are captives and have handed yourselves over with Jeconiah, but to us the land of Israel has been given for an everlasting possession — say, therefore, to them that I have indeed made them far off from the land of Israel and dispersed them into the nations and ordered them to be in foreign lands, but, because they have obeyed my command, I shall be among them, even in strange and hostile places, for a little sanctification, while very many are found among them who by no means submit their necks to idolatry but are mindful of the commandments of God', as Daniel and the three youths were, and it must be believed that others were, after the likeness of such great princes as Scripture now shows. From all of which we learn that we must not insult those who by the judgment of God have been handed over to punishments, nor reproach a man converted from his sins, nor ever say to those who do penance and have gone out of the Church: You have gone far away from the Lord; to us the land has been given for a possession, because thus says the Lord: 'Although I have separated them for a little while from my Church and dispersed them among the nations, yet I will be to them for a small sanctification while they remember their sins, and those who had departed from the land of God because of their vices, may hasten, because of repentance, to return to their former seats'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, your brothers, your brothers, the men your kinsmen and the whole house of Israel, all to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: Go far away from the Lord; to us the land has been given for a possession. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because I have made them far off among the nations, and because I have scattered them into the land, I will be to them for a small sanctification in the lands to which they have come. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, your brothers, your brothers and the men of your captivity and the whole house of Israel is consummated, to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: You have gone far away from the Lord; to us the land has been given for an inheritance. Therefore say: Adonai the Lord says: Because I will drive them away into the nations, and I will sow them abroad into every land, and I will be to them for a little sanctification in the regions into which they shall have entered there.") First we must speak of the variety in translation. Where the Hebrew has 'men your kinsmen' — for this is what 'goolathach' means —, the Seventy translated 'men of your captivity'; then, where there follows: All to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said, in place of 'all' they put 'is consummated', because of the ambiguity of the letters and of the word: for 'chollo', which Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated 'all', they rendered 'is consummated', which does not accord with the sense at all.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore speak: Thus says the Lord God: I will gather you from the peoples, and I will assemble you from the lands in which you have been scattered, and I will give you the soil of Israel. And they shall enter there, and shall take away all the offenses, and all the abominations from it; and I will give them one heart (or another), and a new spirit I will bestow, in their inward parts; and I will take away the stony heart from their flesh, and I will give them a heart of flesh, that they may walk in my precepts, and keep my judgments and do them, and be to me for a people and I be to them for God. But those whose heart walks after their stumbling blocks and their abominations, their way I will set upon their own head, says the Lord God. The divine word speaks to those who were captives in the land of Babylon, and to the brothers of Ezekiel the prophet and to his kinsmen, to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said: You have gone far away from the Lord; to us the land has been given for a possession; and it speaks these things which follow: 'I will gather you from the peoples, and I will restore to you the land of Israel; and when you have entered, you will take away all the idols on account of which you had offended God, and I will give you one heart, of the fear and the service of God, so that you may by no means serve diverse idols, or another than the one you had before; and I will bestow a new spirit in your inward parts, according to what is written: Create a clean heart in me, and renew a holy spirit in my inward parts; and I will take away from you the stony heart — that is, a hard heart, according to what Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, says: Hard of neck and uncircumcised in heart —; and the heart of Pharaoh is hardened, so that he may not let the people of Israel go; and I will give you', he says, 'a heart of flesh, soft and tender, and one which can receive the commandments of God, so that they may be written on the fleshly tablets of the heart' — for this reason a soft heart is given and the hard heart is taken away: so that they may walk in his precepts and keep his judgments and be in the people of God, and the Lord, who before had been an adversary, may be to them for God —; 'but those who have by no means corrected their former sins by repentance, but have walked after their abominations, I will repay', he says, 'with what they deserve: let their ways be set upon their heads'. Most think that these things happened under Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and under Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the great priest, and under Ezra and Nehemiah, to the tribe of Judah and to those who returned with them, and that the inhabitants of Jerusalem who were captured under Zedekiah king of Judah, or who fled with Jeremiah into Egypt, were dispersed into all lands, so that they by no means returned to the city of Jerusalem. But the full conversion, of those who were captives and of the remnant of Israel, is understood in Christ, when the remnant was saved, and in one day three thousand believed, and again five thousand, and others, of whom James speaks to the apostle Paul: You see, brother, so many thousands of believing Jews. These are all zealous for the law. But also daily the proud inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem, whose heart walks after their stumbling blocks and their abominations, earn the displeasure of God, and those who were outside, the stony heart having been taken away and a most soft heart received, return through repentance to the Church, and walk in the precepts of the Lord, and keep his judgments, and become the people of the Lord, and the Lord, whom they had previously offended, becomes God to them.
The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter VI

Behold, therefore, we have been refashioned, as again He says in another prophet, "Behold, saith the Lord, I will take away from these, that is, from those whom the Spirit of the Lord foresaw, their stony hearts, and I will put hearts of flesh within them," because He was to be manifested in flesh, and to sojourn among us.
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 3:1.7

This might lead one to suppose that it was God who gave the power to walk in his commandments and to keep his judgments, if it was he who removed the stony heart, which hindered them from keeping the commandments, and who implanted in them the better and more sensitive one, which is here called a heart of flesh.
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 3:1.15

Now this is what is said by those who wish to prove by the authority of Scripture that nothing lies within our own power. We shall reply to them that these words must not be understood in that sense but as follows. It is as if an uneducated and uninstructed person becoming conscious of the disgrace of his condition, whether by being stirred at the exhortation of another or by a desire to rival those who are wise, should entrust himself to one by whom he is confident that he can be carefully trained and competently instructed. If then he, who had formerly hardened himself in ignorance, entrusts himself, as we have said, with full purpose of mind to a master and promises to obey him in everything, the master, on seeing clearly his purpose and determination, will on his part undertake to take away from him his lack of education and to implant in him education, not promising, however, to do this if the disciple withholds his assent and co-operation but only if he offers and pledges himself to entire obedience.
LETTER 217

Those and other divine testimonies, which it would take too long to enumerate, show that God by his grace takes away the stony heart from unbelievers and forestalls merit in people of good will in such a way that their will is prepared by prevenient grace, but not that grace is given through prevenient merit of the will. This is shown both by thanksgiving and by prayer: prayer for unbelievers; thanksgiving for believers. Prayer is to be made to him that he may do what we ask; thanksgiving is to be offered when he has done it.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the Cherubim lifted up their wings, and the wheels with them, and the glory of the God of Israel was above them; the glory of the Lord went up from the midst of the city, and stood upon the mountain which is to the east of the city. Little by little the glory of the Lord withdraws from Jerusalem: first, deserting the temple, it stands in the court or at the threshold of the house, and afterward at the entrance of the eastern gate; lastly, its wings lifted and the wheels following, it stands upon the mountain which is to the east of the city — no doubt it signifies the Mount of Olives, from which the Savior ascended to the Father; and the glory of the Lord, which had departed from the city of Jerusalem, stood upon the Mount of Olives as a sign of resurrection and of light, so that from there it might behold Jerusalem about to perish and about to burn —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And as for his saying: The glory went up from the midst of the city, in other words the Lord speaks to the disciples: Arise, let us go hence, and to the Jews: Your house will be left to you desolate; Josephus also relates that there was heard in the temple a voice of the angels and of the heavenly strength, which had previously been the city's defense: Let us go away from these seats. And, in a wondrous manner, to the present day the glory of the Lord, which deserted the temple, stands upon the Mount of Olives and, gleaming in the sign of the cross, looks upon the once Jewish temple, dissolved into embers and ashes.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the spirit lifted me up, and brought me into Chaldea, to the exile, in a vision, in the spirit of God; and the vision which I had seen was taken away from me. And I spoke to the exile all the words of the Lord which he had shown me. Where we translated from the Hebrew truth: And the vision which I had seen was taken away from me, the Seventy translated: And I went up from the vision which I had seen; and both signify that the prophet was carried over to Jerusalem from Babylon not in the body but in the spirit, and, when the vision had been taken away which had led him in the spirit to Jerusalem and had shown him all the things which the preceding discourse narrated, he returned from himself, and spoke to the exile all the things which had been shown to him, namely to those of whom it is written above: I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting beside me, and the hand of the Lord God fell upon me there, and I saw. And, in a wondrous manner, while those who had come to visit him were sitting there, the prophet was beholding mystical visions, and he was absent from those who sat before him: absent in spirit, present in body. And all things happen so that those who were captives might receive consolation, in that they are to be led back into the land of Israel, and are to walk in the precepts of the Lord, and to be to him for a people, and he is to be to them for God; but those who have not been converted to repentance, but have walked after their abominations, are to receive what they have done. That in the holy Scriptures words are spoken in place of things, we have often pointed out.

n: Removing. Literally, "vessels of transmigration," (Haydock) or bundles, (Calmet) and what was requisite for travelling, (Worthington) or in exile. (Haydock) --- All this, to chap. xx., happened five years before the fall of Jerusalem. (Calmet) --- See chap. viii. 1. (Haydock)

Be carried. (Septuagint) St. Jerome reads, "thou shalt carry thy bundles on the shoulder," as many explain the Hebrew, (Calmet) and also ver. 7. "I bear it upon my shoulder," ver. 12. (Protestants) (Haydock) --- Cover, to denote the blindness of Sedecias, (Calmet) or his attempt to disguise himself. (Haydock) --- The faces of criminals were covered, Esther vii. The king and nobles escaped through a breach, Jeremias xxxix. 4. (Calmet) --- Sign. Literally, "a prodigy to," &c. (Haydock) --- The actions as well as the words of the prophet indicated what would happen. (St. Jerome, ver. 11.)

Jerusalem. The people regarded not Jeremias. This prediction would be sent to them to confirm what he said, while it would tend to keep up the spirits of those who were in captivity. (Theodoret) (Calmet) --- Israel. The people, or those of the ten tribes who had retired thither. (Menochius)

Net, as was done in war, and to catch wild beasts, Jeremias xvi. 16. (Calmet) --- Not see it, because his eyes shall be put out by Nabuchodonosor. (Challoner) --- The false prophets thought they perceived a contradiction here; (Worthington) and Sedecias, confronting it with Jeremias xxxviii. 18., disregarded both. (Josephus, Antiquities x. 10.) --- This was more pardonable than for Paine to object this as an inconsistency, after the event has so clearly verified the predictions of both, and shewed their consent. (Haydock) --- The unhappy prince saw too late the true meaning. (Calmet) --- He was put in a cage, like a wild beast, and conveyed blind to Babylon. (St. Jerome)
Them. Many joined Godolias, chap. v. 2. (Haydock)
Sorrow. Act like one under great anxiety and distress. (Calmet)

Proverb, or common saying. (Worthington) --- Prolonged. They took occasion from God's long suffering to become more wicked, (Calmet) and even asserted that the prophets told nothing but lies, (Theodoret) and spoke of events at a great distance, that they might not be detected. If what they announced came to pass, they attributed it to chance; (Calmet) if it did not, being only conditional, they ridiculed this idea as a mere subterfuge. (Haydock) --- As the prophets had long before foretold the captivity, and it had not yet taken place, (Worthington) in general, though many were already in exile, (Haydock) they concluded that it would never be realized. Thus heretics deny the general judgment, 1 Peter iii. (Worthington) --- Every vision, on this head, ver. 28. Many events were revealed that regarded the times of Christ, Daniel ix., &c. (Haydock)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, you dwell in the midst of a provoking house, who have eyes to see and do not see, and ears to hear and do not hear, for it is a provoking house. (Where we have rendered: You dwell in the midst of a provoking house, the Seventy put: You dwell in the midst of their iniquities; but from what follows: For it is a provoking house, we understand that the former clause too fits this little verse.) We have often shown, too, that 'bitterness' is said in place of 'provocation', so that the sense is: 'You dwell in the midst of a house that turns God to bitterness, which, by the bitterness of its vices, makes God, who is by nature sweet and merciful, bitter and cruel'; otherwise we read of God: Taste and see that gracious (or sweet) is the Lord. The prophet, then, dwells in the midst of a people provoking God to bitterness, which has eyes and does not see, ears and does not hear, not through a defect of the senses but through the obstinacy of depravity; whence the Lord also says to the Jews: If you were blind, he says, you would not have sin, censuring and condemning in them a voluntary blindness. 'Since, therefore, they have eyes to see and do not see, ears to hear and do not hear, and they despise your words, teach them through an image and a picture, and show them by bodily figures, so that they may recognize the coming captivity not only by hearing but also with their eyes'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

You therefore, son of man, make yourself vessels of exile, and you shall migrate by day before them; and you shall migrate from your place to another place in their sight, if perhaps they may look, for it is a provoking house. (LXX: "And you, son of man, make yourself vessels of captivity, and be taken captive by day before them; and be taken captive from your place to another place in their sight, that they may see, for it is a provoking house.") No one doubts that the whole content of this passage points to the future captivity of King Zedekiah of the tribe of Judah, who was taken together with Jerusalem. But since some would have the captivity of Zedekiah, which means 'righteous Lord', go before as a type of the Savior, who, descending from heavenly things to earthly, took on a human body, and would have these be the vessels of captivity, I therefore think the prudent and cautious reader must be forewarned: that we set these things down, lest we seem to pass over anything, but do not approve them; for a wicked king cannot go before as a figure of him who is the example of all piety. That Zedekiah was taken by the Babylonians and Chaldeans both Jeremiah the prophet and the history of Kings relate, and that he was led from place to place, that is, from Jerusalem to Babylon, and the rest of what Ezekiel says in what follows. But those who refer it to the Lord Jesus Christ think that his captivity and exile from place to place signify the descent from heavenly things to earthly.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you shall carry out your vessels like the vessels of one going into exile by day in their sight, and you shall go out in the evening before them, as one migrating goes out. Before their eyes dig through the wall for yourself, and you shall go out through it; in their sight you shall carry on your shoulders, in the darkness you shall flee: you shall veil your face, and you shall not see the land, for I have given you as a portent to the house of Israel. (LXX: "And you shall bring forth your vessels, vessels of captivity, by day in their eyes, and you shall go out in the evening in their sight, as a captive goes out. Dig for yourself in the wall, and you shall pass through it; in their sight you shall be carried on shoulders, and you shall go out hidden: you shall cover your face, and you shall not see the land, for I have given you as a portent to the house of Israel.") The prophet is commanded to do in figure what Zedekiah is going to do in truth: 'Gather,' he says, 'your baggage — for these are the vessels of one going into exile — while they watch, and after they have seen what you are going to do, you shall go out in the evening in the likeness of one going into exile'; we read that Zedekiah fled by night, the wall having been dug under, to the deserts of the Jordan, and was there seized by the Babylonians, and that this is what the wall dug through signifies; and as for his saying: You shall carry on your shoulders, there is understood: your baggage and whatever those who flee are accustomed to carry for the comfort of the road; in the darkness you shall carry out: so that you may not be seen by anyone; you shall veil your face: either by the blindness that befell him, when his eyes were put out by Nebuchadnezzar, or so that it might not be recognized that he himself was the king and the vigilance of his guards become greater; and what follows: And you shall not see the land, signifies this: that he was led blind into Babylon and did not see it; for I have given you, he says, as a portent to the house of Israel: for both the words and the deeds of the prophets are for a sign and a figure — whence in Zechariah too they are called 'men of portent', because they portend figures; and in Hosea God says: By the hands of the prophets I have been likened —. Those, however, who want Christ to be understood in the person of Ezekiel take the vessels of captivity as the human body; and the wall dug through as that by which he broke through the bars of the underworld and, rising again, was seen by believers alone; and his being carried on shoulders as when he ascended as victor to heaven with the angelic powers; and that he goes out hidden and veils his face, so that the divine majesty may not be seen in mortal flesh; and that he does not see the land, lest that land be illumined by his eyes which does not deserve his gaze: for the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and he turns his face away from the wicked. 'And all these things,' they say, 'he is related to have done so that, through the likeness of a man, he might turn the hard hearts of the Israelite people to faith; and he is given as a portent to the house of Israel, according to what is written: Behold, this one is set for the resurrection and for the ruin of many, and for a sign that will be spoken against'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

So I did as he had commanded me: I brought out my vessels like the vessels of one migrating by day, and in the evening I dug through the wall for myself with my hand; in the darkness I went out, and I carried on my shoulders in their sight. (LXX: "And I did so according to all that he had commanded me: and I brought out vessels like vessels of captivity by day, and toward evening I dug through the wall for myself with my hand, and I went out hidden, I was taken up upon shoulders in their sight.") What he was commanded above to do, he testifies that he accomplished in deed, and it needs no interpretation, according to either sense, since it was expounded above. But this must be noted: that at one and the same time Jeremiah was prophesying in Jerusalem and Ezekiel in Babylon, and the prophecy of the former was sent to the captives, and that of the latter to those who dwelt in Jerusalem, so that the providence of the one God in different regions might be proven, and the hearers might understand that whatever befell the people came about by no means through the power of idols but by the command of the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me in the morning, saying: Son of man, have not the house of Israel, the provoking house, said to you: What are you doing? Say to them: Thus says the Lord God. 'If the provoking house asks you: Why are you doing these things? — or, according to the Seventy, even if they do not ask, you thrust it upon them, so that they may know why you have done these things —, say to them: Thus says the Lord God.'
Commentary on Ezekiel

This burden is upon the prince who is in Jerusalem, and upon all the house of Israel which is in their midst. Say: I am your portent; as I have done, so shall it be done to them: into exile and into captivity they shall go; and the prince who is in their midst shall be carried on shoulders, he shall go out in the darkness; they shall dig through the wall to lead him out: his face shall be covered, so that he may not see the land with his eyes. And I will spread my net over him, and he shall be taken in my dragnet; and I will bring him to Babylon, into the land of the Chaldeans, and he shall not see it; there he shall die. And all who are around him, his guard and his troops, I will scatter to every wind; and I will draw the sword after them. And they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have scattered them among the nations and sown them in the lands. And I will leave of them a few men from the sword and famine and pestilence, that they may tell all their crimes among the nations to which they shall enter; and they shall know that I am the Lord. First let us expound the history: 'Say,' he says, 'O son of man, to those who either ask or do not ask what you are doing, this: that this burden and vision is upon the leader who is in Jerusalem — by the leader signifying Zedekiah —. And say: I am your portent (or, as the Seventy translated: I who make portents, so that future things may be known from present ones), as I have done, so shall it be done to them, to the leader and to all who are in the leader's retinue: they shall be led captive into the Babylonian exile, and the leader who is in their midst shall be carried on the shoulders either of beasts of burden or of those who had fled with him, and he shall go out in the darkness and in the shadows of night; and his companions shall dig under the wall to lead him out: his face shall be veiled, either by the fear of one fleeing or by the injury of blindness, so that, blind, he may not see the land of Babylon. And I will spread my net over him, and he shall be taken in my dragnet — for it was with the Lord's permission that he was taken by the Babylonians, and what he suffered to be done by the enemy, he testifies that he himself did — ; and, led into Babylon, he shall not see the land of the Chaldeans, and there he shall die a captive. And all his companions and helpers and the comrades of his flight, once he has been seized, I will scatter hither and thither, nor will I allow them to get away safe, but I will draw my sword in the hands of the enemy. And when they have been scattered among the nations, let them understand that I am the Lord and that all things were done by my will. And I will leave,' he says, 'of his companions who fled with him and were able to escape, a few who escaped the sword and the famine and the pestilence, so that, when by flight or by captivity they have come to diverse regions, they may tell all their crimes, either by word or by example, on account of which they deserved such great evils; and let them understand that I myself am the Lord'. But he who tries to expound the tropology and the explanation begun concerning the Savior interprets the leader who is in the midst of Jerusalem as him who went before as a portent and a sign, in that both he himself and his companions are captives of this world, and, ascending as victor from the underworld, he was carried on the shoulders of angels, went out in the darkness, unknown to unbelievers, and, the middle wall having been destroyed, made both one; his face is covered, so that he may not look upon the land of the Jews — nor is it a wonder if the Lord has hidden his face, since to this day a veil is placed before the face of Moses for the people that does not believe —. And the Lord spread his net over him — that which the bride says of him in the Song of Songs: Behold, he is behind our wall, looking out through the windows, appearing through the nets; of whom Jeremiah too says: The Spirit of our face, Christ the Lord, was taken in our sins; and: Though he had not done sin, he was made sin for us — ; and he will be brought, he says, into Babylon, the confusion of this world, into the land of the Chaldeans, which means 'as it were demons' — or else, that he might draw back to salvation those who had been enslaved to demons and lead captive the former captivity —, and that very land of the Chaldeans, he says, he will not see, and there he will die, so that by his death he may give life to us all. And all his helpers and companions, the apostles and apostolic men, he scattered into the whole world; and he drew his sword after them, so that they might be crowned with various martyrdoms. And then they might understand, either they themselves or those who had believed through them, that he himself is the Lord, and that he had scattered them among the nations and sown them in the lands for this reason, that they might bear much fruit. And he left of them a few men, such as John the apostle and the others, delivered from sword and famine and pestilence and escaping the onslaught of persecutions, so that they might tell the crimes of the Jews and the iniquities of all the nations to which they had entered, so that, having done penance, they might know that he himself was the Lord. We have said these things leaving the judgment to the reader's discretion; for the rest, there is no doubt that it is dangerous to compare the captivity and death of a wicked king with the mystery of the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Eat your bread in disturbance, and drink your water in haste and grief. And say to the people of the land: Thus says the Lord God to those who dwell in Jerusalem in the land of Israel: They shall eat their bread in anxiety, and drink their water in desolation, so that the land may be made desolate of its multitude because of the iniquity of all who dwell in it; and the cities that are now inhabited shall be desolate, and the land deserted, and you shall know that I am the Lord. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, you shall eat your bread with pain, and you shall drink your water with torment and distress. And you shall say to the people of the land: Thus says Adonai the Lord to the inhabitants of Jerusalem upon the land of Israel: They shall eat their loaves with want, and drink their water with devastation, so that the land and its fullness may be devastated; for in impiety are all who dwell in it, and their cities which are inhabited shall be in desolation, and the land shall be devastated, and you shall know that I am the Lord.") After the prophecy about the prince and his companions, which was shown under a bodily image, he comes to the people, and whatever is said to the prophet is referred through the prophet to the inhabitants of Jerusalem: that in the evil of the siege they will eat their bread in want and distress, and drink their water by no means in abundance, but with torment and tribulation. 'These things,' he says, 'O prophet, are said to you, so that you may speak to the people of your land and say: Thus says the Lord to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, which is in the land of Israel: Besieged by Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans, you shall endure the evil of hunger and thirst, so that the whole land with its fullness may be destroyed', signifying the inhabitants by that which is inhabited. And lest they think this comes upon them without cause: 'Tell them,' he says, 'that because of their crimes and impieties all the cities of Judea are to be reduced to solitude, and the cultivation of the whole land is to perish, so that they may come to know as raging the God whom they would not know as merciful'. According to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], we can call the inhabitants of Jerusalem those believing in Christ who dwell in the church; and if through sins they have deserved his displeasure, let them eat bread with want and drink water with grief and distress, enduring not a lack of the food of bread or of the drink of water, but a famine of the word and teaching of God. For when, either through the fault of the princes who are to be captured and handed over to the Babylonians or through our own hardness, we have lost the word of God and have not deserved to have useful waters, then we shall take our food in pain and penury, and the land will lose the multitude of believers, and the cities, which are understood as the churches throughout the whole world, will be made desolate, and the land will be deserted, so that all may know that this is the Lord's displeasure. This indeed we can also understand of the time of persecution.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, what is this proverb of yours in the land of Israel, of those saying: The days shall be put off far, and every vision shall perish? Therefore say to them: Thus says the Lord God: I will make this proverb cease, nor shall it be commonly said any longer in Israel; and speak to them that the days have drawn near, and the word of every vision. For no longer shall any vision be empty, nor divination ambiguous, in the midst of the sons of Israel; for I the Lord will speak, whatever word I speak, and it shall be done; it shall not be prolonged any more: but in your days, provoking house, I will speak the word and do it, says the Lord God. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, behold the house of Israel, of those saying: The vision that this man sees is for many days, and for distant times he prophesies; therefore say to them: Thus says the Lord God: None of my words shall be prolonged any longer; the word that I speak shall be fulfilled, says the Lord God. What we, following Symmachus, have called 'proverb', all the other translators translated 'parable', which in Hebrew is called 'masal'. (Again, where we have published: Nor will there be ambiguous divination, the Seventy rendered: Nor one divining according to favor, for which all translated 'slippery', what we have called 'ambiguous', so that we may recognize the words of the prophets that deceive their hearers.) And this is the sense of the whole chapter: above he had prophesied against the prince who was in Jerusalem, then he had announced to the people that famine and the burning of thirst were to come; and as the multitude did not believe it, an old and well-worn proverb is taken up: The threat of the prophets is put off for a long time, and every vision will perish, for in vain is it 'seen' — or, according to Symmachus, διαπνεύσει, that is, 'it will be dissolved into wind and a thin breeze' —. 'Tell them, therefore,' he says, 'that my threat is by no means put off, nor is a false and ambiguous divination put forth among the peoples, one with an uncertain end, so that it is spoken at one time and fulfilled at another; but now, while you who speak and those who hear are alive, the word that I have spoken will be fulfilled'. He signifies the impending captivity of the city of Jerusalem, and Zedekiah, with the people of Judah, about to be taken at any moment. Not only at that time, however, but to this day the unbelieving crowd and the hard hearts of mortals do not receive the prophecy of God, but all that the prophets threaten, that the Gospel proclaims, they reckon is to be put off to another time. Let us note that here 'parable', which is used by the Seventy, is taken for 'proverb', according to what we read in the psalm: And I became a parable to them, and in this same prophet: What is this parable to you among the people of Israel, of those saying: The fathers have eaten the sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge. We have touched briefly on the obvious things, so that we may linger over the more obscure.

n: Heart; what pleases them, (Haydock) without being inspired. There were always such impostors. These deluded the people at Jerusalem, (Calmet) or at Babylon, ver. 9. (Sanctius) --- They might be distinguished by the sincere: yet caused irreparable injury to the ignorant people. (Haydock)
Nothing. Yet would lead the blind, though they are not directed by God.
Deserts, or ruins. They sought only to gratify themselves.
Enemy. You do not admonish sinners of their evil ways, nor strive to avert God's indignation, in imitation of true prophets, (Exodus xxxii. 10.) but rather undermine the wall like foxes.

Upon, to punish. --- Counsel. They shall not be consulted, or have any credit. --- Writing. They shall perish in the city, or in banishment. (Calmet) --- Their works shall not be accounted canonical. (Sixt. Bib. ii. 2.)

Straw. Iniquity ruins my people, (Calmet) and these do not endeavour to reform their manners. (Haydock) --- They ought to demolish such a work, and not daub it over. (Theodoret) --- One false prophet builds, and another strives to support his authority; (Junius) or God has given the people his law, but these people corrupt it. (St. Jerome) --- A wall built without proper mortar, will easily be washed down: so vain hopes of security, without amendment, deceive the people. (Worthington)

Hailstones. Literally, "stones," like those which fell on the enemies of Josue, (x. 11.; Haydock) or thunderbolts. (Grotius) (Calmet) --- Such will be the fate of all the buildings of the wicked, Matthew vii. 27. (Haydock) --- None can resist the judgments of God, who will employ the Chaldeans. (Menochius)
You. Literally, "it." But Hebrew and Septuagint have, "ye." (Haydock) --- The wall and the inhabitants shall perish. (Calmet)

Daughters: so false prophets are styled in scorn, (Vatable) or witches; (Rabbins) though it seems rather that there were false prophetesses as well as true ones. Such were Prisca and Maximilla among the Montanists. Women have commonly fostered heresies. (Calmet) --- These pretended to be illuminated, like Debora and Holda; but flattered the people in their sins, instead of reclaiming them. (Worthington)

Cushions, by making people easy in their sins, and promising them impunity, (Challoner) by disguising the truth, or not admonishing people of their danger, chap. iii. 17. He alludes to the cushions used on sofas. --- Pillows. Symmachus, "veils;" (Septuagint and Kimchi) or "nets" designed "to take" the unwary; as mispachot may be properly rendered, ver. 20, 21., and Isaias v. 7. (Calmet) --- Souls. That is, they flattered them with promises of life, peace, and security. (Challoner) (Worthington) --- People are often said to do what they only announce, Leviticus xiii. 11. These impostors pretended to save, while they really destroyed. They shewed a cruel mercy, detaining the people in captivity, or rather Hebrew, "shall you catch?" &c. Do you expect to pass unpunished? (Calmet) --- We might read the Vulgate, "Did they give?" &c. Protestants, "Will ye save the souls alive that come unto you?" (Haydock)

Violated me. That is, dishonoured and discredited me. (Challoner) --- Protestants, "and will ye pollute?" &c. (Haydock) --- They employed the name of God to give credit to their lies, for the smallest advantage. --- Souls, &c. That is, to sentence souls to death, which are not to die: and to promise life to them who are not to live. (Challoner) --- They contradicted Jeremias, who exhorted the people to surrender. (Calmet)
Catch. Hebrew also, "hunt the souls to make them into gardens, (Haydock) or flourishing." Septuagint, "you gather souls there." The original seems to be incorrect, ver. 18.
Just. Jeremias, or any other, particularly the more simple, who were easily seduced and filled with apprehensions. You shall therefore die, (ver. 23.) and your imposture shall be made known. (Calmet)

f: HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 2:1
There is no kind of sin about which Scripture is silent and about which it does not teach its readers.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 2:1
False prophets are teachers of the church whose words or life do not properly accord with the doctrine that they preach.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 2:2
If the Word of God accuses me, I will try to be converted.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 2:2
The word of the present can agree with those who teach in the church, as long as they do not teach other than what the truth demands.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 2:2
If anyone reading the gospel fits its proper sense to the gospel without understanding that the Lord speaks, he is a false prophet speaking according to his own heart in the gospel.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 2:2
If I find in Moses and the prophets the thought of Christ, I speak not according to my own heart but from the Holy Spirit.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy to the prophets of Israel who prophesy; and you shall say to those who prophesy from their own heart: Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God. (This which we have set down: Who prophesy; and you shall say to those who prophesy from their own heart, the Seventy omitted, and in its place they added what is not found in the Hebrew: And you shall prophesy, and you shall say to them.) Now this speech is against the false prophets, who were deceiving the people and prophesying something else, contrary to the commandments of God. Nor should it trouble anyone that they are called prophets, for holy Scripture has this custom, that it names each one the prophet of his own prophesying and speech, just as there are called prophets of Baal and prophets of idols and prophets of confusion; whence also the apostle Paul calls a Greek poet a prophet: A certain one of them, their own prophet, said: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies, and in Hosea we read: As a raving prophet, a man bearing the spirit. But whatever was said at that time to the Israelite people is now referred to the Church, so that the holy prophets are the apostles and apostolic men, while the lying and frenzied prophets are all the heretics, whose leaders invent things from their own heart, while those who have been seduced by them acquiesce in the lies of others.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 2:3

In the same way that a saint prays with the Spirit and prays with understanding and sings with the spirit and sings with understanding, so the false prophet prophesies according to his own heart and follows not the Spirit of God but his own spirit.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Woe to the senseless prophets, who follow their own spirit and see nothing. (LXX: "Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart and do not see at all", leaving out that which has been set down by us: Who follow their own spirit). Since the name of prophets, according to the rule of the Scriptures, is common to the good and the bad, they differ in this, that the good prophets are said to be wise, but the bad stupid and senseless; of these the one is referred to the men of the Church, the other to all the heretics, who, abandoning the Spirit of God, follow their own spirit, because they prophesy not at all by divine inspiration but from their own heart: whence also they see nothing. But he who is wise follows not the thoughts of his own heart but the Spirit of God, according to that passage in which, earlier on, the living creatures and the wheels followed the Spirit of God; and the prophet says: After the Lord your God you shall walk, and in another place: Lead me in the right path, and again: Your Spirit, he who is good, will lead me into the land; and for the people of God the pillar of fire and the cloud was the leader in the wilderness; and Jeremiah says: I have not labored following you. But which of the heretics, who follows his own spirit, does not stumble into darkness and, blind, lead the blind into a pit? Hence, although in their mysteries, or rather their orgies, they seem to themselves to see more than the teachers of the Church, still they see nothing at all, because they have lost the sun of righteousness, and in vain they imitate those who were formerly called 'seers' and to whom it is said: You who see, go; withdraw into the land of Judah, and in Bethel you shall not prophesy; for which reason the 'vision' of Isaiah and of Obadiah is placed in the titles, and the Lord commanded the apostles: Lift up your eyes and see, and the prophet humbly entreats: Unveil my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 2:4
The fox is an animal good for nothing, sly, wild, ferocious.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Like foxes in the deserts were your prophets, Israel. You do not go up from the opposite side, nor did you set up a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord. They see vain things and divine a lie, saying: Says the Lord, when the Lord has not sent them; and they persisted in confirming the word. Have you not seen an empty vision, and spoken a lying divination, and do you say: Says the Lord, when I have not spoken? (LXX: "As foxes in the deserts are your prophets, Israel. They did not stand on the firmament, and they gathered flocks upon the house of Israel; they did not rise up, those who speak on the day of the Lord, seeing lies, divining vain things, who say: The Lord says, and the Lord did not send them; and they began to raise up the word. Have you not seen a false vision, and spoken vain divinations, ※ and you were saying: The Lord says, and I have not spoken?⁚") Let us speak first according to the Hebrew: the prophets of Israel are like foxes, daily committing thefts of domestic fowl, who dwell, according to Aquila and the Seventy, 'in the deserts', according to Symmachus and Theodotion 'in broken walls' and 'ruins'; who cannot go up from the opposite side, nor set up a wall for the house of Israel — we read that Aaron ran to meet the fire that was devouring the people of Israel, and stood in the midst, and set up a wall for the safety of the people; to Jeremiah also it is said that he should not run to meet the Lord, nor stand against his wrath by perseverance in prayer: for just as a wall is set against an enemy, and one is accustomed to meet an adversary from the opposite side and to confront one who is coming on, so the sentence of God is broken by the prayers of the saints; whence also it is said to Moses: Let me go, and I will blot out this people: for in the one to whom it is said: Let me go, it is shown that he has the power of holding back —. These cannot stand in battle on the day of the Lord, so as to fight for the people with prayers and to resist the sentence of God with supplications.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Moreover, according to the Seventy the sense here is this: all the heretics, because of their deceitfulness and wickedness, are like foxes, of whom the Savior speaks: Foxes have holes, and the birds of the sky nests; and of Herod it is written: Tell this fox; and of these same foxes, which deceive the little and simple ones and lay waste the vineyard of Christ, Solomon speaks: Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards; and in the psalm it is sung concerning those who are tripped up by their deceitfulness: They will go into the lower parts of the earth, they will be handed over into the hands of the sword, they will be the portions of foxes.
Commentary on Ezekiel

These prophets, who are like foxes, did not stand on the firmament; nor did they deserve to hear with Peter: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; nor are they like Moses, to whom it was said: But you, stand here with me, nor like him who says: He set my feet upon a rock, but they are tossed about by every wind of doctrine; nor did they stand on the firmament of which we read in Psalm 18 (19): The heavens tell the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands. These gathered all sorts of irrational people, who on account of their excessive innocence are like cattle, against the house of God; hence it is now said: And they gathered flocks upon the house of Israel; nor did they themselves rise up, nor could they raise up others, but whatever they have done and are doing is full of lies.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 14

To such men it is rightly said through the prophet: "You have not gone up against the enemy, nor have you set up a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord." To go up against the enemy is to oppose with the free voice of reason any powers that act wickedly. And we stand in battle on the day of the Lord for the house of Israel and set up a wall if we defend the faithful and innocent against the injustice of the perverse with the authority of justice. Because the hireling does not do this, when he sees the wolf coming, he flees.
Pastoral Rule, Part 2, Chapter 10

Whence it is well said to Ezekiel, "Take unto thee a tile, and thou shalt lay it before thee, and pourtray upon it the dry Jerusalem." And immediately it is subjoined, "And thou shalt lay siege against it, and build forts, and cast a mount, and set camps against it, and set battering rams against it round about. And do thou take unto thee an iron frying-pan, and thou shalt set it for a wall of iron between thee and the city."

But although the ruler may nicely insinuate all these things, he procures not for himself lasting absolution, unless he glow with a spirit of jealousy against the delinquencies of all and each. For by the frying-pan is denoted a frying of the mind, and by iron the hardness of reproof.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 14

To such men it is rightly said through the prophet: "You have not gone up against the enemy, nor have you set up a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord." To go up against the enemy is to oppose with the free voice of reason any powers that act wickedly. And we stand in battle on the day of the Lord for the house of Israel and set up a wall if we defend the faithful and innocent against the injustice of the perverse with the authority of justice. Because the hireling does not do this, when he sees the wolf coming, he flees.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 2:5

All that they want is false, and they can never see the truth. Take an example. To read the Scripture and to hear something other than what is written is to have an untruthful picture of Scripture; but to hear Scripture and interpret it in accordance with the truth, that is to see the truth.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Since, therefore, they behold vain things and divine a lie and say that they have been sent by the Lord, when they have not been sent by him, and persist in their errors and desire to make their own word firm, they are convicted that all the things they preach are empty, since they say that their own lie is the word of the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And what follows: And they began to raise up the word, signifies this: that they wish indeed to rise up and to lift themselves to the heights, but cannot fulfill what they desire; and it is said to them: Have you not seen a false vision, and spoken vain divinations? — and what follows: And you were saying: The Lord says, and I have not spoken, is not found in the Seventy —.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 2:5
Pray for us that our words may not be false.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 2:5
This is what we are looking for, that the Lord will be present as a witness to my words, that he may himself confirm what is said by witness of his holy Scriptures.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have spoken vain things and seen a lie, therefore behold, I am against you, says the Lord God; and my hand shall be upon the prophets who see vain things and divine a lie: in the council of my people they shall not be, and in the writing of the house of Israel they shall not be written, nor shall they enter into the land of Israel, and you shall know that I am the Lord God. (LXX: "Therefore say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Since your words are lies and your divinations vain, therefore behold, I am over you, says the Lord God; and I will stretch out my hand upon the prophets who see a lie and who speak vain things: in the discipline of my people they shall not be, nor shall they be written in the writing of the house of Israel, and into the land of Israel they shall not enter, and they shall know that I am Adonai the Lord.") Under the person of the prophets, the speech is against the heretics who speak vain things and see a lie, and persist in making their own doctrine firm: that the Lord himself comes against them and rises up and stretches out his hand over them to strike, and does not draw it back to spare; and he threatens that they will not be in the council of the people of the Lord, nor in his Church but in the synagogue of the devil, nor will they be written in the house of Israel — of whom it is said in another place: Let them be written upon the earth: not into the land of Israel, which is the land of the living, of which it is now said: Nor shall they enter into the land of Israel, but into the land of the dead and the shadow of death — so that, after they have suffered these things, separated from the assembly of the people of God, they may understand that he himself is the Lord. Where we have rendered: In the council of my people they shall not be, the Seventy translated: In the discipline (or in the correction) of my people they shall not be: for the correction of adversaries is one thing, that of sons another; whence also Jeremiah: Correct, he says, us, O Lord, but in judgment, and not in fury, so that you may by no means make us few. Pour out your fury upon the nations which have not known you, and upon the kingdoms which have not called upon your name.
Interrogation of Job and David 3.3.6

For there is a peace that does not have an offense, and there is one that has it: which is from love, it does not have an offense; which is from deceit, it has. Therefore, the Prophet also says: Peace, peace; but where is peace (Ezekiel 12:10)? Therefore, let us seek the refuge of peace for sinners; for they conspire against the innocent, they gather together to oppress the righteous, to destroy the widow, or to assault her modesty.
LETTER 133.4

How is the cause helped by the people who dance attendance on these people with itching ears who know neither how to hear nor how to speak? They confound old mire with new cement and, as Ezekiel says, daub a wall with untempered mortar; so that, when the truth comes in a shower, they are brought to nothing.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Because they have deceived my people, saying: Peace, peace, and there is no peace; and he himself was building a wall, but they were daubing it with mud without straw. Say to those who daub without tempering that it will fall; for there will be a flooding shower, and I will give very great stones rushing down from above, and a wind of tempest scattering it. For behold, the wall has fallen; will it not be said to you: Where is the daubing with which you daubed? Therefore thus says the Lord God: And I will make the spirit of tempests burst forth in my indignation, and there will be a flooding shower in my fury, and great stones of wrath in consummation; and I will destroy the wall which you daubed without due mixture, and I will level it with the earth, and its foundation will be uncovered, and it will fall and be consumed in its midst, and you shall know that I am the Lord. And I will fulfill my indignation on the wall and on those who daub it without due mixture, and I will say to you: There is no wall, and there are none who daub it; the prophets of Israel who prophesy to Jerusalem, and see for her a vision of peace, and there is no peace, says the Lord God. (LXX: "Because they deceived my people, saying: Peace, peace, and there was no peace; and this one builds a wall, and these daub it with folly. Say to those who daub with folly: It will fall; there will be a flooding rain, and I will give great stones into their joints and they will fall, and a spirit carrying away, and it will be broken apart. And behold, the wall has fallen; and will they not say to you: Where is your daubing with which you daubed? Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: And I will make a spirit carrying away break forth in my fury, and there will be a flooding rain in my wrath, and I will bring great stones in fury unto consummation; and I will dig under the wall which you daubed, and it will fall, and I will set it upon the earth, and its foundations will be uncovered, and it will fall, and you will be consumed with rebukes, and you will know that I am the Lord. And I will fulfill my fury upon the wall and upon those who daub it it will fall, and I said to you: There is no wall, nor those who daub it; the prophets of Israel who prophesy over Jerusalem, and who see peace for her, and there is no peace for them, says the Lord God.") The prophets of Israel, who will not be in the council of the people of God, nor be written in the writing of the house of Israel, nor enter the land of promise, will suffer these things because they deceived my people, wrongfully announcing to them peace and prosperity instead of the rigor of penitence and conversion, according to that which is said elsewhere: Peace, peace: and where is peace? God, then, was building for them μεταφορικῶς [metaphorically], through the commandments of the law and the utterances and threats of the holy prophets, an enclosure — for this is what the Hebrew word 'his' signifies — so as to keep from them every incursion of beasts and every hostile assault, as long as, converted to God, they were girded by this as by a bulwark and a most solid wall —; but the false prophets promised them peace not once but often: for this is what the repeated word of peace signifies. And that very wall, which in what follows is called 'cir', the false prophets were daubing 'without due mixture' — as Symmachus translated, that is, 'with pure mud', which had no straw and could not supply any strength; but as the Seventy and Theodotion have it, they daub it 'with folly'; while Aquila translated the Hebrew word 'thaphel' by ἀνάλῳ, which means 'without salt', passing from one metaphor to another metaphor, so that, just as food without salt has no flavor, so also mud without the straw by which it is made firm and bound together can provide no strength to the wall —.
Commentary on Ezekiel
Also that which we read above: He himself was building (or builds) a wall, many refer to the people of Israel, which was promising itself vain help, either from the Egyptians or from peace.
EXPLANATIONS OF THE PSALMS 96:3

They who choose to declare their own honor have refused to dwell in [God's] house; and therefore they do not sing a new song with all the earth. For they do not share it with the whole world; and hence they are not building in the house but have erected a whitened wall. How sternly does God threaten the whitened wall?… What is the whitened wall but hypocrisy, that is, pretense? Outside it is bright; inside it is dirt.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'Say,' he says, 'to those who promise them vain things and pledge empty help, that this wall, this enclosure, will fall, and I will send a most violent shower, that is, most savage enemies — and he means the Babylonians and Chaldeans —, and these same enemies as stones of hail rushing down from above', all by μεταφορὰν [metaphor], so that a sudden whirlwind may overturn and undermine the unstable enclosure; and that afterward it may be said to them — that is, to the false prophets —: 'Where is the daubing with which you daubed? and where is the help you promised?'.
Commentary on Ezekiel
That which the Seventy translated: And upon their joints, is not found in the Hebrew; and it signifies the joints of the stones in a wall, or the supports of timber by which walls are strengthened.
The Instructor Book 1

The words that follow describe and condemn some sin that has been committed. The judgment contained in these words is just, for it is as if he were giving notice in the words of the prophet that, if you had not sinned, he would not have made these threats.… The inspired Word exists because of both obedience and disobedience: that we may be saved by obeying it and educated because we have disobeyed.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But whatever we have said of the false prophets can be referred also to the heretics: that all their fabrications are dissolved by the wrath of God, and the building of the worst dogmas, which does not have the seasoning of the Holy Spirit, collapses and slides down to its foundations and to dust, and the enclosure itself is leveled with the earth and falls, and both the prophets who were promising and the people to whom it was promised are consumed in its midst, so that, after he has fulfilled his indignation and has said to them: There is no such wall — that is, 'you have no defense' — and there are none who daub it, but all things are vain and come to nothing, then you will know by deed that I am the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel
