And so that we may know who those are who daub the wall, there follows: The prophets of Israel — that is, the false prophets — who prophesy to Jerusalem, and see for her a vision of peace; these are the cause of sin and ruin and foolish security: For there will be no peace, says the Lord, because the Lord did not send them nor did he speak to them.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 3:1

This face, that is to say the ruling faculty in our soul, if it is not fixed toward what it should understand in the manner that it sees, it announces to its hearers that what it looks at has not in fact been seen.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 3:1
It should have a face that wants to be fixed toward what it is striving to understand, and for this reason the order is always first given to those who want to prophecy to make their face firm.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 3:3
Soft are the souls and intentions of those leaders who always compose resonant and harmonious words.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The prophet, then, is ordered to set, or to make firm, his face against the daughters of his people. And first we must say what the face 'set' or 'directed' and 'made firm' means: namely that which is written of the Lord: The face of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth. As indeed wax melts before the face of the fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God; according to which sense it is said in this same prophet: Son of man, make your face firm upon Theman and Darom and Nageb, and again: The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make your face firm upon Jerusalem, and a little after: The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make your face firm upon the Ammonites, and again: Make your countenance firm upon Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and again: Son of man, make your face firm upon Gog and Magog, and in another place: I will make my face firm upon that man, and I will put him into the desert and into dissipation, and I will take him away from the midst of the people, and you shall know that I am the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you, son of man, set your face against the daughters of your people who prophesy from their own heart, and prophesy over them, and say: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand, and make pillows under the head of every age to catch souls; and when they caught the souls of my people, they made their souls alive. And they profaned me before my people for a handful of barley and a fragment of bread, to kill souls which do not die, and to make alive souls which do not live, lying to my people who believe lies. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against your cushions, with which you catch flying souls, and I will tear them from your arms, and I will let go the souls which you catch, souls to fly, and I will tear your pillows, and I will free my people from your hand, and they shall no longer be in your hands for plunder; and you shall know that I am the Lord. Because you made the heart of the righteous grieve falsely, whom I did not sadden, and strengthened the hands of the wicked, so that he should not turn back from his evil way and live, therefore you shall not see vain things, and you shall divine divinations no more, and I will rescue my people from your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord. (LXX: "And you, son of man, make your face firm upon the daughters of your people who prophesy from their own heart, and prophesy over them, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to those who sew pillows under every elbow of the hand, and make veils over every head of every age to pervert souls; the souls of my people have been overturned, and they were saving souls. And they defiled me before my people for a handful of barley and a fragment of bread, to slay souls which ought not to die, and to save souls which ought not to live, while they speak vain words to a people that listens. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am over your pillows, upon which you have gathered souls, and I will tear them from your arms, and I will let go the souls which you pervert, their souls into dispersion, and I will tear your veils, and I will free my people from your hands, and they shall no longer be in your hands for gathering; and you shall know that I am the Lord. Because you were perverting the soul of the righteous unjustly, and I was not perverting him, and you were strengthening the hands of the unjust, so that he should not be converted at all from his most evil way and live, therefore you shall see lies no more, and you shall by no means divine divinations any longer, and I will free my people from your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord.") Above, the divine word was directed to the prophets, who were daubing the wall with mud, because it had no straw and could give no strength to the wall or enclosure; now he is ordered to set his face, or to direct it, or, as the Seventy translated, to make it firm, against the daughters of the people, the prophetesses. And just as other, false prophets were inspired against the prophets by a diabolical spirit, to overturn the commandments of God, so against the prophetesses — such as were Deborah and Huldah and, in the Acts of the Apostles, the four prophesying daughters of Philip the evangelist — other women of the same sex were inspired by a demonic spirit, such as were Prisca and Maximilla, to overturn the faith of the truth by the prophesying of a lie. These, the Hebrews say, were trained in magic arts through necromancies and a pythonic spirit, such as was she who seemed to have raised up the soul of Samuel, and, in the Acts of the Apostles, she whose divination brought much income to her masters, out of whom the unclean spirit was cast at the command of the apostle Paul. But we say this: that some heretics, by the falsity of their dogmas, preach virtue — of whom were Pythagoras, and Zeno, from whom come the Stoics, the Brahmans of the Indians and the Gymnosophists of the Ethiopians, who because of the continence of their diet win the admiration of the nations — and rightly are they said to daub a wall and to promise some strength —, but because they lack the seasoning of Christ, their labor is vain and their building will perish: Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain; others, however, teachers of pleasures and of lust, are said to sew cushions and to place them under every elbow of the hand: the Epicureans and the Pyrrhonists, and among us Jovinian and Eunomius, who say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 3:3

The Word of God must proclaim what is for the salvation of the hearer, what exhorts him to continence, to the practice of sensible actions, to all the things to which the person who is assiduous in works and not pleasures must apply himself in order to be able to obtain what God has promised.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 3:3
When the work of the speaker is deployed in licentious talk, a veil is placed on the head of everyone regardless of age, not just the children and the young but also the elderly.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 3:4
Allow me, O Christ, to break all pillows made for the luxury of souls.
Interrogation of Job and David 1.7.25

The Holy Spirit poured out upon the prophet lamenting the misfortune of our frailty, which neither had rest in this life nor retained anything in the sudden encounter with death, that humanity would not rise again until the one came who did not patch the new onto the old nor put a new piece of cloth on an old garment; but rather made all things new, as he himself said: Behold, I make all things new. For he is the resurrection, he is the firstborn from the dead, in whom we have indeed received a foretaste of the future resurrection, yet he alone has already risen with eternal resurrection.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Woe, then, to these heresies and to these doctrines, which, promising rest, deceive every age and sex, to catch the souls of the wretched and to defile me before my people, while I am believed to love pleasure; and this not for a corus and a hemicorus of barley, as we read in Hosea, but for a handful of barley, on which brute animals feed, and a fragment of bread: not a whole loaf, nor the solid testimonies of the Scriptures, but those which have been broken and cut short and diminished by heretical depravity, so as to deceive all the holy and drag them to death, while they strive to make sinners alive with vain promises.

For from love of himself the ruler's mind is inclined to softness, because, when he observes those that are under him sinning, he does not presume to reprove them, lest their affection for himself should grow dull; nay sometimes he smooths down with flatteries the offence of his subordinates which he ought to have rebuked. It often happens that a Pastor is moved by hatred or favor toward any neighbor; but those who follow their own hatreds or favor in the cases of their subjects cannot judge worthily concerning their subjects. Whence it is rightly said through the prophet: They were putting to death souls that do not die, and giving life to souls that do not live. For he puts to death one who is not dying who condemns the just. And he strives to give life to one who will not live who attempts to absolve the guilty from punishment.

And men, elders of Israel, came to me and sat before me. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, these men have set uncleannesses in their hearts, and have set up the stumbling block of their iniquity against their face; shall I, being asked, answer them? Therefore speak to them, and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: A man, a man of the house of Israel who sets his uncleannesses in his heart, and sets up the stumbling block of his iniquity against his face, and comes to the prophet inquiring of me through him, I the Lord will answer him according to the multitude of his uncleannesses, that the house of Israel may be caught in their heart, in which they have withdrawn from me in all their idols. Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Turn and withdraw from your idols, and turn away your faces from all your defilements. For a man, a man of the house of Israel and of the proselytes, whoever is a stranger in Israel, if he is estranged from me and sets his idols in his heart, and sets up the stumbling block of his iniquity against his face, and comes to the prophet to inquire of me through him, I the Lord will answer him by myself; and I will set my face upon that man, and I will make him an example and a proverb, and I will destroy him from the midst of my people, and you shall know that I am the Lord. And the prophet, when he errs and speaks a word, I the Lord have deceived that prophet, and I will stretch out my hand upon him, and I will blot him out from the midst of my people Israel. And they shall bear their iniquity: as the iniquity of the one inquiring, so shall the iniquity of the prophet be, that the house of Israel may no longer stray from me, nor be polluted in all their transgressions, but may be to me for a people, and I may be to them for God, says the Lord of hosts. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, these men have set their thoughts in their hearts, and have set the torment of their iniquities before their face; shall I, answering, answer them? Therefore speak to them and say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: A man, a man of the house of Israel who sets his thoughts in his heart, and sets the torment of his iniquity before his face, and comes to the prophet to inquire of him in me, I the Lord will answer him in those things by which his mind is held, so as to turn away the house of Israel according to their hearts, which have been estranged from me in their thoughts. Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Turn and withdraw from your inventions and from all your impieties, and turn your faces. For a man, a man of the house of Israel and of the strangers who sojourn in Israel, who is estranged from me and sets his thoughts in his heart, and sets the torment of his iniquity before his face, and comes to the prophet to inquire of him in me, I the Lord will answer him in that by which he is held; and I will make my face firm upon that man, and I will make him a desert and an extermination, and I will take him away from the midst of my people, and you shall know that I am the Lord. And the prophet, if he errs and speaks a word, I the Lord have made that prophet err, and I will stretch out my hand upon him, and I will exterminate him from the midst of my people Israel. And they shall receive their iniquity: according to the iniquity of the one inquiring, the iniquity of the prophet also shall likewise be, that the house of Israel may by no means stray from me, and that they may not be polluted any more in all their offenses, and they shall be to me for a people, and I will be to them for God, says Adonai the Lord.") After he had spoken to the prophets who prophesied out of their own heart and daubed the wall without tempering, and to the prophetesses who sewed cushions and put them under every elbow of the hand, and made veils, and covered the heads of every age — by which the teaching of perverse doctrines is shown —, there came to the prophet not all the old men, lest all should seem to err, but certain of the elders of Israel, and they sat before the prophet, meanwhile deferring in silence the reason for which they had come; and at once the word of God came to the prophet, indicating why they were present — for it is not in the nature of man, however holy, to know the secrets of the heart; hence it is said of the Savior alone: But Jesus, seeing their thoughts and why do you think evil things in your hearts —. And the sense is: 'Son of man, these men who sit before you have set their uncleannesses in their hearts — or thoughts, and, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, idols —, and they have set the stumbling block — that is, the ruin and torment — of their iniquity against their face, and so they have come to inquire after the word of the Lord. Ought I to answer men of this sort, who come to me with their former thoughts, not abandoning the crimes of their impiety even at this time, but believing in idols and deceitful divinations, and having the ruin and torment of iniquity against their face, while they despair of better things and are ready for punishment, and so desire to learn my words through you? Since, therefore, they have come to you with a perverse heart, you answer not in your own person — lest the authority of the one answering be slight —, but by my command, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God'.

Now the meaning of the whole passage, to comprehend a broad explanation in a brief discourse, is this: 'A man, a man not of the other nations — whose error can have pardon —, but of the house of Israel, who comes to the prophet to inquire with his former vices — of which we have spoken above —, I will answer him according to his heart and his uncleannesses, so that he may hear according to what he wishes and believes: for he who asks not in a spirit of learning but of testing does not deserve correction. For they have withdrawn from me and have followed idols; and this is a brief threat, so that they may withdraw from idols and perverse thoughts and turn to me, abandoning their former crimes'; for he who asks deceitfully does not deserve to hear the truth, but is to be caught by his own heart, just as the scribes and Pharisees, questioning the Lord, or rather testing him, hear: Why do you test me?, and again: Neither will I tell you by what power I do these things; but whoever is such a man and asks in this way, God sets his face upon him, or makes it firm, so that by the severity of his countenance the hardness of the brow may be softened and he may be for an example and a proverb, or for a solitude and a destruction, so that, when he has been destroyed out of the people of God, the rest may know that he himself is the Lord, who knows the secrets of the heart and understands the perversity of the mind, and considers not the words of those who speak but their hearts.

And what is said a second time: A man, a man of the sons of Israel and of the strangers who are joined to them, shows, according to the Apostle, a twofold man in us: the outer and the inner — for many, having the bodily face of a man, take on the images of various beasts, whose destruction the prophet desires when he prays: Lord, in your city you will destroy their image; those of whom it is written: Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts of burden, and became like them, are not men who are men, but men who are beasts of burden; again, those who hear in the Gospel: Serpents, brood of vipers, who showed you to flee from the wrath to come?, are not men who are men, but men who are serpents as well; and those of whom it is written: Foxes have holes, and the birds of heaven nests, and of Herod: Tell this fox, are not men who are men, but men who are foxes —; but those who possess both words 'man', if they err, are corrected by punishments for this reason, that they may understand that he himself is the Lord. Moreover, what we have set down according to the Seventy: A man who is estranged from me and sets his thoughts in his heart, and the torment (or punishment) of his iniquity before his face, agrees with that testimony which is written in Isaiah: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame which you have kindled; for each one kindles for himself the blazing of flames and prepares punishments for himself, while he is unwilling to correct his errors by repentance, but remains in errors that deserve the burning of flames.

Those dissatisfied with any facet of your creation are unsound in mind, as I was when many things that you made displeased me. Because my soul did not dare to be dissatisfied with my God, it would not identify as yours whatever dissatisfied it. In this way it had strayed into a belief in two substances, and it got no rest but recounted the opinions of others. Recoiling from that error, it had made for itself a god inhabiting the boundless area of all space, and it had considered that god to be you, and had "set it in its heart" and had become again the shrine of its idol, deserving of your loathing. But after you stroked my ignorant head and closed my eyes so that they should not see vanity, I retired from myself a little, and my madness was lulled to sleep. I awoke in you and saw you infinite in a different way, and that vision was not with the eyes of the flesh.

Then he stretches out his hand upon him — the prophet is understood — and he is blotted out from the midst of his people, so that he may bear his iniquity, because for like error the punishment too is alike, so that both he who asks and he who is asked may bear their iniquity, and the house of Israel, that of those who wish to hear the words of God, may by no means be mocked by perverse prophesyings, but may be the people of God, and may itself deserve to have the Lord as God. With what he said: I the Lord have deceived him, the words of Solomon agree, who, discoursing of God, says: And he will mock the mockers, and that testimony: If they walk perversely toward me, I too will walk against them in perverse fury.

And what follows also seems to raise a question: The prophet, when he errs and speaks a word, I the Lord have deceived that prophet; let us not think that this is said of a true prophet, but of a false prophet, who is called a prophet συνωνυμῶς [by a shared name]. And it can be resolved from that passage of the Scriptures where Ahab king of Israel, going to battle, will not listen to Micaiah the prophet, but acquiesces in the counsels of the false prophets, and Micaiah says that he saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and that a spirit of error offered itself of its own accord to deceive the king; the devil too, in the book of Job, going around the earth, is said to stand in the sight of God and to receive power from the Lord, first over Job's substance, then over his body; and Balaam the soothsayer also is sent by the Lord to deceive Balak the son of Beor. All this, however, is said so that it may not be reckoned to the strength of the false prophets that the people is deceived and would rather hear a lie than lend its ear to the truth, but that it is of the wrath of God that a perverse and unbelieving people listens to false prophets rather than to prophets.

Or if I bring a sword upon that land, and say to the sword: Pass through the land, and I kill from it man and beast, and these three men are in its midst, as I live, says the Lord God, they shall not deliver sons or daughters, but they alone shall be delivered. But if I also send pestilence upon that land, and pour out my indignation upon it in blood, to take away from it man and beast, and Noah and Daniel and Job are in its midst, as I live, says the Lord God, they shall not deliver son and daughter, but they by their righteousness shall deliver their own souls. For thus says the Lord God: But if I also send my four most evil judgments, sword and famine and evil beasts and pestilence, against Jerusalem, to kill from it man and cattle, yet there shall be left in it a deliverance of those who bring out sons and daughters: behold, they shall come out to you, and you shall see their way and their inventions, and you shall be consoled over the evil which I brought upon Jerusalem, in all that I have brought in upon it. But if Noah and Daniel and Job, gathered together and placed in one place, cannot withdraw the sinning land, that is, those who dwell in the land, from the wrath of God, what is to be said of those who think that sinful sons can be delivered from the fires of Gehenna by the merit and virtues of their parents? Hence neither will a martyr father be able to deliver a transgressing son, nor will a mother of holy life give the rewards of chastity to an unchaste daughter; and on the contrary the vices of parents will not harm their children, but: The soul that sins, it shall die. Lot, dwelling in Sodom but a stranger both in spirit and in flesh, did not deliver his wife, who had looked back behind her, but only his daughters, who perhaps had not sinned; and Josiah, a holy man, not only did not save a sinful people by his virtues, but he himself also died in its sins. — It is asked, since Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, Moses too and the other patriarchs and prophets, were righteous, why mention is made of these alone; which is easily resolved: for Noah could not put off the flood impending over the world, because all the earth had polluted the ways of the Lord, but he had his sons preserved, who perhaps were of the same virtue, and also for the sake of a seedbed of the human race; Daniel too softened by no weeping the captivity impending over the people of the Jews; and Job as well, not on account of sins but for the sake of testing, delivered neither his house nor his sons. Others, however, say that because these three men alone beheld both prosperity and adversity and prosperity again, they are for that reason named together, and that this is secretly signified: that, just as they saw both good things and evil and again joyful things, so also the people of Israel, which had first enjoyed good things and afterward bore the yoke of captivity, if it does penance, returns to its former happiness. —

In these three men he no doubt prefigures three classes of mankind to be delivered: in Noah, as I suppose, are represented righteous leaders of nations, by reason of his government of the ark as a type of the Church; in Daniel, men who are righteous in continence; in Job, those who are righteous in wedlock;—to say nothing of any other view of the passage, which it is unnecessary now to consider. Ezekiel the prophet mystically distinguishes them from one another when he foretells that there are only three men who will be delivered when the time of plagues comes, namely: Noah, Daniel and Job. For surely in Noah, who steered the ark over the waves, he shows those who are set over the church; in Daniel, who was zealous to live continently in the royal court, he shows the continent or virgins; in Job, who while married exhibited a wonderful example of patience to all, he shows the life of the virtuous married people.
Dialogue with Trypho, Chapter XLIV

And you deceive yourselves while you fancy that, because you are the seed of Abraham after the flesh, therefore you shall fully inherit the good things announced to be bestowed by God through Christ. For no one, not even of them, has anything to look for, but only those who in mind are assimilated to the faith of Abraham, and who have recognised all the mysteries: for I say, that some injunctions were laid on you in reference to the worship of God and practice of righteousness; but some injunctions and acts were likewise mentioned in reference to the mystery of Christ, on account of the hardness of your people's hearts. And that this is so, God makes known in Ezekiel, [when] He said concerning it: 'If Noah and Jacob and Daniel should beg either sons or daughters, the request would not be granted them.' And in Isaiah, of the very same matter He spake thus: 'The Lord God said, they shall both go forth and look on the members [of the bodies] of the men that have transgressed. For their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be a gazing-stock to all flesh.' So that it becomes you to eradicate this hope from your souls, and hasten to know in what way forgiveness of sins, and a hope of inheriting the promised good things, shall be yours. But there is no other [way] than this,-to become acquainted with this Christ, to be washed in the fountain spoken of by Isaiah for the remission of sins; and for the rest, to live sinless lives.

And besides, they beguile themselves and you, supposing that the everlasting kingdom will be assuredly given to those of the dispersion who are of Abraham after the flesh, although they be sinners, and faithless, and disobedient towards God, which the Scriptures have proved is not the case. For if so, Isaiah would never have said this: 'And unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom and Gomorrah.' And Ezekiel: 'Even if Noah, and Jacob, and Daniel were to pray for sons or daughters, their request should not be granted.' But neither shall the father perish for the son, nor the son for the father; but every one for his own sin, and each shall be saved for his own righteousness.

'Since,' he says, 'these things are so, and the prayer of such great men does not save a sinning land from single plagues, thus says the Lord: Because Jerusalem has sinned abominably, I will bring four plagues upon it at once: the sword by which it is slaughtered by its enemies, and famine which it endures under siege, and beasts by which those who flee are devoured in deserts and forests, and pestilence, which always follows famine and want — for which the common edition translated 'death' —. And these things,' he says, 'I will bring upon it, so that neither men remain in it nor beasts; and yet, in my clemency, while the four plagues impend at once and lay everything waste, I will leave in it some who bring out their sons and daughters, and let them come here as captives — that is, to Babylon and to Chaldea —; and when you see them and have looked closely at their works, then you will understand that they were justly taken captive and that my sentence was just, and your captivity will have consolation, while you understand that I delivered them from sword and famine and beasts and pestilence for this reason: that from their perversity you may learn that Jerusalem was deservedly overthrown and the temple burned and the people led captive, except those whom sword, famine, beasts and pestilence consumed'. These things were said of that Jerusalem upon which, while Ezekiel was prophesying among the Chaldeans, captivity was drawing near.

n: Wood. Small branches or tendrils. The vines of that country were probably small. (Calmet) --- The wild vine (Sanctius) grows very large, and the wood is durable, so that statues, pillars, and ladders were formed of it. (Pliny, [Natural History?] xiv. 1.) --- Strabo (ii., and xi.) mentions the trunk of a vine which two men could hardly clasp, and the bunch of grapes was two cubits high. But the prophet speaks of the small branches, which are fit only for the fire. (Calmet) --- God's Church is often compared to a vine on account of its fruit, and the branches separated form her resemble the useless cuttings. (St. Augustine, tr. lxxxi. in John) (Worthington) --- See Ward's Tree of Life, where this is set in a very striking light. In every age the Church makes fresh conquests, while heretics leave and persecute her. (Haydock)
Thereon. Isaias xxii. 23. (Calmet) --- The Turkish lords have no furniture in their rooms, but hang their arms, saddles, &c., upon such pins, or on strings. (Roger. ii.)

Ashes. It is not even solid enough for fuel. (Calmet) --- When a faggot is consumed in the middle, the ends are also put into the fire; so not one shall escape who dies out of the Church. (Worthington) --- The wicked Jews shall surely suffer, ver. 6. (Haydock)
From fire. If they escape one misery they shall fall into another, as the event shewed. (Calmet) --- They shall be thrown back into the fire. (Menochius)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

According to the spiritual understanding, we can understand the vineyard and Jerusalem as the multitude of believers, which, if it has been negligent and has lost the cultivation of its former religion, and has not borne the fruits of the virtues nor made wine that gladdens the heart of man, will be given up to everlasting flames and reckoned as nothing: for the servant who knows the will of his master, and does not do it, will be beaten with many blows. The Lord too says something of the kind in the Gospel according to John: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch that abides in me and does not bear fruit, the Father will take it away; and every one that bears fruit he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit; but if the Savior is the vine and we the branches and God the Father the husbandman, as long as we keep God's commandments we are continually cultivated, and our cultivation is a cleansing: for it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy; and if, bearing fruit, we are cleansed by the Father so that we may bear more abundant fruit, it is shown that all our effort, by God's help, reaches its end and yields the fruit of fullness; but the branch that has not borne fruit will be taken away by the Father, and once it has been taken away, what the Father does with it Scripture does not say, unless perhaps separation from the body of Christ is everlasting punishment and destruction. What we have understood of the vineyard and the vine, the Savior teaches under another figure in the Gospel: Salt is good; but if the salt has lost its savor, it is useful for nothing except to be thrown out and trodden underfoot by men; and the eye, which gives light to the whole body, if it has been blinded, hears from the Lord: If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be? For in comparison with the transgressor, and with him who has denied the God he first confessed, lighter is the punishment of those who never had knowledge of God. The trees of the woodlands or forests, however, according to the variety of believers, have some usefulness in a great house, in which there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and earthenware, some for honor, and some for dishonor.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, what will become of the wood of the vine, out of all the woods of the groves that are among the trees of the forests? Is wood taken from it to make a work, or will a peg be fashioned from it, so that any vessel may hang from it? Behold, it has been given to the fire for food; the fire has consumed both its parts, and its middle has been reduced to ashes; will it be useful for a work? Even when it was whole it was not fit for a work; how much more, when the fire has devoured it and burnt it up, will no work be made of it! Therefore thus says the Lord God: As the wood of the vine among the trees of the forests, which I have given to the fire to devour, so will I give up the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and I will set my face against them: they will go out from the fire, and the fire will consume them, and you will know that I am the Lord, when I have set my face against them and have made the land pathless and desolate, because they have proved transgressors, says the Lord God. (Where we translated: The fire has consumed both its parts, and its middle has been reduced to ashes, the Seventy translated: The fire consumes its yearly cleansing, and lets it go to the end. Again, where we said: When I have set my face against them, they rendered: When I have set firm. 'Transgression', too, they translated as 'offense'.) By various similitudes, then, which the Greeks call parables, the overthrow of the city of Jerusalem is foretold; and just as above, in the frying pan in which the flesh of the people was fried, and in the brick on which the siegeworks and mounds and the engines of rams and of mantlets were drawn, the siege and famine of that same city were described, and as we shall read later in this same prophet — in Jeremiah too it is written that the 'pot' which is kindled from the face of the north signifies the city of Jerusalem; and the forest of Nageb and Theman and Darom [three Hebrew words for the south], cut down, foretells this very thing —, so in the present passage the same Jerusalem is compared to a vineyard and a fruitful vine — of which it is written in another place: I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly true; how have you been turned into bitterness, O alien vine?, and in Isaiah: I planted, he says, a vine 'sorec', which means 'chosen' and 'beautiful'; and in the Psalms we read: You brought a vine out of Egypt, you cast out the nations and planted it; you were the guide of its way before it; and we learn it more plainly when Scripture says: But the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel —. As long as this vine bears fruit, among all the trees of the woodlands nothing is more precious than it; but if it ceases to have grapes, it is useful for nothing except to be given to the fire with its root and its layered shoots. The other trees of the forests — to say nothing of the fruit-bearing trees, of which Scripture here makes no mention —, though they have no fruit, once cut down provide a great deal of usefulness and serve both all of agriculture and the making of arms, while they are thinned into shields and shaved into spear-shafts; they close doorways, they hold things as cupboards, as chests and coffers, and they furnish all the equipment of a house. But the vine, once it has ceased to bear grapes, is so useless that not even a peg can be made from it on which something might hang; and when you have cut off its shoots, the fire first seizes both their parts, then the flame consumes them; and it is of no use whatever once it has been reduced to ashes, seeing that even when it is whole it offers no usefulness without its fruit.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now the ambiguity of the Hebrew word 'sene', which is written with three letters, 'sin' and 'nun' and 'iod', is this: if it is read 'sene' it means 'two', if 'sane', 'years'; hence it came about that for its two extremities, which we translated 'both its parts', the Seventy translated 'its yearly cleansing', whereas Aquila said 'its two last parts', Symmachus and Theodotion 'its two extremities'; and the sequence is this: 'As a fruitless vine is given to the fire to no use, so Jerusalem too, or rather its inhabitants, will be given up to the flames, so that they go out from the fire and the fire consumes them, that is: even if they escape from the city, outside they will be consumed by the enemy's sword, and those who remain, crushed by the very weight of their miseries, will recognize that I am the Lord, when I have set, or set firm, my face against them and have given them up to everlasting desolation: for they proved not sinners like the other nations, but transgressors' — for it is one thing to neglect what you do not know, and another to despise what you have worshiped —.

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make known to Jerusalem her abominations, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God to Jerusalem. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, bear witness to Jerusalem of her iniquities, and you shall say to her: Thus says Adonai the Lord.") Where the compass of the individual prophecies was brief, we set down whole passages, adding at once beneath them what seemed right to us; here, however, because a long discourse is directed to Jerusalem by one who bears witness to her and teaches her the sins she has committed, and the prophecy extends to nearly two hundred lines, namely up to that place in which it is written: When I have been appeased toward you in all that you have done, says the Lord God, we must set out the whole prophecy in parts, and fit the due explanations to the parts we have set out. Under the person of a harlot woman, who was first joined in union with a husband, there is woven together the birth and upbringing and youth and marriage and adultery and divorce and recall again of Jerusalem, so that both the clemency and the judgment of the husband and the crimes of the adulteress and harlot may be recognized, when after all the punishments he raises up for her an everlasting covenant, that she may remember her iniquity and be confounded, and it may no longer be hers to open her mouth because of her confusion, when he has been appeased toward her in all that she had done; and it greatly profits sinners to know what they have done: whence the penitent too says: For I know my iniquity, and my sin is ever against me. Now Jerusalem can be understood in four ways: either this one which was set on fire by the Babylonian and the Roman flame, or the heavenly one of the firstborn, or the Church, which means 'vision of peace', or the souls of individuals who by faith behold God. And what many think should be interpreted of the heavenly Jerusalem the Church does not accept, lest we be compelled to take all that is woven together in the present prophecy as referring to the fall and torments of the heavenly powers, and to their restoration to their former state.

Why is it that I admire Ezekiel? Because the order was given him to make known to Jerusalem its abominations, and he did not place before his eyes any danger that would result from his preaching, but in order to keep only the precepts of God, he spoke whatever he was told. Let us realize that there was a mystery, that there was the revelation of a mysterious kind on the subject of Jerusalem and all that is said against it. Nevertheless, he prophesied, and accused it of fornication.
HOMILIES ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES 43

And again, Ezekiel makes this an accusation against them, that they did not grieve for the afflicted. What sayest thou, O Prophet? God punisheth, and shall I grieve for those that He is punishing? Yea verily: for God Himself that punisheth wisheth this: since neither does He Himself wish to punish, nay, even Himself grieves when punishing. Then be not thou glad at it. You will say, "If they are justly punished, we ought not to grieve." Why, the thing we ought to grieve for is this—that they were found worthy of punishment. Say, when thou seest thy son undergoing cautery or the knife, dost thou not grieve? and sayest thou not to thyself, "What is this? It is for health this cutting, to quicken his recovery; it is for his deliverance, this burning?" but for all that, when thou hearest him crying out, and not able to [bear it], the hope of health being restored is not enough to carry off the shock to nature. So also in the case of these, though it be in order to their health that they are punished, nevertheless let us show a brotherly feeling, a fatherly disposition. They are cuttings and cauteries, the punishments sent by God: but it is for this we ought to weep, that they were sick, that they needed such a mode of cure.

If so many things are said in Jerusalem about which such great and wonderful things are written that have been promised to her, what future is there for unhappy me, if I sin? Who will I have for a father, who will I have for a mother?
Commentary on Ezekiel

Your root and your generation from the land of Canaan, your father an Amorite and your mother a Hittite. Great is the faith, great the boldness of the prophets, that one man should charge a whole city with ignoble birth; admirable is Daniel who, to an elder who was sinning and joining murder to adultery, dared as a boy to say: Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you; great too is Isaiah, who cries out to the princes and to the people of the Jews: Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom; give ear to the words of the Lord, people of Gomorrah; but no less is Ezekiel, who speaks confidently to the whole city: Your root and your generation from the land of Canaan, your father an Amorite and your mother a Hittite. Although Stephen too, the first martyr of the Gospel, spoke thus to the raging people: Stiff of neck, and uncircumcised in heart, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit, and although we can take the root of Jerusalem and her generation, the land of Canaan, in the sense that the people was called in Egypt and dwelt there a long time — for Ham, the father of Canaan, was the founder of the Egyptian nation —, yet, according to the likeness of their crimes, let us say that the root of Jerusalem is the land of Egypt; whence also her father is called 'amorrhaeus' [Amorite], which means διαδούμενος, that is, 'celebrated by much talk', and her mother 'chethaea' [Hittite], that is, ἐξιστῶσα, 'she who' either 'is herself mad' or 'drives others into madness': Everyone, indeed, who commits sin is born of the devil, whence also in the whole world the name of this ancient father is notorious, and it turns many into madness. And Jerusalem is commanded, whether according to the letter or according to the spirit, to leave her ancient father, and it is said to her: Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house; and the king will desire your beauty, and it is promised her, if after sin she is willing to return to her true father: I will restore you as you were when you were born. Such is the nobility of the city of Jerusalem, which, descending from the stock of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, had God as her father, and yet, because she sinned and left her true parent, deserves to hear: Your root and your generation from the land of Canaan, your father an Amorite and your mother a Hittite! If she heard this, what will become of us, who, called out of the filth of the nations, lost every stain in the washing of the Savior, if we defile the garment of Christ and do not have the wedding garment at the banquet? Surely this: that, with hands and feet bound, we be handed over to everlasting fires, in which there is weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 6:5
Not everyone is washed for salvation. We who have received the grace of baptism in the name of Christ are washed, but I do not know who is washed for salvation.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 6:5

It is quite difficult that he who is washed should be washed in order to be saved. Listen, catechumens, listen, and from what is said, prepare yourselves, while you are catechumens, while you are not yet baptized, and come to the bath and be baptized for salvation. Do not be so baptized that you are washed but not for salvation.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 6:6
It is a great work to be rubbed with salt. If we are seasoned with salt, we are full of grace.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 6:6
The soul that is reborn is barely out of the bath before being enveloped with towels.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 6:6
To take an example from human relationships, if the Holy Spirit gives, then I travel on to Jesus Christ and God the Father.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when you were born, on the day of your birth, your navel was not cut, and you were not washed in water for salvation, nor salted with salt, nor wrapped in swaddling cloths. No eye spared you, to do for you one of these things, having pity on you, but you were cast out upon the face of the earth in the abjection of your soul on the day on which you were born. (LXX: "And your generation: on the day on which you were born, they did not bind your breasts, and you were not washed in water for salvation, nor salted with salt, and you were not wrapped in swaddling cloths. Nor did your eye spare you, that I should do for you one of all these things, and that it should suffer anything over you, and you were cast out upon the face of the field for the depravity of your soul on the day on which you were born.") Let us discuss each point in the order of the reading. When Jerusalem was born of an Amorite father and a Hittite mother and poured forth from the womb, her navel was not cut, the navel by which fetuses are nourished in the belly, like trees and shrubs which are nourished through their roots by the hidden moisture of the earth — and just as the seed-bed of men is signified in the loins, so the genitals of women, by a decent expression, according to the custom of the Scriptures, are called the navel, on the testimony of Job who, under the figure of the dragon, speaks of the devil: His strength is in his loins, and his might in the navel of his belly; for this dragon, the ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan and deceived the whole world, has his strength against men in the loins, against women in the navel —, and this signifies of Jerusalem that she did not at once receive the Law, nor were the beginnings of her shameful birth cut away from her, but she first lived a Gentile life; for which the Seventy translated: On the day on which you were born, they did not bind your breasts, since Holy Scripture has this custom, that for the heart it names the little breast, or the breast, and the breasts, as it sees fit for each place — the priests, in whom there ought to be doctrine, and from whose mouth they seek the Law, receive the little breast; John reclines upon the breast of the Lord, to draw the streams of wisdom from the richest fountain; the virgin's two breasts in the Song of Songs are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, which feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows are removed; a careful mother, as soon as her baby girl is born, binds her breasts, so that they may refrain from tender swelling and keep their virginal beauty, but when she has come to the age of puberty, it is said of her: Will a bride forget her adornment, or a virgin her breast-band? —. There follows: And you were not washed in water for salvation; the bloody bodies of infants are usually washed as soon as they are sent forth from the womb; so too the spiritual birth needs the saving washing: For no one is clean from filth, not even if his life has been of one day, and in the Psalms we read: In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother conceived me; the second birth undoes the first birth, for it is written: Unless one is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God; and there are many washings which the pagans, in their mysteries, and the heretics promise, who all wash but do not wash for salvation; therefore it is added: And you were not washed in water for salvation, which indeed can be understood not only of heretics but also of churchmen who do not receive saving baptism with full faith, of whom it must be said that they received the water but did not receive the Spirit — just as that Simon the magician, who wished to buy the grace of God with money, was indeed baptized in water but was by no means baptized for salvation —. Thirdly it is said: Nor salted with salt; the tender bodies of infants, while they still keep the warmth of the womb and with their first wail bear witness to the beginnings of a toilsome life, are usually touched with salt by the midwives, so that they may be drier and be firmed; but Jerusalem, born of evil parents, obtained no savor, no care; to those, however, who are reborn in Christ it is said: You are the salt of the earth, and they are commanded by the Apostle: Let your speech always be seasoned with salt in grace — whence also in common speech the wise are called 'salty' and the foolish 'unsalted', and in Leviticus it is enacted by law: Every sacrifice of yours shall be salted with salt, the salt of the covenant of the Lord shall not cease from your sacrifices: in all your gifts you shall offer salt; he who has been seasoned with this salt and by its admixture has dried up all stench and harmful moisture will no longer say: My scars have putrefied and become corrupt before the face of my foolishness. I know that I have read in a certain volume about the Lord Savior that he himself is the heavenly salt, and has seasoned with his savor not only earthly and infernal things but heavenly ones too, and that what is written is fulfilled: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will —. Fourth is: Nor wrapped in swaddling cloths; the Savior too was wrapped in the swaddling cloths of infancy, and everyone who is born needs the protection of God through the wrappings of swaddling cloths. It is natural, where at least the care of the parents is not lacking, for newborn infants first to have the navel cut, then to be washed with water to wash off the blood, thirdly for the moisture of the little bodies to be dried by the application of salt, fourthly for the tender bodies of infants to be wrapped in swaddling cloths, for a twofold reason: both so that the body may be dried by the salt, the body being kept and held tight by the cloths so that it does not run off, and so that the most tender limbs may not easily become misshapen — whence also the bodies of the barbarians are straighter than Roman bodies: for up to the second and third year they are always wrapped in swaddling cloths —; but not so Jerusalem, whose navel was not cut off, nor were her breasts bound, nor was she washed with water for salvation, nor salted with salt, nor wrapped and bound in the swaddling cloths of infancy.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But why she deserved none of these things, the following Scripture testifies: No eye spared you, to do for you one of these things, having pity on you, for which the Seventy put: Your eye did not spare you, that I should do for you one of all these things, and the twofold edition must have a twofold understanding; the former signifies this: No eye spared you, to do for you one of these things, having pity on you, and the sense is: 'No one had pity on you, since God was offended; no one's heart was moved over you, so as to do for you at least one of the four things above, since you did not deserve to receive them all together'; in the other it is said: Your eye did not spare you, that I should do for you one of all these things, and it has this sense: 'You acted so, and were so born in sins, and in sins your mother conceived you, that not even you yourself had pity on yourself. And since you behaved so as to be cruel against yourself through evil works, what could I do for you, who did not deserve to receive even one of the things above? Since, then, none of these things which are usually done for infants was done in you, and this not without cause nor without judgment but through your own fault and sin, since not even you yourself had pity on yourself, therefore: You were cast out on the face of the earth (or of the field), and cast out because of the depravity of your soul on the day on which you were born' — let us pray that we be not cast out through depravity of soul onto the face of the field, in which wide and spacious is the way that leads to death, in which the cavalry of the Chaldeans runs riot —. And at the same time it must be considered that no one, on the day on which he is born, can commit anything depraved, except at the time of the washing, when a wise generation is taken up by the faith of the believer.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 6:7

But see the mercy of God, see his extraordinary goodness. Even though Jerusalem was thrown into the open field, he does not look down on it as thrown out forever, he does not leave it in a state of perversion as entirely forgotten, as not in the end to lift up the fallen. You were thrown out, but I still return to you; my visit is not lacking after your ruin."
Commentary on Ezekiel

But passing by you I saw you trampled in your blood, and I said to you, when you were in your blood: Live. I said, I say, to you: In your blood live. I made you multiplied like the sprout of the field, and you went in and came to womanly finery, your breasts swelled and your hair sprouted; and you were naked and full of confusion. (LXX: "And I passed by you and saw you mixed in your blood, and I said to you: From your blood, life; be multiplied. Like the growth of the field I made you, and you were multiplied and were magnified; and you entered into the cities of cities, your breasts were raised and your hair sprang up; but you were naked, full of disgrace.") 'After you were cast out on the face of the field, or upon the face of the earth, because of the depravity of your soul, you no longer deserved my help. Nevertheless: Passing by you I saw you trampled (or mixed) in your blood, that is, guilty of deadly crimes, and I summoned you, granting repentance, and I said to you: Although you are in blood, yet live, converted.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And so great was the abundance of all things in you, that you had the likeness of a most fertile field — and the blessing of Jacob with which his father blessed him, saying: Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed —, and that you entered the inner chambers of the Lord — and said with the bride: The king has brought me into his chamber —, and came to womanly finery'; for which the Seventy translated: And you entered into the cities of cities, so that, just as one speaks of the Song of 'Songs' and of an age of 'ages', so cities are called cities of 'cities', of which it is said in the Gospel: 'Have authority over ten (or over five) cities, so that you are called not only a city but a metropolis city', according to what is written in Isaiah: Faithful Zion, mother of cities; moreover, what Symmachus translated: And you came to the adornment of women, or Theodotion: And you entered to the adornment of adornments, for which we, following the Hebrew sense, said: And you came to womanly finery, shows the time of puberty, when girls are called 'marriageable' and can be joined in the embraces of husbands. Then there follows: Your breasts swelled and your hair sprouted: the maturity of young girls is decently indicated, when the breasts swell, or are raised, and the hair sprouts. And although she was ready for marriage and had beauty of body, she did not have the covering of garments nor was she protected by the help of God; if anyone does not have the garment of Christ, he is naked; if anyone is not clothed with the bowels of mercy, of goodness, of humility, of modesty, of meekness, of patience, he lies upon the face of the earth, and his beauty is disfigured by confusion and nakedness.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 6:8
When we are of a greater age and can therefore sin, angels look for a chance to influence us, and that is as true of the angels of God as it is of the angels of Satan.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 6:9
Let us pray that the mercy of God will come on us and wash away the blood from our souls.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 43:5

But from hence infer not thy punishment only, but also the boundless longsuffering of God. How often at least have we put our hands to the same evil deeds, and yet He suffers long! But let us not be sanguine, but fear; since Pharaoh too, had he been taught by the first plague, would not have experienced the later ones; he would not afterwards have been drowned, his host and all together.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I passed by you and saw you; and behold, your time, the time of lovers. And I spread my cloak over you, and covered your disgrace. (LXX: "And I passed by you and saw you; and behold, your time, the time of those turning aside. And I spread my wings over you, and covered your disgrace.") What great clemency! It had not been enough to have seen her once trampled in blood and to have called her to repentance, but when she sins again he visits her and, because she was naked and full of confusion, he comes again and visits; and behold, her time, the time 'of lovers' — or according to the Seventy 'of those turning aside', and according to the second translation of Aquila, συναλλαγῆς, namely 'of betrothal' and 'of the time of the nuptials', but according to the first edition of the same and Theodotion μαστῶν, which means 'of breasts', for which Symmachus rendered ἀγαπῆς, which signifies 'love' —; that, then, was the time when women can be joined and sustain marital intercourse. Nevertheless the merciful God spread his wings, took them up, and carried them on his shoulders — according to what is written in the Gospel: How often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not —, or he spread a 'cloak' in place of 'wings' — for this is what πτερυγίῳ [wing; also the skirt of a garment] means, with which Ruth too was covered as she slept at the feet of Boaz; and on the border, that is, the πτερυγίῳ, of our garment we are commanded to fasten ὑακίνθινας [hyacinth-blue] fringes —; and he did these things to cover the disgrace of Jerusalem — indicating by this name the genital body of women; for indeed, according to the Apostle, we surround the uncomely parts of our body with greater honor, whence also the psalmist sings: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; and because Ham did not cover these in his father, he is marked with an everlasting curse —. What we have said of Jerusalem, let us refer to our soul, which, as long as it is set in infancy, is without sin; but when the time of its age has come, there are many lovers — of demons and of heretics and of perverse dogmas — who desire to turn aside to it; they are repelled by the protection of the Lord, so that it may receive not the satellites of the devil but the ministers of the Savior. For 'of those turning aside', 'love' and 'of breasts', the Hebrew has 'dodim', which, according to the peculiar character of their language, signifies all the things translated above. The time 'of love' and 'of breasts', or 'of the lovers of God', can be understood as Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, when the Lord promised them that his people would be freed after the Egyptian servitude.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I swore to you, and entered into a pact with you, says the Lord God. (LXX: "And I swore to you, and entered into a covenant with you, says Adonai the Lord.") 'Because I spread my cloak, or my wings, over you and covered your confusion, therefore I swore to you and entered into a pact, or covenant, with you, so that you might be joined to me rather than to the others who wished to turn aside to you' — according to that: The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek; for an oath is the end of every dispute, and: As I live, says the Lord, 'I would rather have the repentance of the sinner than his death' —. At the time of the nuptials, then, Israel received the oath of God in place of every dowry gift — and because David had said of himself: Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness, who swore to the Lord, vowed a vow to the God of Jacob, the Lord himself also swears to him, as Scripture says: The Lord has sworn truth to David, and will not frustrate him.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you became mine. And I washed you with water, and cleansed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil. 'Because I spread my wings and covered your disgrace and swore to you and entered into a pact with you, therefore you have become my possession, so that you, who were another's when you were seen unclean, began to be mine when I confirmed my pact with you by an oath', or, according to the custom of the prophets: 'You became mine', he says, 'stands for: you were joined to me in marriage; and I washed you', he says, 'with the water of saving baptism': Unless, indeed, one is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God; and elsewhere we read: He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire, of which baptism Isaiah too speaks, saying: The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning. And when he has washed, and cleansed her of the blood — the blood from which, by the touch of his fringe, he also healed the αἱμορροοῦσαν [woman with a flow of blood] who for twelve years had been running with gore —, it is not enough to wash with water and cleanse from blood, unless he also anoints with oil, according to which the Samaritan, which means 'guardian', first soothed the wounds of the half-dead man by pouring in oil, then checked them with the sharpness of wine; but our Lord was anointed with another oil, which would not soothe the pain of wounds but grant gladness, as the Holy Spirit says to him: Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of exultation above your fellows. The opposing powers too have the smoothness of a counterfeit oil, promising sweet things through the heretics: things which are turned into bitterness, and which the prophet detests, recalling: But let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head. But if from anointing the anointed one, that is, Christ, is so named, see how far Jerusalem had advanced, that she too, anointed with spiritual oil, received the name of Christ, according to what we read in the Psalms of Abraham: Do not touch my christs, and do no evil among my prophets.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I clothed you in parti-colored garments. (LXX: "And I dressed you in varied garments.") In the ceremonies of the Law, so that, occupied in the study of them, you would forsake idols. These are the varied garments with which Joseph was clothed, and his brothers could not sell him until they had first stripped him of the variety of his tunic; and of the bride it is said in Psalm 44 (45): The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety; this is the garment of which the Apostle too speaks: Having put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the Creator. Do we want to know what the varied garments are? Let the same Apostle teach us, writing to believers: Put on therefore the bowels of mercy, of goodness, of humility, of meekness, of patience — what is more beautiful than this variety? —, of which Job too spoke: Who gave women the wisdom of weaving or the skill of variety?, and the high priest, once a year, when he burned incense for the people and entered the Holy of Holies, used varied vestments. Certainly, if riches, and not holiness and diversity of virtues, made the variety of garments, Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar would be written to have had these garments, and not Joseph, who under a sojourning and shepherd father could not have parti-colored and royal garments.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I shod you with violet. (LXX: "And I shod you with hyacinth.") Aquila and Symmachus translated 'violet', the Seventy and Theodotion 'hyacinthine', for which in the Hebrew is written 'thas'. And beautifully, because the discourse is directed to Jerusalem and, under the person of a woman, all her adornment is set out, ὑακίνθινα [hyacinth-colored] or ἰάνθινα [violet] shoes are spoken of, which do not suit the person of men — indeed, those who are to keep the Passover are commanded, without any variety of color, to have their loins girded and their feet shod; these are the shoes of which the Apostle writes: Feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace; Philo, the most eloquent man among the Jews, compares the ὑάκινθον [hyacinth] in the vestments of the high priest to the air, by which he thinks the higher and heavenly things are signified —. Nor is Jerusalem shod with hyacinthine shoes until she has been washed with water — whence also the apostles, whom the Lord had earlier commanded to shake off the dust of their feet, have their feet washed by the Savior; and the bride says in the Song of Songs: I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?; and the divine word testifies to Moses and Joshua that they should loose the latchet of their shoe, because the place in which they stand is holy —; but when the feet have been washed and purged of all filth, they are shod with ὑακίνθινις or ἰάνθινις — both of which are of an ἀέριον [air-like] and κυανέου [dark blue] color — so that they may be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, and hasten to the heavenly kingdoms.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I girded you with fine linen. Jerusalem is not only clothed in parti-colored garments and shod with ὑακίνθινις, but is also girded with fine linen, from which the finest threads are woven in the vestment of the high priest; and the wife in Proverbs, who wove two cloaks for her husband, of the present age and of the future, is said to have made garments for herself of fine linen and purple. With this fine linen the reins are girded whenever the rich incitements of lust are to be thinned, and nothing of gross moisture is left in them, and we fulfill the precept of the Apostle, who says: Stand therefore with your loins girded in truth — as though he said in other words 'with fine linen' —. And the Lord says to the apostles: Let your loins be girded, and lamps in your hands: for unless we bind up the flowing humors of the loins, we cannot have lamps in our hands; whence God also says to Job: Gird up your loins like a man. And those who are to eat the lamb, with feet shod, holding a staff, standing in the truth of the Gospel and prepared for the blood of Christ, are said to have their loins girded; with this belt, which mortifies the loins, Elijah too and John the Baptist are girded; of these the penitent too groans tearfully, saying: For my loins are filled with illusions.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I clothed you with fine stuffs. (LXX: "And I surrounded you with trichaptum.") For which Aquila put 'flowery' or 'palpable', Symmachus 'garment', Theodotion the Hebrew word itself, 'messe'; and when I was diligently inquiring what the word 'trichaptum', which the Seventy translated, meant, and could find from none of the Greeks either the usage or the ἐτυμολογίαν [etymology] of the word, at last I learned that it was coined by the Seventy — for new names must be fixed to new things —, because the garment was of such fineness that it was believed to have the thinness of hairs and of the hair of the head; whence I too, wishing to express the thinness of the garment, translated 'subtilibus' [fine stuffs] for 'trichapto', because it was woven with fine warp and weft. And fittingly, to those whom he had rebuked, saying: The heart of this people has grown fat, and Jacob ate and drank and was filled and grew fat, and the beloved kicked and forsook God his maker, fineness of garments is now granted; for in the book of Wisdom too, which by some is ascribed to Solomon, the spirit of wisdom is called only-begotten and manifold, fine and mobile; and the manna, of which it is written: Man ate the bread of angels, is said to have been very fine, in the likeness of hoarfrost and of coriander seed. We can, according to the interpretation of the second edition of Aquila, who translated 'flowery', understand the 'garment' through a μεταφορὰν [metaphor] as the fertility of the land of Judea, or as the beauty of divine worship.
LETTER 31.2

It is true that a festival such as the birthday of Peter should be seasoned with more gladness than usual; still our merriment must not forget the limit set by Scripture, and we must not stray too far from the boundary of our wrestling ground. Your presents, indeed, remind me of the sacred volume, for in it Ezekiel decks Jerusalem with bracelets.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I adorned you with adornment. Here he sets down the adornments in general, which in what follows he enumerates one by one: bracelets and torque, earrings and crown, and the rest, which adornments he bestowed on Jerusalem, and in Isaiah it is said that by her own fault she lost them all: for it is written: Because the daughters of Jerusalem were lifted up (that is, were proud) and walked with lofty neck, and the rest: instead of a girdle they were girded with ropes, and instead of the adornment of the head disfigured with baldness, and instead of beautiful and soft clothes surrounded with the roughness of sackcloth.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I put bracelets on your hands. (LXX: "And I surrounded your hands with bracelets.") When God gives us good works, he puts bracelets around our hands. Whence also he says that he was likened in the hands of the prophets, and we frequently read that the word came in the hand of Haggai or Jeremiah and the others; in Job too the lip of the dragon is pierced with a bracelet, and all his venomous hissings, which are understood in perverse dogmas, are pierced by the ring of good works.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And a torque around your neck. For 'torque', which we translated following the second edition of Aquila and Symmachus, the Seventy and Theodotion translated κάθεμα [pendant] — which is written not only here but also in Isaiah: The Lord will take away the glory of their garment, and the little lamprey-chains and the clusters and the rings, and the κάθεμα —; and I think that by κάθεμα they meant a necklace of various gems descending onto the breast of women, which itself too is a most beautiful adornment of women.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 6:10
Almighty God, grant to us to be worthy of the crown and glory on our head.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 6:10
We are not only anointed with this oil, but we also live.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I gave an earring over the mouth (or your nostrils). The Hebrew word 'nezem', except for Symmachus, who translated ἐπιρρίνιον [nose-ring], all translated 'earring', not that earrings are put in the nostrils — they are called 'inaures' [earrings] from the fact that they hang from the ears [aures] —, but that a ring, made in the likeness of earrings, is called by the same word; and to this day, among the other adornments of women, golden rings are wont to hang from the forehead over the mouth and to overhang the nostrils. These we receive according to mystical understanding when with the Apostle we can say: We are the good odor of Christ in those who are being saved, and in those who perish: to some an odor of death unto death, to others an odor of life unto life; when we live and it can be said of us: The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, but we the living, then God smells the odor of our sacrifice of good fragrance, and we have the golden ring of divine senses and dogmas in our nostrils; but when we are dead and wallow in the mire and in the filth of lusts, we have in our nostrils that earring of which Solomon wrote: As golden earrings in the nostrils of a swine, so is beauty to an ill-mannered woman.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And rings for your ears. (LXX: "And little wheels upon your ears.") He who stops his ears so as not to hear the judgment of blood, and hedges them with thorns so as not to become a partaker with the envious and the detractors — of whom it is written: Do not mingle with detractors; for their destruction will come suddenly, and who knows the ruin of both? —, namely both of him who detracts and of him who gladly listens, this man has rings and little wheels in his ears — not the wheels which follow the Cherubim: for that belongs to the evangelical powers, but little wheels, in the diminutive —, which befit human frailty. Therefore it is also said to God: The voice of your thunder in the wheel: for in those who pass over earthly things and touch the earth with scarcely the slightest footprints — of whom it is written: Holy stones are rolled upon the earth —, the voice of the Lord's thunder and of lofty dogmas resounds; but those who are led by human errors and have no solid footing but are carried about by every wind of doctrine and, cast out of the paradise of firmness, dwell in the region of Naid [Nod], which means 'fluctuation', deserve to bear the sentence of a lying tongue, which sets on fire the wheel of our birth.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And a crown of beauty on your head. (LXX: "And a crown of boasting upon your head.") We translated 'beauty' following Symmachus, for the elegance of the sense; otherwise both in the Hebrew, 'thopherth', and in the other translators, καύχησις, it is called 'boasting'. The other adornments belong to individual members; the adornment of the head is the dignity of the whole body; and he calls crown the diadem of women, by which the abundance of the hair is bound and adorned. Do we want to know what the crown of beauty on the head of Jerusalem is? Let us unroll Exodus, in which it is written: And he made a plate of gold, and wrote on it letters formed with the seal of the sanctification of the Lord, and put it upon the head of Aaron; 'the sign of the Lord's holiness' is the name of almighty God, which is written with four Hebrew letters and among them is called 'ineffable', since his name cannot be spoken — whose majesty even paganism is not ignorant of, and the altar of the Athenians bears witness, 'To the Unknown God', whence also the Apostle: What you, he says, worship as unknown, this we proclaim to you —. This I think is the crown of which he also speaks thus in the Psalms: The light of your countenance is sealed upon us, O Lord, and the Apostle says: I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; for the rest there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the righteous judge will render to me, and in another place to believers: My joy and my crown: for the glory of fathers is their sons; and in Solomon it is written: Old age is a crown of glory, namely of those who have destroyed the things that belong to little ones and, after the age of the perfect man, have come to old age and to the name of fathers, to whom John writes after the children and the young men, who can say: When I was a little one, I spoke as a little one, I understood as a little one, I thought as a little one; when I became a man, I destroyed the things that belong to a little one.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you were adorned with gold and silver. We have often said that gold pertains to the mind, silver to speech. And may the Lord grant us that we may deserve to receive the divine sense and wisdom, and to bring forth with grace of eloquence what we conceive in the mind, and by no means to make idols of these, as the heretics do, of whom it is written: I gave them silver and gold; but they made Baal of the silver and gold. And this, according to the spiritual understanding, is the more fitting for the adornment of women; otherwise silver, the cheaper material, is the adornment of country women and of poor women and maidservants, which does not befit Jerusalem, who is said to have advanced to be queen.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you were clothed with fine linen and many-threaded stuff and many colors. (LXX: "And your cloaks of fine linen and trichapta and variegated things.") The Hebrew word 'mesi' Theodotion here too set down as it stands, as above, Aquila ἄνθινον [flowered], Symmachus 'polymitum' [many-threaded], and we, what above we called 'subtile' [fine], here, following Symmachus, called 'polymitum'; the Seventy translated 'trichapta', keeping their former interpretation, so as to show garments fine like hairs. Now the whole adornment of women is described: that she is washed, that she is cleansed, that she is anointed with oil, and is clothed in parti-colored garments, is shod with ὑακίνθινις, is girded with fine linen, is clothed with trichapta or fine stuffs, receives bracelets, and the golden torque, rings hanging over the mouth, and little wheels in the ears, a diadem on the head, is decorated with gold and silver — although silver is the cheaper material —, and after all this there is added: You were clothed with fine linen and many-threaded stuff and variegated colors — or, as the Seventy translated, 'with cloak and mantles', for this is what περιβόλαια signifies —, so that she was not only adorned in the care of her body and had all the necklaces of women, but the husband's diligence was also solicitous for her bedding and her couch, so that, when he had completed these things, he might come to the delights of foods, and would not allow anything to be lacking to her even in these. All of which, following the explanation above, we have fitted to the spiritual understanding: that she is covered with fine linen and fine stuffs, so that the delicate limbs of the wife may not be weighed down by the heavy burden of mantles, but may display usefulness and beauty alike.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Fine flour and honey and oil you ate, and you became beautiful greatly, exceedingly. After the clothing he takes care of food, that Jerusalem may eat fine flour and honey and oil, either separately, as many reckon, or, by a mixture of the three, a sweeter bread, the bread which came down from heaven; and under three names, as some think, it indicates the mystery of the Trinity, not that there is one substance and another, but that by the diverse names of fine flour and honey and oil the one sweetness of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is shown. And this is to be noted, that in many sacrifices fine flour is offered, the marrow of the wheat and the purest, of which it is written: And he satisfied them with the fat of wheat, not of barley nor of meal, which is offered only when a husband is moved by a spirit of jealousy. In the volume of Judges we read of 'Debboram' [Deborah], which means 'bee', whose prophecy is the sweetest honey, and this is referred to the Holy Spirit, who among the Hebrews is called by a feminine name: in the Gospel of the Hebrews too, which the Nazarenes read, the Savior is introduced speaking: Just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, took hold of me; moreover the fine flour, which is made from wheat, is referred to the Lord, who says of himself: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit; and the oil, which sustains and refreshes the limbs of the weary, and is the nourishment of light, and with which the light of the lamp is kindled continually in the tabernacle of God, is said to befit the Father; and all these grant one grace to believers, as the Apostle says: There are divisions of graces, but one Spirit; and divisions of ministries, but one Lord; and divisions of operations, but one and the same God.
