Your crime and your wickedness you will bear; Theodotion in this way: And Sodom your sister was not in the hearing of your mouth in the day of your pride, before your wickedness was uncovered, as the time of the reproach of the daughters of Syria, and of all the daughters of the foreigners round about her, who abhor you on every side. Your fornication and your abominations you have borne, says Adonai the Lord; our translation agrees with the edition of Aquila. All these I have set down so that from the comparison of them all we may be able to find a trace of some sense; and meanwhile, without prejudice to others, the order of the reading seems to us to be rendered thus: 'In the days of your pride, when you were sinning, you did not remember the overthrow of Sodom your sister, before your wickedness lay open, which at this time has been uncovered to such a degree that you became a reproach to all the cities of Syria and Palestine which are round about you; since, therefore, you surpassed your sister in crime, and were not frightened by her example so as not to suffer like things and to hold back your foot, but now your disgrace has been uncovered, hear the sentence of God: either 'bear' — according to the Seventy —, or 'you have borne' — according to Aquila and Theodotion, or 'you are going to bear' — according to Symmachus — your crime and disgrace, so that, after you have endured the punishment for sacrilege, you may obtain pardon, not from your covenant but from my clemency'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'Syria' in the Hebrew tongue is called 'aram', which means 'loftiness'; and according to the explanation of that passage of the prophet Isaiah in which Aram and Ephraim conspire against Judah and Jerusalem, the subtle wisdom of the heathens, which promises itself the loftiness of knowledge, in all the wickedness of the heretics, attacks Judah, in which is the true confession, and cannot prevail; here too the same arrogance of Syria, that is, of the philosophers, together with the daughters of the foreigners, in whom is shown the manifold error of the diverse doctrines among the nations, mocks Jerusalem and holds in reproach her by whose vices it has been surpassed.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For thus says the Lord God: And I will do to you as you despised the oath, so as to make void the covenant. And I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I will raise up for you an everlasting covenant. And you will remember your ways, and you will be ashamed when you receive your sisters with you, the greater with your lesser ones; and I will give them to you as daughters, but not by your covenant. And I will raise up for you my covenant with you, and you will know that I am the Lord, that you may remember and be ashamed, and that it may no longer be yours to open your mouth because of your shame, when I have been appeased toward you in all that you have done, says the Lord God. (LXX: "Thus says Adonai the Lord: And I will do in you as you have done, as you despised these things, so as to transgress my testament. And I will remember my testament which I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will raise up for you an everlasting testament. And you will remember your way, and you will be despised when you receive your sisters greater than you together with your younger ones; and I will give them to you for proving, and not by your testament. And I will raise up my testament with you, and you will know that I am the Lord, and you may remember and be ashamed, and it may no longer be yours to open your mouth before the face of your disgrace, when I have been propitiated toward you according to all that you have done, says the Lord God.") 'For this reason I said to you: Your crime and your disgrace, you, bear them (or you have borne or you are going to bear), : that you may receive what you deserve, because you despised my oath and made void my covenant. But when there has been fulfilled: I will kill and I will make alive, I will strike and I will heal, then I will remember my covenant which I once had with you. And I will raise up for you a covenant, by no means that of the law, which has passed away, but the everlasting covenant of the Gospel, so that, when you have remembered your ways and received your sisters, greater or lesser, Samaria and Sodom and their companions, I may grant them to you as daughters — or for proving: For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest to each —, not from your merit, but from my mercy; and then you may know that I am the Lord, and remember my benefits and be ashamed, and say with the Apostle: I who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God'.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 10:5
After receiving the price of my sins and being re-established, and the covenant made with me, then do I understand my evil deeds, and I am confounded, and within I punish myself.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 10:5
Let us pray with all our heart that God would grant us to fight for truth to the very end of our mind and body.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And that it may no longer be yours to open your mouth because of your shame: for it belongs to the saints to open the mouth — according to the Apostle, who says: My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians —, and to the Lord Savior — who, opening his mouth, taught them, and who says in the psalm too: I will open my mouth in parables —; but to the sinner it is said: You have sinned, be still, and: Why do you take up my testament through your mouth?, and: Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner; and the holy man deserves to hear: Open your mouth and I will fill it. From this we understand that even when, through the mercy of the Lord, we have received back our former glory, nay rather have received the everlasting covenant of the Gospel, after the Lord has been appeased toward us in all that we have done, we keep the memory of past sin and always close our mouth, because we have been saved not by our works but by the grace of God.

n: Riddle. Thus the prophets and Christ often delivered their doctrine. (Calmet)

A large eagle. Nabuchodonosor, king of Babylon. (Challoner) --- The multitude of his subjects, and his rapid and cruel conquests, are designated. (Calmet) --- He spoils the vineyard of Jerusalem, notwithstanding the Jews had applied to another eagle, the king of Egypt, ver. 12. (Worthington) --- Libanus. That is, Jerusalem; (Challoner) or invaded the country, (Calmet) entering by Libanus. (Haydock) --- Cedar. King Jechonias (Challoner) and his nobles, (4 Kings xxiv. 11.) with the most precious effects.

Twigs. The young king and his officers, who had scarcely got established. (Calmet) --- Chanaan. This name, which signifies traffic, is not taken here for Palestine, but for Chaldea; and the city of merchants here mentioned is Babylon. (Challoner) --- It was so corrupt as to deserve this appellation, as Rome was afterwards styled Babylon. Its situation was very favourable to traffic, and its dominions were very extensive. (Calmet)
Land. Sedecias, whom he made king. (Challoner) --- He was brother of the dethroned king, and had every prospect of reigning long, if he had proved faithful. (Calmet)

Towards him. Nabuchodonosor, to whom Sedecias swore allegiance. (Challoner) --- Literally, "to it," eam, the eagle. (Haydock) --- The dominions of Sedecias were extensive, but weak, and dependant on a foreign king.

Eagle. The king of Egypt, (Challoner) Vaphres, who came at the request of Sedecias, to oppose the Chaldeans, but was routed; and they returned to the siege of Jerusalem, Jeremias xxxvii. 4. --- Plantation, as the waters of the Nile were conducted to different parts by ditches, Deuteronomy xi. 10.

Prosper. Will God countenance perfidy? (Calmet) --- "Faith must be kept even with enemies." (St. Jerome) --- Arm. The conquest did not cost the Chaldeans much. Sedecias fled by night, but was soon taken, 4 Kings xxv. 6. (Calmet)

Shall, or, "hath taken," &c., (Challoner) as also (ver. 13.) Sedecias was seized five years after, chap. viii. 1. Jechonias, the princes, mighty warriors, (ver. 13.) and expert artists, had been taken away six years before, with the prophet. Protestants, "is come,...and hath taken," &c. (Haydock)
Die. He had sworn fidelity, and was justly punished, dying blind, and in prison, chap. xii. (Worthington)
Souls. Some refer this to Pharao; others to the enemy. The former did not attempt to surround the besiegers, but after losing a battle retired, chap. xxx. 21. (Calmet)
Hand. Swearing perhaps to both (Haydock) the Egyptian and to the Chaldean monarch.
Net. Chap. xii. 13. (Calmet) --- Judge, punish. (Haydock) --- His sentence was pronounced at Reblatha, 4 Kings xxv. 7. (Calmet)

Cedar. Of the Royal stock of David. --- Twig. Jesus Christ, whom God hath planted in Mount Sion, that is, the high mountain of his Church, to which all nations flow. (Challoner) --- The Jews in vain apply this to Zorobabel or to the Machabees. Their power was never great enough to verify these expressions. (Calmet) --- But Christ has united in his Church all the birds, or those who have strength enough to raise themselves above earthly things. (St. Jerome) (Theodoret, &c.) --- The kingdom of Sedecias and that of Nabuchodonosor prospered not, or was soon at an end: Christ remains for ever. (Worthington)

High and green denote Sedecias; low and dry Jechonias, who was exalted at Babylon, while his rival was hurled down from his present high estate. The prophets speak of that as past, which God has decreed. See Jeremias xxii. 30. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, propound a riddle and tell a parable to the house of Israel, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: A great eagle with great wings, long in the extent of its limbs, full of feathers and of variety, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar; it plucked off the top of its foliage and carried it over into the land of Canaan; in a city of merchants it set it. And it took of the seed of the land and set it in the ground for seed, that it might make firm its root upon many waters; on the surface it set it. And when it had sprouted, it grew into a broader vine of low stature, its branches looking toward it, and its roots were under it; so it became a vine, and bore fruit in vine-shoots and sent out offshoots. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, narrate a narration and speak a parable to the house of Israel, and you shall say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: A great eagle with great wings, of long extent, full of talons, which has the leading to enter into Lebanon, and it took the choice parts of the cedar; it plucked off the tops of the tenderness and brought them into the land of Canaan; in a walled city it set it. And it took of the seed of the land and gave it in a plain as a planting upon many waters, that it might be looked upon, and it set it, and it sprang up and became a weak vine and small in size, so that only its branches appeared under it, and its roots were beneath it; and it became a vine, and made offshoots and stretched out its branches.") When it is said to the prophet: Propound a riddle, tell a parable (or, as the Seventy translated: Narrate a narration and speak a parable), it is shown that what is said is obscure; for no one doubts that both a riddle and a parable put forward one thing in the words and hold another in the sense: for the Savior too spoke to the people in parables, which he explained privately to the apostles; therefore we must understand the riddle and the parable in just this way, as a riddle and a parable.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 11:5
He came to that Lebanon, which is the church, where the offerings of God and the incense of his prayers are celebrated, that great true evil, Nebuchadnezzar, that is, the devil, and he sees it.
Commentary on Ezekiel

According to anagogy — although the interpretation may seem forced — this must be known: that, just as the other living creatures are customarily referred both to a good and to a bad sense, so also is the eagle. Of the lion it is said in a good sense: A lion's whelp is Judah; in the contrary sense: Our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, and that in the psalm: He lies in wait in secret, like a lion in his den. He lies in wait to seize the poor. In a good sense it is said of the eagle that the righteous man, having become rich, may make himself wings like an eagle, that he may be able to return to the house of his superior, and in Isaiah it is written that the righteous may put forth feathers like eagles, may run and not grow weary, may walk and not hunger; but rightly he who had said: I will do strength and wisdom of understanding, I will remove the boundaries of the nations and plunder their strength, and I will shake the cities that are inhabited, and I will grasp the whole world in my hand like a nest and like broken eggs, is now described in the person of an eagle: in that he by no means wishes to strip from Lebanon — which means 'whiteness' and is referred to incense — the small and low shrubs, but the tops of the cedars, and of the princes and the royal stock, according to that saying of Habakkuk: His food is choice. And he makes a covenant with those whom he has captured, that they may bow their necks to the Babylonian king and fulfill what the Apostle says: Whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme, and in another place: Whom I have delivered, he says, to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved. We ought not, then, if perhaps on account of some sin we are cast out of the congregation of the brethren and out of the house of God, to struggle against it, but to bear with an even mind the sentence brought against us and to say with the prophet: I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause, and so on. And it often happens that, being subject to one, we go over to another who promises us his help and does not make us abide in the former sentence; which must be avoided by every means, lest our vine-shoots be dried up and our sprouts wither, and we be believed to act against the compact of God.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now in the present prophecy of Ezekiel two eagles are set forth; of the first we must speak now, of the other we shall treat in what follows. And meanwhile let us gather the simple history. A great eagle with great wings, long in the extent of its limbs, full of feathers and of variety (or, as the Seventy rendered, full of talons) is Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, of whom Hosea also speaks: As an eagle over the house of the Lord. He, ruling over many nations and hedged about by a countless army, came upon the house of God — no doubt it means the temple — or, as Scripture now says, to Lebanon, of which Zechariah speaks: Open your gates, O Lebanon; and let fire devour your cedars. Howl, fir tree, for the cedar has fallen, since the magnificent have been laid waste; and often the temple, which was renowned and lofty, is called Lebanon in the holy Scriptures. And it took the marrow of the cedar, and plucked off the top of its foliage and carried it over into the land of Canaan; in a city of merchants it set it (for 'merchants', or 'commerce', the Seventy translated 'walled'); and it indicates Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar captured together with his mother and the princes of the people and all the wealth of Jerusalem and the vessels of the temple, and carried over to Babylon, which is in the land of Canaan, and there he grew old; of whose line afterward, as the writing of Matthew the evangelist testifies, our Lord and Savior was born, through Shealtiel and Zerubbabel.
Commentary on Ezekiel

In his place he took of the seed of the same land, that is, of the royal stock, Mattaniah, the paternal uncle of Jeconiah, whose name he changed, and he called him Zedekiah and set him as king in Jerusalem, and put him over many peoples. And yet he set him on the surface, and did not make his power firm with a deep root of rule, but set him so that he might be looked upon and be under Babylonian power, or: Of low stature, its branches looking toward it, so that he would indeed rule over the peoples of the Jews, but would look to the authority of the Babylonian who gave the orders: for this is what Scripture says: Of low stature, its branches looking toward it — understand: toward the eagle — which the Seventy rendered more plainly: And it sprang up — what had been planted — and became a weak and small vine, so that only its branches appeared, and he would seem indeed to have a kingdom, but his kingdom itself, low and weak, would be ruled by the will of the Babylonian prince. So much for the present passage for now; let us join the rest to it as well.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 11:4
As long as it was on holy ground, the vine was huge; but when it was taken to the land of sinners, it was made infirm and small.
HOMILIES CONCERNING THE STATUES 19:9

Afterwards, intending to speak of the oaths and treaties, "He took," saith he, "of the seed of the land, and planted it in a fruitful field, that it might take root by great waters. He placed it to be looked upon; and it grew, and became a weak vine, and of small stature, and it stretched out its branches towards him, and its roots were under him." Here he calls the city of Jerusalem a vine; but in saying that it stretched out its branches towards the eagle, and that its roots were under him, he refers to the treaties and alliances made with him; and that it cast itself upon him.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 11:2

Another crowd was taken by him, and it became a vine, less vigorous than it was when it was in the vineyard of God and on holy ground, where the sacrifices of God are celebrated, but it was transferred to Babylon as a weak vine.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And there was another great eagle with great wings and many feathers; and behold, this vine, as if sending its roots to it, stretched out its vine-shoots to it, that it might water it from the beds of its growth. In good land upon many waters he planted it, that it may make foliage and bear fruit, and become a great vine. Say: Thus says the Lord God: Shall it then prosper? Will he not pull up its roots and strip off its fruit, and dry up all the vine-shoots of its growth, and it will wither? And not with a great arm nor with many peoples, so as to pull it up by the roots. Behold, it is planted; shall it then prosper? Will it not, when the burning wind touches it, be dried up, and wither in the beds of its growth? (LXX: "And there was another great eagle with great wings, with very many talons; and behold, this vine was entwined toward it, and its roots toward it, and it stretched out its branches toward it, that it might water it with the clod of its planting. In a good plain upon much water it was fattened, that it might make sprouts and bring forth fruit, and become a great vine. Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Shall it be guided aright? Will not the roots of its tenderness and its fruit rot, and all that has sprung from it wither? And not with a great arm nor with a numerous people, so as to pull it up from its roots. And behold, it is fattened; shall it be guided aright? Will it not, as soon as the burning wind touches it, wither, and be dried up with dryness? With the clod of its growth it will wither.") The second eagle, that is, the other one, itself also great, full of feathers and of many talons, because of its rapacity and its devastation of very many nations, is Pharaoh king of Egypt. And behold, this vine — understand: King Zedekiah, who had been set up in Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar — began, it says, to send its offshoots to it, that is, to direct envoys to the king of the Egyptians and to ask him for help against the king to whom he was subject — for this is what Scripture now says: That it might water it from the beds of its growth —.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 11:2

One who was condemned by God does not escape his sentence and does not want to change the will of he who judges him, but he will bear it with all patience until God frees the one who he has condemned.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 11:3

When the association of such different natures is made in faith in Christ, the lion will no longer be impure, and all the animals called impure in the law of God will receive the purity of their former condition.
Commentary on Ezekiel

It had been planted in good land by Nebuchadnezzar, that it might make foliage and bring forth fruit and grow into a broader vine; therefore the prophet is commanded to speak to the vine which had been planted by Nebuchadnezzar and had sent its branches to the Egyptian eagle: 'Shall it prosper because it has attempted to do this, and will not all its offshoots and vine-shoots at once be dried up? And not,' it says, 'with a great arm nor with a numerous people'; for Zedekiah, fleeing and left destitute of the help of the Egyptian king, was caught by the leaders of Nebuchadnezzar in the deserts of Jericho, and all his companions were scattered here and there, as is written in the volume of Kings and in Παραλιπομήνῳ [Chronicles] and in Jeremiah.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 12:1
I am inclined to think that by the good quality of their conduct they increase yet more the agreeableness of the words of God, mixing the sweetness of the life with the sweet savor of the word.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 12:2

If we who appear to stand over the church have sinned and given place to the devil against the teaching of Paul when he says "do not give any place to the devil," in the same way the faults committed at Jerusalem mean that we provide Nebuchadnezzar with the chance to enter into the holy city and to take away those whom he chooses.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Say to the provoking house: Do you not know what these things signify? Say: Behold, the king of Babylon comes to Jerusalem, and he will take its king and its princes, and lead them to himself into Babylon; and he will take of the seed of the kingdom, and strike a covenant with him, and receive an oath from him; but he will also take away the mighty of the land, that the kingdom may be lowly and not lift itself up, but keep his compact and observe it. But he, withdrawing from him, sent messengers to Egypt, that it might give him horses and a numerous people; shall he prosper or obtain safety who has done these things? And shall he who has broken the compact escape? As I live, says the Lord God, surely in the place of the king who made him king, whose oath he made void and whose compact, which he had with him, he broke, in the midst of Babylon he shall die. And not with a great army nor with a numerous people will Pharaoh make war against him, in the casting up of a mound and the building of ramparts, to kill many souls. For he had despised the oath so as to break the covenant, and behold, he gave his hand; and when he has done all these things, he shall not escape. This is the riddle and this is the parable: that under two eagles and a vine Scripture was showing two kings, of Babylon and of Egypt, and King Zedekiah, who, against his oath, abandoning his friendship with Nebuchadnezzar, transferred himself to the Egyptian king: And he will strike, it says, a covenant with him, and receive an oath from him, that he may keep his compact and observe it. He who has dissolved, it says, the compact, shall he escape? From this we learn that faith must be kept even among enemies, and that one must consider not to whom but by whom you have sworn; for far more faithful is he found who, on account of the name of God, trusted you and was deceived, than you who, under pretext of the divine majesty, plotted snares against your enemy, nay rather, by now your friend.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 12:3
If you have the covenant with us in a blessing, Nebuchadnezzar cannot make a covenant with you.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 12:3
God makes covenant with us in a blessing; Nebuchadnezzar establishes his covenant in abuse.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 12:3
As holy Scripture tells us, God intends that the covenant with Israel is an abuse against Nebuchadnezzar.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Surely, it says, in the place of the king who made him king, whose oath he made void and whose compact, which he had with him, he broke, in the midst of Babylon he shall die; for we read that Zedekiah was captured, led to Riblah, and there, after his sons had been killed, blinded, and, shut in a cage like a wild beast, carried over to Babylon — whence also Scripture, though it seems to be contrary to itself, is nevertheless most true in both: it had been said to Zedekiah: And you shall enter Babylon and: You shall not see it: for he entered, because he was led to Babylon, and he did not see it, because he had been blinded —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But what follows: And not with a great army nor with a numerous people will Pharaoh make war against him, in the casting up of a mound and the building of ramparts, to kill many souls, is understood in two ways: either the Egyptian king, coming against Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, will not be able to give battle nor with a small army resist so great a multitude; or Zedekiah himself will be conquered by Pharaoh, from whom he hoped for help, not that Pharaoh conquered him — or that Scripture anywhere attests this —, but that Nebuchadnezzar's conquest was brought about on the occasion given by the king of Egypt; and that not he who was besieging seemed to conquer Jerusalem, but he in whom Zedekiah had hoped in vain.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Behold, it says, he gave his hand to the king of Egypt, and handed himself over, and committed the sacrilege of perjury against God: 'Will it,' it says, 'profit him?'. And when he has done all these things, he shall not escape.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore thus says the Lord God: As I live, surely the oath that he despised and the covenant that he transgressed I will lay upon his head, and I will spread my net over him and he shall be caught in my dragnet, and I will bring him into Babylon, and I will judge him there in the transgression by which he despised me. And all his fugitives with the whole column shall fall by the sword; and the rest shall be scattered to every wind, and you shall know that I the Lord have spoken. It is a worldly maxim: Deceit or valor, who would ask, in an enemy?, which those who say that enemies are to be deceived by fraud are wont to set against us; yet even if we were to assent to it, Zedekiah did much worse: for he did not deceive an enemy, but a friend to whom he had been bound by a covenant of the Lord. Therefore, so long as you do not swear and do not enter into a compact under the name of God, it belongs to prudence and courage either to deceive or to overcome the adversary in whatever way you can; but when you have bound yourself by an oath, he who trusted you is by no means an adversary but a friend, and he was deceived under pretext of an oath, that is, of the invocation of God. That is why Scripture now says: The oath that he despised and the covenant that he transgressed I will lay upon his head; and lest we should think that the oath and the covenant and the compact belonged to the king of Babylon or to Zedekiah who had made it, there follows: In the transgression by which he despised me. So he who scorns an oath despises him by whom he swore, and does wrong to him in whose name the adversary trusted; for which reason: I will spread, it says, my net over him and he shall be caught in my dragnet, and I will bring him into Babylon, and I will judge him there. Whatever, then, Nebuchadnezzar did against Zedekiah, he did not do by his own strength, but by the wrath of God, in whose name perjury had been committed.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 12:4
There is one who dishonors the judgment of God; there is another who honors it.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 12:4
To the one who has transgressed and has dishonored the judgment of God, Pharaoh cannot come to the rescue; he will die in the center of Babylon for his transgressions.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord: And I myself will take of the marrow of the lofty cedar, and will set it; from the top of its branches I will strip off a tender shoot, and I will plant it upon a high and eminent mountain. On the lofty mountain of Israel I will plant it, and it will break forth into a sprout and bear fruit, and it will become a great cedar, and all birds will dwell under it, every winged creature nesting under the shade of its foliage. And all the trees of the region shall know that I the Lord have brought low the lofty tree and raised up the low tree, and dried up the green tree and made the dry tree flourish: I the Lord have spoken and have done it. (LXX: "For thus says Adonai the Lord: And I will take away of the choice parts of the cedar from the top ※ and I will give from the head of its branches ⁚, from their heart I will take away, and I will plant upon a high mountain; and I will hang it on the lofty mountain of Israel, and I will plant, and it will bring forth a sprout and bear fruit and will become a great cedar, and every bird will rest under it, and every winged creature will rest under its shade ÷ and its branches will be restored ⁚. And all the trees of the field shall know that I am the Lord who bring low the lofty tree and exalt the low tree, and make the green tree dry and make the dry tree sprout: I the Lord have spoken and I do it.") What is read in the Seventy: And I will give from the head of its branches, has been added from the edition of Theodotion; and again what follows: And its branches will be restored, must be marked with an obelus, because it is not found in the Hebrew. The real Nebuchadnezzar takes of the marrow of the lofty cedar, from the top of its branches, for this purpose: That the kingdom may be lowly and not lift itself up; but the Lord God, the Father almighty, who spoke to Ezekiel, takes from the royal stock and from the line of David: And plants it upon a high and eminent mountain; he it is who speaks in the psalm: But I have been set up as king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain. For the prince had failed from Judah and the leader from Israel, until he should come for whom it is reserved: And he shall be the expectation of the nations.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 12:5

Consider the sublime grandeur of the church of Christ, to understand that according to the promise of God the word has been realized.… It will become a noble cedar; and under it will dwell all kinds of beasts; in the shade of its branches birds of every sort will nest.
HOMILIES ON EZEKIEL 12:5
Take the wings of the word of God, and you will be able to repose under this tree that has been planted over a high mountain.
Commentary on Ezekiel

He broke forth into a sprout and bore fruit, and surpassed all the cedars by his loftiness, so that all the birds of heaven dwell under him, and all winged creatures are protected by his shade — he of whom Habakkuk says: Horns in his hands: there his strength is hidden, and who desires to gather, like a hen, the chicks under his wings —, so that all the trees of the region may know that he himself is the Lord; τροπικῶς [figuratively] speaking of believers: he who brought low Israel, once a lofty tree, and exalted the lowly people of the Gentiles; who dried up the green tree of the Jews, flowering and sprouting in the Law and the Prophets, and made the dry tree of the nations flourish, so that what he had always spoken he might fulfill in deed; the same thing is signified also by the words of Simeon in the Gospel, saying: Behold, this one is set for the ruin and for the resurrection of many, and by the grain of mustard seed which, though it is the smallest of all seeds, once it has grown is a dwelling place for birds.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Some interpret it otherwise, referring the lofty tree brought low and the low tree exalted to the passion of the Lord Savior: Who, though he was in the form of God, did not count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; and after the resurrection the very tree was afterward raised on high which, at first green, was dried up in death and afterward, reviving, recovered its former greenness. Others, in Jewish fashion, refer both to Israel: that at the first coming it was brought low and dried up, and at the second it will be restored to its former state, when that is fulfilled which the apostle Paul says: When the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved.

n: Edge. Those in captivity would not allow that they were punished for their own sins: God convinces them of the contrary. (Worthington) --- They knew that he often visited the sins of the fathers upon the children, (Exodus xx. 5., and xxiv. 5.; Calmet) when they also hated him, (Haydock) and that many had suffered for their parents' faults, like those of Saul, David, &c. (Calmet) --- But these were all guilty of original sin at least, and death is not always a real misfortune. (Haydock) --- God seems to allow that the complaints had hitherto had some grounds, (Jeremias xxxi.) but that they should be removed after the captivity, and still more effectually by the death of Christ, who came to redeem sinners, and rejected none. By baptism he cancels original sin, the sour grape, and those who cannot receive it are not innocent. (Calmet) --- God chastises the body, but not the soul of children, for their parents' faults: (Menochius) and this conduct is a trial for them, which may increase their glory. (Haydock)
Mine. He insinuates the vocation of the Gentiles and the general redemption. All will be treated according to their works. (Calmet)

Mountains: of the sacrifices there offered to idols; (Challoner) or partaken in their usual feasts. Some irregularly worshipped God in these high places, under many pious kings; and were tolerated, (Calmet) though condemned for so doing. (Haydock) --- Woman. The pagans abstained by the light of reason. (Calmet) --- The contrary practice, "it is said," would give rise to lepers or monsters, (St. Jerome) as experience evinces. (Calmet) --- It was forbidden in the Christian Church. (St. Augustine, q. 64. in Leviticus xx. 18.; St. Gregory, resp. 10. ad Aug.) (Calmet) --- But no such questions are now asked. The prophet insists on this no more, ver. 11, 15.
Wronged. Literally, "contristated." (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "oppressed," maliciously.
Increase more than what he lent, on any pretext. (St. Jerome) (Calmet)
Robber. Hebrew, "breaker;" rude and lawless. Septuagint, "pestilent."
Abomination. This refers to the woman, (ver. 6.) or to idolatry.
Him. He alone is answerable, and shall suffer.

Sinneth. God never acted otherwise, though the Jews seem to have thought so. Temporal afflictions are the source of merit, and generally fall to the share of the saints, particularly under the new law.
Penance. The end determines all. If a person be then found just or unjust at his departure, he will be treated accordingly. (Worthington)

Will. God sincerely wishes that the sinner should be converted. If he refuse grace, it is only in punishment of former transgressions. (St. Augustine, ep. 217.) --- He wills antecedently their salvation, (1 Timothy ii. 4.) though he has a consequent will to punish them, as they speak in the schools, because they themselves will not be saved. (Sanctius) (Calmet) --- God's absolute will is always fulfilled, not that which is conditional. (St. John Damascene, Fide ii. 29.; St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae p. 1. q. 19. a. 6.) --- He does enough by offering his graces and the death of Christ, to shew that his will is sincere; though by a consequent will his justice punishes the impenitent. Thus a virtuous judge would have all to observe the laws and live: but finding some transgress, so as to become pernicious, he punishes them with death. (Worthington)
Remembered, to procure him pardon; yet he will suffer less than if he had never done any good. (Calmet)
Not right, in thus punishing or rewarding for the last act; (Theodoret) or rather, God shews that those who complain are guilty.
Alive. Mortal sin destroys that life of grace. (Calmet)
Do penance. This is requisite, as well as a change of conduct. (Worthington)

New. We can do no good of ourselves: but we are admonished of our free-will, that we may do what we can, and ask for grace. (Council of Trent, Session vi. 5, 11.) (James i. 5., and 2 Corinthians iii. 5.) (St. Augustine, &c.) (Calmet)

f: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 56

For both this man hath sinned and his parents, but his blindness proceedeth not from that. And this He said, not signifying that though this man indeed was not in such case, yet that others had been made blind from such a cause, the sins of their parents, since it cannot be that when one sinneth another should be punished. For if we allow this, we must also allow that he sinned before his birth. As therefore when He declared, "neither hath this man sinned," He said not that it is possible to sin from one's very birth, and be punished for it; so when He said, "nor his parents," He said not that one may be punished for his parents' sake. This supposition He removeth by the mouth of Ezekiel; "As I live saith the Lord, this proverb shall not be, that is used, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." And Moses saith, "The father shall not die for the child, neither shall the child die for the father."
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 14: ON REPAYING THE FATHERS' SINS UPON THE CHILDREN

WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT GOD, WHO IS PROCLAIMED AS JUST, HAS PROMISED TO REPAY THE SINS OF THE FATHERS UPON THE CHILDREN TO THE THIRD AND FOURTH GENERATION? — Anyone who doubts that God does nothing and says nothing unjust is out of his mind. Therefore, if the words of the Lord are not suppressed, but everything that relates to this same question is set forth, what seems obscure will come to light, and what is thought hardly just will be recognized as devout. For whoever suppresses the words of a question is either ignorant or shifty, preferring accusation to teaching. Further, the Lord indeed promised that He would repay the sins of the fathers upon the children, but upon those who hate Him, that is, those who, involved in their fathers’ evils, have served idols just as their fathers did. For he is an enemy of God who transfers the honor of His name to a creature. Just as the sons of the righteous, being themselves righteous, dignify the line of righteousness in themselves, while both the righteousness of the fathers and their own are exalted; so also the sons of the utterly wicked, being themselves wicked, increase hatred, because they are children of the evil and have copied their wickedness to the ruin of many. God therefore appears to speak with terror; but it is true, and it has its basis. For who does not detest both an evil man and the son of an evil man in a double way, just as he judges both a good man and the son of a good man deserving of double honor? He therefore promised to repay to the third and fourth generation so that, if after an evil father the son does not follow his father’s treachery, but the grandson becomes an imitator of his grandfather’s evils, he may know that he will not be exempt from the severity of judgment; or if the grandson, not following his grandfather but his father’s footsteps, loves the Covenant of God, the great‑grandson may not be ignorant that the sentence reaches to him, if he rivals the disloyalty of his great‑grandfather. By this revealing of the Law God wished to deter wicked fathers, so that, recognizing how much evil the pursuit of idolatry produces, they might be recalled to reverence for the Creator by affection for their children; or so that the children, fearing lest they experience their fathers’ sins, might obey the Law of God. But those who add to their wickedness began to interpret this differently, saying, “Our fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge,” so that, feeling secure about exemption, because the sins would be repaid to their children, they would have no devotion either in spirit or in flesh. Therefore it is said to them, “The son shall not die for the father, nor the father for the son; but the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:2, 4). In order that they might learn that it would not be without penalty for them, but that the sins of the fathers are repaid to the children in this way: since they have followed the wickedness of their parents and have repeated the evils which should have been blotted out, they are punished more bitterly. After God showed what evil idolatry produces, He immediately added what good follows for those who love Him, saying, “And showing mercy to thousands upon thousands of those who love Me and keep My commandments” (Exod. 20:6): so that the good of a father is repaid not only up to the great‑grandson, but up to thousands upon thousands. Suppose, for instance, that someone from the seed of David loves God, knowing for certain that David lived a thousand years earlier: to this man the mercy of God is added, so that in time of need, with two reasons to support him, he may merit to receive mercy, because he himself is a worshiper of God, and because he is of the seed of one who loved God. And in this the mercy of God is praiseworthy, that He repays to those who hate Him only up to the third and fourth generation, and not to thousands upon thousands: so that, if evil is drawn out into a fifth generation, from there it again begins to have its starting‑point, so that from that point it is counted up to a third and fourth generation. But someone will say: It seems more just that more should be repaid to the originator than to the imitator. Vengeance is rightly given to the originator; but what is said about more being repaid to the sons is a punishment upon the fathers. And if you seek the reason, by the coming of the Law sinners become more guilty, like Lamech and those after Lamech. Yet it seems to some that the sins of the fathers were repaid to the children in this way: when they were led into captivity because of their fathers and remained there up to the fourth generation. If this is true, He repaid the sins of the fathers not only to those who hated Him, but also to those who loved His name: for Daniel was taken away, and the three youths, and Baruch, and Ezekiel, and Ezra was born there. It clearly appears, then, that what we said above fits the question that has been proposed.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What is it that you turn a parable into this proverb among you in the land of Israel, saying: The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge? (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ÷ Son of man, ⁚ what is the parable among the sons of Israel, of those who say: The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge?") What the Seventy said, Son of man, is not found in the Hebrew. Now divine Scripture warns that what was said in Exodus, I am the Lord your God; a jealous God, who render the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation for those who hate me, and show mercy to thousands for those who love me and keep my precepts, and again, The Lord descended in a cloud and stood beside Moses, and Moses called on the name of the Lord, and the Lord passed before his face, and he called on him, saying: Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and of much mercy and true, and keeping righteousness and mercy to thousands, taking away iniquities and injustices and sins, and he will not cleanse the guilty, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons and upon the sons of the sons to the third and fourth generation, ought to be taken thus, as a parable and a proverb, so that it sounds one thing in the words and holds another in the sense; which we also said above on the parable of the two eagles. Hence the Lord in Psalm 77 (78): I will open, he says, my mouth in parables, I will utter propositions from the beginning; and in the Gospel he sets forth the parable of the sowing, and of the darnel, and of the mustard seed, which, though it is the least of all seeds, rises up into a great tree, in such a way that he presents one thing in the words and holds another in the sense; and we, up to the present day, think that the two testimonies of Exodus which we set down above are not a parable, but set out a simple statement. And although we would not dare to say anything, nor would the earthen vessel speak against the potter, 'why have you made me thus or thus', yet we suffered a hidden stumbling block, because it seemed an injustice on God's part that one should sin and another pay for the sins. For if he renders the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one should sin and another be punished; but from what follows, for those who hate me, the stumbling block of the threat, or of the precept, is resolved: for they are not punished to the third and fourth generation because their fathers transgressed, since it is rather the fathers, who were the sinners, who ought to have been punished, but because they proved to be imitators of their fathers and hated God, by an inherited evil, the impiety growing from the root into the branches as well. At this place the heretics who do not receive the Old Testament are accustomed to say against the Creator: How good and righteous is the God of the Law and the Prophets, who, resting and silent at the sins of the fathers, repays those who have not sinned; nay rather, how great is the cruelty in him, that he should extend his wrath even to the third and fourth generation! To them we shall reply that even in this the clemency of God the Creator is shown: for it is not a mark of ferocity and severity to hold back wrath until the third and fourth generation, but a sign of mercy to defer the punishment of sin; for when he says, The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and of much compassion, and adds, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons and the sons of the sons, he indicates this: that he is of such great mercy that he does not punish at once but defers the sentence of punishment. But if the vengeance on sinners is deferred to the third and fourth generation, what more will he do with the righteous and the holy? There follows: And keeping righteousness and mercy to many thousands for those who keep his commandments and do his precepts. It is written in Proverbs: As a sour grape is harmful to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who practice it; from which it is clear that it is not the teeth of others that ache and are set on edge, but the teeth of those who have eaten the sour grape. And this is the sense of this passage: just as, if anyone should wish to say, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge, it is ridiculous and has no logical consequence, so it is unjust and perverse that the fathers should sin and the sons and grandsons be tormented. There are those who expound what is written in Exodus, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation, in such a way as to refer the statement to the human soul, saying that the father in us is the light prick of the senses and the incitements of the vices; the son, if the thought has conceived the sin; the grandson, if you carry out in deed what you have thought and conceived; and the great-grandson, that is, the fourth generation, if you not only do what is evil and wicked but glory in your crimes, according to what is written: The impious man, when he has come into the depth of evils, despises. God therefore by no means punishes the first and second goads of thoughts, which the Greeks call προπαθείας [pre-passions, the first movements of the mind], without which no human being can exist, but only if someone has resolved to do what he has thought, or has been unwilling to correct by repentance the very things he has done; whence it is written: No human being is without sin, not even if his life be of a single day. But the years of his life are numbered; and in another place: Who will boast that he has a chaste heart?; and again: The stars too are not clean in his sight, and against his angels he has devised something perverse. But if that sublime nature is not free of sin, what is to be said of human beings who, surrounded by fragile flesh, must say with the Apostle: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?, and that word, that when we have done all things we must say, We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done, and: Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it has kept watch in vain? Now in proof of this point, that the first impulse of thoughts, or rather the slight prompting of the mind, is by no means punished by God, but only if you complete in deed what you have conceived in the mind, that passage of Genesis must be brought forward: Ham sinned in mocking his father's nakedness, and the sentence was received not by him who laughed but by his son Canaan: Cursed, he says, be Canaan; a servant he shall be to his brothers. For what righteousness is there in this, that the father should have sinned and the sentence be pronounced against the son? Likewise what the Apostle sets down in the opposite direction, that the woman is saved if her son remains in faith and holiness and chastity, would seem not to have the righteousness of a sentence, namely that if the sons and grandsons are good, the parents are saved; for how many parents are holy and have wicked sons, and, on the contrary, how many are sinners and beget holy sons? Therefore all that we said above is to be taken according to this sense: that the sins of parents and begetters are punished in the branches, not in the root. Let it suffice for the present to have said this about the proverb, or the parable: that the Law and the Prophets, that is, Exodus and Ezekiel, or rather God himself, who spoke both here and there, should by no means seem to disagree in their statements, or to correct here what he had said badly there. But if anyone can find either a better sense or another one, which removes the stumbling block of testimonies contrary to one another, it is rather his opinion that is to be accepted.
Enchiridion 46

It was this new covenant that was prophesied about when it was said by Ezekiel that the children should not bear the iniquity of the parents, and that it should no longer be a proverb in Israel, "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." Here lies the necessity that each person should be born again, that he might be freed from the sin in which he was born. For the sins committed afterwards can be cured by penitence, as we see is the case after baptism.
Commentary on Zephaniah

But if they wish to say that after the return from Babylon these nations were subjected to the people of Israel, first we shall demand the authority of the Scriptures by which they may prove that this happened; then, when they are quite unable to demonstrate it, we shall grant it to them out of superfluity and say: Suppose that what you say happened; what justice of God would it be that the grandfathers blasphemed and the forefathers reproached, and afterwards it was repaid to the grandsons? Especially since that sentence by which it was formerly said in the law that the sins of the fathers are repaid upon the sons in the third and the fourth generation has been loosed through Ezekiel: As I live, says the Lord; this parable shall no longer be spoken, but the soul that sins, it shall die. And at the same time notice that what was said is a parable, and does not mean what they bring forward on the surface of the letter.
Commentary on Ezekiel

As I live, says the Lord, if this parable shall be any longer to you as a proverb in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sins, it shall die. (LXX: "As I live, says the Lord Adonai, if it shall be any longer that this parable is spoken in Israel; for all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sins, it shall die.") What As I live, says the Lord means, and parable or proverb, we have said more fully above; it will by no means be spoken in Israel, but among those who do not have the knowledge of God and cannot discern the truth.
DIALOGUE WITH HERACLIDES
I know also another kind of death, in which a man dies for God; of it it is said: "The soul that sins shall itself die."
On the Death of Satyrus 2.36
The soul dies to the Lord, not through natural infirmity but through the sickness caused by guilt. This type of death is not the release from this life but is the fall resulting from sin.
Against the Pelagians 3.11
Show me a body that has never been sick or one that is sure of enjoying good health forever after sickness, and I will show you a soul that has never sinned.
LETTERS 60:8

The soul therefore that has not sinned shall live. Neither the virtues nor the vices of parents are imputed to their children. God takes account of us only from the time when we are born anew in Christ.
Commentary on Ezekiel

All, he says, souls are mine, according to creation, not according to merit, as Moses was called a man of God, of whom it is written, A prayer of Moses, the man of God, and Elijah, who said to the captain of fifty soldiers, And if I am a man of God, let fire come down upon you and upon the fifty men; but the man of sin and son of iniquity is not called a man of God, just as those are called servants and attendants of God of whom it cannot be said, Everyone who commits sin is the servant of sin, and again, For by whom anyone is overcome, to him he is also a servant. Just as the sins of the sons do not harm the fathers, so the sins of the fathers do not overflow onto the sons, but the soul that sins, it shall die: not by the abolition of its substance, but out of the fellowship of him who says, I am the life, and who says elsewhere, Everyone who lives and believes in me shall not die for ever, and, Amen, amen I say to you, whoever keeps my word shall not see death for ever; for our life indeed is hidden with Christ in God, the life by which we shall live when Christ, our life, appears in glory, and that which is written will be fulfilled: Amen, amen I say to you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but passes from death to life. But what is said by Balaam, Let my soul die the death of the righteous, has this sense: that he desires to die to the world and to sin, and to live with the souls of the righteous, whose life is Christ, and who can sing, I will please the Lord in the land of the living; he is not indeed the God of the dead, but of the living; and if Balaam, translated into our language, means 'a vain people', which is most true, it is clear that the formerly vain people of the nations desired to have fellowship with the souls of the righteous Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who are called εὐθεῖς, that is, 'upright' and 'righteous'; whence also the book of Genesis received its name from their designation.
LETTER 1*.1
The spiritual penalty always pertained only to the sinner.
SERMON 35:2

This whole passage is so constructed as to show that bad children are not given relief because of good parents or good children oppressed because of bad parents. So having first established this absolutely true and rock-firm principle on our own account, we go on now to examine what our obligations are in our relations with others; and here we must be very careful to distinguish between the effect of salvation, which we must seek for ourselves, and the consideration that we must show to our neighbors. If you are good, you are good with your own goodness, not with someone else's. And yet through that goodness of yours with which you are good you also rejoice over another's goodness together with him, not by exchanging goodnesses but by exchanging love.
Commentary on Ezekiel

·i· If, he says, a man is righteous and does judgment. It is written in Proverbs: The thoughts of the righteous are judgments. He who possesses this virtue, so as to do nothing without reason and judgment, can say that prophetic word, The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves; and when he has judged all things rightly, so as not to accept the person of the poor in judgment, he will fulfill the precept of the Lord, As the lesser, so also shall you judge the greater, saying boldly, My soul has longed to desire your judgments at all times, and again, I have chosen the way of truth, I have not forgotten your judgments, and in the same psalm, I have known that your judgments are righteousness; and he will advance to such great blessedness that he understands the judgments of the Lord, which are a great deep, and says with the Apostle, O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and his ways unsearchable!, and recalls in prayer, For your judgments are delightful. ·ii· After judgment follows 'righteousness', and he who has it will clearly possess Christ, who, according to the Apostle, was made for us righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that he does true righteousness and does not regard persons in judgment, but knows that, in his judgment of others, he must be judged on his own righteousness.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And a man, if he is righteous and does judgment and righteousness, does not eat on the mountains and does not lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, and does not violate his neighbor's wife, and does not approach a menstruous woman, and does not grieve a man, returns the pledge to the debtor, seizes nothing by force, gives his bread to the hungry, and covers the naked with a garment, and does not lend at usury, and does not take more, turns his hand away from iniquity, does true judgment between man and man, walks in my precepts, and keeps my judgments so as to do truth: this man is righteous and shall live with life, says the Lord God. (LXX: "But a man who is righteous, who does judgment and righteousness, does not eat upon the mountains and does not lift up his eyes to the thoughts of the house of Israel, and does not defile his neighbor's wife, and does not approach a woman flowing with blood, and does not oppress a man, returns the pledge owed, and does not seize plunder, gives his bread to the hungry, and covers the naked with a garment, and does not give his money at usury, and does not take more, turns his hand away from iniquity, will do righteous judgment between a man and his neighbor, and walks in my precepts, keeps my justifications so as to do them: this man is righteous, he shall live with life, says Adonai the Lord.") 'Do you wish', he says, 'to know that what was said, I will render the sins of the fathers to the third and fourth generation, does not mean what most people suppose, and is not like this saying, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge? Hear what I am about to add: if a father is righteous, who has done these things and has not done those, and has a very wicked son who, abandoning his father's virtues, gives himself over to crimes, will not the one live with life because he is righteous, and the other die by death because he has committed all the things by avoiding which his father was made righteous?' Let us look at the catalogue of the father's virtues, which seem to me to be divided into seventeen parts; of which the first is: to have done judgment; the second, similar to this: to have joined righteousness to judgment; the third: not to have eaten on the mountains; the fourth: not to have lifted the eyes to the idols — or, as the Seventy translated, the thoughts — of the house of Israel; the fifth: not to have violated his neighbor's wife; the sixth: to have avoided the embraces of a menstruous wife; the seventh: not to have grieved a man — or, as the Seventy rendered it, oppressed through power —; the eighth: to have returned the pledge to the debtor; the ninth: to have seized nothing by force — or, according to the Seventy, not to have seized plunder —; the tenth: to have given his bread to the hungry; the eleventh: to have covered the naked with a garment; the twelfth: not to have given money at usury; the thirteenth: to have taken nothing more from what you have given; the fourteenth: to have turned his hand away from iniquity; the fifteenth, which seems similar to the first but is different in part: to have done true judgment between man and man — or, his neighbor —; the sixteenth: to have walked in the precepts of the Lord; the seventeenth: to have kept his judgments and justifications. What each of these means we shall say in what follows.
Commentary on Ezekiel

·iii· The third is: He does not eat on the mountains, which the Jews think pertains to the sin of idolatry; for we read frequently in the books of Kings and of Chronicles: Nevertheless he did not depart from the high places; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the heights, Scripture signifying this: that on mountains and in groves they sacrificed victims to idols and kindled incense. We, however, say that he eats on the mountains who says with the Pharisee: I give you thanks, God, that I am not like this tax collector. I fast twice in the sabbath, I give tithes of all my substance, and so on; but on the contrary the tax collector, hearing him who had said, Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, struck his breast with his hand, that is, the treasury of the worst thoughts, and did not dare to raise his eyes to heaven. But that too which is said elsewhere, Do not seek things greater than you, and do not search out things stronger than you, convicts all heretics of eating on the mountains of pride, and of despising the simplicity of the Church, and of not knowing that it is written of them: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. ·iiii· In the fourth place is set: And does not lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, for which the Seventy translated 'thoughts'. Now idols, that is, images which they have fashioned from their own heart, all heretics make, and to them they lift up the eyes of the heart, since they have supposed their falsehood and lie to be the truth. And those are called images of the house of Israel which are found in the Church and, by occasion of knowledge falsely so called, seduce all the simple, as they bring the dogmas of the philosophers into the house of Israel, that is, of those who behold God with the mind. ·v· In the fifth place is set: And does not violate his neighbor's wife (or defile), which plainly forbids adultery; but from the fact that it says 'his neighbor's', unless every human being is understood as a neighbor, the precept would seem to be that we abstain from the wives of friends, but freely pollute the spouses of enemies and strangers. Every human being, therefore, is to be taken as the neighbor of every human being, according to the Gospel parable set forth by the Savior about a certain man who, going down to Jericho, was wounded by robbers, when the Pharisee asks, 'who was his neighbor?', teaching that he is the neighbor who has done good. According to the mystical understanding, the wife of the holy man can be understood as wisdom, as Solomon says: Love her and she will embrace you, cherish her and she will guard you; and he desires to defile her who finds fault with the good words of others and, kindled by the torches of envy, violates holy things, corrupts chaste things, defiles pure things. ·vi· The sixth is: And does not approach a menstruous woman. Each month the heavy and sluggish bodies of women are relieved by the outflow of unclean blood, and if at that time a man has intercourse with a woman, the fetuses conceived are said to contract a defect of the seed, so that lepers and elephantiacs are born from this conception, and corrupted gore makes bodies, foul in either sex, degenerate through the smallness or the enormity of their limbs. Men are therefore commanded, not only with respect to other men's women but also with their own, to whom they are seen to be joined by law, Scripture saying, Increase and multiply and fill the earth, to know fixed times for intercourse, when they must come together and when they must abstain from their wives; which indeed both the Apostle and Ecclesiastes express: A time to embrace and a time to be far from embraces. Let the wife therefore beware lest, overcome by the desire for intercourse, she conceal it from her husband, and the husband lest he do violence to his wife, thinking that the pleasure of marriage ought to be subject to him at every time; whence Paul too: That each one, he says, may know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and chastity. It is finely said in the little maxims of Sextus the Pythagorean: An adulterer is the too ardent lover of his own wife; a book which a certain man, translating it into the Latin language, wished to adorn with the name of the martyr Sixtus, not considering that in the whole volume, which he pointlessly divided into two parts, the name of Christ and of the apostles is entirely passed over in silence; nor is it surprising if he turned a pagan philosopher into a martyr and bishop of the city of Rome, since he also changed the first book of Eusebius of Caesarea in defense of Origen to the name of the martyr Pamphilus, so that with such a eulogist he might more easily commend the most impious books Περὶ Ἀρχῶν [On First Principles] to Roman ears.
Commentary on Ezekiel

·vii· There follows in the seventh place: And does not grieve a man (or, as the Seventy translated, does not oppress through power). I do not know who is free of this vice and sin; for the Egyptians too oppressed the Hebrews through power, whence Habakkuk also complains that the impious oppresses the righteous. And would that this were said only of those who are outside, and not of those who are within! For the princes of the churches too are accustomed to oppress the people through pride, of whom it is written: They have made you prince: do not be lifted up; be among them as one of them, and the Savior commanded: Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be the least of all. But what is said according to the Hebrew, And does not grieve a man, agrees with the apostolic testimony, Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, who dwells in you; and in the Gospel according to the Hebrews, which the Nazarenes are accustomed to read, it is placed among the greatest crimes: he who has grieved his brother's spirit. But if the sadness of another kills the one who causes the grief, what must be said of iniquity and a tyrannical mind, when that saying fits, Why do earth and ashes glory?, so that a man, forgetful of his condition, how he is full of phlegm, bile and dung, and shortly to be ploughed through by worms, sets his mouth in heaven, and his tongue passes through even to the earth, and he says with the true Nebuchadnezzar, I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my throne and I will be like the Most High? ·viii· The eighth is: If he returns the pledge to the debtor; not to every debtor, otherwise for many the occasion of receiving back their pledges would become a means to riches, but to that debtor of whom it is written in the Law that he is poor and has put up his own garment, and ought to receive back his covering before sunset, lest, tormented by cold, he cry out to the Lord, who is the avenger of his injury. But if, according to what follows, we ought to give bread to the hungry and cover the naked with a garment, how much more to return what is his own, provided the debtor's poverty is beyond doubt? We can also return the pledge to the debtor when, to one to whom we are joined in love and who owes us mutual charity, we return his pledge, retaining with us nothing further of his debt. ·viiii· The ninth place is held by: Seizes nothing by force (or, according to the Seventy, does not seize plunder). The Apostle too speaks of plunderers, that among the other sinners one must not even eat with such men; and every plunder is mixed with violence, for unless force has been applied, plunder does not succeed. But there is also a holy violence and a desirable plunder, of which the Gospel writes: From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent tear it away; of which Jude the brother of James also speaks: And some indeed seize from the fire; but have mercy on others who are judged. On the contrary, the adverse powers hasten to seize their prey to the destruction of those whom they seize, which Jacob too signifies when he says: An evil beast has devoured him, an evil beast has seized Joseph. Hence also the sheep of the Lord which follow him are not seized from his hands, and he himself says: What the Father has given me is greater than all, and no one can seize it from the hand of the Father; from which is seen the one power, might and substance of the Father and the Son: for if no one can seize from the Son's hand what the Father has given, and these same things are in the Father's hand and are not seized from him, it is clearly proved that all things are common to the Father and the Son, and that the Father holds in the Son's hand, just as the things that are the Son's are held in the Father's hand. ·x· The tenth is: Gives his bread to the hungry; by which we are taught that alms are to be given not to the sated but to the hungry, and that bread is to be given not to those who belch with fullness but to those who are tormented by emptiness. In bread, moreover, every food is contained, and 'his' is said significantly, lest we turn into an act of mercy bread acquired from plunder and usury and the misfortune of others: for the redemption indeed of a man's soul is his own riches; which we see many doing who oppress their clients and the poor and the farmers through power, or commit thefts against them, to say nothing of the violence of soldiers and judges, so that out of much they bestow a little on the poor and glory in their crimes; and the deacon reads out publicly in the churches the names of the offerers, 'She offers so much, he has promised so much'; and they are pleased with themselves at the applause of the people, while their conscience torments them; and we give the wretches occasion to rejoice over what they bestow and not to mourn over what they have seized. But it is better for us to understand that the bread of righteousness is he who said, I am the bread who came down from heaven, and whom we pray in prayer to be granted to us: Our substantial bread (or that is to come) give us, so that him whom we shall afterwards receive always, we may deserve to receive daily in the present age. This bread the righteous man gives to the hungry, of whom it is written, Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled, because he who is righteous makes the common bread of all his own, the bread which had failed in Judea, as the prophet says: I will take away from them the strength (or the staff) of bread. What we are saying, provided that we are Christ's, or rather what the prophet records, is the bread of believers and of the hungry, which is by no means to be given to those who have eaten and drunk and been sated and, grown fat, have kicked, of whom it is said, Woe to you who are sated now, for you will hunger, lest they vomit it up, as Solomon says: For he will vomit it up and will defile your good words; which the Savior says in other words: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine. ·xi· The eleventh place is held by: And has covered the naked with a garment, a saying which, according to the explanation of the preceding little verse, must be expounded in two ways: that we both give covering to the naked, as the Savior says, I was naked, and you covered me, and give to those who are naked of faith and virtues the garment of Christ, of whom it is written, For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. Naked of this garment was he who, not having a wedding garment, was thrown out of the banquet. Of this nakedness the Lord also speaks to Jerusalem: You moreover were naked and full of confusion.
Commentary on Ezekiel

·xii· The twelfth number is held by: And does not lend at usury (or, as the Seventy translated, does not give his money at usury). In the Hebrew usury on all kinds of goods is forbidden, in the Seventy only on money, according to what is also written in Psalm 14 (15), Who has not given his money at usury, and as it is said, To your brother you shall not lend at interest, but to a foreigner you shall lend at interest. But see the progress: at the beginning of the Law interest is removed only from brothers; in the prophet usury is forbidden from all, as Ezekiel says, He has not given his money at usury; and further, in the Gospel there is an increase of virtue, as the Lord commands, 'Lend to those from whom you do not hope to receive back'. ·xiii· There follows in the thirteenth place: And does not take more. Some think that usury applies only to money; foreseeing this, divine Scripture removes the surplus on everything, so that you may not receive back more than you gave. In the country it is customary for 'usury', or, as the divine word calls it, 'abundance', to be exacted on grain and millet, wine and oil, and other kinds of goods; for example, that in winter we give ten modii and at harvest receive back fifteen, that is, more by half. He who thinks himself most just will take a fourth part more; and they are accustomed to argue and say: 'I gave one modius, which, when sown, made ten modii. Is it not just that I should receive half a modius more of what is mine, when he, by my generosity, has nine and a half from what is mine?' Do not err, says the Apostle: God is not mocked. For let the merciful moneylender answer us briefly whether he gave to one who had or to one who did not have. If to one who had, he certainly ought not to have given; but he gave as if to one who did not have: why then does he exact more as if from one who has? Others, in return for money lent at interest, are accustomed to accept little gifts of various kinds, and do not understand that whatever it is is called 'usury' and 'surplus' if they have received more than what they gave. ·xiiii· The fourteenth step: From iniquity, he says, he turns away his hand, so that he flees iniquity in every work. For iniquity is committed not only with the hand but with the other members too, as Solomon says, Remove iniquitous lips far from you, and in the Psalms, They have spoken iniquity on high; the foot too runs to iniquity, and the eye, if it covets another man's wife; nor would he be an imitator of him of whom it is said, He did no iniquity and no deceit was found in his mouth. Hence also we are commanded to make friends for ourselves from the unrighteous mammon, who may receive us into the eternal tabernacles. ·xv· The fifteenth is: Does true judgment between man and man (or his neighbor), which seems to mean the same as the first, where it is written, If he is righteous and does judgment; but it adds the 'truth' of the judgment which he does between man and man, or his neighbor: it is seen to have an ἐπίτασιν [intensification] of the virtues. Hence also at the opening of Proverbs, after many precepts, the 'correction' of judgment is added: To know, it says, wisdom and discipline, and to understand the words of prudence, to receive the subtleties of words, and to know true righteousness, and after all things to correct judgment. For this reason the Apostle too rebukes those who are established in the Church, because they have lawsuits among themselves, and the least and despised one is chosen, who according to the Gospel is first, to judge between man and man, he who has put away the things of a child and has attained to the perfect man; and yet he needs a greater discernment to be able to attain to the 'truth' of judgment.
Commentary on Ezekiel

·xvi· There follows in the sixteenth place: Walks in my precepts, ·xvii· and in the seventeenth: Judgments (or my justifications) he keeps, so as to do them, and keeps them once done; each of which has a manifold understanding, if we wish to go over all the commandments of the Law, in which there are said to be precepts of the Lord and in which justifications. Psalm 118 (119) is full of precepts and justifications, and in part Psalm 18 (19), in which it is written, The righteousnesses of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts and the precept of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes; in this the question is raised how God said in this same prophet, I gave them justifications not good, in which they should not live in them; and the answer is easy, and fuller in what follows: that the Jews, following the killing letter, do not live, and the Christians, understanding the life-giving spirit, do live. It would be long, if we wished to prove by testimonies where there are said to be precepts of the Lord and where justifications, and in what differences or obscurities they are each wrapped. Hence too in the present place it is added: This man is righteous, he shall live with life, says the Lord God; he who has done these things and has not done those will by no means be punished for the offenses of his father, but will live by his own virtues.

But if he begets a son who is a robber, shedding blood, and does one of these things (or, as the Seventy translated, and does sins, does not walk in the way of his righteous father), and who does not do all these things, but eats on the mountains, and pollutes his neighbor's wife, grieves the needy and the poor (or oppresses), seizes plunder, does not return the pledge, and lifts up his eyes to idols, commits abomination, gives at usury and takes more: shall he live? For 'robber' in the Hebrew is written 'pharis', which the second edition of Aquila translated 'sinner', Symmachus 'transgressor', the Seventy and Theodotion 'pestilent'.
