Certainly he will not live, but will be guilty of his own blood. Further, according to the spiritual understanding, if a righteous man of the Church has preached the evangelical faith, and his son and disciple has been deceived by heretical error, the son will be called pestilent, of whom it is written also in Psalm 1, And has not sat in the chair of pestilence, and in Proverbs, The bold and insolent and proud man is called pestilent. He has shed the blood of the deceived and doubles all sins upon himself, eating on the mountains of pride and polluting his neighbor's church, grieving the needy and the poor in the knowledge of the Scriptures, oppressing and supplanting them, seizing as plunder those whom he has seduced from the Church, not returning the pledge which he had received from his teacher so as to fulfill what is written, Freely you have received, freely give, and lifting up his eyes to the idols and images which he has fashioned from his own heart, and committing all abominations, and giving money at usury, so as to increase the teacher's error by the diligence of the disciples, and demanding back from those to whom he gave more than he had given: certainly he will not be able to live, but will die in his own blood.

But if he begets a son who, seeing all the sins of his father which he did, fears and does not do likewise, does not eat upon the mountains and does not lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, and does not violate his neighbor's wife, and does not grieve a man, does not retain the pledge, and does not seize plunder, gives his bread to the hungry, and covers the naked with a garment, turns his hand away from injury to the poor, does not take usury and surplus, does my judgments, walks in my precepts: this man shall not die in the iniquity of his father, but shall live with life. His father, because he practiced calumny and did violence to his brother, and wrought evil in the midst of his people, has died in his iniquity. 'And do not wonder', he says, 'if the son of a righteous man, turning aside to vices and sins, dies by death, since, on the contrary, the son of a sinner and impious man, if he sees the perversity of his father's ways and turns himself so as not to do evil things and to do good things, is not held guilty of his father's crimes'. This can be taken also of us, to whom it is said in the Psalms, Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and the father's house; and the king will desire your beauty, and who have been born of the stock of the nations: that we should leave behind the crimes of our parents and do judgment and righteousness and live in it. He therefore repeats what we have treated more broadly above, and so we run through everything briefly, wishing to pass on to the things that are more obscure and new.

And you say: Why has the son not borne the iniquity of the father? QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 126: ON THE PERSON WHO HAS RECEIVED FAITH IN CHRIST

ON THE PERSON WHO HAS RECEIVED FAITH IN CHRIST. — It is written: “The righteousness of the righteous shall not benefit him on the day that he goes astray; and the wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him when he turns back” (Ezek. 18:26–27). And the Lord in the Gospel says: “He who does not believe is already judged” (Jn. 3:18); by this indicating that the one who believes is not subject to judgment for the reception of a sentence, but will be found worthy of praise by the merit of faith. Therefore, the knowledge of God has this privilege, that it obtains the remission of sins. For the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God is deemed worthy to be freed from all sins. Long wandering in error, tossed by the waves of ignorance in various ways, he has at last been enlightened and has received the flashing light of truth, in which, after great storms, he rests in safety. It is fitting that after this knowledge he restrain himself from those things which he used to do long before when he was set in ignorance. For what does knowledge profit if the former way of life remains? One is seen to have known God if he changes his life and corrects his conduct. For once God is known, he must be feared, because he is proclaimed as the one who will judge: so that the faithful may receive the fruit of their righteousness, and the wicked, that is, the unbelieving, may pay the due penalties for their faithlessness. It is fitting that the righteous rejoice in the future, where Christ will reign with his own: so that righteous as in this world, where the Devil is prince, they are exposed to reproach and injuries, so in the kingdom of Christ they may appear glorious for the sake of him for whom they were judged shameful by worldly people. But the unrighteous, who seem to flourish falsely, resisting the truth by lies, are to be afflicted in punishment; so that those who appeared glorious by hoax may appear exceedingly despised and humbled by the reality. Then the righteous will rejoice that they have believed, when they see the faithless tormented; and the faithless will not even regret that they did not believe except when they see the glory of those whom they considered foolish and shameful because they believed, and their own punishment. Therefore, from the fact that someone professes to be a Christian, he must strive not to sin and arm himself against vices; and because it is impossible always to win, if he is overcome he should grieve lest he be overcome again; for the one who is grieved that he has been beaten restores himself. Whoever, then, resists has a basis on which he can excuse himself if he has been overcome. He shows that he had the desire to win, though he was by no means able. From this there is hope that he can repair himself, so that by constant reflection he may be found more skillful and stronger in the contest. But the one who rises for the purpose of sinning, having become inexcusable, bears a very serious charge. It is worse to live under the profession of God and yet have the will to sin than for someone to be ignorant of God and live shamefully and in defilement. For such a person does not know whom he ought to fear; the other one, knowing, despises. Believers therefore receive remission of sins; yet they will not be glorious unless, after receiving faith, they live in the fear of God, so that, having struggled against the enemies of the Christian name, they may win victory and therefore deserve the reward by conquering more than they are conquered. But the one who understands God and does not approach his faith so as to live as a Christian, but instead wants to receive faith at the end so that he may die a Christian, either is ashamed to live as a Christian, or devotes himself to sins which he thinks can be forgiven him when he has believed, this person, I think, does not have a good case. For he does not want to become or live as a Christian as long as he is in the world, but wants to sin; or he is ashamed to become a Christian. What sort of God does he hope for, from whom, while he is ashamed to serve as a soldier, he wants to receive wages? Such a man is a mocker. Knowing he no longer has time to sin, with death at hand, then he wants to become a Christian; so that, because he can no longer sin, he may say that he believes in Christ, who hates sinning, not that he no longer wishes to sin, but that he cannot, because death has come first. To such people it ought to be read that “God is not mocked” (Gal. 6:7). Indeed, such persons are even accustomed to give such instructions that faith should be given only to those already failing and out of their senses, merely still breathing, fearing that they might recover and be ashamed because they have become Christians. For them the words of the Gospel must be recited: “Whoever,” says the Lord, “is ashamed of me and of my words in this generation, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in the kingdom of his Father” (Matt. 10:33). But perhaps they say: knowing that the human race is frail, therefore we want to receive faith at the end of life, so that we may no longer sin. Yet faith must be received in such a way that one knows what he is receiving. Then it will bring its benefit, if he both knows it and professes it. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). And therefore, one who by then no longer knows where he is, how can he be said to receive? He has received who professes that he has received, knowing that he has received. If they believe that remission of sins is given to those who believe, they ought to know that this one believes whose heart bears witness that he believes. For God, who promised, is the inspector of the heart: he accepts the one whom he sees believing in his heart. Therefore, whose heart does not regard the words of faith, how will he have its benefit? So the person who does not lightly become a Christian upon receiving faith can be seen to act rightly, in that he is observed to strive not to sin easily. But the one who rushes to sin does not want to receive faith, specifically so that he may not be compelled to live well, which he appears unwilling to do; but he wants to obtain faith at death, hoping for exemption and remission of past evils, so that he may be secure both regarding the past and the future, since as a dying man he can no longer sin. But this is done neither with good counsel nor with a clean conscience, that he should want to receive faith then, when he can no longer sin, rather than when he does not want to sin. To such people the saying applies: “Let us do evil that good may come”—that is, let us sin now, and at the last let us believe, and it will be forgiven us. And so it is added: “Their condemnation is just” (Rom. 3:8). For it is not fitting that forgiveness of sins be granted to those who, already knowing God, who wills that no one should sin and hates sinners, are eager to sin, refusing to consider that the gift of God benefits those who, ignorant of God, sin in such a way that they do not know God will judge. But the one who has heard and reflected within himself, and has the intention of sinning, not because he is overcome by some compelling cause, but because he wishes to sin, is hardly to be forgiven. For there are two causes which bring about the remission of sins: one is the gift, the other is repentance, so that whoever has sinned after receiving the gift should be restored through repentance. For since he did not remain in the grace received so as to persevere in freedom, but again subjected himself to sin, he obtains the blotting out of sin by weeping and groaning; for he sinned knowingly and deliberately: not that anyone is ignorant of sin itself, but the one who does not know that God will judge thinks that what he does in sin will be without punishment. Therefore, if a Gentile begins to grow weak and, in the very despair of life, considers within himself the faith and hope that have been promised, he has a complete case for his sins to be forgiven when he believes, and for him not to be held in the underworld, bearing with him the sign of death overcome and despoiled, even though he does not possess dignity or reward. For there ought to be some difference between the one who, stirred by love of his Lord, did not fear to fight against His enemies, arming himself with self‑control and with the observance of all virtues, so that he might resist evil, always anxious as to how he may defend the dominion of his Lord; and the one who, having made common cause with the enemies of his Lord and standing by their side, at the end of life returned to his Lord, not in order to claim the kingdom of his Lord, but so that it might benefit himself alone to be a citizen before being a soldier. For he who wishes to live as a Christian so as to be rewarded after death knows that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). And therefore, having taken up the armor of faith, he does not hesitate to engage with principalities and powers, so that, being a victor in this world, he may be crowned after this world. For it is fitting that the one who, among the faithless and rebels, bears witness to the kingdom of his Lord in the present should receive a reward for this in the future: so that the enemies of God, seeing the witness of Christ appear exalted in the kingdom of God because of the truth of his confession, may grieve in confusion that they judged false what has been shown to be true; and also that those who believed late, confessing God not in life but in death, when they see how great is the glory of those who, fighting under the armor of Christ, have waged the battles of their Emperor devoutly and faithfully, may regret not that they lived as Christians, but that they were Christians only in death. For one who had no intention of living as a Christian can seem hardly suitable to die as a Christian: perhaps already on the point of death he wished to be called a Christian precisely because the time for sinning was now past. “Lest,” he says, “what is believed should prove true, I wish to become a Christian, losing nothing if what is believed is false”; and because at death it is not the will to sin, but the act of sinning, that ceases, he tests whether faith may be able to profit after death, whereas its usefulness would certainly have been this: that vices and sins should be corrected here, where they had been committed. For a person then shows that he has condemned his past deeds when, following the rule of faith, he appears to change his conduct and his life. For if before he sinned on this account, that he did not know God, when he comes to know Him, he ought no longer to sin, lest it be pointless that he has come to know Him. For a person ought to be made perfect by the knowledge of God. Indeed, before his profession, a Christian ought to understand that he must prove himself more by his works than by his name. For this reason the commandments were given, superior to all other laws and belonging to holiness, so that from these the worship of God might be seen: otherwise they will hear, “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46). By which He then indicated that it is beneficial to call the Lord “Lord” if His commandments are kept: for he seems a mocker who calls him Lord whose precepts he despises. To such a person the words of the Law must be recited, which say that God is not mocked. Therefore he will be condemned by his own words, because he calls Him Lord whom he shows by his deeds that he is in no way afraid of.

Rods. The king had many children, and confided in them, but they were slain.
Dry; unfit for vine-trees. He speaks of the prison of Babylon. (Calmet) --- The country was naturally wet. (Haydock)
Fire. Ismael, who slew Godolias, was of the royal family, Jeremias xli., &c. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

From this it is plain that both the earlier reading, in which it is said: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions?, and this one, in which it is written: Your mother is like a vine in your blood, planted upon water, pertain to Jerusalem, which lost her lions and her shoots, and there did not remain in her a rod that might rise up into a tribe or into the scepters of rulers. For it begins from a lament and ends in a lament: Take up a lament over the princes of Israel, that is, at the beginning, and now at the end: It is a lament; and the royal stock is to be attended by the lamentation and lament of the parable. Moreover, according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], what others refer to the heavenly Jerusalem — so as to say that from it very many fell down into this valley of tears, and that kings ceased to be, and that the once most beautiful vine was dried up by the burning wind, so that none of its green shoots remained in it, the vine which Jeremiah afterwards laments under the figure of the city — we understand of the Church — because in the last time, iniquity having been multiplied, the love of many grows cold, so that if it can be, even the elect of God are tested, and her princes are caught in the nets of the devil, who is not content with the capture of one king but hastens daily to capture kings and princes, according to what is written: His foods are choice —. The shoots of the Church too, which formerly were equaled to flowers and to the redness of blood, are afterwards dried up by the burning wind; and this exposition the parable of the Gospel also sounds forth, in which, when the sun had risen, the things that had sprouted were scorched and suddenly dried up, so that scarcely one of the shoots remains to rise up into a rod and become a worthy prince of the people, which Isaiah says in other words: I will bring famine and thirst upon the land, and not a famine of bread and a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God. Hence we must lament and wail over the princes of Israel, through whose vice and pride Judea was deserted, and Jerusalem was captured.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you, take up a lament over the princes of Israel, and you shall say: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions, in the midst of young lions rear her whelps? And she brought out one of her young lions, he became a lion, and he learned to catch prey and to devour man. And the nations heard of him, and not without wounds of their own they caught him, and they brought him in chains into the land of Egypt. And when she had seen that she was weakened and her expectation had perished, she took one of her young lions, she made him a lion. He went about among the lions and became a lion, he learned to catch prey and to devour men; he learned to make widows, and to bring their cities into a desert, and the land and its fullness was made desolate by the sound of his roaring. And the nations gathered against him from every side, from the provinces, and they spread their net over him; in their wounds he was caught. And they put him into a cage, in chains, and they brought him to the king of Babylon; and they put him into prison, so that his voice should no longer be heard upon the mountains of Israel. (LXX: "And you, take a lamentation over the prince of Israel, and you shall say: Why has your mother become a whelp in the midst of lions, in the midst of lions she multiplied her whelps? And one of her whelps sprang forth, he became a lion, and he learned to seize spoils, he devoured men. And the nations heard against him, in their corruption he was caught, and they brought him in a muzzle into the land of Egypt. And she saw that he had been taken away from her and that her substance had perished, and she took another of her whelps, she made him a lion. And he went about in the midst of the lions, he became a lion, and he learned to seize spoils, he devoured men; and he fed in his boldness, and he brought their cities to a desert, and he laid waste the land and its fullness by the sound of his roaring. And he set nations against him round about from the regions, and they spread their nets over him, in their corruption he was caught. And they put him in a muzzle and in a cage, he came to the king of Babylon; and they brought him into prison, so that his voice should not be heard any longer upon the mountains of Israel.") I know that I have read in this place a manifold explanation, and one entangled in such great obscurities that it did not so much open up the reading as wrap it up, since it refers everything that is written to the opposing powers and describes lions and wars in the heavenly Jerusalem, how one of them was captured and another was in turn set up in his place; and it sets out many testimonies that the devil and his companions are customarily called lions, such as that saying of the apostle Peter: Our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion and seeks how he may enter, and that of the Psalms: Do not hand over to the beasts the souls that confess to you; certainly, when it comes to the history, it says that Johanan the son of Kareah was led into Egypt (how he, fleeing with a few men, is to be called a lion, I am unable to know), and that the other lion is Zedekiah, who was himself also led into Babylon. But we, leaving explanations of this kind to the judgment of the reader, say that, with the captivity close at hand, the prophet is not so much foretelling things to come as narrating things past. For after the sixth year of King Zedekiah — since immediately in what follows we read: And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth of the month — a lament is taken up over the princes — or the prince — of Israel, and it is said: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions? The lament, then, is over the princes, namely all who were begotten of the stock of Josiah. Jerusalem, the mother of the princes, is called a lioness, who bore and reared young lions, and brought out one of her young lions and made him a lion, signifying Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, whom Pharaoh Neco led into Egypt, and in his place he set up Jehoiakim; and when he had died, Jeconiah his son, having been made king, was led to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar together with his mother and the nobles of the city; of him is born Shealtiel, the father of Zerubbabel, who received his name from the fact that he was born in Babylon. And it is plain that under the μεταφορᾷ [metaphor] of the lioness, of the young lions and of the lion, and again of another lion, those things are described which had already been done at the time when the prophet was saying these things.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For after Jerusalem had brought out Jehoahaz the son of Josiah from the royal stock and made him king, he proved so cruel in a short time that he is related, tropologically, to have caught prey and devoured men.
Commentary on Ezekiel

When the Egyptian had come against him, he caught him not without wounds — or in a pit, as is properly contained in the Hebrew, so as to preserve the tropological capture of lions, which are always caught in pits — and he brought him in a muzzle, or in chains, into the land of Egypt, and there he died.
Commentary on Ezekiel

When his mother Jerusalem, who had borne him, who had reared him, who had set him in the kingship, had seen that her expectation had perished, she took from among the other kings Jeconiah, the son of Jehoiakim, and set him up as king.
Commentary on Ezekiel

He too, having imitated the cruelty of his predecessor, is described under the ferocity of a lion, in that he devoured men, made many widows, brought cities to a desert, and at the sound of his roaring the whole province was terrified, so that the nations gathered against him and spread their net and caught him in a pit and put him in a cage and in chains — not that this was done to Jeconiah: for he gave himself up to the king of Babylonia and was carried off into Chaldea; but so that the metaphor of the lion may be preserved, which is caught in pits and bound with chains and kept in cages —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Otherwise, according to the history, we read this of Zedekiah, who was set up as king of Jerusalem after Jeconiah — and this is what gave occasion for most people to understand Zedekiah rather than Jeconiah, because chains are read of, and cages, and a prison is named —; he was, then, kept in prison and not put to death, and was only removed from the kingship. But the history relates that Zedekiah was led blind into Babylon and there immediately killed.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Your mother is like a vine in your blood, planted upon the water; its fruits and its leaves grew from many waters; and it had solid rods for the scepters of rulers, and its stature was exalted into leaves, and it saw its height in the multitude of its shoots. And it was plucked up in wrath, and cast down to the ground, and the burning wind dried up its fruits; the rods of its strength withered and were dried up, fire devoured it. And now it is transplanted into the desert, in a land impassable and thirsty. And fire went out from the rod of its branches, which devoured its fruit; and there was not in it a strong rod, a scepter of rulers. It is a lament, and it shall be for a lament. (LXX: "Your mother is like a vine, like a flower on pomegranates, planted in water; its fruit and its sprout came from much water; and it had a rod of strength for a tribe of leaders, and it was exalted in its greatness in the midst of its offshoots, and it saw its greatness in the multitude of its shoots. And broken in fury, it was cast to the ground, and the burning wind dried up its choice parts; they were avenged, and the rod of its strength was dried up, fire consumed it. And now they have planted it in the desert, in a land without water. And fire went out from the rod of its choice ones, and devoured it, and there was not in it a rod of strength. A tribe is in a parable of lamentation, and it shall be for a lament.") One thing is said in different words; and just as in the earlier passages we read that Jerusalem was compared to a beautiful woman, and again to a lioness who reared lions in her lair, so now she is compared to a vine-stock or a most beautiful vine planted upon many waters; and that therefore its shoots, nourished by the moisture, grew so much that one shoot, which Scripture calls a most solid or most strong rod, advanced 'into the scepters of rulers' — for which the Seventy rendered 'into a tribe of leaders' — so, namely, that kings should be made from it. And the vine itself was of such beauty that the splendor of its greenness was made equal to the flowers of the pomegranate, which is what is said in the Hebrew, like a vine in your blood, the redness of its flowers being compared to blood.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The vine, then, was exalted and raised up; because God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, it was plucked up in the fury of the Lord and cast down to the ground, so that the elegant metaphor of the vine-stock might preserve the ruins of Jerusalem; for however beautiful a vine may be and however far it stretches out with long runners, unless you raise up stakes and reeds, joined to the earth it dries up from the heat, especially if the burning wind, which the Greeks call καύσωνα [the scorching wind], has dried up its fruits, so that it withers and is burned as though by the blazing heat of fire. But as for what has been added in the Seventy, And they were avenged, in place of what is written in the Hebrew, They withered, what coherence it can have I am unable to know.
Commentary on Ezekiel

That vine, then, of such abundance and of such fruits and of such beauty, how is it now carried over into the desert, in a land impassable and thirsty? And it signifies the land of Babylon, to which they were carried over, or Egypt, where they fled for refuge, or the land of Judea itself, in which a few poor people remained, over whom Gedaliah was set to gather and rule the remnant of the people; against him there rose up, from the royal stock and from the rod of the branches of the vine, Ishmael, who killed him at Mizpah and devoured all the fruit of the vine; and from then on there was not in that vine a strong rod and a scepter of rulers: for none of the kings remained to govern the people, but with Johanan, the son of Kareah, they fled to Egypt. Therefore it is a lament and a parable of lamentation, so that the royal line may be lamented, which will thenceforth cease in Judea until he should come for whom it is reserved: And he was the expectation of the nations.

n: Month: the year of the world 3411, August 27. (Usher) --- Ezechiel had prophesied in the fourth year; then was silent a year and two months, or 430 days. He opened his mouth again in the sixth year, (chap. viii. 1.) and now in the seventh year he is ordered not to answer. (Worthington) --- We know not what the ancients wanted to know; but their design was evil. (Calmet)

Judgest them; or, if thou wilt enter into the cause, and plead against them. (Challoner) --- Lay before them the iniquities of their fathers, and their own, which bring on the reprobation of the greatest part. God will form his Church out of a few of them and of the Gentiles. The return of a small number from captivity is also insinuated.
Excelleth. Hebrew, "is beauty or a desire." Septuagint, "a honeycomb." (Calmet)

Scandals, &c., (offensiones) that is, the abominations or idols, to the worship of which they were allured by their eyes. (Challoner) --- Moses found them in this condition in Egypt, and he could not entirely reclaim them. (Calmet) --- Many still secreted their idols, chap. xxiii. 1., and Acts vii. 42. (Haydock)

Egypt. Their disorders called for such severity. But God was restrained by the dangers (Calmet) of blasphemy, &c., to which the faithful and idolaters would thus have been exposed. (Haydock) --- He saved them as he had promised, though they did not deserve it. (Worthington)
Brought. Literally, "cast," (Haydock) as if they had been reluctant.
Live, and enjoy temporal felicity, which was chiefly promised, though the faithful observers of the law would obtain an eternal reward.
Sign, as also to promote piety and instruction.

Sabbaths. We only read of one man gathering sticks, and the people manna once on those days, Exodus xv., and xvi. But Moses does not mention all. (Calmet) --- Sabbath often denotes the whole law, which they transgressed; and as long as they retained an affection for idols, they could not observe the sabbaths so as to please God.

But. Literally, "And I did for," &c. This motive caused me to spare them. (Haydock) --- I punished only the most guilty adorers of the calf, and murmurers, &c., Numbers xiv. 28. (Calmet) --- Some were always preserved for a succession, ver. 9, 22. (Worthington)

Again, or also. (Haydock) --- Four times are specified [in] ver. 13, 15, 21., which may allude to the adoration of the calf, the graves of concupiscence, the murmuring, and commerce with the women and idols of Moab, Exodus xxiii., and Numbers x., and xiv., and xxv. (Calmet)

Not good. The laws and ordinances of their enemies: or those imposed upon them by that cruel tyrant the devil, to whose power they were delivered up for their sins; (Challoner) which may be styled the statutes of your fathers, &c., ver. 18. (Haydock) --- God is often said to do what he only permits. (Calmet) --- He abandoned them to their own perversity. (St. Jerome) (Deuteronomy xxxii. 21, 37.) --- If God had spoken of the Decalogue, &c., would he say such laws were not good, after he had testified that the observers shall live in them? ver. 11. He established the ceremonial law, at the same time. See Kimchi; Menochius, &c. Chaldean, "I have given them up to their foolish desires. They have established bad statutes and laws which will not give them life." This seems the best explanation. (Calmet) --- Hebrew, "Have I given....(26) and have I polluted them?" &c. (Manasse Ben. Israel.) The precepts had also a bad effect, and were given in condescension to the weakness of the people, (Origen) particularly the ceremonial part. (St. Just.[St. Justin Martyr?]; St. Chrysostom; St. Jerome, &c.) --- They did not justify, (St. Augustine) and were not good, compared with those of the new law. (St. Gregory, mor. xxviii. 9.) --- Thus Solon gave the Athenians "the best laws that they would receive," (Plutarch) though others more perfect might have been devised. (Calmet)

I polluted them, &c. That is, I gave them up to such blindness, in punishment of their offences, as to pollute themselves with the blood of all their first-born, whom they offered up to their idols in compliance with their wicked devices. (Challoner) (Menochius) (Leviticus xviii. 21., and 4 Kings iii. ultra[last verse], and xxi. 6. (Calmet) --- Offered. Protestants, "caused to pass through the fire all,["] &c., chap. xvi. 21. --- For their. Protestants, "that I might make them desolate to the end, that," &c.

Called high. Hebrew, "Bamah," (Haydock) out of contempt. (Calmet) --- The Jews were so much attached to the high places, that they called the altar of the Lord by the same name. Thus heretics are convicted by the very names they use, calling sacrifice service, &c. (Worthington)
Stones. This was the secret intention of the ancients, (ver. 1.; Haydock) and of many in captivity, who were only praise-worthy compared with those at Jerusalem, chap. xi. 15.
Out. I will not allow you to follow idols with impunity. (Calmet)
Of people. That is, a desert, in which there are no people; (Challoner) meaning Judea, to which they should return.
Covenant of the gospel, by the powerful attractions of grace, Luke xiv. 24., John vi. 69., and vii. 46., and 2 Corinthians x. 4.
Israel. They shall continue in exile; or the rebel Jews who will not believe in Christ, shall be cast off. (Calmet)

Walk, &c. It is not an allowance, much less a commandment to serve idols; but a figure of speech, by which God would have them to understand, that if they would walk after their idols, they must not pretend to serve him at the same time: for that he would by no means suffer such a mixture of worship. (Challoner) (St. Jerome) --- Continue, if you dare, to serve idols. I will still bring you back. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "take away each your devices; and then if you hear me, (Grabe's copy adds, not) and defile not my," &c. (Haydock) --- God would rather have idolaters leave him wholly, than halt between two, (3 Kings xviii.) neither hot nor cold; (Apocalypse iii.) for such dishonour God's name the most, Romans ii. 24. (Worthington)

Mountain. The foregoing verse, to make the sense complete, must be understood so as to condemn and reject that mixture of worship which the Jews then followed. In this verse God promises to the true Israelites, especially to those of the Christian Church, that they should serve him in another manner in his holy mountain, the spiritual Sion, and shall be accepted of by him. (Challoner)
Committed. This is a picture of the converts to Christianity. (Calmet)

Of the south. Jerusalem lay towards the south of Babylon, where the prophet then was, and is here called the forest of the south field, and is threatened with utter desolation. (Challoner) See chap. xxi. (Calmet) --- In Jerusalem there were good and bad. (Worthington)
Burned, with war and famine, Jeremias xxi. 14. (Calmet) --- North, from Egypt to Mesopotamia. (Theodoret) --- Nabuchodonosor invaded those parts. (Haydock)

Parables. They were easy enough to understand, but the Jews would not comprehend them no more than our Saviour's words, John x. 24. (Calmet) --- Much of this prophecy was so hard, that all seemed to be parables. (Worthington)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth, on the tenth of the month, there came men of the elders of Israel to inquire of the Lord, and they sat before me. Eleven months and five days after the previous vision, the word again comes to the prophet, after some of the elders of the house of Israel had come to inquire of the Lord and had sat before him. That it was the custom of the people of Israel to seek from the Lord through the prophets whatever they desired to know, many examples testify: Saul, looking for the asses, goes to Samuel and received advice from the servant boy to offer the prophet the fourth part of a shekel; when the son of Jeroboam fell ill, his wife is sent to Shiloh to the prophet Ahijah, bringing little gifts, loaves and cakes, grapes and a small jar of honey, to learn about her son's sickness; David too, a prophet, inquires of another prophet, Nathan, whether he ought to build a temple to the Lord; and Ahab asks whether he should go up to Ramoth-gilead or not; in Isaiah also and in the volume of Kings the things that were to come upon Sennacherib are announced. Nor is it surprising if in the Old Testament the prophets announce to individuals the things that are to come, since we read that Agabus prophesied the things that were to come upon Paul; for it is written in Deuteronomy: The nations which the Lord is about to destroy in your sight, these will listen to dreams and divinations; but to you the Lord your God has not granted it so: for it belongs to the nations to resort to Chaldeans, soothsayers, haruspices, diviners, lot-casters, the oracles of demons, by which their error is mocked. Hence now too the elders of Israel approach the prophet in order to inquire of the Lord through him, and yet they are silent about their question, while he who was to be questioned knew what they were asking, so that in this too there might be a miracle: to know why they had come and to answer the things that a silent speech held within their mind.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Have you come to inquire of me? As I live, I will not answer you, says the Lord God. To the saints and to those who ask fitting things a promise is given: 'While you are still speaking I will say: Behold, I am here'; but to sinners, such as the elders of Israel were, whose crimes the prophet describes in what follows, no answer is given, but a rebuke for their sins, and he adds an oath: As I live, so that the sentence of the one who refuses may be the firmer. What the Seventy said: If I answer you, Symmachus translated more plainly: I will not answer you.
Commentary on Ezekiel

If you judge them, if you judge, son of man. (LXX: "If I avenge them with vengeance, son of man.") 'They indeed came to inquire, wishing to learn the future concerning the things about which they are in doubt. But you, son of man, judge them, so that there may be no prophet's answer, but the sentence of one who judges, for the iniquities which they have committed, and they have followed the crimes of their fathers'; or certainly: If I avenge them with vengeance, so that the sense is: 'They are covered with such great iniquity that they are not worthy even of correction and reproof', according to what is said in the prophet: I will no longer visit your daughters and your daughters-in-law, when they have committed adultery. Hence sinners too, who have come into the depth of sin, are let go to do the desires of their heart.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Show them the abominations of their fathers. And you shall say to them. (LXX: "Testify to them the iniquities of their fathers, and you shall say to them.") If the sins of the fathers do not overflow onto the sons, how is it that the abominations and iniquities of the fathers are now set before the elders? For this reason, evidently: that they may be shown to act like their parents and, by a hereditary evil, to drag a very long rope of sins, so that they may dread the punishments of those whose vices they imitate.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God: On the day when I chose Israel, and lifted up my hand for the stock of the house of Jacob, and appeared to them in the land of Egypt, and lifted up my hand for them, saying: I am the Lord your God. On that day I lifted up my hand for them, to lead them out of the land of Egypt into the land which I had provided for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is excellent among all lands. (LXX: "Thus says the Lord God: From the day on which I chose the house of Israel, and became known to the seed of the house of Jacob, and was known to them in the land of Egypt, and took them up, saying: I am the Lord your God. On that day I took hold of them with my hand, saying, to lead them out of the land of Egypt into the land which I prepared for them, a land flowing with milk and honey, it is a honeycomb beyond all lands.") For what the Seventy said: It is a honeycomb beyond all lands, for which we translated: It is excellent among all lands, the first edition of Aquila put 'firm support', the second 'renowned', Symmachus 'region', Theodotion 'strength', namely because this land is the foundation of all lands, because in it are the religion of God and the temple and the ceremonies and the knowledge of God; and so far was the people of Israel, settled in Egypt, from knowing God, that Moses, sent to them: If they ask, he says, me: Who sent you?, what shall I say to them? Say, he says, to them: He who is, sent me. In Egypt, then, he became known to the people and to the seed of the house of Jacob, when he lifted up his hand for them against the Egyptians, and said: I am the Lord your God, and he chose them to lead them out of the land of Egypt to a land flowing with milk and honey; for they were not yet able to take solid food, but like little children and sucklings they needed the honey and milk of infancy. According to the letter, however, that the land of Judea is renowned and more fertile than all lands, no one will be able to doubt who has considered the whole land from Rhinocorura as far as Mount Taurus and the river Euphrates, and the power of its cities and the pleasantness of its regions, namely Palestine and Phoenicia, Arabia, Coele-Syria, Cilicia, and the other regions which the Lord promised to Israel if he had kept the precepts of God; and that he did not receive them was the fault of his unbelief. For even in Palestine itself and the province of Judea very many nations remained which were not driven out; for the guarantor is not to blame if the one to whom the promise is made has made himself unworthy of the pledge, especially since the one who promises sets out a choice: If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land. But if you are unwilling, the sword shall devour you. They are chosen, then, according to the present, and it does not follow that one who is chosen cannot be tempted or perish, since both Saul, chosen as king, and Judas, chosen as apostle, afterward fell by their own fault. The lifting up of the hand, or its stretching out, shows the posture of one who strikes: that he might strike the Egyptians for them and free the people of Israel from Egypt.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he said to them: Let each one cast away the offenses of his eyes, and do not be defiled with the idols of Egypt: I am the Lord your God. (LXX: "And he said to them: Let each one cast away the abominations of his eyes, and let him not be defiled with the inventions of Egypt: I am the Lord your God.") For 'offenses', which in Hebrew are called 'seccuse', Symmachus translated 'nauseating things', the second edition of Aquila 'cuttings-off', so as to signify that bleariness must be cast away from the eyes, and a kind of nausea which not only hinders the sight but also produces vomiting in those who look at it; 'gelule' too is a Hebrew word, which the Seventy translated 'inventions', the first edition of Aquila 'defilements', the second, and Symmachus and Theodotion, 'idols', whom we too have followed for the present. He commanded them, as they were first going out of Egypt, to forget the idols which they had served for a long time; to cast them away from their eyes, so as not to hold them worthy even of a glance, and no longer to give consent to the things by which they had long been defiled. I, he says, am the Lord your God, not the portents of Egypt, not the fabrications of various monsters. But we too, when we go out of Egypt, are commanded to cast away the offenses of our eyes, namely so that we may not take delight in the things in which we formerly took delight in the world, lest we be defiled with the images of Egypt, that is, with the inventions of the philosophers and of the heretics, which are rightly called idols. Let us also turn our eyes away from the spectacles, or rather the offenses, of Egypt: of the arena, the circus, the theaters, and all the things that defile the purity of the soul and enter the mind through the senses; and what is written is fulfilled: Death will come in through your windows.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And they provoked me. (LXX: "And they withdrew from me.") Or, as Symmachus translated: They did not consent to me; and as soon as they are called, they withdraw from God, so that there is no interval between the calling and the withdrawal. And this is to be noted, that no one withdraws from God except one who was formerly with him; hence the dragon too in the book of Job is called ἀποστάτης, a transgressor and one who withdraws.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And they would not listen; each one did not cast away the abominations of his eyes, nor did they abandon the idols of Egypt. (LXX: "And they would not listen to me; they did not cast away the abominations of their eyes, and did not abandon the inventions of Egypt.") 'For this reason', he says, 'they provoked me and withdrew from me: because they would not listen, while man's free will is preserved, and they did all the things which I commanded in the law that they should not do, at once despairing of salvation and muttering against Moses, and distrusting the promises of God'. There follows:
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I said that I would pour out my indignation upon them, and fulfill my wrath on them in the midst of the land of Egypt. 'As soon as I commanded them to leave or cast away the offenses of their eyes and by no means to be defiled with the idols of Egypt, they provoked me and would not listen to what I said, but on the contrary did what I had commanded should not be done. Therefore I had decreed to pour out on them my fury and my indignation and to fulfill my wrath, which I had conceived in my mind, in the midst of Egypt, upon those who had not yet gone out of Egypt'. For there follows: I therefore cast them out of the land of Egypt and led them down into the desert, from which it is shown that they had not yet gone out of the land of Egypt when he wished to pour out his indignation and fulfill his wrath upon them and to strike them in the midst of the land of Egypt.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations in whose midst they were, and among whom I appeared to them, to lead them out of the land of Egypt. 'What I was thinking of doing on account of justice I did not do on account of the greatness of my clemency, lest my name be defiled and I should seem not to have been able to fulfill what I had promised to Israel. I spared my name, then, lest the nations among whom I became known to them in the land of Egypt should have occasion to blaspheme'. Up to this point the prophet describes what he promised them while they were settled in the land of Egypt, and how they at once gave offense, and what the Lord thought of doing against them and yet did not do; what follows he spoke to them after they had gone out of Egypt.
Commentary on Ezekiel

I therefore cast them out of the land of Egypt, and led them out into the desert. And I gave them my precepts, and showed them my judgments, which a man should do and live in them. Moreover I also gave them my sabbaths, that it might be a sign between me and them, and that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctifies them. And the house of Israel provoked me in the desert: they did not walk in my precepts, and they cast away my judgments, which, if a man does them, he shall live in them, and they violated my sabbaths exceedingly. I said therefore that I would pour out my fury upon them in the desert and consume them. And I acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations from which I cast them out in their sight. These things are said to those who were led out of Egypt into the desert, so that, freed from the vices of the Egyptians, they might more easily fulfill the precepts of God in the wilderness and do his judgments and keep the sabbaths, which were given as a sign between the one who gave them and those to whom they were given, as Scripture says: The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command the children of Israel and you shall say to them: See that you keep my sabbaths, for it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you; and keep the sabbath, for it is holy to you: whoever violates it shall surely die; everyone who does work on it, that soul shall be put to death from the midst of its people. So the sabbath and circumcision were given as a sign of the true sabbath and the true circumcision: that we may know that we must rest from earthly works in the perfect and true sabbath, and that we should circumcise not the foreskin but the heart. Hence, working for six days, we rest on the seventh day, so that day and night we may do nothing else than recognize that all that we live is owed to the Lord, and, as the week comes round again, consecrate ourselves wholly to his name, so that through the sanctification of the day we may remember the Lord who sanctifies us.

For indeed the Sabbath did at the first confer many and great benefits; for instance, it made them gentle towards those of their household, and humane; it taught them God's providence and the creation, as Ezekiel saith; it trained them by degrees to abstain from wickedness, and disposed them to regard the things of the Spirit.

It is this truth that we shall realize perfectly when we shall be perfectly at rest and perfectly see that it is he who is God.
Commentary on Ezekiel

These precepts and ordinances and the observance of the sabbath the Lord gave in the desert, so that doing them they might live in them, not that they should pass from them to greater things, as is promised in the Gospel; and these they violated, not once nor a little but exceedingly, so that the ἐπίτασις [intensification] of the violation might be shown. He said, therefore, and decreed in his mind, that he would pour out his fury upon them in the desert and consume them, when he spoke to Moses: Let me alone, and, angered with fury against them, I will destroy them; but he would not do it, sparing the Egyptians and the other nations, lest they be scandalized, and them as well, on whom he had mercy, awaiting the repentance of those who would turn back. And it is to be noted that, when he was speaking to them while they were settled in Egypt, after the offense: I acted, he says, for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations, but now he says: I acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations from which I cast them out in their sight; for then they were still in their midst, not yet having gone out, but now, after they have gone out, it is said: From which I cast them out in their sight.
Commentary on Ezekiel

I therefore lifted up my hand over them into the desert, not to bring them into the land which I gave them, flowing with milk and honey, the foremost of all lands; because they cast away my judgments, and did not walk in my precepts, and violated my sabbaths, for their heart went after idols. And my eye spared them, so that I did not kill them; nor did I consume them in the desert. (LXX: "And I lifted up my hand over them in the desert, so as not at all to bring them into the land which I gave them, a land flowing with milk and honey, it is a honeycomb beyond every land; because they rejected my ordinances, and did not walk in my precepts, and violated my sabbaths, and they walk after the thoughts of their hearts. And my eye spared them, so that I did not wipe them out; and I did not kill them to consumption in the desert.") 'I had indeed decreed to pour out all my fury upon them and to wipe them out and consume them, but I acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned among the nations — namely the Amalekites and the rest, which fought against them in the wilderness —, so that I would by no means bring them into the land which I promised them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the foremost of all lands — or a honeycomb —'. The cause of the punishment and of this sentence is: Because they cast away my judgments, and did not walk in my precepts, and violated the sabbaths; and the cause of that cause is this: that they did not do these things because their heart followed the idols of Egypt.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'But my eye', he says, 'spared them, so that I did not kill them and wipe them out: so that I did not consume them altogether'; in which it is asked how he spared those whose corpses lay in the wilderness and, except for Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, no one entered the land of promise. From this we understand that they live, and are not reserved for eternal punishments, nor blotted out of the book of the living, nor consumed before the face of the Lord; for if, because they were not brought into the land of promise, they must be believed to have perished, then Moses too perished, who only saw the land of promise and did not enter it, of whom the Lord speaks in the book of Joshua: Moses my servant is dead, and in Malachi: Remember the law of Moses my servant, and in Jeremiah God speaks of him as of his friend and most intimate: If Moses and Samuel should stand in my sight? Otherwise we must also believe that the prayers of Moses were heard, when, interceding for the people, he says: If you forgive them their sin, forgive; but if you will not, blot me too out of your book. And that the sentence of the Lord against sons and servants is not perdition but correction, let us hear the testimonies of the Scriptures: Son, do not be saddened at the discipline of the Lord, nor faint when you are rebuked by him: for whom the Lord loves he corrects, and he scourges every son whom he receives, and in another place: When he slew them, then they sought him, and in the song of Deuteronomy: I will kill and I will make alive. We can also say this according to the letter: that he did not wipe them out nor consume them along with their stock and offspring, but, when the fathers had been killed, he spared the sons, whom he brought into the land of promise.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But he said to their sons in the wilderness: In the precepts (or statutes) of your fathers do not walk, and neither with their idols nor keep their judgments (or be defiled by thoughts). I am the Lord your God: walk in my precepts, and keep my judgments and do them, and sanctify my sabbaths, that it may be a sign between me and you, and that it may be known (or that you may know) that I am the Lord your God. After the slaying of the fathers who fell in the wilderness, he gives precepts to the sons, in whose salvation he had mercy on the fathers: 'And the eye of the Lord', he says, 'spared them, so as not to kill them altogether and wipe them out, but to preserve the fathers in the sons'; and he testifies to them the same things that he also spoke to the fathers: that, after they have walked in his precepts and kept his judgments and observed the sanctification of the sabbath, which was given as a sign, they may then know that he is the Lord their God. By the precepts and statutes of the fathers and their judgments he signifies ingrained error, so that they may not imitate the sins of those whose torments they behold.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the sons exasperated me; they did not walk in my precepts, and did not keep my judgments to do them, which, when a man has done them, he shall live in them, and they violated my sabbaths; and I threatened to pour out my fury upon them, and to fulfill my wrath on them in the desert. But I turned back my hand and acted for my name's sake, that it might not be profaned before the nations from which I cast them out in their eyes. 'But the sons too', he says, 'followed the crimes of their parents and did all that those had done; hence they too deserved a like sentence; but they were preserved by the same greatness of my mercy as their fathers too, and for the same reasons for which I also had mercy on the fathers, so that I, the one and the same Creator of both, might soften my wrath with a like patience'. We run through the plain things so as to pass on to the more obscure.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 44: HOW THE PROMISE TO ABRAHAM WAS FULFILLED IN CHRIST

How could it be shown from the testimony of the prophets, already received among the Gentiles in the New Testament, that the promise which God made to Abraham has been fulfilled through the coming of Christ? — It is written in the prophet Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. 56:7). But perhaps the Jews will say: The house of God, that is, the synagogue, is open to all. Nor do we object; yet in such a way that, as always, the circumcised join themselves to the Law. For their Law is that by which they were commanded, after the manner of Abraham, to be circumcised. Therefore, nothing new can seem to be signified by this example of the prophet; since anyone coming from any nation has never been forbidden from the beginning of Judaism to join himself to the Law. Nothing new spoken by the prophet can be thought, indeed it would be unessential, if the Gentiles have always been admitted to serve the God of Abraham and are never found to have been forbidden. And this is true, because those who submit themselves to the Law are never found not to have been received. If, therefore, these things are so, it seems needless that the prophet admonished about what, once handed down, has always been observed. And could anyone so dull be found as to say that the prophet spoke something unnecessary and empty? I do not know for whom it would be safe even to hear this and not oppose it. For since the Jewish people, on account of the sins which they committed against God, seeking help from idols, were often rebuked by the prophets but refused to enter upon the path of repentance so as to return to God, God, in reproach of them, indicated that He would open His house to all nations to pray, so that, the Jews being cast off, He would show that He would place others in their place. For if the nations have always been admitted to the Law, as was said above, how could the prophet say that this would happen in the future, unless he meant something different from what had been previously commanded? He could not speak of a thing which was done daily as though it were going to come. Therefore it is clear that this tends to the ruin of the Jews, to whom the prophet shows that, with them removed, others were to be called and were to receive the house of God’s grace, which had been promised to the Jews. What that promise is, the prophet Isaiah teaches, saying: “There shall come out of Zion one who shall deliver and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob; and this shall be my covenant with them” (Isa. 59:20–21). Therefore this covenant is the removal of sins. This is the New Covenant, which was promised through Jeremiah, who says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will accomplish for the house of Israel and the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I arranged for their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not continue in my covenant, and I neglected them, says the Lord” (Jer. 31:31–32). This is their transgression, when they made the image of a calf; then they corrupted His covenant. Therefore also the tablets on which the Law had been given were shattered under the mountain (Exod. 32:4, 19), because they deserved to receive more severe precepts. But because God is mild and merciful, He promised through the prophets that He would change the Law, so as to give another Covenant, which would differ from that which He had given before: that not only what was burdensome might be changed, but also those things which were given in figure, that is, the sabbath and circumcision; so that, since they had long been oppressed, being relieved in all things, they might give grateful thanks to God as petitioners. And because, persisting in their fathers’ transgression, they refused to turn their minds away from idols, He testifies that the nations, together with the remnant who kept the faith, will enjoy the Covenant which He had said would come: so that the faithless Jews might be tortured in a twofold way. For they were burdened for a time by the precepts, and in the future they will pay fitting penalties, because they were found faithful neither in the Old nor in the New Covenant. So He said that He would give a New Covenant, so that the Old, which had been given to the Fathers, would cease. And therefore, whoever serves God in this Covenant does not observe the sabbath, nor new moons, nor circumcision, nor distinctions of foods; but has only the fear of God in faith: because he will not be justified by the Law, but by faith, as the prophet Habakkuk says: “For the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. 2:4); so that he no longer uses many precepts to gain favor with God, but few. Isaiah again, speaking with the same meaning, says: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of them shall be saved. For the Lord shall accomplish and cut short His word in righteousness, because the Lord will make a short word upon the whole earth” (Isa. 10:22–23). For the remnant who will persevere in the faith of the promise, while the others do not believe, He shows the shortened word of the Law: this is the New Covenant which He promised. It would not otherwise be called a Covenant, unless in a similar way this too were confirmed by the witness of blood, just as the Old Covenant, so that both might have one and the same name: but in the Old, many precepts, in the New, however, few, as He promised. So that, since He had said that Abraham would be the father of many nations (Gen. 17:4–5), in the same way the sons might be justified as the father had been justified: so that, once those things ceased which began after the faith of Abraham, those who receive the faith by which that same Abraham was justified might be sons of Abraham, as was said by the Lord. And this is neither strange nor unheard of, that men should be justified without care for the sabbath and circumcision and the rest of the commandments of this sort. For Enoch did not please God by this, that he might be translated; nor was Noah found righteous in the flood by observing this alone; nor was Abraham himself justified after he was circumcised: “Abraham,” it says, “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Heb. 11:5, 7, 8; Rom. 4:3). Then he was circumcised, so that there might be in him a sign that, though he was old, he believed that he would have a son. Therefore it is not circumcision that commends Abraham, but faith. And so, for those who believe, faith is sufficient for justification, that they may be sons of Abraham in faith, not in circumcision, because they have no need of circumcision. For what Abraham believed is not what is believed in their case. But the Jews were therefore ordered to be circumcised, so that they might have the sign of Abraham’s faith, not of their own faith, but so that they might be known as his sons according to the flesh. Yet if they believe, they will be his sons also in justification. For what advantage is it to be called the son of a powerful man if one is powerless, except that it is even more harmful? For it is a disgrace to be the son of a noble and glorious man without honor. Indeed, bodily circumcision is so far from being a merit that God says through the prophet Jeremiah that He will take vengeance on all the circumcised in foreskin, if they are not circumcised in heart (Jer. 4:4). Yet He is not angry with those who are circumcised in heart but uncircumcised in flesh, because no one has ever pleased God without the circumcision of the heart. Whoever, therefore, are circumcised in the flesh signify the lineage of Abraham according to the flesh; but those who are circumcised in heart signify the lineage of God according to faith, because, being circumcised from all worldly error, they confess God as their Father. What then does the circumcision of the flesh profit, if, when faith is lacking in the Jew, he cannot attain to the merit of Abraham? Or what harm is there in foreskin, when no one attains to his righteousness except the one who has followed the faith of Abraham? They therefore glory in the circumcision of the flesh in vain, since they see that it has no merit before God. And since, as has been shown, it is better to have faith than circumcision, the Gentiles are better than the Jews; for the Gentiles have faith, the Jews have circumcision. And whom do you think He recognizes more as sons of Abraham: those who are like him according to the flesh, or those who are like him in faith? But the faith of Abraham bears witness. And therefore he glories not in the flesh but in faith. For this reason he has received as sons those whom he sees to be imitators of his glory. For how can he call those sons from whom he sees a shrinking back from that by which he pleased God and was justified? He will therefore be able to judge them not as his sons, but as his enemies. For they appear to be envious of him, despising the faith through which he was glorified. Nor is it surprising if the Jews are found untrusting, not at all accepting the New Testament, when we know that they were not faithful even in the Old. They were always rebellious and disrespectful against God, and therefore they received such commandments by which their necks, which were unbending, might be pressed down. For they never wished to hope for good things from God, whose such great benefits and such wondrous powers they had come to know. Therefore it is that, among other things, the prophet Ezekiel says: “I lifted up my hand to them in the desert, that they should be scattered among the nations and dispersed in the lands, because they did not perform my ordinances and rejected my commandments.” And in what follows: “I gave them laws that were not good, and judgments whereby they should not live in them” (Ezek. 20:23–25). He shows for what reason such great and so harsh commandments were given to them: because they proved ungrateful for such great benefits, and, justice dictating, they were to be pressed by more severe precepts. Therefore He called them “not good,” although they are just: because they did not lead them to justification, but to destruction; and although a punishment rightly inflicted, yet for the one who suffers it, it is not a good. After these things, however, because God is merciful, He promised that He would give the New Testament, in which the shortening of the Law would justify believers, just as Abraham was justified: so that, with new moons and the sabbath and circumcision and the other precepts ceasing, not those that belong to the natural law, that is, murder, adultery, and such things, they might be justified as Abraham was. For, with the faith of Abraham renewed, He willed that all things should cease, so that the time might be such as it was when Abraham believed. But perhaps the Jews say: “If those things that were given by Moses are said to cease through the shortening of the Law, was circumcision given by Moses so that it should cease? And therefore we have the sign of our father, because we are the sons of Abraham, a sign which, for the sake of the testimony of our lineage, ought not to cease.” Circumcision indeed had to be observed in its time, that is, before the New Testament which had been promised was given. But when, by the grace of God, the burdens of the Law were ordered to cease, what need is there of circumcision? Therefore a new Law was given, that is, a spiritual one, so that carnal things might cease, and those who received it might accept its sign: so that just as in the Old Testament they had the sign of Abraham, from whom the Old Testament began, so also in the New they might have the sign of the Savior, who is the institutor of the New Testament. For just as from Abraham they were called Hebrews, so from Christ they are called Christians. Whoever, therefore, are still called Hebrews have not received the New Testament which God promised, bringing to nothing the kindness and mercy of God: for He no longer wished His people to be designated by the name of a man, but agreed to establish them under the name of His Son. With what courage, then, do the Jews say that we do not use our Law but theirs, when David says, “I will give thanks to you among the nations” (Ps. 17:50), and again, “Rejoice, O nations, with his people”? And to the prophet Jeremiah the Lord says, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you; and I appointed you as a prophet to the nations” (Jer. 1:5). Judaism certainly has its own particular signs: for this people is signified either in Jacob, or in Samaria, or in Jerusalem, or in Judea, or in Israel. As for the nations, however, it is clear that He signifies them in a different way than He does the Jews. Therefore Jeremiah is our prophet. For although in all the Prophets God showed that the nations would share in His gift, yet to Jeremiah in particular He says that He has given him to us as a prophet. For he signified that the New Testament would come, which would profit the Gentiles more than the Jews, as now appears clearly. For since the preaching of the New Testament is spread over the whole earth, a faithful Jew is so rarely and with such difficulty found that all the Churches of the New Testament are called “of the nations,” as it was said in the prophet Hosea: “I will call that which is not my people, my people; and her that was not beloved, beloved” (Hosea 2:24; Rom. 9:25). Therefore, the Jews having been rejected, He calls the nations with the same mercy and grace with which He agreed to call Abraham. For Abraham did not come to know the Lord without being called. Therefore, He who agreed to call Abraham likewise agreed to call the nations. Why then do they say, “The Law is ours,” when it is clear that the gift of God is for all who are willing? Let this careless violation cease, since the grace of God is common to all. With what shame do they deny that our Christ was promised in the Law, when they see in Him all the signs which the Law foretold as to come? For both according to the promise made to Abraham all nations are justified by believing in Him (Gen. 22:18); and according to the prophet Isaiah He was born of a Virgin (Isa. 7:14) in Bethlehem from the tribe of Judah, as was promised, from the seed of David (Micah 5:2); and in accordance with what Jeremiah prophesied (Jer. 31:31–32), He proclaimed the New Testament which God then promised would come; and after all the signs of power had been shown, He humbled Himself, according to the words of the Prophets; and having suffered all that had been foretold, He rose on the third day, as it is written in the prophet. And if they inquire about the time of the promise, as it is shown in the prophet Daniel (Dan. 9:24 ff.), they will find it fulfilled in the time when Christ was born and suffered: for from the first year of Darius, king of the Persians, down to the birth and passion of the Lord and the destruction of Jerusalem, which was carried out by Vespasian, chief of the Roman Empire, the seventy weeks were completed, which are four hundred and ninety years, a reckoning made clear through the kingdoms and the successors of the empire. Therefore also it is found calculated by Tertullian in the book which he wrote against the Jews; but, lest this should backfire to his disadvantage, although he calculated correctly, we have passed it over in silence. And who can doubt this number, when now about three hundred years are found in addition to that number? It is therefore shameless, after so many years have been added beyond the time of the coming of the Saviour, to say, “He has not come.” Under the Apostles, or at the time when the Lord was living among men, hatred opposing the truth could still hide itself; so that, although it saw all the signs of the Christ who had been promised in the Savior, it could say that it doubted about the time, to conceal its unbelief. But afterwards, when many years began to exceed the promised number, what shamelessness it is to deny that He has come, whose coming is known to have been fulfilled both by signs and by times! For when something is full and does not overflow, a combative person may say that it is not full; but overflow closes the mouth of the argumentative. So the Jews, in the time of the Saviour, could say, though deceitfully, that the calculation from the time of Darius to the Lord Christ was not correctly made, so that He might not be acknowledged as the one who had been promised. We are mistaken, they might say, in the years and in the months and in the days of the emperors, and we do not make an exact reckoning. But when the times have extended beyond the prescribed number of years of the promised Christ, no excuse can be put forward to deny that He who has come is the Christ, unless, which God forbid, the one who promised is said to have lied. For when the time of the promise has elapsed, and it is denied that the one who was promised has come, what else is charged against the promiser but falsehood? Yet that He who made the promise is truthful, all the signs teach which were foretold in Christ and are known to have been found in Christ. The Jews, however, while they are ashamed to change themselves, do not consider that there will be a judgment to come. For nothing is worse than for someone to deny that a thing is true when he understands that it is not a lie.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Again I lifted up my hand against them in the wilderness, to scatter them among the nations and winnow them into the lands, because they had not done my judgments, and had rejected my precepts, and had violated my sabbaths, and their eyes had been after the idols (or thoughts) of their fathers. Therefore I too gave them precepts not good, and judgments in which they shall not live; and I defiled them in their gifts, when they offered (or made pass over) everything that opens the womb, for their transgressions (for which the Seventy translated that I might destroy them. And what they passed over:), and they shall know that I am the Lord. Where in the Old Testament the Lord lifted up his hand against the sons of those who fell in the wilderness, wishing to scatter them among the nations, Scripture does not say, but from what he relates here we must believe that it happened; or else this signifies that, after they had entered the land of promise, at various times on account of many sins they were handed over to diverse nations and kings, and at that time the precepts of the Lord and the judgments, which were good by their nature and in which believers could live, were made not good for them, since in captivity they were by no means able to keep the precepts of the law and do what the divine word commanded; nor did he say: I gave them 'evil' precepts, but 'not good' — for it does not at once follow that what is not good is evil, as the Apostle too teaches: that it is good for a man not to touch a wife or a woman, but, because of incontinence, for each one to possess his own vessel in sanctification and chastity; and if he does this, it is neither good nor evil —; so God gave them, scattered among the nations, precepts not good — that is, he gave them up to their own thoughts and desires —, so that they did what is not fitting; and he defiled them in their gifts, like a priest separating the lepers from the people and declaring them to be defiled, while they offer to idols what they ought to offer to God; and they make everything that opens the womb, that is, the firstborn, pass through the fire to Baal, so that, after they have been abandoned by God and handed over to the worship of idols, they may then understand that he is the Lord whom by their own fault they roused to anger. Symmachus translated this passage more plainly, putting the future for the past: Therefore I too will give them precepts not good, and judgments on account of which they shall not live, and I will defile them on account of their gifts; because they consecrate and make pass over what opens the womb, that I may destroy them, and they may know that I am the Lord; and the sense is: 'Because I saw that the sons were equaling the crimes of their fathers and doing the same things for which those had offended God, I wished to divide them among the nations, and scatter them through the whole world, and give them precepts not good, and judgments in which they would not live, so as to defile them in their gifts, because they were consecrating all the firstborn to idols, and to destroy them forever, and that they might know that I am the Lord'. He shows that he did not give the precepts not good to those who were staying in the desert, but that to those whom he wished to scatter among the nations and make strangers throughout the whole world he had thought of giving what he did not give, so that there, by their own fault, they would make the good precepts of God not good, while they present to idols what God had commanded to be presented to himself.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Wherefore speak to the house of Israel, son of man, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Still in this too your fathers blasphemed me, when they had spurned me with contempt, and I had brought them into the land over which I lifted up my hand to give it to them; they saw every high hill and every leafy tree, and they sacrificed their victims there, and there they gave the provocation of their offering, and there they set their odor of sweetness and poured out their libations. And I said to them: What is the high place to which you go in? And its name was called 'high place' to this day. (LXX: "Therefore speak to the house of Israel, son of man, and you shall say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: Even to this your fathers provoked me to anger in their transgressions by which they fell away against me, and I brought them into the land over which I lifted up my hand to hand it over to them; and they saw every high hill and every leafy tree, and they sacrificed there to their gods and set the fury of their gifts, and set there the odor of their fragrance, and poured out there their libations. And I said to them: What is ἀβανὰ [abana, a transliteration], that you go in there? And they called its name ἀβανὰ to this present day.") 'I wished', he says, 'to scatter them among all the nations when they sinned in the wilderness and to give them precepts not good, so that they would sacrifice to idols what they ought to have offered to me, and consecrate to them all their firstborn through fire, so that I might kill them and wipe them out'. — When he says 'I wished', he shows that he did not do what he wished. And what follows: They shall know that I am the Lord, is not found in the Seventy; for it did not seem to them consistent that after the slaying they should know that he is the Lord —.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 7

For as regards the former people, what good or perfect thing could be commanded to those who murmured and contradicted? Indeed, a little later they even turn to idols, and forgetful of the benefits and wonders of God they set up the head of a calf. For this reason, therefore, precepts are given to them, in which they may be tested. Hence it is that also through the prophet Ezekiel the Lord says to them: "I gave you precepts and ordinances that were not good, in which you shall not live by them"; for being tested in the precepts of the Lord they are not found faithful.
AGAINST CELSUS 7:20
