We hold, then, that the law has a twofold sense—the one literal, the other spiritual—as has been shown by some before us. Of the first or literal sense it is said, not by us but by God, speaking in one of the prophets, that "the statutes are not good, and the judgments not good"; whereas, taken in a spiritual sense, the same prophet makes God say that "his statutes are good, and his judgments are good."
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 46: WHY THE LAW IS BOTH HOLY AND WORKS WRATH

This Law, then, he says, works wrath; for these things were added by God when angry, so that they might be a burden upon the unbelief of the Jews. In matters so many, it is inevitable that something be omitted. Therefore the Apostle Peter says: “Why,” he asks, “do you put a yoke upon the neck of the brothers which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (Acts 15:10). Finally, God says through the prophet Jeremiah: “I gave them statutes that were not good” (Ezek. 20:25). For after many offenses and temptings of God, and insults against Moses and detractions from God, these things were given for them to observe, so that their stiff neck might be pressed down, and wherever they turned, they would have the Law, so that there might be no refreshment for them.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 10: WHY WERE CIRCUMCISION AND PRECEPTS GIVEN?

WHY WERE CIRCUMCISION AND PRECEPTS GIVEN TO THE PEOPLE, WHICH PREVIOUSLY DID NOT EXIST AND NOW ARE NO LONGER HELD IN AUTHORITY? — Circumcision is a sign of Abraham’s faith, so that when this sign was seen in his sons, it might be known that they were his sons, who, believing God, had received this sign (Gen. 17:10–11). But the commandments about Sabbaths and things past were given as testimony, and about things to come which were to have a figure (Exod. 20:9–11). For the future Sabbath, in which He will grant rest in eternity, is foreshadowed by this Sabbath that was made in the completed week. The law of foods, however, was not given at the beginning of the Law, but when, under a leader, they were faithless and did not want to give faith to God’s words and promises, they received, because of the hardness of their heart, precepts that were not good, as the prophet Jeremiah says (Ezek. 20:25). This was done so that their neck might be pressed down, for their own improvement. For the whole creation ought not to have been subjected to proud and stubborn men. Later, however, when the mercy of God came, freedom to eat was restored. Therefore the apostle Peter says: Why do you put a yoke upon the neck of the brothers, which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? (Acts 15:10).
Letter 74.2

For a paedagogus, as the word is rendered in the Latin, is the teacher of a boy; and he cannot apply perfect precepts to an imperfect age, because it cannot bear them. Again, the God of the Law says by the Prophet, I gave them also statutes that were not good, that is, not perfect. But the same God has preserved more perfect things for the Gospel, as He says, I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil the Law.
HOMILIES ON 1 CORINTHIANS 7:9

They, it is well known, when they led not a life of toil but indulged in relaxation, not being able to bear prosperity, fell away into ungodliness. What then did God upon this? He laid upon them a multitude of laws with a view to restrain their licence. And to convince you that these laws contribute not to any virtue, but were given to them as a sort of curb, providing them with an occasion of perpetual labor; hear what saith the prophet concerning them; "I gave them statutes which were not good." What means, "not good?" Such as did not much contribute towards virtue. Wherefore he adds also, "and ordinances whereby they shall not live."
LETTER 79.10
[Israel] received statutes that were not good and commandments that were altogether evil whereby it should not live but should be punished through them.
Commentary on Galatians

And Ezekiel, in the person of God: "I led out", he says, "them", that is, the people of the Jews, "from the land of Egypt: and I led them into the desert: and I gave them my precepts, and showed them my justifications: which a man shall do, and live in them" (Ezek. 20:10). But concerning that law which works wrath, to which the Apostle too died, he adds afterward: "And I gave them precepts that were not good, and justifications in which they shall not live in them" (ibid., 25).
Commentary on Galatians

But let us not think that to live in them are the words of the Apostle, but of the prophet Ezekiel, who says: "And I led them out into the desert, and I gave them my precepts, and showed them my ordinances, which a man shall do, and shall live in them" (Ezek. 20:10, 11). And when he had said that those who had walked in the precepts and ordinances live, he added: "And I gave them precepts not good, and ordinances in which they should not live in them" (ibid., 25). How much care in the words! Where he said: "I gave them precepts and ordinances in which they should live in them", he did not add "good". But where he put "in which they should not live in them", he added: "And I gave them precepts not good, and ordinances in which they shall not live in them". But these things more fully in Ezekiel: now let us return to the order of the Epistle.
Commentary on Galatians

In another way, however, we shall affirm that the weak and needy elements are the traditions of the Jews and the base understanding according to the letter, which are statutes that are not good and precepts that are not good. For the spiritual understanding of the Law is strong and rich (Ezek. 20), so that either it ought not to be called an element at all, or it is indeed an element by comparison with the age to come and with the life in Christ Jesus, by which the angels and the heavenly powers now live. But compared with the Jewish sense, it should be called not so much an element, that is, a beginning, as perfection.
Commentary on Ezekiel

This too can be said: that before the offense they received only the Decalogue, but after the idolatry and blasphemy the manifold ceremonies of the law, so that they would rather offer to God the victims which they were offering to demons, and, by comparison with sacrilege, what was not good in itself would become lighter: by no means evil, because they were offered to God, and yet not good, because they had offended the author of good.
LETTER 82

But, why should I not say that the requirements of ancient ceremonies are not good because people are not justified by them; they are figures that foreshadow the grace, by which we are justified.… They are not bad, because they were precepts of divine origin, adapted to times and people, although in this estimate I am supported by the prophetic statement in which God said that he had given to that people "statutes that were not good." It happens that he did not say that they were bad but only that they were not good: that is, such that with them, people become good; without them, they do not. I would like your kind sincerity to inform me whether any oriental saint who comes to Rome and fasts on Saturday—except the eve of Easter—is acting deceitfully. If we say that is wrong, we shall condemn the Roman church and also many places near it and others somewhat further away, where the same custom continues to be observed.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'But you, son of man, speak again to them, that is, to the elders of the house of Israel who came to inquire of you: Your fathers, from whose stock you are descended, blasphemed me in this too and held me for nothing: after I had brought them into the land, which they possessed by my strength, which I had given them to possess, they turned it to provoking me; for when they had seen every high hill and leafy tree, they sacrificed on the mountains and in the groves and in the woodlands, and sacrificed victims to idols, and poured out offerings; and when I saw this, I said to them: What is 'bama' — for this means 'high place' —, or why do you go into such a place, which you have chosen for yourselves on all the hills, so that to this day places of this kind are called 'bamoth' and the ancient error keeps its former name?'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For 'bama', which we rendered as 'high place', an error has prevailed in the edition of the Seventy, so that ἀβανὰ is written, which means nothing in the Hebrew language; 'bama', if you divide its two syllables into two words, can mean 'in what', but that sense does not fit the present passage; but wherever it is written in the books of Kings and Chronicles: Still the people burned incense and sacrificed on the high place, 'bama' in the singular and 'bamoth' in the plural mean 'high places'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore say to the house of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: You are defiled in the way of your fathers, and you commit fornication after their stumbling-blocks, and in the offering of your gifts, when you make your sons pass through the fire, you are defiled with all your idols to this day; and shall I answer you, house of Israel? As I live, says the Lord God, I will not answer you. 'You imitate the vices of your fathers and walk by the same ways, so that like offenses deserve a like punishment too; and you have advanced so far in crimes that you consecrate your sons to demons through fire, nor is it enough to have done this once, but even at present you do the same things; not that the elders in captivity do these things, but that those who were staying in Jerusalem and over whom captivity was hanging do not cease to do all these things. And when you are bound by such great outrages, do you seek', he says, 'my answer? As I live, says the Lord, and I swear by my own self, I will not answer you'. And what follows:
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 7

The first Passover is of the first people; the second Passover is ours. For we were "unclean in soul", we who "worshiped wood and stone" and "not knowing God served those who by nature were not gods". We also were those who "were journeying far", of whom the Apostle says that we were "strangers and sojourners from the covenants of God, having no hope and without God in this world".
Commentary on Ezekiel

Nor shall the thought of your mind come to pass, of you who say: We will be like the nations and like the families of the earth, to worship wood and stones. As I live, says the Lord God, with a strong hand and with an outstretched arm and with fury poured out I will reign over you, has this sense: 'Do not think that your thoughts, by which you blaspheme against me, can be fulfilled; for you say: We do not wish to be under the Lord nor to be called his people, but, as all the nations in the whole world are, and each people lives by its own will, so as to worship wood and stones and serve idols, we too will be one nation out of many'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

To which God replies, and swears by himself, and says: 'I will not leave you nor despise you, as negligent masters are accustomed to despise runaway slaves, but I will drag you back to my rule, and with arm outstretched and striking I will reduce you to your former servitude and reign over you, so that, whether you will or not, you may have me as king, and may feel as an angry king him whose clemency you neglected'.
THE CHAPLET 10:7
He commands us to be completely separated from idolatry and have no close dealing with it, because even the earthly serpent sucks people into its jaws at a distance with its breath.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will lead you out from the peoples, and gather you from the lands in which you are scattered; with a mighty hand, and an outstretched arm, and with fury poured out I will reign over you. 'I will not suffer you', he says, 'to be among the nations nor to be held in eternal captivity, but I will lead you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands into which hostile necessity has scattered you here and there to be slaves; and I will do these things not to destroy you and wipe you out, but to be your king'. From this we understand that even what the heretics call the cruelty of the Creator sounds of clemency, since he is angry and rages and pours out all his fury for this purpose: to draw back to his kingdom those who had chosen the tyranny of demons, and that to be its slaves.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will bring you into the desert of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face. As I contended in judgment against your fathers in the desert of the land of Egypt, so will I judge you, says the Lord, and I will subject you to my scepter, and bring you into the bonds of the covenant. And I will pick out from you the transgressors and the ungodly, and I will lead them out of the land of their sojourning, and they shall not enter the land of Israel, and you shall know that I am the Lord. 'I will do', he says, 'to you who are in Babylon and now serve idols what I did to your fathers in Egypt: I will lead you out into the desert of the peoples and there enter into judgment with you face to face, as I contended in judgment against them when they went out of Egypt; and after I have judged you, I will subject you to my scepter and rule, and enter into a covenant with you, and bring you into your land in the bonds of love, so that, bound by my love, you may by no means be able to depart from me.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But the transgressors and the ungodly, who in hardness of heart persevere in evil works, I will pick out from you, not to possess them but to cast them away; and I will indeed lead them out of the land of their sojourning, so that, once led out, they may not enter the land of Israel but perish in diverse regions, and that, by the distinction of the good and the evil, you may know that I am the Lord who do all things with judgment'. The discourse hastens on to what remains, and we run briefly through each point, so as to offer readers only the sense.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you, house of Israel, thus says the Lord God: Walk each of you after your idols, and serve them. But if in this too you do not listen to me, and pollute my holy name any more with your gifts and with your idols. (LXX: "And you, house of Israel, thus says Adonai the Lord: Let each one take away his inventions; and after this, if you listen to me, and do not pollute my holy name any more with your gifts and with your pursuits.") Symmachus translated this passage more plainly: Each of you, go and serve your idols, since you would not listen to me. But my holy name do not pollute any more through your gifts and images. But on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says the Lord God, there all the house of Israel shall serve me. Symmachus' translation has this meaning: 'Since you do not wish to serve me, go, serve idols and tread in the footsteps of your images; for you do not wish to listen to me: by no means sacrifice victims to me, nor burn incense, nor be called my people — for my worshipers will by no means serve me in groves and shrines and the places of idols, as you do, but on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel —'. The Seventy, for their part, unfold a sense of their own: 'Abandon your former thoughts, and take away the evil sins of your inventions; and if after this you listen to me and do not pollute my name with your gifts and images, then on my holy mountain you shall offer me victims and serve me, all the house of Israel'. Aquila, however, agreeing in part with Symmachus, disagrees in part: Go, he says, after your idols and serve them, since you are unworthy of my rule, nor does your worship delight me; but if in this too you by no means listen to me, but pollute my holy name, while you pretend to offer to me what you offer to idols, and do such blasphemy to my name that, being worshipers of idols, you say that you are mine, know this: that on my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, there all the house of Israel shall serve me, not you who serve idols, but all the house of Israel which is afterward to believe.
Commentary on Ezekiel

On my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says the Lord God, there all the house of Israel shall serve me: all, I say, in the land in which they shall please me; and there I will require your firstfruits and the beginning of your tithes in all your sanctifications. In an odor of sweetness I will receive you, when I have led you out from the peoples and gathered you from the lands into which you were scattered, and I shall be sanctified in you in the eyes of the nations. And you shall know that I am the Lord. Of this mountain, on which all the house of Israel is to serve God, Isaiah and Micah sang with one voice: In the last days the mountain of the house shall be manifest on the summit of the mountains and shall be raised above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways and we will walk in his paths; for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and again Isaiah: Go up onto a high mountain, he says, you who proclaim to Zion; lift up and exalt your voice, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem. This mountain, Zion, we understand either as the Church, which means 'watchtower' and is set on the height of holy doctrines, or as the Lord Savior himself, in whom the firstfruits and the tithes and all worship are turned into an odor of sweetness, so that all the nations round about, seeing that the people of the Lord has been saved, may glorify God, and those who have been saved may know that he is the Lord.
TO THE MARTYRS 2:4

Consider yourselves as having been transferred from prison to what we may call a place of safety. Darkness is there, but you are light; chains are there, but you are free before God. It breathes forth a foul smell, but you are an odor of sweetness.
Commentary on Ezekiel

When I bring you into the land of Israel, into the land for which I lifted up my hand to give it to your fathers. 'Then you shall know that I am the Lord, when I bring you', he says, 'into the land of Israel, for which I lifted up my hand to bring your fathers into it, which they lost by their own fault and which you have received back not so much by your own merit as by my clemency'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you shall remember your ways and all your crimes, with which you were defiled in them; and you shall be displeasing to yourselves in your own sight in all your wickednesses which you have done. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have done good to you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways nor according to your most wicked crimes, house of Israel, says the Lord God. We cannot remember our crimes and vices unless we have been brought into the land of Israel and, set there, say with the Apostle: I who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. And you shall be displeasing, he says, to yourselves in your own sight in all your wickednesses which you have done (or, as Symmachus translated: And you shall seem little to yourselves because of all your wickednesses which you have wrought), so that, after they have been exalted, they may believe themselves to be lowly, because: The Lord gives grace to the humble, and in another place it is written: Before crushing the heart of a man is exalted, and before height it is humbled: for crushing follows pride, and exaltation follows humility.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have done good to you: and we came to know the Lord Savior the more at that time when he did good to us and suffered for our sins and bore our iniquities and grieved for us, not for any merit of those who are saved but for his name's sake; otherwise our ways and most wicked crimes deserved not mercy but punishment. But whatever we have said of the people of Israel, which, freed from Egypt, committed many things in the wilderness and offended God, and afterward, brought into the land of promise, venerated idols and worshiped wood and stones, and afterward was preserved by the clemency of God, let us refer to those who have been freed from the Egypt of this world by the high hand of the Lord and, brought into the wilderness of vices, sighed again for Egypt and did the things for which they ought to have been punished, but nonetheless, through repentance, not by their own merit but by the clemency of the Lord, have been preserved.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And beautifully, at the beginning: Drip, he says, toward the southwest, so that not the whole wrath of God may seem to be poured out, but a kind of drip and a part. But if there is such savagery in a drip, what must be reckoned of whole downpours, so that all flesh, which is to see the salvation of God, may know through the burning of the woods and through the flame that is extinguished by no one's help that he himself is the Lord?
Commentary on Ezekiel

Tropologically, however, Theman and Nageb and Darom can be understood as Egypt; for we read in Daniel that the south is frequently taken for Egypt; and Egypt refers to the straits of this world. Ezekiel therefore prophesies the evils that are to come upon the world, which he calls a forest, one that has no fruit-bearing trees but is a dwelling-place of beasts, of which it is also said in Psalm 28 (29): The voice of the Lord perfecting the stags, and he will uncover the thickets of the woods. These are the woods and forests that devoured more of Absalom's army in the battle than the sword killed. And in the forests the green wood is kindled first, and then the dry: those who live in evil, and those who are dead to righteousness. And what is said, And every face shall be burned in it from the south to the north, says this: from those who seemed to be fervent in spirit to those who, as iniquity increased and the love of many grew cold, have lost their former warmth, so that all flesh may perceive that the flame of the Lord is not extinguished.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against the way of the south, and drip toward the southwest, and prophesy to the forest of the southern field. And you shall say to the southern forest: Hear the word of the Lord: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and I will burn up in you all green wood and all dry wood; the flame of the kindling shall not be extinguished, and every face shall be burned in it from the south to the north: and all flesh shall see that I the Lord have kindled it, and it shall not be extinguished. And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God; they say of me: Does not this man speak in parables? (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make firm your face upon Theman, and look toward Darom, prophesy upon the forest, the leader Nageb. And you shall say to the forest Nageb: Hear the speech of the Lord: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it shall devour in you all green wood and all dry wood; the kindled flame shall not be extinguished, and every face shall burn in it from the midday to the north: and all flesh shall know that I the Lord have kindled it; it shall not be extinguished. And I said: By no means, Lord, Lord; they say to me: Is not this which is spoken a parable?") What Set (or make firm) your face means, we have said more fully above; for there is need of firmness of countenance and hardness of brow, so that the prophet may speak fearlessly the things he is commanded, above all when sad things must be announced to the whole multitude of the people. Now what 'Theman' and 'Darom' and 'Nageb', and again 'Nageb', for which the Seventy translated ἀπηλιὼτην [Apeliotes, the east wind], signify in the Hebrew, our translation has expressed. And as for their saying 'leader Nageb', the Hebrew has it better, 'of the field' or 'of the southern region'; for what is written is not 'sare', as the Seventy supposed, a word that means 'leader' and 'prince', but 'sade', which properly signifies 'field' and 'region'; and the error grew up because of the likeness of the letters 'daleth' [d] and 'res' [r].
Commentary on Ezekiel

The divine word, then, speaks through the μεταφορὰν [metaphor] of a forest against Jerusalem, which is a dwelling of beasts and of fierce men, saying that he will set it on fire and that all its wood will be burned up together; by no means does he call trees those that were lacking in fruit, but wood, as if made ready for burning. And first he burns in it the green wood, according to what we read in this same prophet: And begin from my holy ones, and afterward the dry, which could have nothing living in itself; that is, the saints and the sinners together, so that some by captivity may escape an evil death, while others are handed over to eternal punishments. And what he adds, From the south to the north, indicates this: from Jerusalem to Babylon, so that the whole road of those going into captivity may be filled with those falling by sword, famine and pestilence; for to those who are in Babylon, Jerusalem lies to the south, just as, conversely, the pot of Jeremiah, which signifies Jerusalem, is kindled from the face of the north, that is, of Babylon.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Understanding this, the prophet answered: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God (or, as the Seventy translated: By no means, Lord), and he adds: They say to me: Does not this man speak in parables? (or: Is this a parable which is spoken?), and the sense is: 'Speak more plainly; we do not understand what you are saying in a parable; open to us the meaning of God in plain speech'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the prophet prays that what the Lord has threatened may not come to pass, that is, that the forest may not be set on fire and all the wood burned up together, so that either they may still receive room for repentance, or the necessity of announcing sad things may not be laid upon him, especially since the people do not understand them and are provoked rather to madness by the obscurity of the sayings.

n: Just. But had not God declared the contrary, chap. xviii? The time was not yet arrived; or, he rescued the just from death, though he permitted them to experience the other common miseries. (Calmet) --- He preserved them from eternal death. (Estius) --- The just often means those who are so only in appearance, chap. xvi. 51. (Calmet) --- Temporal afflictions fall upon all; but the just derive benefit from them, while the wicked fall into eternal misery. (St. Jerome) (Worthington)
North, including all the country belonging to Israel.
Back, (ver. 30.) without doing execution, Jeremias l. 9. (Calmet)
Bitterness. Septuagint, "pains," like those of child-bearing, Isaias xxi. 3.
Melt. Literally, "decay," Josue vii., &c. --- Knee. Chap. vii. 17. (Haydock)

My son. He speaks, according to St. Jerome, to the sword of Nabuchodonosor; which was about to remove the sceptre of Israel, whom God here calls his son. (Challoner) --- This title belonged to all Israel, Exodus iv. 22. (Worthington) --- The Hebrew seems to be corrupt, and we may adhere to the Vulgate or to the Septuagint, (Calmet) which has, (9.) "Sword be sharp, and raging to slay victims; be sharp to shine, ready for destruction; cut, reduce to nothing, remove all wood." (Haydock) --- Syriac, "be ready to scatter the race of my son," &c. Hebrew, "Where shall we rejoice, sceptre of my son, thou sword which despisest every tree?" (Calmet) --- Protestants, "It contemneth the rod of my son as every tree?" (Haydock)
Slayer. He had conquered many nations before he attacked Israel. Let none boast of being the scourges of the Lord.
Fled, with Sedecias, by night. --- Thigh, in surprise and grief, ver. 17.

God. Perhaps you will say it is only a trial: but what will be your sentiments, when you behold the king and his people led away? (Calmet) --- Protestants, "Because it is a trial; and what if the sword contemn even the rod? it shall be no more, saith." (Haydock)
Tripled. Let the war be very bloody. Nabuchodonosor often invaded Judea. (Calmet) --- He raised the siege, but returned. (Vatable)
Ready. Literally, "covered," (amicti. Haydock) in the scabbard, and quite new and sharp.
Rabbath. They had formed a league with Sedecias, and Nabuchodonosor thought of punishing them first. (Haydock) --- But they joined his forces, Jeremias xii. 6., and xxvii. 3.

Shuffling. Hebrew, "polishing." Syriac, &c., "shooting an arrow upwards." He was undetermined which to attack first, and perhaps wrote Jerusalem on one and Rabbath on another arrow; (St. Jerome, &c.; Calmet) or which way the arrow fell the army followed. (Haydock) --- Many nations have adopted such superstitious practices. --- Idols. Hebrew Teraphim, Genesis xxxi. 19. (Calmet) --- Entrails. The Chaldeans taught the Lydians and they the Tuscans. (Grotius) --- At first this was done only to see if the victims were sound. (Cicero, Div.)

Right of one going by Thapsacus and Damascus, and not through the Desert Arabia, for thus Rabbath would have been to the right. God permitted this divination to succeed in his wrath. The devil pushed the Chaldeans forward, lest the Jews might be converted. (Calmet) --- If they had attacked Rabbath first, they would probably have succeeded, as they did five years after. But the time of vengeance was come for Jerusalem, (Haydock) and they were directed to assault it. (Worthington) --- Voice: the din of war, (Haydock) or of soldiers, trumpets, &c.

Vain. They shall think that Nabuchodonosor is wasting his time. --- Sabbaths. Hebrew, "they have people who swear to them;" false prophets, or the Egyptians, on whom they depend. Septuagint, "and counting the weeks," like Aman, Esther iii. 7. --- Iniquity, or perfidy of Sedecias, chap. xvii. 15. (Calmet)
Remembered. Hebrew, "caused....to be remembered," (Haydock) sinning publicly. (Calmet)
Thou profane, &c. He speaks to king Sedecias, who had broken his oath, and was otherwise a wicked prince. (Challoner) --- Hebrew, "Criminal, (sentenced to die) wicked," &c. (Calmet)

Diadem, (cidarim.) Some think this was the ornament of the high priest, (St. Jerome; Chaldean) denoting that he should perish as well as the king. (Haydock) --- This. The royal crown of Juda had exalted Sedecias from a private state and condition to the sovereign power, as the loss of it brought down Jechonias, &c. (Challoner) --- It shall be given to Godolias. (Chaldean) Hebrew, "it is not (Haydock) or shall be no more" the same, or for the posterity of Sedecias. None of the tribe of Juda was truly king after him, till the Messias. (Sanctius; Tirinus, &c.) (Genesis xlix. 10.) (Calmet)

Iniquity. Or, I will overturn it, viz., the crown of Juda, for the manifold iniquities of the kings: but it shall not be utterly removed till Christ come, whose right it is; and who shall reign in the spiritual house of Jacob (that is, in his Church,) for evermore. (Challoner) --- Hebrew also, "sideways." Thou shalt no more wear the tiara erect, (Haydock) like a king: (Hesychius) or rather, thy iniquity or punishment shall be most grievous. --- Him; Christ, or (Calmet) Nabuchodonosor. (Vatable) (Menochius)

Reproach, by which they had reproached and insulted over the Jews, at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem. (Challoner) (chap. xxv. 6., and Sophonias ii. 8.) --- They were punished five years later (Calmet) by the same Babylonians whom they had encouraged. (Worthington)

Sheath. The sword of Babylon, after raging against many nations, was shortly to be judged and destroyed at home by the Medes and Persians. (Challoner) --- After Nabuchodonosor had chastised the nations around for 18 years, after the ruin of Jerusalem, he returned and died in peace. Yet he first became like a beast, ver. 31., and Daniel iv. 30. The rest of the prophecy regards his successors. Cyrus waged war upon them, and Baltassar was slain in a conspiracy. See Isaias xlvii., and Jeremias l. (Calmet) --- At last the sword fell upon Babylon itself. (Worthington)
Brutish, or devoid of sense. (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "burning;" smiths. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem, and distil toward the sanctuaries, and prophesy against the ground of Israel. And you shall say to the land of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I will cast out my sword from its sheath, and I will kill in you the righteous and the wicked. But because I have killed in you the righteous and the wicked, my sword shall go forth from its sheath against all flesh, from the south to the north, and all flesh shall know that I the Lord have drawn my sword from its sheath, irrevocable. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Therefore prophesy, son of man, and set firm your face against Jerusalem, and look toward their holy places, and prophesy over the land of Israel. And you shall say to the land of Israel: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, and I will draw out my sword from its sheath, and I will slay out of you the lawless and the unrighteous. Because I will destroy out of you the lawless and the unrighteous, so shall my sword go forth from its sheath upon all flesh, from the south as far as the north, and all flesh shall know that I the Lord have drawn my sword from its sheath; it shall not return any more.") Because he had said above: They say of me: Does not this man speak in parables?, and the people were demanding a plain statement, therefore the Lord now says more plainly what he had spoken through a metaphor, or 'parable', and, as others rendered it, 'proverb': that the forests of Nageb and Darom and Theman [Hebrew words for the south] are Jerusalem and its temple and the Holy of Holies and the whole land of Judea, and that the flame which was to burn up the forest is to be understood as the devouring sword, which has been drawn from its sheath to kill the righteous and the wicked — for this is the green wood and the dry; whence the Lord also says: If they do such things, he says, in the green wood, what will they do in the dry? —; in place of which the Seventy, intending I know not what, translated 'the lawless and the unrighteous', as though both did not signify the same thing.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And what he had said there: And all flesh shall see that I the Lord have kindled it, that is, the forest or the flame, and it shall not be quenched, here he says in other words: That all flesh may know that I the Lord have drawn my sword from its sheath, irrevocable. For truly, for Jerusalem the flame has not been lulled to sleep, nor the fire quenched, nor the sword recalled, because there was a short time in between, and Jerusalem, with its temple, was set ablaze by Babylonian fire.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you, son of man, groan in the breaking of the loins, and in bitternesses groan before them. And when they say to you: Why do you groan?, you shall say: For the report, because it comes, and every heart shall melt, and all hands shall be loosened, and every spirit shall grow weak, and waters shall flow down all knees; behold, it comes, and it shall be done, says the Lord. (LXX: "And you, son of man, groan in the breaking of your loins, and in griefs groan in their sight. And it shall be, if they say to you: Why do you groan?, then you shall say: Because of the tidings, because it comes, and every heart shall be seized, and all hands shall be loosened, and all flesh and every spirit shall be tested, and all thighs shall be defiled with moisture; behold, it comes, and it shall be, says the Lord God.") First he had said: 'Prophesy, or distil, toward the south, the southwest and the noonday, and toward the southern forest'. Because this seemed obscure, and the people did not understand the prophet's words, in the second place it is set down more plainly that the southern forest is Jerusalem, and that all the unfruitful trees, at whose roots the axe has been laid, are to be understood as its inhabitants, and that the sword is to be interpreted in place of the fire. In the third place the prophet is commanded that, since they are silent and do not ask why he has prophesied these things, he should do something by which he may be questioned, and should answer what the Lord has spoken. 'Groan', he says, 'and wail, not with a light voice nor with moderate grief, but in the breaking of the loins, so that your groaning may be brought forth from your inmost bowels and from bitterness of soul; and you shall do this before them so that, when they have asked you why you are crushed with such great groaning and what evil has befallen you that you groan so, you may answer them with my word: This is why I lament and cannot hide the grief of my heart, because the report which had always sounded in my ears is being fulfilled in deed, and it comes — the menace, that is, of the raging Babylonian army; and when it has come and has hemmed Jerusalem in with a rampart, then every heart shall melt and all hands shall be loosened, so that, with panic seizing men's minds, no one dares to resist; for the spirit of all the warriors shall grow weak, and such trembling and dread shall seize them all that, under the compulsion of fear, their limbs and bowels are loosened and the bladder cannot hold its moisture, so that their knees are defiled with urine' — for it is natural that, under the compulsion of fear, the bladder is relaxed and, against a man's will, the moisture flows down; which indeed also tends to happen in the severity of illnesses, that, after the strength of the sick has failed, not only the knees but even the beds are defiled —. 'Behold', he says, 'it comes, what I have often foretold and what is being fulfilled in deed, and it shall be done, which not I but the Lord has spoken'. I know that a certain man unrolled many testimonies on the breaking of the loins and the flowing waters, so that the prophet's chastity might be made out, and the bitterness of soul and the inward pain of mind, namely that the waters of seed defile the knees; but this exposition does not belong to the present passage.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: Speak. The sword, the sword is sharpened and filed; it is sharpened to slaughter victims, and it is filed that it may gleam: you who move the scepter of my son, you have cut down every tree. And I have given it to be polished, that it may be held in the hand; this sword is sharpened, and this one is filed, that it may be in the hand of the slayer. Cry out and howl, son of man, because this one has come among my people, this one among all the leaders of Israel who had fled; they have been handed over to the sword with my people, therefore clap upon your thigh, because it has been proved, and this when it has overturned the scepter and it shall be no more, says the Lord God. You therefore, son of man, prophesy, and strike hand against hand, and let the sword be doubled, and let the sword of the slain be tripled. This is the sword of great slaughter, which makes them stand aghast, and melt in heart, and multiplies the ruins. In all their gates I have set the confusion of the sword, sharpened and filed to flash, clad for slaughter. Be sharpened, go to the right or to the left, wherever the desire of your face is. Moreover I too will clap hand against hand, and I will fulfill my indignation; I the Lord have spoken. (It is too much if I set down both editions, and the length of the books is drawn out, especially where there is either no difference or a small one; I will therefore set down some of the things that disagree. Where we said: You who move the scepter of my son, you have cut down every tree, they translated: Kill, despise, reject every tree; again, where we said: Who had fled, have been handed over to the sword, both they and others translated: My guests, or inhabitants; and where we said: Clap upon the thigh, they put: Strike the hand; and where we translated: And this when it has overturned the scepter, their edition has: The tribe has been rejected.) He speaks, moreover, to the sword of Nebuchadnezzar, that it should come against Jerusalem and be sharpened and filed, for many must be slaughtered; and he makes an apostrophe to it: 'You are the one who moves and overturns the scepter of my son, namely the rule of the people of Israel, and you cut down every tree, the whole multitude of the people. I have given', he says, 'this sword to be held in the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, and to be in the hand of a most powerful man.
Commentary on Ezekiel

According to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense] we can take the sharpened sword, prepared for slaughter, as the devil, of whom the Apostle says: To hand over such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved; and in another place: Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme; and in the Psalms it is written: He sent fury and wrath and distress, a sending by most evil angels. Some think that this sword was also in the hand of the angel when Jerusalem was struck under David. Others, however, suspect that it is also said of that sword of which it is written in the Gospel: 'I came not to send peace upon the earth, but a sword, and to divide among themselves every bond of kinship, so that the wicked may fall and the saints rise again'. But it is impious to believe this of the Savior's sword, and not rather of the devil, who overturns the scepters of the Lord in the Church, who slays all among the people, both the leaders and the guests of God, and is then approved by the Lord, when he has overturned Judas the traitor and those like him; into whom, after he had eaten the morsel, Satan entered. And the sword of the slain is doubled and tripled, so that the sin of Jerusalem may be loosed, because she has received from the hand of the Lord her sins twofold. The Lord, moreover, rejoices and exults, and is the exhorter of the raging sword, that it may go either to the right or to the left, and wherever the desire of its face carries it, so that, the wicked being slain, the good may remain, and that which is written may be fulfilled: What has chaff to do with wheat?, says the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore, O prophet, cry out and howl, and bear witness to the impending evils with the lamentation of your voice. This sword has spared no one, nor left anyone without a share in the impending evils. It has come among the people, it has come among the leaders of Israel, it has come among my guests and the priests who dwelt in my temple. Therefore strike your thigh, or your hand, and take on the bearing of a mourner. For this sword has been proved by me, and this when it has overturned my scepter and kingdom, which shall be no more and shall come to its end in King Zedekiah.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Again I command you, prophet, that you, who had struck your thigh in astonishment and wonder, should strike your hands also, so that not only once but a second and a third time the sword may come to slay'. For Nebuchadnezzar had come the first time when he carried off Jeconiah, and the second time when Jehoiakim reigned, the third time when Zedekiah did. 'And this is the tripled sword, when a great slaughter took place, and it multiplied the ruins to such a degree that they were stunned in mind and melted in heart, and it caused confusion in all their gates'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

It is commanded therefore to it, that is, to the sword sharpened and filed to flash, clad and ready and prepared for slaughter, that it go to the right if it so wishes, or to the left. 'Wherever', he says, 'it pleases your face, enter boldly, having me as your leader and helper. I will clap hand against hand, so that, as your patron and exhorter, I may spur you on as you rage against my adversaries. Do not hesitate, do not dread and fear to suffer what Sennacherib suffered; I the Lord have spoken; you are the minister of my will, carry out my sentence'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'When', he says, 'the divine word had said to me: Prophesy, son of man, and speak to the sword, and say: The sword, the sword, and the rest that the prophecy of the sword contains, a second time the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Do you wish, son of man, to know who this sword is, and to learn more openly the person of the raging sword? Listen to what I say: Set two ways, so that by them the sword of the king of Babylon may come, who will indeed go forth by the one road of the Chaldeans but, when he has come through the desert and the wilderness to the fork of the land of Arabia which is called that of the Ammonites, of which one way leads to Jerusalem on the right-hand side, but the left to Rabbath of the Ammonites' — which is a metropolis and today is named Philadelphia.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, set for yourself two ways, and let the sword of the king of Babylon come: both shall go forth from one land; and with his hand he shall take a conjecture, at the head of the way of the city he shall cast it. You shall set a way for the sword to come to Rabbath of the Ammonites, and to Judah, into Jerusalem the most fortified. For the king of Babylon stood at the fork, at the head of the two ways, seeking divination, mixing arrows; he questioned idols, he consulted entrails. At his right hand the divination came out against Jerusalem, to set battering rams, to open the mouth in slaughter, to lift up the voice in howling, to set battering rams against the gates, to heap up a mound, to build siege works. And in their eyes he shall be as one consulting an oracle in vain, and imitating the idleness of the sabbaths; but he himself will remember the iniquity, so as to capture. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have called your iniquities to remembrance, and have uncovered your transgressions, and your sins have appeared in all your thoughts; because, I say, you have called them to remembrance, you shall be taken by the hand. I know that in this place, following the Seventy translators, I have read a manifold exposition, which refers Rabbath of the Ammonites to the people of the nations, but Judah and Jerusalem to those who are gathered under the name of Christ and are given by their deeds the dignity of the name; and holds that the king of confusion, the devil, stands at every head of the ways and lies in ambush in secret, and that that little verse is fulfilled: Beside the path they have set a stumbling block for me; and that he stands at the fork, desiring either to hold those who are his own or to acquire new servitude for himself, and always goes to the right, namely to those who are placed on the right side, to storm them, to exult in slaughter, to capture wretched Jerusalem with battering rams and the heaping up of earthly works; and that at first indeed he seems to her to do nothing and to strive in vain, but, as he recalls the iniquities of those who dwell in the Church — or rather, by their evil works they bring the adverse powers back to the remembrance of their former crimes —, all the sins of the people and their thoughts are laid bare, and therefore they are captured, because they have heaped new offenses upon old ones. Another may have said these things; we must pursue the truth of the history we have begun.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'Mindful', he says, 'of the slaughter that befell the Assyrian king when a hundred and eighty-five thousand were cut down in one night, he will be afraid to turn aside to the right-hand side and go against most fortified Jerusalem, but he will stand at the very crossroads and, according to the rite of his nation, will consult the oracle, putting arrows into the quiver and mixing them, inscribed or marked with the names of each, to see whose arrow comes out and which city he ought to attack first' — this the Greeks call βελομαντίαν [belomancy, divination by arrows] or ῥαβδομαντίαν [rhabdomancy, divination by rods] —. 'He questioned the idols, therefore, he consulted the entrails. To the right came his divination, that he should go against Jerusalem and attack it, heap up mounds, set battering rams, build siege works and shut in the city, and in slaughter open his mouth and rouse the roar of an exulting and howling army.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Doing this', he says, 'he will seem to the inhabitants of Jerusalem to consult the oracle in vain, and as it were to wear away the idleness of the sabbaths, namely to play and accomplish no work. But the king of Babylon will trust not in his own strength but in the iniquity of the people, by which he knows that they have offended God and have heaped up the sins of their fathers with new offenses, and that their transgressions have been laid open to all; and therefore he will not doubt of victory, because he will trust in the iniquity of Jerusalem'. This is according to the Hebrew, from which the Seventy disagree in most places, not so much in sense as in words.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But you, profane, wicked leader of Israel, whose day has come, foreordained in the time of iniquity, thus says the Lord God: Take off the miter, take away the crown; is not this that which raised up the lowly and brought low the lofty? Iniquity, iniquity, iniquity I will set it; and this shall not be until he comes whose is the judgment, and I will deliver it to him. (LXX: "And you, profane, lawless leader of Israel, whose day has come in the time of iniquity, the end, thus says the Lord God: You have taken off the miter and put on the crown; this shall not be alike; you have humbled the lofty and raised up the lowly. Iniquity, iniquity I will set it; nor shall this be such, until he comes to whom it is due, and I will give it to him.") Symmachus translated this passage thus: But you, profane, lawless leader of Israel, whose day has come, appointed in the time of iniquity, thus says the Lord God: He has taken off the miter and taken away the crown; neither this nor that; he has raised up the lowly and brought low the lofty. Iniquity, iniquity, iniquity I will make it; and this was not he whose is the judgment, whom I am going to give. After the overthrow of the city of Jerusalem and the captivity of the people, the word is directed to the leader of Israel, whom no one doubts to signify Zedekiah, in whom the rule of the kings of Israel from the stock of David came to an end. 'There has come to you', he says, 'the day which was foreordained against you long ago, and because of you the priesthood and the kingdom of the Jewish people perished'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For the miter is the insignia of the high priest; the crown, that is, the diadem, is the mark of a king. 'Is not this the miter and this the crown, which did nothing by judgment but, in imitation of the Babylonian king: Whom he wished he exalted, and whom he wished he humbled?
Commentary on Ezekiel

In the place where we translated: Is not this, Symmachus rendered beautifully: Neither this nor that; for because he had said: Take off the miter, take away the crown, he added: 'Neither this nor that is', that is: 'Both the kingdom and the priesthood shall cease'. Hence, of those who afterwards, until the coming of Christ, were kings and priests alike, one, Hyrcanus the high priest, placed a diadem on his own head and wished in vain to claim both this and that for himself, since the kingdom was not owed to him after Zedekiah, but to him for whom it was laid up and who was the expectation of the nations; of whom Malachi also speaks: You priests, who defile my name, and a little after: My will is not in you, and I will not accept victims from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is offered to my name; which pure offering, without the blood of goats, rams and bulls, is fulfilled at the coming of Christ, when he who is desired by the nations has come, and the sun of righteousness has risen, in whose wings is healing.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore, not once nor — according to the Seventy — twice, but a third time I will set iniquity upon you forever, which was not reckoned to you at once, but until Christ comes, whose is the judgment, and the Father delivers to him the kingdom and the priesthood, or the Church gathered from the nations'. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son; and in another place: O God, he says, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son; this is he for whom the everlasting rule and priesthood are laid up, of whom Jacob also spoke: A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is laid up; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you, son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God, to the Ammonites and to their reproach; and you shall say: Blade, blade, unsheathe yourself to slay, file yourself that you may kill and flash, while vain things were seen for you and lies were divined, that you might be set upon the necks of the wounded wicked, whose day has come, foreordained in the time of iniquity; return to your sheath, to the place in which you were created; in the land of your birth I will judge you, and I will pour out my indignation upon you, in the fire of my fury I will blow upon you, and I will give you into the hands of foolish men and of those who fashion destruction. You shall be food for the fire, your blood shall be in the midst of the land; you shall be given over to oblivion, because I the Lord have spoken. That the sword of the king of Babylon stood at the head of two ways, at the crossroads of the right and the left, of which one led to Jerusalem, the other to Rabbath of the Ammonites, and that the lot came out that he should go first against Jerusalem, we have read above; and, now that it has been stormed and taken, he foretells that its kingdom also and its priesthood have perished forever. What remained concerned the Ammonites, and the very order of the division called for it: what had become of the left-hand way. Hence the prophet is commanded to speak to the Ammonites and to their reproach, that they themselves are to be captured, and he directs his speech to the same sword: 'O blade, blade, you who are prepared for slaughter, who are filed so that you may flash and kill, although the idols have given you answers, and all that is answered by demons is vain, so that you might, namely, hang over the necks of the wounded and that through you might be fulfilled what the Lord had long threatened, nevertheless, once your work is completed which you did against the Ammonites, return to your sheath, that is, into Babylon, to the place in which you were made and created, so that in the land of your birth I may judge you and pour out my indignation upon you, and you may be captured by the might of the Medes and Persians'; which is said more fully in the volume of Isaiah, in the vision against Babylon: Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them; and a little after: And that Babylon, glorious among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, shall be as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. It shall not be inhabited to the end.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And because he was once speaking under the person of the sword about the king, or rather the kingdom, of Babylon, he keeps the μεταφορὰν [metaphor]. 'In the fire', he says, 'of my fury I will blow upon you, so as to have you consumed by fire; and I will hand you over to the hands of foolish and unskilled men, who have not the art of forging and sharpening swords, so that you may by no means be sharpened any more, be filed and flash to kill, but may be food for the fire, and your blood, which you shed with all looking on, may rather flow back upon you; and you shall be handed over to eternal oblivion; and may you perish forever, because I the Lord have spoken these things, for whom to have said is to have done'.

n: Blood. Why dost thou cease to admonish and rebuke the people? (Worthington) --- Pronounce sentence on Jerusalem, (Haydock) for her cruelties. (Calmet)
Hath. Septuagint, "was mixed with his relations," ver. 10., &c., (Haydock) fighting against them. (Theodoret)
Sabbaths, by servile works, and by their sinful deportment.
Slanderers, hateful to all, Leviticus xix. 16., and Proverbs xi. 13. --- Mountains. Chap. xviii. 6.
Father, his widow, their mother-in-law, or one of his wives.
Increase. Chap. xviii. 18. (Calmet) --- Me. "The remembrance of God excludes all sins." (St. Jerome)
Hands, through surprise and sorrow. (Calmet) --- God wishes the sinner's salvation, Genesis vi. 6. (Worthington)
In thee. I will purify thee by violent medicines. (Calmet)

Possess, "as an inheritance:" (Septuagint; Haydock) "I will defile:" (Aquila) "wound thee." (Symmachus) Hebrew is very different: (Calmet) "thou hast inherited in thyself," (Haydock) being no longer willing to be subject.
Dross. Hebrew, "a mixture." Septuagint, "God will purify the silver," Isaias iv. 4.
Rained upon, or watered with the instructions of the prophets, chap. xx. 46.
Conspiracy. The false prophets defend each other, (Calmet) while the priests connive at their proceedings, (Haydock) and set the example of wickedness.
Without. Septuagint, "they shall fall, seeing," &c.
None like Abraham, Moses, &c. (Calmet) --- The prayers of the just are very powerful; and God wishes them to exert themselves for sinners. (St. Jerome) (Worthington)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, will you not judge the city of bloods? And you shall show her all her abominations, and you shall say: Thus says the Lord God: A city shedding blood in her midst, so that her time may come; and which made idols against herself, so as to be polluted. By your blood, which has been shed by you, you have sinned; and in your idols which you made you are polluted; and you have made your days draw near, and you have brought on the time of your years. Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all lands. Those that are near and those that are far from you will triumph over you (or will mock you), filthy one, noble one, great in ruin. Behold, the princes of Israel, each in his own arm, have been in you to shed blood. Father and mother they have treated with insults in you (or they have cursed father and mother), the stranger they have falsely accused in your midst, the orphan and the widow they have grieved (or have oppressed) in you. My sanctuaries you have despised and my sabbaths you have polluted. Men who are detractors (or robbers) have been in you to shed blood, and upon the mountains they have eaten in you; wickedness (or, as the Hebrew has it more expressively, 'zemma', that is, incest) they have wrought in your midst. The more shameful parts of the father they have uncovered in you, and the uncleanness of the menstruous woman they have humbled in you; and each one has wrought abomination with his neighbor's wife, and the father-in-law has wickedly defiled his daughter-in-law; the brother has oppressed (or humbled) his sister, his father's daughter, in you. They have taken gifts in you to shed blood; usury and excess you have taken, and greedily you have falsely accused your neighbors (or and I will fill up the consummation of your malice in your oppression), and you have forgotten me, says the Lord God. Behold, I have clapped my hands over your avarice which you have practiced, and over the blood which has been shed in your midst. Will your heart endure, or will your hands prevail, in the days which I shall make for you? I the Lord have spoken and I will do it; and I will scatter you among the nations, and I will winnow you into the lands, and I will make your uncleanness fail from you; and I will possess you in the sight of the nations (or, according to the first edition of Aquila and Theodotion, and I will defile you; or, according to Symmachus, and I will wound you in the sight of the nations), and you shall know that I am the Lord. 'And you', he says, 'son of man — for I will use the word I am accustomed to use with you —, judge the city of bloods and show her all her abominations, so that she may know that she deservedly endures the imminent captivity and that by many bloods she has brought on the time of her ruin.
Commentary on Ezekiel

First of all crimes, in place of God you have worshiped idols, and you have adored the works of your hands, and you have made the time of your years draw near, which for a long time was being announced and postponed, so that you might do penance. But according to your impenitent heart you treasure up wrath for yourself against the day of wrath. Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all lands that are round about you, both near and far, which will triumph over you, or mock you, filthy, noble, great in ruin: filthy, because you have ceased to be clean; noble in evil, you who once surpassed all cities in nobility in good; great in ruin, so that the more lofty you were, the more heavily you should fall.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And meanwhile, to pass over the rest, I will enumerate a few things that took place in you: your princes, judging not by righteousness but by the strength of their might and of their arm, shed innocent blood in you; others treated father and mother with insults, or cursed their parents, though Scripture says: Whoever curses father and mother shall die the death; the stranger and the sojourner they oppressed in your midst, as though sojourning and exile from their homeland were not enough for them in place of every distress; the orphan and the widow they grieved, or oppressed, in you, so that those whose whole protection lies in the justice of the laws were not only grieved but oppressed by you; my sanctuaries, or holy things, you despised, and my sabbaths you polluted, so that you did not distinguish between holy and polluted, between the day decreed for religion and the rest of the sabbath for the worship of God, and the other days on which it is permitted by the law to work and to serve the needs of the flesh; men who were 'detractors' — or, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, 'deceitful', which in the Hebrew is called 'rachil' — and murderers were in you, so as to blaspheme God or to do everything by deceit or violence; and they ate on the mountains, minding high things and lifted up against God in pride; wickedness, or incest, they wrought in your midst, so that what is rarely done even in corners and in secret, when the awareness of men is shunned by the wicked, this you did in the open — and what the incest is, the following passage indicates: They have laid bare the more shameful parts of the father in you, coupling with a stepmother against what is right and lawful, and they have humbled the uncleanness of the menstruous woman in you, not sparing nature nor granting a truce to their foulness, and neighing after their neighbor's wife; and, what is more wicked than this, the father-in-law burned for his daughter-in-law, and the brother knew nothing of a sister's rights, so as to violate a sister born not of the same womb but of the same father —; they took gifts so as to shed innocent blood; they turned the need of the poor into gain, so as to take usury and excess; and out of avarice they falsely accused their friends. This you have done', he says, 'O Jerusalem, because you have forgotten me; for the remembrance of God shuts out all shameful deeds.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Hence I have taken on the bearing of the Lord in anger and have clapped my hands against your avarice and against the blood that has been shed in your midst, so that you may understand and recognize in your mind whether you can endure my wrath either in spirit or with your hands; for I the Lord have spoken and I will do it, so that, after you have been captured, Jerusalem, I will scatter you among the nations and winnow you into the air like useless chaff to be swept this way and that.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I am of such great clemency that my severity is turned into mercy; for I will do everything so that your uncleanness may fail from you and you may recover your former purity; and when you have recovered it, I will possess you in the sight of all the nations, so that, when you have been possessed by me, you may then understand that I myself am the Lord'. If, however, we follow the interpretation of Symmachus and Theodotion, of whom the one says: And I will wound you (or I will pierce you through), the other: I will defile you in the sight of the nations, everything must be referred to the bad sense, although what is said above is contrary to this sense: And I will make your uncleanness fail from you; for the failing of uncleanness is the restoration of purity. I have discussed both editions together, so as to avoid enlarging the books.
Commentary on Ezekiel

What we have understood of Jerusalem, let us understand of the state of souls, which were created pure by God and received gold in understanding and wisdom, and silver in speech and eloquence, so that what they have conceived in the mind they may unfold in words. Of silver we read: The utterances of the Lord are chaste utterances, silver tried by fire, proved for the earth, purged sevenfold. Of gold and silver alike Psalm 67 (68) speaks, in which it is written: If you sleep in the midst of the lots, the wings of a dove covered with silver, and the hinder parts (or the inner parts) of her back in the greenness (or paleness) of gold. All indeed the glory of the king's daughter is within, she who speaks in the Song of Songs: The king has brought me into his chamber. Whoever has slept and rested between the two testaments at once takes up the silvered wings of the dove, and will shine with the brightness of gold in the treasury of the heart. To this sense, I think, those passages too are to be referred: that for sinners and for those who have deserved God's displeasure the heaven is bronze and the earth iron, and above all the land of Egypt, out of which the Lord leads Israel as out of an iron furnace; in Zechariah, too, iniquity sits upon a talent of lead, and in the song of Exodus it is said: They sank like lead in the most violent water; for they were pressed down by the heavy weight of their sins and could say: Like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me. And just as the counterfeit likeness of bronze feigns the appearance of gold, so tin imitates the whiteness of silver, which the simple and rustic man does not easily tell apart. And it often happens that gold and silver, mixed with heretical depravity, are separated by the fire of the Holy Spirit in the judgment of the Lord, and the gold remains pure, and the silver of which the prophet says: I gave them gold and silver, but they made Baal out of them, to which this is similar: I brought them out with silver and gold, and there was not a feeble one among their tribes. And let the end of all punishments be to know that he himself is the Lord. A tin stone, or a mass of tin, we read in Zechariah too; what it signifies we have explained in its place.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, the house of Israel has been turned into dross for me; all these are bronze and tin and iron and lead in the midst of the furnace; they have become the dross of silver. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have all been turned into dross, therefore behold, I will gather you into the midst of Jerusalem, with a gathering of silver and bronze and iron and tin and lead into the midst of the furnace, so that I may kindle a fire in it for smelting: so will I gather in my fury and in my anger, and I will rest, and I will smelt you, and I will kindle you in the fire of my fury, and you shall be smelted in the midst of it. As silver is smelted in the midst of the furnace, so shall you be in the midst of it; and you shall know that I am the Lord; that I have poured out my indignation upon you. The Hebrew word 'sig' Symmachus translated 'dross', the first edition of Aquila and Theodotion στέμφυλον and γίγαρτον, both of which signify the 'pip' of the pressed grape; but the second translation of the same Aquila and the Seventy rendered it 'mixture'. Now dross denotes the filth and refuse of metals; and accordingly, with captivity near, nay, with the destruction of the city already impending, fire is applied so that, under the metaphor of smelting, pure silver may remain, which had been mixed with and corrupted by bronze, tin, iron and lead; of these, three — bronze, tin and lead — are of a fusible substance and are melted by fire, while iron is softened and thinned between anvil and hammer and takes various forms, according as the will of the craftsman may be.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Just as, then, silver, which the metals mentioned above have corrupted, is put into the furnace so that, once the filth and the counterfeit substances have been removed, it may remain pure: 'so', he says, 'I will gather you into the midst of Jerusalem and surround you with the Babylonian siege, so that I may kindle a fire in you for smelting; and what the immense heat of the flames does there, famine and pestilence do here, so that, after I have gathered you and kindled you in the fire of my fury, I may then rest and quell the pain of being despised by the vengeance of your punishments; and all this I will do so that, after I have poured out my indignation upon you, the end of your torment may be the knowledge of me, and you shall know that I am the Lord, the judge and requiter of all'. That he is said to be a smelter we read in many other places too, but above all in Malachi and Isaiah, of whom the one says: Behold, he says, the Lord enters like the fire of a smelter and like the herb of the washers, and he will sit smelting as gold and silver, and he will smelt the sons of Levi, the other: And the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and he will cleanse the blood from their midst by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning; and I think that this is also the sense of what is said in the Psalms: Prove me, O Lord, and try me, after which is added: Burn my reins and my heart, so that all the phlegm of the harmful humor in my loins may be dried up.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, say to her: You are a land unclean, and not rained upon in the day of fury. A conspiracy of prophets in her midst, like a lion roaring and seizing prey; they have devoured souls, they have taken wealth and price, they have multiplied her widows in her midst. Her priests have despised my law and have polluted my sanctuaries; between holy and profane they made no distinction, and between polluted and clean they did not discern, and from my sabbaths they turned away their eyes, and I was defiled in their midst. Her princes in her midst like wolves seizing prey, to shed blood and to destroy souls and greedily to pursue gains. And her prophets daubed them without tempering, seeing vain things and divining her falsehood, saying: Thus says the Lord God, when the Lord has not spoken. The people of the land they wronged with false accusation and plundered violently; the needy and the poor they afflicted, and the stranger they oppressed with false accusation without judgment. And I sought among them a man who would set up a wall and stand opposed against me for the land, so that I should not destroy it, and I did not find one. And I poured out my indignation upon them, in the fire of my anger I consumed them, I rendered their way upon their head, says the Lord God. A careful hearer might have asked what the dross was that violated the purity of the silver and mixed it with bronze, lead, tin and iron. What was expressed there, then, in the person of a city and a furnace is proclaimed here under the image of a land that has not been watered nor received rains — those rains of which it is written: I will command the clouds not to rain a shower upon it, the shower we await when the early and the late rain is given us, of which it is written: A voluntary rain you will set apart, O God, for your inheritance. And the day of fury is the one which each person procures for himself by the multitude of his sins.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But in our Jerusalem too we often see this: those who, according to the Seventy, devour souls in power and take a price, so as to make many widows who have lost the Lord, their bridegroom; and these prophets form a faction and a conspiracy, so as to be one another's supporters and to do everything for the sake of shameful gain; the priests, who ought to be the guardians of the temple and from whose mouth the knowledge of the law is sought, violate the sanctuaries and make no distinction between holy and profane except that of money; they turn their eyes away from the sabbaths and do not ponder the rest of God, which lies in the knowledge of the Scriptures, nor do they say with the prophet: Unveil my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law, nor that word of the Apostle: But we all with unveiled face behold the glory of the Lord. Among such prophets and priests the Lord, standing in their midst, is defiled, of whom it is written: In the midst of you stands one whom you do not know.
Commentary on Ezekiel

We wish to know what the dross of the city is, what the squalor of a land most hard and full of brambles and thorns. A conspiracy, he says, of prophets (or, according to the Seventy, of leaders) in her midst, who bear the likeness of a lion, of which Peter too writes: Our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion; and this lion and all his companions seek to devour not bodies but souls, and they take rewards and decide everything by money. That this happened to the people of the Jews at that time indeed, no one doubts; for because of the priests and the princes and the prophets the Lord brought evil upon them.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The prophets, then, or leaders, are compared to lions; but the princes, whom we understand as men of a lower rank, imitate the rapine of wolves, so as to shed the blood not of bodies but of souls, and greedily pursue gains, by no means content with this: Those who serve the altar live by the altar, but, once they have come to the ministry of God, they amass the riches of Croesus.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Her prophets also, who foretell things to come, daubed them without tempering — which we also discussed above, that of the soothsaying prophets who, without an admixture of chaff, plastered a wall that is broken down by the rains; men of this kind see vain things, and do not so much prophesy as divine falsehood, saying to the wretched land: 'Thus says the Lord, this he promises', when the Lord has not spoken to them; and the people of the land, being an imitator not of God at all but of the earthly works of the princes and priests, did everything through false accusation and power, oppressing not the rich but the poor, of whom it is written: But the poor man does not bear threatening, and: The ransom of a man's soul is his own riches; the stranger, too, and the sojourner, who had not yet become a citizen of the Church but was only a hearer, possessing the beginnings of faith, they oppressed with false accusation, so that, after one had gone around sea and dry land to make one proselyte, they made him a son of Gehenna.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'Amid such great', he says, 'vices and a multitude of crimes, I sought among them a man who could resist my anger and, after the pattern of Moses and Aaron and Samuel, set himself against my fire and my burning, and I could not find one — whence he said to Moses: Let me alone, and I will destroy this people —; and because I could not find one to resist me and hold me back, therefore I poured out all my indignation upon them and consumed them, not without measure and judgment, but so as to render their ways upon their own heads', either assigning to their authors the very sins they had committed, or surely upon the heads of the leader of the people, the prince and the prophets, of whom there was none who dared to resist the Lord in his anger, and on whose account the land, squalid and deserted, did not deserve to receive the rain of the Lord.

intro: THE PROPHECY OF EZECHIEL. INTRODUCTION. Ezechiel, whose name signifies the strength of God, was of the priestly race, and of the number of the captives that were carried away to Babylon with king Joachin. He was contemporary with Jeremias, and prophesied to the same effect in Babylon as Jeremias did in Jerusalem; and is said to have ended his days in like manner, by martyrdom. (Challoner) --- He strove to comfort the captives, who began to repine that they had listened too readily to Jeremias, exhorting them to submit to the king of Babylon. Some think that part of his prophecies is lost, as Josephus mentions two books: but the nine last chapters, regarding the new city and temple, might form the second division. The Jews hesitated whether to allow his works to be canonical, as they seemed to differ from Moses, and from the dimensions given of Solomon's temple. But the same God might surely suggest some improvements, and the morality of the prophet is most excellent. (Calmet) --- His style may be compared to that of Homer (Grotius) and Alcæus. Many have thought that (Calmet) Pythagoras was his disciple; (Eusebius, præp. xiii.) yet the latter seems to have lived after the prophet, who was led into captivity with Jechonias, the year of the world 3410, and prophesied twenty years. He dates from this period, (Calmet) and from the renewal of the covenant under Josias, (chap. i. 1.; Haydock) when the captivity was first announced. (Worthington) --- The Jews allowed none to read the first and the nine (Haydock) last chapters, nor the beginning of Genesis, nor the Canticle of Canticles, before they were thirty years old; and they never attempted to explain the vision nor the building of the temple, supposing it to be above the power of man. (St. Jerome)
